Prologue This work begins from a simple but demanding premise: Christianity from the first to the fourth century cannot be reconstructed as a finished institution onto whose origins the doctrinal, legal and episcopal forms of Late Antiquity are projected back. It must instead be studied as a historical constellation of communities, texts, practices, objects, memories and conflicts whose configuration varied with period, language, city and networks of circulation. The volume brings together literary, papyrological, epigraphic, numismatic, archaeological, iconographic and legal evidence under a single principle of critical scrutiny: no documentary series serves merely to embellish another. A codex has a material history distinct from the tradition it transmits; an inscription cannot be reduced to the doctrine a later reader recognises in it; an imperial law must be dated, situated and read within its legal genre before it can be used to describe a religious practice. This relative autonomy of the sources makes comparison possible without erasing their differences. The research therefore adopts a deliberately cumulative structure. The main chapters reconstruct historical processes; documentary windows isolate evidence that requires closer examination; tables set out chronologies, attributions and degrees of certainty; and appendices provide prosopographies, networks, bilingual loci and reference materials. The apparatus does not seek to create an impression of absolute certainty. Its purpose is to distinguish firmly attested evidence from probable conclusions, reconstruction from direct observation, and matters still debated from established findings. The reader will encounter divergent positions wherever the evidence does not permit the debate to be closed: manuscript chronologies, relationships between gospel traditions, the scope of categories such as “Gnosticism”, the reconstruction of groups known chiefly through their opponents, the formation of ministries, the transformation of meeting spaces, and the interpretation of images and objects. In such cases, the work gives priority to making the problem explicit rather than offering false simplicity. xxxi

xxxii early christianity Early Christianity is thus offered both as a monograph in critical history and as a reference work. Its unity rests not on an all-encompassing thesis but on a delimited historical one—that later Christian unity was historically produced rather than given at the origins—and on a shared discipline applied to heterogeneous corpora: critically established chronology, a hierarchy of sources, analysis of transmission, attention to material culture, and a consistent distinction between evidence, inference and reception.

How to read this book The book offers two complementary routes. It can be read continuously, following the transformation of Christian movements from the first to the fourth century, or consulted by topic, beginning with a particular problem, corpus, historical figure or body of material evidence. The contents, lists of figures and tables, Index locorum and specialised indexes support this second approach. The codes for access to evidence indicate how sources have been consulted; they do not automatically establish their truth. [AUT] denotes direct physical examination; [IMG-HR], consultation of high-resolution digital images; [FAC], a facsimile or reproduction; [ED], a critical edition, catalogue or specialist description; and [LAB], published material analysis. [REC-GRAF] identifies a modern reconstruction or visualisation by third parties, and [REC-GRAF/IA] an original graphic reconstruction prepared for this edition. The historical value of a claim depends on the quality of its evidence and reasoning, rather than on a code taken in isolation. Diplomatic transcriptions retain, where methodologically appropriate, the spellings and symbols of the source or the cited institutional edition. These should not be confused with a general typographic standardisation of the volume. Thus, the crescent-shaped sigma of certain papyri is retained when it forms part of the chosen mode of documentary representation, while Greek cited for philological purposes may be presented according to modern editorial conventions. In historical social networks, metrics are read as properties of an explicit model, not as political or ecclesiastical hierarchies. High centrality may depend on the selection of the corpus; a regional aggregation, such as that used for certain African recipients of the Cyprianic dossier, is not directly comparable to an individual or a see. The book points out these asymmetries to prevent the visualisation from producing more precision than the data allow. Images should be read together with their complete captions. For a reconstruction, a modern colour treatment or a reproduction of an ancient object, the status of the object is distinguished from that of the image. Licensing and provenance information belong to the editorial apparatus. For the print edition, reproductions lacking xxxiii

xxxiv early christianity documented commercial clearance have been removed or replaced, where analytically necessary, by original reconstructions explicitly labelled [REC-GRAF/IA]. Finally, dates and categories are used historically. A provision of 321 is not identified with a later norm of 386; a heresiological term does not in itself demonstrate the existence of a unitary organisation; a religious similarity does not prove dependence; and the late reception of a memory is not automatically projected onto the first century. This discipline of reading runs throughout the volume.

Editorial Note to the Present Edition This monograph, Early Christianity: History, Texts, and Material Culture of Christian Origins, examines the emergence and transformation of Christian movements between the first and fourth centuries CE. Later literary testimonies, ecclesiastical catalogues, and retrospective traditions are used only where they illuminate the diachronic history of transmission, material reception, or the retrospective construction of institutional memory, and such use is explicitly signalled. The study integrates comparison of the canonical gospels, Christian apocalyptic literature in Jewish, Roman, and Iranian settings, asceticism and the formation of monasticism, protective and exorcistic practices, childhood and household organisation, and the imperial cult, together with the other historical, philological, social, and archaeological dossiers developed throughout the volume. The volume is organised according to three principles of historical-critical discipline: 1. Exclusion of speculation unsupported by evidence. Numerological or gematric correspondences without documentary verification, esoteric genealogies and speculative Neoplatonic interpretations are excluded from the evidentiary apparatus. The ancient calculation in Rev 13:18 is a specific philological and historical problem involving manuscript variants; it does not serve as a universal hermeneutical key. Where Neoplatonism is relevant as a historical phenomenon of Late Antiquity, it is treated as a context that can be documented. Historical analysis rests on positive evidence, critically disciplined comparison and explicit chains of cultural transmission. 2. Hierarchy and traceability of primary sources. Ancient texts are cited by book, chapter, section, verse or document number; crucial loci are checked against standard modern critical editions. Abstract This monograph studies the formation of early Christianity as a historically plural process of constructing identity, authority, memory, ritual practice, and material representation, developed between Second Temple Judaism and the Greco-Roman Mediterranean world during the first to fourth centuries. Its central argument is that the later doctrinal and institutional configuration cannot be retrospectively projected onto the first decades of the Jesus movement. Reconstruction must begin with the critical convergence of texts, epigraphy, papyrology, archaeology, and iconography, weighing each witness according to its nature and date. The research adopts a historical-critical methodology that distinguishes between highly reliable documentary data, widely accepted historiographical reconstructions, and open hypotheses. Numerological, gematric, esoteric, or symbolic correspondences for which no positive chain of transmission can be demonstrated are rejected as historical arguments. Religious comparison is used to contextualise and formulate problems, not to replace historical evidence. The first chapters examine the Jewish origins of the Jesus movement, the centrality of Jerusalem, Paul’s mission, the incorporation of Gentiles, and the historiographical problem of differentiating between Judaism and Christianity. Subsequent chapters study the plurality of the second century, canon and authority, community practices, persecution and martyrdom, material culture, iconography, Constantinian transformation, and institutionalisation in Late Antiquity. xlix

Methodological abstract The method combines three operations. The first is chronological: each witness is located according to its date of composition, its date of copying and its context of transmission, so that the undisputed Pauline letters, the gospels, second-century literature and imperial legislation are not read on a single plane. The second is documentary: objects, inscriptions, papyri and buildings are described according to their material status before they are interpreted, and the control sigla ([AUT], [IMG-HR], [FAC], [ED], [LAB], [REC-GRAF], [REC-GRAF/IA]) declare the actual degree of access to each piece of evidence. The third is comparative: similarities between Jewish, Greco-Roman, Iranian and Christian traditions are recorded as problems that require a demonstrable chain of transmission, not as proofs of dependence. Degrees of certainty are expressed on three levels—attested datum, widely accepted reconstruction and open hypothesis—and are applied also to prosopography and to social network analysis, whose metrics depend explicitly on the selected corpus. The ancient calculation of Revelation 13:18 is examined as a specific philological and historical problem, paying attention to its manuscript variants, without making it a universal key to interpretation. l

General Introduction The origins of Christianity do not constitute the history of a fully formed institution progressing linearly from Jesus to the imperial Church. First-century sources, instead, reveal a movement born within Second Temple Judaism, initially organised around the memory of Jesus, the conviction that God had raised him from the dead, and eschatological expectations that needed to be articulated in the language of Israel’s Scriptures. During the following decades, this movement spread through the cities of the Mediterranean, gradually incorporating non-Jews and producing new forms of authority, interpretation, and practice. This book argues that the category of “early Christianity” is useful if employed as a historiographical tool and not as the name of a homogeneous reality. In the first century, there was not yet a single social, liturgical, or doctrinal form that could be identified without nuance with the Christianity of later centuries. Paul’s letters, the Gospels, Acts, the Didache, 1 Clement, Ignatius, the Shepherd of Hermas, and apologetic literature belong to different contexts and should not be harmonised as if they were equivalent voices of the same institution. Chronology imposes an initial hierarchy of sources. The undisputed Pauline epistles are the earliest surviving Christian documents and allow particular communities to be observed from within their own controversies. The Synoptic Gospels and Acts belong to a later phase of narrative and theological development; the Gospel of John represents another literary trajectory; the writers of the early and mid-second century already document processes of differentiation, the construction of authority, and disputes over apostolic memory. Temporal distance does not invalidate a source, but it modifies the kind of question that can be put to it. The central problem is not to determine when an already defined essence called “Christianity” separated from another essence called “Judaism”. Research over the last few decades has shown the difficulty of that scheme. The relationships between Jewish groups following Jesus, mixed communities, and predominantly Gentile congregations varied according to region and generation. The image of a single “parting 1

2 early christianity of the ways” has been largely replaced in contemporary discussion by models that recognise multiple, asymmetrical, and protracted processes.1 The same caution applies to terms such as “orthodoxy”, “heresy”, “Gnosticism”, or “Jewish Christianity”. The ancient term αἵρεσις could designate an option, school, or group; its transformation into a negative theological category was a historical development. In this work, “heresy” is used when an ancient source or a particular ecclesiastical tradition classifies a doctrine as deviant. For the historical description of second-century groups, terms such as “tendency”, “school”, “community” or “doctrinal position” are preferred where possible. The methodology of this investigation rests on a simple rule: the strength of a claim must be proportional to the strength of the evidence. The execution of Jesus under Pontius Pilate, the existence of a community of Jesus’ followers in Jerusalem, the role of James in it, or Paul’s missionary activity among Gentiles can be affirmed with a high degree of certainty. In contrast, the exact identification of the meeting narrated in Galatians 2 with the episode in Acts 15, the nature of certain later apostolic traditions, or the precise chronology of some communities require a more cautious formulation. This gradation does not lead to historical minimalism. Its purpose is precisely to allow for a positive narrative where the sources permit it. Critical history does not consist in indefinitely suspending judgement, but rather in explaining what we know, why we know it, and what remains disputed. 1 Becker and Reed 2007; Fredriksen 2018; Lieu 2002. The argument distinguishes local processes of differentiation and avoids a single universal date of separation.

Method and documentary corpus The research combines literary criticism, historical criticism, philological analysis, and the study of material culture. Literary sources are first read as documents produced in specific contexts: a letter is not interpreted as a chronicle, an apologetic work is not used as a neutral description of its adversaries, and a later historiographical account does not automatically replace contemporary testimony. Where a question depends on vocabulary, the relevant original form is given with a brief English translation. Notes identify the loci and standard editions. The documentary appendix distinguishes specific checks from comprehensive consultation of the apparatus of variants; bibliographical identification of an edition is not presented as a new textual collation. Material culture is treated as an independent body of evidence. Images, inscriptions, papyri and architectural spaces do not serve as decorative illustrations of conclusions reached in advance. Provenance, dating, writing material, archaeological context and preservation all form part of the argument. The Alexamenos graffito, the house-church at Dura-Europos and manuscripts containing staurograms are therefore analysed as evidence in their own right. Comparisons with religions of the Empire are limited to verifiable historical issues. Formal similarity does not amount to dependence. Proposing cultural transmission requires compatible chronology, routes of contact, and positive evidence. This criterion excludes numerological, gematric, and esoteric genealogies from the argument. The bibliographical apparatus distinguishes three levels: primary sources and critical editions; reference tools and corpora; and secondary scholarship. Engagement with contemporary research extends beyond citing names: each debate presents positions, arguments and evidence. Particular attention is given to developments in Pauline studies, Jewish-Christian relations, the ancient construction of heresy, and material culture. 3

4 early christianity Social history, urban networks and circulation The reconstruction of the early Christian communities systematically incorporates the social and economic history of the Roman Mediterranean. Mission, hospitality, patronage, artisanal and commercial mobility, domestic structure, and urban inequalities provide a necessary context for interpreting the Pauline epistles and the formation of translocal networks. This approach makes it possible to engage with the tradition of social history represented by, among others, Wayne A. Meeks, Ekkehard and Wolfgang Stegemann, and Martin Goodman, without reducing religious experience to a purely socioeconomic explanation.2 Cities are not treated as mere points on a missionary itinerary. Corinth, Ephesus, Antioch, Philippi, Thessalonica, and Rome are analysed as specific urban environments, with civic structures, associations, houses, markets, ports, and mobility networks that conditioned the forms of gathering and transmission. Orality, memory and written culture The transmission of traditions about Jesus is studied within a culture in which orality and writing coexisted. The presence of a written text does not imply that oral transmission ceased, just as an oral tradition should not be imagined as a mechanical and immutable reproduction. The Gospels are considered literary products embedded in prior and parallel processes of memory, performance, teaching, and rewriting. Contemporary discussion of orality, memory, and written culture are incorporated through specialised works, including the contributions of Werner H. Kelber and Chris Keith. This framework allows for a more precise description of the formation, circulation, and stabilisation of traditions without postulating a fixed text from the outset or, at the opposite extreme, a completely free transmission.3 The state of research 2 3 Meeks 1983; Stegemann and Stegemann 1995; Goodman 2018. Associations, households and support relationships constitute social contexts; they are not equated without evidence with the legal status of each community. Kelber 1983; Keith 2020. Orality and manuscripts are studied as coexisting practices of transmission; the material medium alone does not establish the degree of stability of a narrative.

method and documentary corpus 5 1. From linear models to historical complexity For much of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, the history of Christian origins was narrated through relatively linear sequences: Jesus founded a community recognisable as Christian; Paul universalised his message; a progressively unified Church defined orthodoxy against lateral deviations; and the canon, the episcopate, and doctrine crystallised as the logical development of an initial core. This framework produced works of enormous documentary value, but it tended to read the first and second centuries retrospectively through institutional configurations better attested in the third and fourth centuries. Research in recent decades has replaced this teleology with models that privilege local processes, uneven chronologies, competition for authority, the circulation of texts, and the overlapping of identities. The German historical-critical tradition was decisive in formulating the problem. Adolf von Harnack combined a monumental reconstruction of Christian expansion with a strongly articulated account of doctrinal formation and demarcation in relation to Marcion. Walter Bauer, in turn (Rechtgläubigkeit und Ketzerei im ältesten Christentum, 1934; Eng. trans. Orthodoxy and Heresy in Earliest Christianity, 1971), recast the relationship between “orthodoxy” and “heresy” as a historical question of regional distribution and institutional success. Subsequent historiography has challenged both the simplicity of a homogeneous early orthodoxy and the possibility of replacing it with an inverse model of originally unrestricted diversity. It is now more productive to ask what forms of authority operated in each city, which texts circulated, which practices groups shared or used to distinguish themselves, and when particular networks succeeded in presenting their own genealogies as universal. The Anglo-American tradition broadened the field to include social history, the sociology of knowledge, Pauline studies, material culture, and network analysis. Wayne A. Meeks showed that Pauline communities should be studied within the structure of the Greco-Roman city; Peter Lampe reconstructed Roman Christianity as a constellation of domestic groups rather than a monolithic institution; subsequent work on associations, mobility, and networks has deepened this approach. At the same time, French and Italian research has made decisive contributions to the analysis of ancient heresy, Christian archaeology, episcopal institutions, and the construction of martyr memory. The present work adopts this methodological plurality as a working condition: no single discipline is by itself sufficient to reconstruct Christian origins. This survey of scholarship does not attempt an exhaustive history of the discipline. Its purpose is to identify the debates that materially affect the interpretation

6 early christianity of the sources examined in this volume. Each section distinguishes questions of evidence from interpretative models and from the methodological choices adopted here. Schools and scholarly traditions are therefore not invoked as badges of authority: a historiographical position is preferred only insofar as it offers the most persuasive account of the available evidence while keeping its uncertainties explicit. 2. The Jewish origins of the Jesus movement: from Sanders to Paul within Judaism The modern renewal of Pauline studies fundamentally altered the image of Judaism against which Paul had traditionally been read. E. P. Sanders (Paul and Palestinian Judaism, 1977) challenged the caricature of Judaism defined by the attempt to “earn” salvation through the accumulation of merits and proposed describing many forms of Second Temple Judaism through the category of “covenantal nomism”: belonging to the covenant people precedes observance, which expresses and maintains that relationship. James D. G. Dunn popularised the term “New Perspective on Paul” (“The New Perspective on Paul”, Bulletin of the John Rylands Library 65, 1983, 95–122) to encompass, despite significant internal differences, readings that reinterpreted Paul’s polemics on “works of the Law” within conflicts concerning identity, circumcision, table fellowship and belonging, rather than as a simple opposition between Christian grace and Jewish legalism. N. T. Wright developed a narrative reading of Paul centred on Israel, covenant, messianism, and new creation, while John M. G. Barclay reopened the question of grace through a comparative analysis of the concept of gift. These developments show that the New Perspective never constituted a uniform school. Its historiographical importance lies less in a common solution than in having compelled the reconstruction of the letters within real Jewish controversies and a wariness of theological oppositions inherited from modern debates. A second phase, usually associated with the Paul within Judaism movement, has taken this shift further. Mark Nanos, Magnus Zetterholm, Paula Fredriksen, and Matthew Thiessen, among others, have insisted that the undisputed letters can be read as the discourse of a Jew convinced of the eschatological significance of Jesus, addressed primarily to Gentiles brought into allegiance to the God of Israel without needing to become ethnically Jewish. From this perspective, the warnings against circumcision in Galatians do not necessarily express a universal abolition of the Torah, but rather a debate about what Gentiles should do in the messianic age. The scope of this proposal continues to be debated, especially when attempts are made to extend

method and documentary corpus 7 it to all Pauline passages or to reconstruct with excessive certainty the social status of each recipient. This monograph adopts a position of critical convergence. It takes Paul’s Jewish identity as a fundamental historical fact; it distinguishes what Paul demands of Gentiles from what can be presupposed for Jewish followers of Jesus; and it avoids describing Paul’s mission as the conscious foundation of a separate religion. At the same time, it does not turn Paul within Judaism into a universal key: the internal tensions of the letters, regional diversity, and subsequent reception show that the reconfiguration of belonging was an ongoing process. From the “parting of the ways” to multiple differentiations and overlapping configurations The second structural debate concerns the relationship between Judaism and Christianity. Previous models sought a relatively definable moment of rupture: the mission to the Gentiles, the destruction of the Temple in 70 CE, a supposed decision at Yavne, the Bar Kokhba revolt, or the episcopal consolidation of the second century. Recent research has shown that these dates mark real transformations, but they do not function as a universal boundary. Mediterranean cities produced distinct ecologies; a community could share scriptures, social spaces, kinship ties, or practices with Jewish groups and, at the same time, construct discourses of intense opposition. Judith Lieu has insisted that “Jewish” and “Christian” are categories whose apparent literary stability should not be confused with identically stable social boundaries. Daniel Boyarin has studied the production of these boundaries as a discursive process, while Adam H. Becker and Annette Yoshiko Reed have brought together studies that challenge the paradigm of a single separation. The value of these proposals lies not in asserting that there was never a separation, but in shifting the question: where, for whom, in what practice, and with what sources can a boundary be demonstrated? An anti-Jewish homily, a synagogue sanction, a funerary inscription, and an imperial decree describe different levels of interaction and should not be automatically assembled into a single chronology. The Johannine occurrences of ἀποσυνάγωγος, the controversies of Matthew, the birkat ha-minim, the homilies of John Chrysostom, and Late Antique legislation must be situated within their own contexts. The chronological distance between them is precisely part of the evidence. Polemical language can reveal competitive proximity as well as entrenched separation. For this reason, the present work uses expres-

10 early christianity 4. Marcion, Luke and the formation of textual authority Research on Marcion is one of the fields in which philology most directly reshapes historical narrative. The surviving sources are mostly adversarial and later: Tertullian, Epiphanius, Irenaeus, and other authors cite or describe the Marcionite Gospel and Apostolikon within polemical projects. The problem lies in reconstructing, from these quotations, a lost text and then establishing its relationship with Luke and the Pauline collections. This operation requires distinguishing three levels: the text actually attested by a source; the critical reconstruction of the Marcionite text; and the genealogical hypothesis regarding priority or dependence. Dieter T. Roth (The Text of Marcion’s Gospel, 2015) has advocated an exceptionally cautious reconstruction, restricted to what the evidence allows. Jason BeDuhn has proposed a reading of Marcion that gives more weight to his scriptural programme as a coherent collection. Judith Lieu has shown the extent to which the historical figure of Marcion was produced by his adversaries and has demanded a careful separation of the teacher from the literary “arch-heretic”. Matthias Klinghardt has formulated the most radical thesis: the gospel used by Marcion predated canonical Luke and is therefore crucial evidence for the formation of the Synoptic Gospels. This hypothesis forces a reconsideration of the direction of dependence and cannot be dismissed by mere appeal to patristic tradition. This monograph adopts a deliberate methodological asymmetry. For the reconstruction of the Marcionite text, it takes as its primary evidentiary constraint the data that can be reliably attributed to the sources; for literary history, it keeps hypotheses of priority open without conflating them with directly preserved readings. The fact that a reconstruction is possible does not imply that all its words have the same degree of certainty. Similarly, the explanatory success of a synoptic model is not the same as the existence of a manuscript that proves it. For this reason, the apparatus in Chapter II explicitly records the source, state, and effect of each locus. This debate also alters the history of the canon. If Marcion possessed a defined collection comprising a gospel and Pauline letters, his project constitutes a decisive moment in textual delimitation; but describing it as the “first New Testament” may suggest a material and conceptual stability greater than the evidence warrants. Irenaeus’s response in favour of the fourfold Gospel, later lists, and manuscript practice show a process of selection, collection, and authority that did not advance at the same pace in all regions.

After “Gnosticism”: categories, schools and practices The term “Gnosticism” was long used as if it designated a coherent religion, characterised by radical dualism, a fall myth, a rejection of the cosmos, and salvation through knowledge. This synthesis proved useful as a classificatory tool, but it conflated very different systems and relied too heavily on the taxonomies of heresiologists. Michael A. Williams proposed abandoning the category as a unitary historical entity; Karen L. King examined its modern genealogy and showed how the opposition between “Christianity” and “Gnosticism” partly reproduced the polemical architecture of ancient sources. David Brakke has advocated a more restricted use of the term for certain formations, while Einar Thomassen and Ismo Dunderberg have reconstructed Valentinianism as a network of schools, rituals, exegesis and lifestyles, not simply as a deviation from the “Great Church” of the heresiologists. The methodological consequence is decisive. A Nag Hammadi text should not first be classified as “Gnostic” and then explained from a supposed essence. One must begin with its language, literary form, scriptural traditions, cosmology, reading practices, possible location, and relationships with other texts. Only then is it legitimate to discuss whether the comparative label contributes anything. The same applies to names transmitted almost exclusively by adversaries, such as “Ophites”, “Cainites”, or certain genealogies of teachers: their existence as stable groups cannot be automatically deduced from a heresiological list. Valentinus offers a particularly instructive case. The evidence places him within sophisticated Christian intellectual debates of the second century; Valentinian traditions used exegesis of texts that also circulated in communities that would later be considered proto-orthodox. The boundary is, therefore, contested from within. This monograph retains “Gnosticism” only as a secondary historiographical term, always defined and never used to explain a text in itself. It prefers to identify specific schools, authors, corpora, and practices. Material culture, manuscripts and the turn towards artefacts The history of Christian origins can no longer be written solely from literary works. The material turn has placed manuscripts, inscriptions, coins, architecture, funerary objects, and images within the same evidentiary field. Larry Hurtado drew attention to graphic features such as the nomina sacra, the staurogram, and the early Christian preference for the codex. Roger Bagnall and Brent Nongbri have forced a reassessment of dates, archaeological contexts, and assumptions about how quickly certain formats can be associated with religious identities. Chris Keith has insisted that the Gospels must also be studied as manuscript objects and as a social practice of reading. This shift changes the questions that can be asked. A papyrus is not merely a medium for recovering a reading: its size, format, handwriting, corrections, page layout, and signs of use provide evidence for production, cost, readership, and circulation. Similarly, the Christian building at Dura-Europos is not a “church” in an abstract sense, but a building transformed within a precise archaeological sequence; and the Alexamenos graffito is not generic evidence of persecution, but a situated act of mockery whose interpretation depends on the medium and the social context of the Palatine Hill. Digital humanities expand these possibilities through image databases, handwriting comparison, mapping, and network analysis, but they also introduce new risks.

The present work treats material culture as an independent archive and as a corrective to literary narrative. When text and object converge, the conclusion gains strength; when they diverge, the divergence is preserved. An inscription, a building, or a codex is not forced to confirm the history transmitted by Eusebius, Irenaeus, or the martyrdom accounts. 7. Prophets, miracle workers, and messianic pretenders: a comparison without equivalence The comparative study of Jesus with sign prophets, miracle workers, and charismatic figures has oscillated between two extremes: the isolation of Jesus as a phenomenon without historical analogues and the reduction of his activity to a supposedly welldefined religious type. Research on prophetic figures of late Second Temple Judaism, holy men of the Mediterranean, and miracle literature allows for a more disciplined comparison. Theudas, the Egyptian, Honi, Hanina ben Dosa, Apollonius of Tyana, and Alexander of Abonoteichos do not form a homogeneous class; they belong to different eras, genres, and agendas. Rebecca Gray demonstrated the importance of the popular prophets described by Josephus; studies of miracle stories and holy men have explored formal parallels with Greco-Roman narratives. The comparative value lies in isolating variables: charismatic authority, signs, healing, prophecy, relationship with crowds, response of authorities, and posthumous memory. Similarity in one of these dimensions does not demonstrate literary dependence or social identity. Apollonius, for example, is known primarily through a biography by Philostratus written in the third century; using him as an immediate mirror of the Galilee of Jesus without considering this distance would produce an anachronism. Chapter VIII enters this debate through a disciplined typological comparison. The historical singularity of the Jesus movement is not formulated as an absence of parallels, but as a specific combination of eschatological proclamation, remembrance of the execution, affirmation of resurrection, and the capacity to generate lasting

method and documentary corpus 15 translocal networks. The comparison serves to clarify differences, not to fabricate equivalences. 8. Historiography in Spanish and the position of this monograph Research in Spanish is not a secondary appendage to Anglophone or Germanophone debates. In recent decades, it has produced collective syntheses, studies of the historical Jesus, sociology of the early Christian communities, analyses of the New Testament, and works on Christian diversity capable of engaging with international discussions. The collective work coordinated by Rafael Aguirre, Así empezó el cristianismo (How Christianity Began), is especially relevant for its attempt to reconstruct the origins as a social, historical, and plural process; the works of Santiago Guijarro have contributed to the study of the Gospels and the early Christian communities; and Antonio Piñero has disseminated in Spanish a non-confessional historical-literary approach to the formation of the New Testament. This monograph belongs to that scholarly conversation, while seeking to strengthen it through a more systematic integration of material culture, philology of individual loci, papyrology, epigraphy, and international historiographical comparison. The distinctive contribution of this volume lies in bringing into a single analytical framework bodies of evidence that are often studied separately. Paul’s letters are read against urban and economic structures; canon formation is set beside manuscript evidence and competing collections; episcopal lists are treated as documents of institutional memory; groups labelled heretical are reconstructed, where possible, from texts produced within those traditions; and archaeology is treated not as illustration but as evidence capable of qualifying, constraining, or contradicting literary narratives. The result is a history of convergence: the Christian unity visible in later centuries was historically real—if normative, partial and contested, as the Arian, Donatist and Melitian controversies of the fourth century show—but it was not present fully formed at the outset. It emerged through textual selection, ritual negotiation, episcopal authority, economic networks, doctrinal controversy, and legal transformation. This stance also implies limitations. The book does not attempt to resolve ongoing debates or transform every uncertainty into a thesis. Where a date, authorship, textual reconstruction, or archaeological identification is uncertain, the degree of certainty is preserved. The aim of a reference work is not to maximise assertions, but to make explicit what is known, why it is known, what depends upon inference, and what remains open to revision.

Thesis and research question The book asks how the identities, doctrines, practices, forms of representation and community structures of Jesus’ followers took shape between their Jewish origins in the first century and their gradual institutionalisation within the Roman Empire by the end of the fourth century. The thesis defended here is that this configuration was not the linear unfolding of a pre-existing identity, but rather the result of successive processes of scriptural interpretation, incorporation of Gentiles, circulation of texts, competition for authority, ritual development, and negotiation with institutions of the Roman world. The later unity—normative, partial and always contested—was real, but it was historically produced. That process can be reconstructed only if texts, objects and spaces are treated as independent bodies of evidence and every claim is kept proportional to the evidence that supports it: material culture therefore does not merely confirm the literary narrative but can correct it. That production was, moreover, a case of convergence among diverse fields of influence—Second Temple Judaism, Greco-Roman culture, imperial administration and, on the eastern margins, Syriac and Iranian traditions— whose articulation was decisively Pauline: the problem of Gentile belonging, the epistolary and communal medium, and the vocabulary that was later debated, canonised or combated all start with Paul.

chapter i From the Jesus Movement to the First Mediterranean Communities 1. The starting point: a Jewish movement of the first century The reconstruction of early Christianity begins within Second Temple Judaism. Jesus, his first disciples, Paul, James, and Peter were all Jewish; their conflicts, expectations, and religious language developed in a world structured by the Scriptures of Israel, the Temple, the practice of the Torah, and a wide diversity of interpretations concerning purity, eschatology, the restoration of Israel, and divine action in history. Presenting this movement as a “sect” can be useful if the term is used in a sociological sense, but it is misleading if it suggests that a separate religion existed from the beginning. The vocabulary of the New Testament itself does not offer a uniform selfdesignation. In Acts, for example, αἵρεσις can be used for both Jewish groups and the movement associated with Jesus, showing that the term could still mean “current” or “party” before fully acquiring the later technical meaning of “heresy” (cf. Acts 5:17; 15:5; 24:5, 14; 26:5; 28:22). Eschatological expectation constituted one of the most important frameworks for interpretation. The proclamation that God had raised Jesus from the dead was not initially received as an isolated event, but as a sign of a decisive divine intervention. This conviction appears particularly early in Paul’s letters, where Christ’s resurrection is linked to the future resurrection of believers and to the imminence of eschatological fulfilment. The importance of this Jewish matrix does not compel us to imagine uniformity. First-century Judaism encompassed a diversity of groups, practices, and positions; nor did the early communities of Jesus react in a single way to issues such as the observance of the Law, sharing meals, or the admission of Gentiles. This diversity is 18

Roman power and the conditions of provincial life The Judea in which the Jesus movement arose was not a uniform political landscape. The death of Herod the Great led to a dynastic partition; from 6 CE, Judea, Samaria, and Idumea came under direct Roman administration, while Galilee and Perea remained under Herod Antipas during Jesus’ ministry. Distinguishing these jurisdictions avoids presenting every Galilean conflict as an immediate action of the Roman prefect of Judea. Local authorities, the priesthood in Jerusalem, dynastic clients, and imperial representatives all had a share in an unequal distribution of power. The prefect Pontius Pilate administered Judea from approximately 26 to 36 CE. The Caesarea inscription, which preserves part of his name and title, provides epigraphic confirmation of the office of praefectus Iudaeae. Tacitus retrospectively uses the title procurator in Ann. XV.44; the two designations should not be confused or harmonised by eliminating the discrepancy. The inscription and the Roman account belong to different genres and dates. Neither alone describes the trial of Jesus with the precision of a preserved court record.4 The Gospels place Jesus in villages, on roads, in homes, in synagogues, and finally in Jerusalem. This spatial variety is historically more important than an abstract opposition between “countryside” and “city.” Galilee was connected to administrative centres and markets, but movement through these environments does not prove that Jesus received a specific urban education, nor does it entitle us to reconstruct his occupation or level of literacy from geographical proximity. Mobility and contact are conditions of possibility; a detailed biography requires further evidence. It is also important to distinguish between ancient forms of taxation. Imperial taxes, agrarian obligations, religious dues, and debt relationships could coexist without constituting a single levy administered by the same agent. The parables and gospel controversies reflect a world of day labourers, tenants, landowners, moneylenders, and tax collectors, but they are literary compositions. Their historical use requires comparing the motifs with independent social documentation and not turning each story into a statistical description of Galilee. 4 Josephus, Ant. Later Christian resistance to public sacrifice cannot be projected onto the early followers of Jesus as a fully defined legal regime. Provincial history helps explain why a movement born in Judea could be perceived differently in Corinth, Rome, or Bithynia. 1.2. The Temple and the transformations of 70 and 135 The Temple in Jerusalem was a centre of worship, pilgrimage, authority, and resources. Its importance does not mean that all of Judaism was limited to the priestly institution. Diaspora communities, domestic practices, the reading of Scripture and local meeting places all belonged to a plural religious world that maintained different relationships with Jerusalem. The Theodotus inscription shows, within the city itself, the combination of reading of the Law, teaching and hospitality without displacing the sacrificial function of the Temple. The war of 66–73 and the destruction of the sanctuary in 70 radically altered this organisation. Josephus is an indispensable source, but he wrote from a position committed to his own justification and to the Flavian dynasty. His account must be compared with archaeology and epigraphy. The Iudaea capta coins, issued in various denominations and types, document the imperial celebration of the victory. On them, the vanquished personification and military attributes construct a message of domination, not a neutral description of the experience of the inhabitants of Judea.5 The coinage obliges us to separate three levels: the military event, its propaganda, and its subsequent reception. The fact that the destruction of the Temple fostered new Jewish and Christian formulations does not demonstrate an immediate separation between two religions. Nor does the lament or theological interpretation of the catastrophe establish an identical reaction in all communities. Christian writings after 70 CE must be analysed according to their location, probable date, and literary strategy. The Bar Kokhba revolt, between 132 and 135, brought about another transformation. The consequences of the reorganisation of Jerusalem as Aelia Capitolina are known through uneven documentation and later sources. The Christian corpus of the first century that has come down to us is written in Greek. This does not prove that all previous preaching, teaching, or memory circulated exclusively in Greek. The transition between multilingual orality and Greek writing should not be represented as a single act of translation. It included reformulation, vocabulary selection, adaptation to Greek scriptural repertoires, and circulation among different communities. Therefore, terms such as Χριστός, κύριος, ἐκκλησία, or εὐαγγέλιον must be studied simultaneously as Greek vocabulary and as ways of expressing traditions rooted in Jewish Scripture and practice. 1.4. Textual ecology in the first half of the first century: Scriptures, archives and orality before Paul The first half of the first century CE must be reconstructed as a multilingual ecology of texts, memories and reading practices, not as a landscape governed by a closed canon in the later sense. For the Jesus movement, moreover, the documentary situation is especially asymmetrical: before the Pauline epistles, we do not possess a securely identifiable Christian written corpus. This does not imply an absence of stable formulations. Traditions of sayings, passion narratives, formulas of faith, hymns, confessions, and scriptural arguments could have circulated orally or on media now lost; some of these units appear to have been incorporated later into letters and gospels. The historian must therefore distinguish between texts actually preserved from the period, works whose composition can be placed at that time, and traditions whose early existence can only be inferred retrospectively. The immediate textual framework of Jesus and his first followers was Jewish. In Judea and Galilee, Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek coexisted, each with different functions depending on the region, institution, education, and type of document. The liturgical reading of Scripture, oral interpretation, the copying of scrolls, documentary production, and everyday communication were not evenly distributed among these languages. The diaspora added even greater diversity: in Alexandria, Asia Minor, Syria, Rome, and other urban centres, Greek played a decisive role in the trans-

The Scriptures of Israel: authority without a “canon” identical to the later one The Torah held an exceptional normative position, and the Prophets possessed widely recognised authority; the body of Writings, however, should not be described as if its scope and status were fixed in the same way as the medieval Masoretic canon. The Judean Desert manuscripts simultaneously demonstrate stability, textual plurality, and a diversity of repertoires. During this period, Hebrew forms of biblical books circulated that did not always coincide word for word with the later Masoretic text, along with Greek translations and parabiblical compositions that could function as Scripture or as authoritative interpretations within certain groups. Aramaic was also part of this ecology. Daniel 2:4b–7:28 and Ezra 4:8–6:18; 7:12–26 contain extensive Aramaic passages; Jeremiah 10:11 preserves a short Aramaic phrase. In addition, there is a large body of extra-biblical Aramaic production documented at Qumran. The existence of Targumic practices of oral translation and interpretation is historically plausible, but this should not be confused with the early dating of the complete literary forms of the Targums that we know from later manuscripts. 1.4.2. The Septuagint and the Greek Scriptures of the Diaspora The Greek translations of the Scriptures of Israel, conventionally grouped under the name Septuagint, form one of the fundamental archives for understanding Hellenistic Judaism and, subsequently, the scriptural language of Greek-speaking Christians. This was not a single, uniform edition comparable to a modern printed Bible: different books show distinct histories of translation, revision, and transmission. By the first century CE, however, a broad repertoire of Jewish Scriptures in Greek existed, used in diaspora contexts and also known in Palestine. Alongside translations of books that would later become part of the Hebrew canon, the Greek tradition transmitted works such as Tobit, Judith, Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach, and 1–2 Maccabees. Their presence in later Christian manuscript traditions does not warrant the retrospective reconstruction of a single “Septuagint Bible” finalised in the year 30. It does, however, demonstrate that the textual world available to Hellenised Jews and early Christians was broader than the modern opposition between “canonical” and “apocryphal.”

Qumran and the Jewish literature of the Second Temple The manuscripts found at Qumran and other sites in the Judean Desert offer an exceptional sample of contemporary textual diversity, although they should not be automatically confused with the books that “all Palestine read”. They document what was copied, preserved, and used by specific communities and, in some cases, preserve works known beyond that context. Among the sectarian and para-sectarian texts are the Community Rule (1QS), the Damascus Document (CD), the War Scroll (1QM), the Hodayot or Hymns (1QHᵃ), and various pesharim. The archive also includes numerous biblical copies and parabiblical compositions. Aramaic production occupies a prominent place: the Genesis Apocryphon (1QapGen), fragments of 1 Enoch, the Book of Giants, and other texts reveal a literary landscape in which biblical rewriting, revelation, interpretation of patriarchal figures, and eschatological speculation could coexist. This plurality is crucial for contextualising early Christianity, but it does not justify direct genealogies between Qumran and Jesus without an independent chain of evidence. 1.4.4. Philo, Hellenistic Jewish authors and Greco-Roman literary culture Philo of Alexandria belongs entirely to this first half of the first century and constitutes a privileged source for observing how a Greek-speaking Jewish intellectual could read the Pentateuch using tools of allegorical exegesis, Hellenistic philosophy, and the political categories of the Roman world. Works such as De opificio mundi, Legum allegoriae, De vita Mosis, De specialibus legibus, and De migratione Abrahami show that Scripture could become the object of a sophisticated literary culture while still functioning as a core element of Jewish identity. The exact dating of each treatise and its circulation must be addressed on a work-by-work basis. Also circulating, with varying degrees of dissemination, were compositions by earlier Hellenistic Jewish authors, now preserved only in fragments, such as Ezekiel the Tragedian, Artapanus, and other authors transmitted by later compilers. Their existence reminds us that Jewish production in Greek was not limited to biblical translations. In cities of the diaspora and among educated sectors of Palestine, this literature coexisted with Homer, historians, rhetoric, popular philosophy, and administrative documents in Greek and, in certain circles, Latin. 1.4.6. Before Paul: orality, formulas and absence of a preserved Christian corpus For the years c. 30–50 CE, still greater caution is needed. We possess no Christian manuscripts that can be reliably dated to those decades, nor any complete Christian work predating the undisputed Pauline epistles. The Jesus movement, in its first generation, was fundamentally oral in the production and circulation of its memory: proclamation, teaching, scriptural debate, stories about Jesus, prophecy, prayer, and ritual formulas. Orality, however, does not preclude the use of auxiliary writing, lost letters, collections of quotations, lists, or notes; it simply does not warrant treating them as preserved documents. Paul’s letters preserve material that many scholars consider to predate the epistolary composition itself—for example, confessional or traditional formulations in 1 Corinthians 15:3–5, Romans 1:3–4, and Philippians 2:6–11—but their scope, original form, and dating are debated. Therefore, they should be described as pre-Pauline traditions proposed by literary analysis, not as recovered independent manuscripts. This point is crucial to avoid a double anachronism: imagining, on the one hand, a Christianity without texts or Scriptures and, on the other, projecting onto the 30s a Christian library similar to that of the second century.

The Latin horizon: literature, administration and education in the first century Latin was part of the written landscape of the first century, but its importance varied drastically depending on the region and function. In Italy and large areas of the Roman West, it was the language of administration, law, the army, education, and literary production; in the eastern Mediterranean, however, Greek continued to be the main language of written communication, urban culture, and often even of interaction with the imperial administration. In the first half of the first century, numerous authors from the Republic and the Augustan period remained fundamental. Cicero served as a model of prose, oratory, and philosophical argumentation; Caesar and Sallust continued to be historiographi-

Tacitus begins his preserved production towards the end of the century, so his usefulness in contextualising nascent Christianity lies both in the political culture he describes and in his later testimony about Nero and the christiani. The relevance of this literature to a history of Christian origins is contextual, not genealogical. Paul and the earliest surviving Christian authors wrote in Greek, and there is no basis for postulating direct dependencies on Virgil, Seneca, or Cicero without specific textual evidence. Nevertheless, the Roman educational system, rhetoric, legal categories, administrative vocabulary, and Latin literary genres were part of the imperial environment in which communities moved, were classified, and subsequently began to produce literature in Latin. Qumran and the sectarian diversity of Second Temple Judaism The Dead Sea Scrolls are indispensable for contextualising the diversity of Jewish life before and during the time of Jesus’ first followers. The Community Rule (1QS) and the Damascus Document (CD) show communities that reinterpreted the Torah, regulated admission, purity, discipline, and communal life, and situated their existence within an intense eschatological expectation. Philo and the Judaism of the Diaspora First-century Judaism cannot be reconstructed solely from Jerusalem. Philo of Alexandria testifies to a Jewish milieu deeply integrated into Greek language and intellectual forms without abandoning the centrality of the Scriptures of Israel. Works such as Legatio ad Gaium illuminate questions of citizenship, imperial cult, and communal conflict, while De vita contemplativa documents an early representation of ascetic and exegetical life. Philo’s importance to this monograph does not lie in making him a direct source for Paul or the Gospels. His value lies in showing that allegorical interpretation, the philosophical use of the vocabulary of λόγος, and dialogue with Hellenic categories were part of Jewish possibilities prior to the Christian expansion. Contact between Judaism and Greek culture did not begin with Paul.8 1.7. The Greek translation of the Torah is linked to Hellenistic Judaism in Alexandria; other writings were translated, revised, and transmitted in different processes. The great later Christian Bibles bring together materials whose history predates that codicological form. Therefore, “the Septuagint” can refer to a translation tradition, a modern edition, or the content of a particular codex: these are not equivalent. A verbal match with the Greek may demonstrate the use of a Greek scriptural tradition; it does not guarantee that the writer possessed the same set of books or the same text as a current edition. The use of words like κύριος, νόμος, or διαθήκη drew on pre-Christian Greek-speaking Jewish traditions, even though their Christian contexts introduced new referents and associations. Philological analysis can describe these operations without postulating a complete doctrine behind each word. To do so, it must distinguish between lexical equivalence, explicit quotation, probable allusion, and subsequent interpretation. The transmission of the divine name also requires a material approach. Jewish and Christian Greek manuscripts present diverse solutions: Hebrew characters, specific palaeographic forms, transliterations, or substitutions. Representations of the Tetragrammaton do not, in themselves, constitute mathematical equivalences or architectural codes. A historical reading identifies the manuscript, the hand, the support, and the function of the script. Interpretations that visually relate letters from different alphabets do not replace this investigation. The result is a history of written and communal reception. The authority of the Scriptures of Israel did not depend solely on possessing a text: it involved reading it, translating it, memorising it, and debating it. The controversies surrounding Marcion and the arguments of Justin or Irenaeus are better understood within this history than through the opposition between a supposed original Jewish book and an entirely new Christian book. 1.7.1. from the jesus movement to the first… 37 1.9. Yavne, Rabbinic Judaism and the problem of the “separations” Reconstructing the relationship between Judaism and Christianity after the destruction of the Temple requires abandoning two schemes that long dominated historiography: the idea of an instantaneous break in 70 CE and the image of a “Yavne Academy” that supposedly reorganised Judaism uniformly and simultaneously expelled Jesus’ followers from the synagogues. Contemporary research tends to describe a longer process, regionally uneven and only fragmentarily documented. Rabbinic evidence must be treated according to its own chronology. The Mishnah was compiled around the beginning of the third century and preserves traditions of varying antiquity; the Tosefta and the Talmuds are even later. None of these corpora can be read, without qualification, as a direct record of Jewish institutions from the last third of the first century. The same is true, in reverse, for Christian literature: Matthew, John, Acts, Ignatius, and Justin do not describe a uniform relationship with “Judaism,” but rather situated controversies, identity constructions, and different rhetorical strategies. Yavne—ancient Jamnia—was undoubtedly a significant place for certain sages after 70 CE, but the reconstruction of a formal council that would have definitively established the Hebrew canon and decreed a general exclusion of Christians lacks sufficient documentary support. The so-called birkat ha-minim presents a similar problem. Rabbinic sources attest formulae directed against groups considered deviant, but the identification of minim exclusively with Christians and the uniform dating of a centralised measure are hypotheses that must be argued on a case-by-case basis. The studies of Shaye J. D. Cohen, “The Significance of Yavneh: Pharisees, Rabbis, and the End of Jewish Sectarianism” (Hebrew Union College Annual 55, 1984), and Reuven Kimelman, “Birkat Ha-Minim and the Lack of Evidence for an AntiChristian Jewish Prayer in Late Antiquity” (1981), set the terms of this revision. For the history of early Christianity, the consequence is methodological. The expression “parting of the ways” is useful only if understood as a metaphor for multiple processes and not as a single event. In some cities, followers of Jesus and other Jews were able to continue sharing spaces, Scriptures, family networks, and practices for decades; in others, tensions may have taken on an exclusionary character sooner. Geography, social composition, and local history matter as much as doctrinal formulations. Paul’s letters show that controversies about circumcision, table fellowship and belonging to Israel existed long before 70 CE, but they do not prove the existence of two completely separate religions. Galatians 2, Romans 9–11, and Philippians 3 should be

38 early christianity read as the interventions of a Jew convinced of a mission to the nations, not as retrospective treatises on a Church already detached from Judaism. The literature of the late first and second centuries, on the other hand, documents a growing process of discursive differentiation. This differentiation was not linear: the most intense polemics may be precisely an indication of social proximity and competition for texts, traditions, and legitimacy. The destruction of the Temple decisively altered the horizon for all Jewish groups, but its effects varied. For the followers of Jesus, the Temple traditions could be reinterpreted Christologically; for other Jews, the Torah, prayer, the synagogue, and domestic practices took on new forms. This process should not be described as if a fully established rabbinic Judaism immediately replaced a Temple religion while, in parallel, an equally established Christianity separated from it. Both institutional formations emerged only gradually. This approach also allows for a more precise treatment of so-called “Jewish Christians”. The category encompasses heterogeneous phenomena: communities that combined confession of Jesus and observance of the Torah, gospel traditions transmitted in Jewish environments, groups later labelled as Ebionites or Nazarenes, and heresiological accounts produced by adversaries. The label should not be projected backward as if it designated a unified Church of the first century. Each testimony must be dated, located, and evaluated according to its genre. Accordingly, the analysis employs the terms “differentiation”, “demarcation”, and “separations” in the plural. The aim is not to identify a single moment at which an independent religion was “born”, but to reconstruct the processes by which particular communities defined authority, Scripture, practice, ethnicity, and apostolic memory. This approach does not deny real processes of separation; it places them within a more complex and documentable chronology. from the jesus movement to the first… 39 1.10. Egypt, Exodus and Akhenaten: a historical comparison without speculative genealogies Egypt, the Hyksos, the Exodus, and Akhenaten require a comparison grounded in the history of traditions, with careful consideration of chronology, language, and transmission. This context remains subordinate to the core of the work, the formation of Christianity: the first Christians read the Scriptures of Israel and inherited narratives whose literary form is linked to memories of Egypt. General similarities and speculative etymologies are insufficient to establish a direct historical genealogy. The Second Intermediate Period and the presence of Asiatic populations in the eastern delta constitute an archaeological field independent of the biblical narrative of the Exodus. Avaris/Tell el-Dabʿa documents dynamics of migration, settlement, and political power that help reconstruct Egypt in the second millennium BCE; however, it does not demonstrate the historicity of the Exodus nor does it allow for the direct identification of the Hyksos with Israel. The similarity between an episode of expulsion and a tradition of departure is insufficient to establish historical identity. Ancient historiography already established associations between Hyksos, Jews, and accounts of expulsion. Josephus, in Against Apion, preserves and debates traditions attributed to Manetho. This material is important because it shows how, in Hellenistic and Roman times, Egypt could become a stage for identity disputes and conflicting memories. Its value for our topic lies in the reception and reformulation of traditions, not in using Josephus as a direct witness to the second millennium BCE. The figure of Akhenaten requires similar caution. Atenism was a specific religious reform of the 18th Dynasty and must be studied through inscriptions, hymns, monuments, and the archaeology of Amarna. The old hypothesis of a simple genealogical relationship between Akhenaten, Moses, and biblical monotheism belongs to an intellectual history that can be studied, but should not be presented as a historical conclusion. The chronological, institutional, ritual, and theological differences are too great to substitute a general analogy for proof of transmission. The comparison between the Great Hymn to Aten and Psalm 104, however, deserves a controlled philological treatment. Thematic similarities exist in the celebration of cosmic order, light, the cycles of nature, and the dependence of living beings on the divine. But the analysis must distinguish motifs widely disseminated in the hymnography of the ancient Near East from demonstrable literary borrowings. A similarity of imagery does not in itself establish textual contact, and differences in theological structure are as important as parallels.

40 early christianity Wisdom literature offers another, more productive field of comparison. The Instruction of Amenemope and Proverbs 22:17–24:22 have been the subject of philological discussion because they present more precise correspondences of form and content than broad symbolic analogies. This type of case shows what it means to argue responsibly for a literary relationship: sequences, vocabulary, structure, and chronology are compared, and plausible routes of transmission are evaluated. For the history of Christianity, these problems matter because Christian authors inherited a Bible already shaped by centuries of cultural interaction. Matthew reinterprets the Exodus from Egypt; Paul uses traditions from the Exodus typologically; the Fathers develop readings of the sea, the manna, and the desert in baptismal, ecclesial, or ascetic terms. The scholarly interest lies not in making Egypt the “hidden origin” of Christianity, but in understanding how a scriptural tradition with a long history of contact was reread in new contexts. Accordingly, Egypt is approached in three carefully delimited ways: as historical context for the biblical world; as a field for the history of traditions and controlled philological comparison; and as a setting for the Christian reception of scriptural motifs. Undocumented identity equations—Hyksos = Hebrews, Akhenaten = Moses, Aten = YHWH, or comparable chains of equivalence—are excluded from the historical argument. from the jesus movement to the first… 41 1.11.1. Documentary status and historical method The Gospels are confessional documents composed and edited several decades after Jesus’ public ministry. Their historical value lies at the intersection of memories of earlier practices, literary composition and controversies within the communities that transmitted them. This section distinguishes (a) practices widely attested by Jewish sources and archaeology, (b) debates within Judaism and (c) theological formulations particular to each evangelist. Comparative verification draws on Josephus, Philo, Judean Desert manuscripts, epigraphy, miqvaʾot, stone vessels, early synagogues, and, with explicit stratification, Mishnah, Tosefta, and later rabbinic materials. Late Antique rabbinic halakha is not retrospectively projected onto the first century. 1.11.2. The Temple of Jerusalem: worship, economy and conflict Luke 2 situates the presentation and purification within the cultic system; Mark 11:15– 19, Matthew 21:12–17, Luke 19:45–48, and John 2:13–22 transmit different versions of Jesus’ action in the Temple precinct; Mark 13 and parallels rework the horizon of destruction. The money changers presuppose the sacrificial and monetary economy of the sanctuary, but the episode should not be reduced to a modern denunciation of commerce. Criticism of the Temple has Jewish prophetic antecedents and does not automatically equate to a rejection of the Temple, the Torah, or Israel. The memory of the period after 70 CE intensified the symbolic weight of these narratives; therefore, a distinction must be made between the historical setting and post-70 redaction. 1.11.3. The synagogue—συναγωγή—as a local institution Mark 1:21–28; 3:1–6; 6:2; Luke 4:16–30; John 6:59 presuppose the synagogue as a space for gathering, reading, teaching, and conflict. Archaeology confirms early synagogue institutions, but not a uniform architecture or liturgy. John 9:22; 12:42; 16:2 and the term ἀποσυνάγωγος require caution: they may reflect later conflicts of the Johannine communities and do not prove a universal and coordinated expulsion of all believers in Jesus. 1.11.4. The sources and their unequal chronological value The evidence for the first decades is fragmentary. We have no contemporary records of the Jerusalem community nor a chronicle written during Jesus’ public ministry. Reconstruction depends on documents produced for specific purposes and at different times. To these must be added material culture—inscriptions, coins, built spaces—which should be interrogated as an autonomous body of evidence, not as mere illustration of the texts. The undisputed Pauline epistles are the primary point of reference for the middle years of the first century. They are not systematic treatises: they respond to specific conflicts and presuppose shared information between author and recipients. Precisely for this reason, they possess extraordinary historical value. When Paul mentions Cephas, James, John, Barnabas, or communities in Judea, he does so incidentally within the context of problems that were not invented to narrate the origins of the movement. The Acts of the Apostles is later and presents a coherent narrative of expansion from Jerusalem to Rome. Its historical value is considerable, but it must be evaluated episode by episode. Where it can be compared with Paul, agreement corroborates certain data; the differences also reveal the author’s literary and theological perspective. XV.44, written at the beginning of the second century CE, describes the Neronian repression following the fire of Rome in 64 CE and explains that the name of the Christians derived from Christus, executed during the reign of Tiberius by order of Pontius Pilate. The historian calls Pilate procurator, while the Caesarea inscription identifies him as praefectus; this terminological discrepancy does not invalidate the testimony, but it is worth remembering that Tacitus wrote several decades after the events. The passage is particularly relevant for documenting how a Roman senatorial author understood the origin of the group and its presence in Rome.14 Pliny the Younger, in Epistulae X.96–97, offers a different kind of testimony. Around 110–113, as governor of Bithynia-Pontus, he consulted Trajan about the legal procedure to follow against people denounced as Christians. Pliny reports that some met before dawn and alternately sang a hymn to Christ quasi deo, “as to a god,” in addition to swearing an oath to certain behaviours. The document does not describe a complete liturgy and comes from interrogations conducted by a Roman magistrate; precisely for this reason, it constitutes an exceptional source for the social, ritual, and administrative history of provincial Christianity at the beginning of the second century.15 Suetonius, in Claudius 25.4, states that Claudius expelled from Rome the Jews who were causing disturbances, impulsore Chresto (“at the instigation of Chrestus”). The identification of Chrestus with Christus is possible and has often been argued, but it is not certain: Chrestus was also a known name, and the phrase may refer to a person present in Rome. If the passage alludes indirectly to disputes about Christ, it would be an early indication of conflicts within Jewish communities in the capital; if not, it remains evidence of the instability of the Roman diaspora under Claudius. The source should therefore be used as contested evidence, not as unequivocal proof of a fully differentiated Roman Christian community in 49.16 Taken together, these external sources do not, on their own, suffice to reconstruct the history of Jesus or the early communities, but they do provide independent points of reference. Jerusalem: Jewish memory, authority and continuity Jerusalem appears as a centre of authority in the oldest testimonies. Paul, in retrospectively narrating his activity, presupposes that certain figures in Jerusalem enjoyed particular recognition. In Galatians 1:18 he states that, three years after his calling, he went up to Jerusalem to meet Cephas and remained with him fifteen days; he adds that he saw none of the other apostles except James, “the Lord’s brother” (Gal 1:18– 19). This passage is historically more important than a later list of office-holders. It shows that, for Paul, Cephas and James belonged to a network of authority that he could not ignore, even though his own apostolic legitimacy did not depend on them. The phrase does not describe a later episcopal hierarchy, but rather recognised prestige within the movement.17 The Jerusalem community should not be imagined as a Gentile proto-church. Paul’s own letters show that the debate about the incorporation of non-Jews took place within a Jewish framework. The question was not whether Israel remained relevant, but how Gentiles could participate in Israel’s promises and what practices they should adopt. The centrality of Jerusalem is also expressed in the collection organised by Paul for “the saints” in the city (Rom 15:25–31; 1 Cor 16:1–4; 2 Cor 8–9). The collection was more than just financial assistance: it served as a gesture of communion between the Gentile Pauline communities and the Jerusalem community. Its importance confirms that, even in a mission oriented towards the nations, the relationship with Jerusalem remained fundamental. 17 Gal 1:18–19; 2:1–10; 1 Cor 15:3–7; Acts 1–5. Paul: calling, mission and communities Paul is the best-documented figure in mid-first-century Christianity. His importance does not compel us to consider him the “founder of Christianity” in an absolute sense. Rather, his letters show that he joined a pre-existing movement, received earlier traditions, and had to negotiate his place in relation to other missionaries and authorities. In Galatians 1:15–16 he describes his calling through prophetic language: God separated him from the womb and revealed his Son “to announce him among the nations”—ἵνα εὐαγγελίζωμαι αὐτὸν ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν—(Gal 1:15–16). Thessalonica, Philippi, Corinth, and the communities of Galatia were not simply points of a geographical campaign: they were social groups with their own conflicts concerning authority, sexuality, food, status, charismatic gifts, resurrection, and relationships with non-believers. The First Letter to the Thessalonians is especially revealing because of its early chronology. Paul reminds his recipients that they turned “from idols to God”—πρὸς τὸν θεὸν ἀπὸ τῶν εἰδώλων—to serve the living God and await his Son from heaven (1 Thess 1:9–10). This formulation presupposes recipients from non-Jewish cultic practices and shows the radical nature of their religious reorientation. Paul’s mission, therefore, did not simply consist of converting pagans to a new religion already separate from Judaism. His project was to integrate Gentiles into the eschatological horizon of the God of Israel without necessarily requiring them to become Jews through circumcision. It is precisely here that one of the most intense debates in contemporary scholarship arises. The so-called “New Perspective on Paul”—a label coined by James D. G. Dunn in 1982 (published in the Bulletin of the John Rylands Library 65, 1983) on the basis of E. P. Subsequent research has further developed this revision, insisting that many of Paul’s statements about the Law are directed at Gentiles and do not constitute a general denial of Jewish identity (Thiessen 2016, 1–17; 73–102; Fredriksen 2017).
