A later line of thought, usually called Paul within Judaism, proposes reading Paul as a Jew who directs his instructions on circumcision, idolatry, and belonging primarily to Gentiles incorporated into the Messianic movement, without assuming that he himself abandoned Jewish practice or identity. The volume edited by Mark D. Nanos and Magnus Zetterholm programmatically formulates this perspective and compels a careful distinction between what Paul prescribes to Gentiles and what can be inferred from his own practice. The usefulness of this approach does not require its adoption as the sole explanation. Its main contribution is methodological: it avoids transforming all of Paul’s critique of the Law into a rejection of Judaism. At the same time, works such as John M.G. Barclay’s Paul and the Gift have shown that the debate on grace, gift, and obedience cannot be reduced to the alternative of “Jewish legalism” versus “Christian grace.” Barclay distinguishes several ancient ways of ‘perfecting’ the notion of gift and locates Paul’s radicalism above all in the incongruity of the gift, given without regard to the recipient’s prior worth. This monograph uses these currents as interlocutors, not as school labels. For each passage, it asks who the intended audience is, what specific problem is being discussed, and what inference about Jewish or Gentile identity is actually authorised by the text.20 4.3. Work, house-workshop and logistics of the urban mission Paul’s mission had a material dimension that cannot be reduced to itineraries on a map. Paul repeatedly states that he worked with his hands (1 Thessalonians 2:9; 1 Corinthians 4:12; cf. Acts 18:3). Acts refers to him as σκηνοποιός, a term whose exact translation—tentmaker, leatherworker, or related trade—continues to be debated. What is certain is that Paul presents manual labour as part of his missionary economy. In Roman cities, production, trade, and housing could coexist in spaces like the house-workshop or a taberna (shop or workshop). It is not possible to prove that each Pauline community literally arose in one of these settings, but the model helps us understand how work, hospitality, and sociability could overlap. Galatians 2: Jerusalem, communion and conflict Galatians 2 is the most important surviving testimony for studying the relationship between Paul and the authorities in Jerusalem. Paul states that he returned to Jerusalem “after fourteen years” with Barnabas and Titus. There he expounded the gospel that he proclaimed among the Gentiles and received from James, Cephas, and John “the right hand of fellowship”—δεξιὰς ἔδωκαν... κοινωνίας—, with a division of missionary fields: they to the circumcised, and Paul and Barnabas to the Gentiles (Gal 2:1–10). The agreement did not eliminate the conflicts. According to Paul himself, at a point he does not date relative to that agreement, a public dispute arose with Cephas in Antioch. Paul declares: κατὰ πρόσωπον αὐτῷ ἀντέστην, “I opposed him face to face” (Gal 2:11–14). The reason was Cephas’s withdrawal from the table shared with Gentiles after the arrival of people associated with James. The episode shows that formal fellowship did not automatically resolve the practical consequences of Gentile inclusion. This conflict should not be reduced to an abstract opposition between “Pauline Christianity” and “Judaism.” The concrete question was who could share a table with whom and what that practice meant for community identity. Food was a space where purity, ethnicity, belonging, and authority converged. The intensity of Paul’s reaction, our only surviving account of the incident, indicates that coexistence between Jews and Gentiles in Christ remained an open problem. The narrative also qualifies F.C. Baur’s classic model, which organised early Christianity around two coherent and opposing blocs, Petrine and Pauline. The sources show real conflicts, but alliances and positions were more fluid. Peter/Cephas could

Acts 15 and the problem of comparison Acts 15 recounts a meeting in Jerusalem prompted by the question of whether Gentiles should be circumcised and observe the Law. The episode has traditionally been identified with the visit in Galatians 2. The identification is plausible and remains common, but it cannot be considered definitively proven. The two narratives share important elements: Jerusalem, Paul and Barnabas, a discussion about Gentiles, the participation of key figures, and a resolution that avoids imposing circumcision on non-Jews. However, they differ in structure, emphasis, and outcome. Galatians does not mention the so-called apostolic decree; Acts does not reproduce the conflict in Antioch with the same narrative function. The comparison must follow a methodological sequence: first, each text is reconstructed within its own argument; then, convergences and divergences are identified; only then is a historical relationship proposed. Harmonising them from the outset would produce a third narrative that does not fully coincide with either of the two sources. The minimum consensus is more solid than the detailed identification: during the middle decades of the first century, there was a real controversy about the conditions for incorporating Gentiles, and leaders linked to Jerusalem and the Pauline mission participated in it. This transformation should not be described as an immediate replacement of a “Jewish Church” with a “Gentile Church.” In different cities and regions, Jews and Gentiles continued to interact in various ways for generations. Differentiation did not progress at the same pace in all cities. Jerusalem and Judea were shaped by the centrality of the Temple, warfare, and the reconfigurations after 70 CE; the diaspora communities operated within different civic, legal, and linguistic frameworks. Alexandria, Antioch, Rome, and the cities of Asia Minor should not be seen as mere stages in a single chronology. Urban geography altered the possibilities for interaction between Jews, Gentiles, and groups of followers of Jesus, and consequently, the speed and manner in which boundaries were constructed. Recent historiography has challenged the idea of a single separation between Judaism and Christianity datable to the year 70, at Yavne, or at some other isolated event. The volume edited by Adam Becker and Annette Yoshiko Reed influentially articulated this problem through the image of “ways that never parted” in any simple fashion (Becker and Reed 2007). The value of this historiographical shift lies less in denying all differentiation than in compelling us to situate it historically. The destruction of the Temple in 70 CE was undoubtedly a decisive transformation for multiple Jewish currents and for communities following Jesus. But its effects varied depending on the group. The Gospels composed after the war reflect new configurations of memory and conflict; Gentile communities could find themselves increasingly distanced from Jewish institutions; at the same time, Jewish practices, Scriptures, and categories continued to structure Christianity. Therefore, this book uses the expression “differentiation between Judaism and Christianity” rather than “definitive separation” when referring to the period of the first and second centuries. In some contexts the boundaries became clear relatively early; in others they remained porous for longer.26 8. Authority and memory before institutionalisation The early Christian communities did not lack authority; they lacked a single, unified form of authority. Paul appeals to his calling, to the received tradition, to Scripture, to his missionary work, and to his relationships with other apostles. Jerusalem possesses 26 Gal 2:15–21; 3:1–29; 5:1–6; Rom 3–4. Thiessen 2016 and Fredriksen 2017 allow us to clarify the problem of the Gentile recipients.

This plurality explains why apostolic memory subsequently became such an important resource. As new generations debated doctrine, discipline, and authoritative texts, proximity to the apostles became an argument for legitimacy. But that stage should not be projected retrospectively onto the decades of Paul. The circulation of letters was one of the material mechanisms for constructing memory. Paul wrote to specific communities, but his letters began to circulate beyond the original recipients. This process contributed to a set of occasional documents acquiring translocal authority. The history of the canon begins precisely with this materiality: texts copied, exchanged, read, and collected before being included in normative lists.27 9. Women beyond Paul: prophecy, martyrdom, patronage and ministries in the second–third centuries Female agency does not end with the Pauline networks. In the second and third centuries, women appear in archives of a different nature: apocryphal narratives, martyrdom accounts, charismatic prophecy, inscriptions, ecclesiastical discipline, and normative literature. Comparison requires distinguishing between historically identifiable individuals, literary characters, and institutional categories. Thecla belongs to second-century Pauline reception; Priscilla/Prisca and Maximilla show that women’s prophetic authority could be central while also contested by heresiologists. Perpetua and Felicity permit analysis of martyrdom, status and slavery without treating the Passio as social statistics. Widows, virgins, and deaconesses require terminological precision. The Didascalia Apostolorum and other normative sources show women exercising functions of assistance, access to domestic spaces, and mediation, but these should not be mechanically translated into modern categories of ordination. 27 Gal 1:1; 1:11–24; 1 Cor 9:1–2; 15:8–11; 2 Cor 10–13. Apostolic defence is not equivalent to a unified institutional regulation.

62 early christianity 10. Pre-Constantinian Christian buildings: comparison and degrees of certainty Dura-Europos remains the clearest case for examining a house adapted to Christian use before the Constantinian settlement: the architectural sequence, baptistery, and wall paintings allow space, ritual, and image to be related without reconstructing a premature “basilica”. The Megiddo/Kefar ʿOthnay complex, with its paved hall and Christian mosaic inscription, offers an important third-century comparandum, although the precise function of the complex, its relationship to the camp of Legio VI Ferrata, and the fine chronology of its phases require caution. The find at Kefar ʿOthnay (Legio), in the Megiddo prison compound (2005), allows this point of comparison to be made more precise. It is a plain assembly hall with a mosaic pavement decorated with geometric motifs and fish, and several Greek inscriptions. The principal one records that Akeptous, “lover of God”, offered the table “to God Jesus Christ” as a memorial (τὴν τράπεζαν θεῷ Ἰησοῦ Χριστῷ μνημόσυνον); another states that a Roman officer, Gaianus, also called Porphyrius, paid for the mosaic. The editors (Tepper and Di Segni 2006) date it to about 230; other proposals lower it to the late third or early fourth century, and its functional interpretation remains debated. In any case it is neither a basilica nor a monumental building, and no comparable building is known for the first century: the evidence indicates that by the third century some Christian groups had halls of their own, a ritual “table” and explicit Christological language in a space of worship, before any imperial patronage. This case, together with Dura-Europos, corrects a generalisation of the literary sources. Minucius Felix’s Octavius has the pagan opponent say that Christians have “no altars and no temples” (Minucius Felix, Oct. 10.2), and the apologist accepts this in a theological sense (Oct. 32.1). That formula describes a rhetoric of difference from pagan temples, not a general material condition: in the third century there were Christians with a dedicated hall, a table offered to God and a decorated space. The correction is limited: it does not prove that such halls were the norm or that they existed in the first century, only that the literary argument cannot be read as a description of the communities’ actual equipment. A second body of testimony concerns the memory of the apostles at Rome, and in it veneration must be separated from worship. The theological distinction between the latria owed to God alone and the honour given to martyrs is formulated with precision only later; what the sources and finds document for the second and third centuries is a cult of memory beside tombs: the monument, the visit, the funerary meal and invocation. The literary sources are of unequal weight. 1 Clem. 5–6 presents Pe-

from the jesus movement to the first… 63 ter and Paul as examples of endurance unto death, alongside “a great multitude of the elect” who suffered, but does not name Nero or specify where Peter died; Ignatius, Rom. 4.3, presupposes that both apostles held special authority before the Roman community (“I do not command you as Peter and Paul did”); Dionysius of Corinth, c. 170, asserts that both founded the churches of Corinth and of Rome and suffered martyrdom “at the same time” (Eusebius, HE II.25.8), a claim with an evident apologetic interest in the unity of the two sees. The most important testimony is that of the presbyter Gaius, c. 200, against the Montanist Proclus: “I can show you the trophies (τρόπαια) of the apostles; if you go to the Vatican or to the Ostian Way, you will find the trophies of those who founded this Church” (Eusebius, HE II.25.7). Tertullian, c. 200–210, ascribes to Peter a death like the Lord’s and to Paul one like John the Baptist’s (Tertullian, Scorp. 15.3; Praescr. 36.3). This is a body of evidence datable to the late second century, not the first, and none of it proves by itself a cultic practice in the first century. Archaeology allows what Gaius implies to be made more precise. The Vatican excavations of 1940–1949 identified in the necropolis beneath St Peter’s an aedicula of the mid-second century set against the so-called “red wall”, which scholarly tradition identifies with Gaius’s “trophy”; the monument shows that by about 160–170 there was at the site a point of apostolic memory, not that it simply contained the apostle’s remains, a question that remains debated. The graffito Πέτρ(ος) ἔνι, read and proposed by Margherita Guarducci on the adjoining wall, is disputed in both reading and date and should not be made to carry more weight than it bears. Firmer is the evidence of the Memoria Apostolorum on the Via Appia, at San Sebastiano (ad catacumbas): hundreds of graffiti, most from the later third century, attest refrigeria— funerary meals in honour of the apostles—and invocations such as “Paul and Peter, pray for Victor”. The association with the year 258, when the relics are said to have been moved there during the persecution of Valerian, is a plausible but late reconstruction that depends on fourth-century sources. The value of the whole for this book is twofold: it confirms that the cult of apostolic memory took shape in the second century around the paired figure of Peter and Paul, and it shows that its material support was the funerary monument and the ritual meal, not a building for worship. It is worth adding that this chronology should not be confused with that of the synagogues. In the first and second centuries there is no conversion of synagogue buildings into churches: the movement was born within the diaspora synagogues, which Paul uses in Acts as a platform (Acts 17:1–2; 18:4), coexisted with them, and separated from them unevenly and regionally, not all at once. The two milestones usually given as causes—the destruction of the Temple in 70 and the Birkat ha-Minim—

64 early christianity must be taken with the caution set out in the relevant chapter, since the second can be neither dated nor read as a general synagogue measure in 85–90. The oldest surviving Christian spaces are adapted houses, such as that of Dura-Europos (remodelled c. 240–256), which coexisted with its synagogue as an independent structure; the term domus ecclesiae is a modern category and not a standardised second-century architectural form. Conversions of synagogues into churches are later than the Constantinian peace and cannot be projected back onto the period this book studies. The house gatherings can be described more precisely if the sources are distinguished from what is inferred from them. Justin, 1 Apol. 65–67 (c. 150–155, written at Rome), gives the earliest description of a Sunday meeting: reading of “the memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets”, exhortation by the president, standing prayers, the kiss of peace, bread and wine mixed with water, thanksgiving and distribution by the deacons, with exclusion of the unbaptised; it is an apologetic description addressed to a pagan audience, not a liturgical ordo. Pliny (Pliny, Ep. X.96, c. 112) places the gatherings “before dawn” and in two stages, with hymns to Christ “as to a god” and a later meal “common and harmless”; Tertullian (Tertullian, Apol. 39) describes the common chest, prayer for the emperors and the agape, not a secret cult; Minucius Felix (Oct. 8–9) transmits, in the mouth of the pagan opponent, the suspicions of nocturnal rites and recognition signs, which the Christian text refutes and which therefore cannot be taken as a neutral description. The figure of the ostiarius is attested at Rome c. 251 in Bishop Cornelius’s letter (Eusebius, HE VI.43.11), which lists forty-two acolytes and fifty-two “exorcists, readers and doorkeepers”; the formal dismissal of catechumens and the discipline of the secret come from third-century and, above all, fourth-century sources, and the Apostolic Tradition attributed to Hippolytus is a text of debated date and composition. The picture of an adapted triclinium, a common table and a separate baptismal space rests, for this period, chiefly on Dura-Europos, and everything else—the doorkeeper recognising each attendee, the low voices of the psalms, the oil lamps—is plausible inference, not datum. Irenaeus (Haer. III.3.2–3), for his part, does not describe meetings but grounds the authority of the Roman tradition in the preaching of Peter and Paul and in the succession of Linus, Anacletus and Clement, which links to the cult of memory treated above. Comparison with other meeting places must separate positive evidence from retrospective inference. A large house mentioned in a letter, a room capable of accommodating an assembly, and a building later transformed into a church are not equivalent kinds of evidence. Before Constantine, archaeology points to a plurality of solutions—domestic adaptation, association-like meeting rooms, and complexes

from the jesus movement to the first… 65 with specific ritual functions—but not to a universal Christian building type. Archaeology here does more than illustrate the texts: it can contradict the retrospective picture they project. The fourth-century transformation lies less in the ex nihilo invention of a form than in a new scale of patronage, urban visibility, and monumentality. Conclusion The first generation of the Jesus movement can be reconstructed with sufficient historical depth without turning uncertainties into voids. The movement arose within Judaism; Jerusalem functioned as a centre of memory and authority; Paul developed an intensive mission among Gentiles; and the incorporation of these Gentiles produced concrete conflicts regarding circumcision, table fellowship, the Law, and belonging. The sources do not show an instantaneous break between Judaism and Christianity. Rather, they show a process of differentiation accompanied by profound continuities. Nor do they show two monolithic, opposing parties, but rather networks of people and communities whose positions could coincide, diverge, and transform. This configuration forms the starting point for the second century. There, the question is no longer merely how to incorporate Gentiles, but who has the authority to interpret Scripture, which texts should be read, how correct teaching is defined, and how diverse groups construct apostolic genealogies. The shift from local controversies to more stable systems of authority is one of the central themes of the following chapter. Summary This chapter situates the Jesus movement within first-century Judaism and the political and social conditions of Roman Judea. It compares Paul’s letters, the Book of Acts, and external literary and epigraphic testimonies, distinguishing contemporary evidence from later memory. Jerusalem, the incorporation of Gentiles, disputes over commensality, and the interpretation of the Law are examined as uneven processes of community formation, rather than an instantaneous separation between two religions. Keywords: Second Temple Judaism; Paul; Jerusalem; incorporation of Gentiles; Roman Judea.

chapter ii Marcion, Scripture and the Formation of the Canon The second century demands a change of scale. Controversies no longer concern only the inclusion of Gentiles or the authority of specific missionaries, but also the relationship between the Scriptures of Israel and the Gospel, the identity of the God proclaimed by Jesus, the authority of the Pauline epistles, and the delimitation of texts that could be read as normative. Marcion of Sinope occupies a central place in this process, not because the history of the canon can be reduced to a reaction against him, but because his activity reveals that, by the middle of the second century, the selection, arrangement, and interpretation of Christian writings had become explicit problems of authority. 1. The historical problem of Marcion Marcion was an active Christian figure in Rome during the second century and was later condemned by authors who presented themselves as defenders of the apostolic rule of faith. The exact chronology of his arrival in Rome, his break with the local community, and the spread of his churches depends on later testimonies, so it is important to avoid transforming a heresiological biography into a sequence securely established by documentary evidence. The conventional date of the Roman break, c. 144 CE, derives from a polemical computation by Tertullian (Adv. Marc. I.19), which places Marcion one hundred and fifteen and a half years after the preaching of Jesus, and should be treated as an estimate. What can be stated with confidence is that, in the second half of the second century, authors such as Irenaeus were aware of communities and doctrines associated with his name, and that Tertullian, at the beginning of the third century, was able to dedicate five books to refuting them. The methodological difficulty is immediate: no work by Marcion survives in independent manuscript transmission. His Gospel, his Pauline collection, and the Antitheses must be reconstructed from adversaries—especially Tertullian, 66

marcion, scripture and the formation of… 67 Epiphanius, Irenaeus, and the Dialogue of Adamantius—who quote, paraphrase, or describe Marcionite materials for polemical purposes. Judith M. Lieu has emphasised precisely this point: the Marcion accessible to the historian is also the product of a long “construction of the heretic” by his opponents (Lieu 2015). Therefore, the correct question is not “What did Marcion teach?” in the abstract, but “What elements of his thought and his texts can be reconstructed, through which witnesses, and with what degree of certainty?” The distinction is crucial if we are not to repeat as fact the rhetorical characterisations of his adversaries. 2. Heresiological sources and their value Irenaeus offers one of the most influential early accounts. In Adversus haereses I.27, he attributes to Marcion an opposition between the God proclaimed by the Law and the Prophets and the Father of Jesus Christ; he adds that Marcion used a gospel related to Luke and a collection of Paul’s letters. The passage is indispensable, but it is not neutral: Irenaeus presents these operations as deliberate mutilation of received texts and integrates them into a genealogy of heresy. His testimony must be used simultaneously as a source on Marcion and as a source on Irenaeus’s polemical strategy. Tertullian is still more important for textual reconstruction. Adversus Marcionem IV extensively discusses the gospel used by Marcion, and Book V discusses his Pauline epistles. The fact that Tertullian argues against specific readings allows for the recovery of numerous passages, but his procedure is not equivalent to a diplomatic transcription of the Marcionite text. He may quote from memory, summarise, combine formulations, and adapt his discussion to Latin. Dieter T. Roth has shown that any modern reconstruction must evaluate the form of each attestation individually and distinguish degrees of certainty (Roth 2015). Epiphanius of Salamis, in Panarion 42, offers a later inventory of differences attributed to the Gospel of Marcion. He is chronologically more distant and no less polemical than Tertullian, yet he preserves details not always found in Tertullian. Tertullian and Epiphanius are treated as independent witnesses only where the history of literary dependence warrants it; agreement between them cannot by itself establish independent access to the same Marcionite exemplar. Methodological note on witness dependence. Panarion 42 should not be mechanically counted as a second independent witness alongside Tertullian. Epiphanius works within a heresiological tradition that reuses earlier materials, and his relationship to Irenaeus, Hippolytus, and intermediate texts must be evaluated locus by locus. When Tertullian and Epiphanius agree, the agreement increases

68 early christianity the reconstructive value only if a literary dependence can be excluded or limited; otherwise, there is a risk of circular collation. 2.1. Justin as contemporary witness Before Irenaeus and Tertullian, Justin Martyr offers one of the earliest surviving testimonies about Marcion. In 1 Apol. 26 he states that Marcion of Pontus was still alive and teaching his disciples to believe in a god distinct from and superior to the Creator; he adds, with evident polemical intent, that he had persuaded people “of every nation.” In 1 Apol. 58 he again presents him as an active teacher with a wide following. Justin’s demonological rhetoric prevents us from using his description as a neutral portrait. Its historical value lies in other aspects: it establishes Marcion as a contemporary, confirms that his activity was known in Rome by the mid-second century, and shows that his movement had acquired sufficient visibility to be mentioned in an apology addressed to imperial power. Justin must therefore precede Irenaeus in the chapter’s documentary sequence.28 3. The Gospel of Marcion and its relationship to Luke Ancient adversaries identify the Marcionite gospel with a form closely related to Luke. Irenaeus describes it as a truncated Luke; Tertullian sets out his refutation by accepting, for the purposes of discussion, the gospel that Marcion acknowledges; Epiphanius lists passages present, absent, or altered. The modern task is to avoid accepting uncritically the direction of change presupposed by the accusation of “mutilation.” Roth’s reconstruction offers a significant methodological advance because it does not propose a homogeneous text with the same degree of confidence in all its verses. His study classifies the evidence and reconstructs readings only when the combination of witnesses allows it. Consequently, this monograph does not print a continuous “Gospel of Marcion” as if it were a preserved manuscript; it presents only the loci necessary for the argument and expressly indicates the level of certainty of each reconstruction. Roth’s work, published by Brill in 2015, constitutes a central reference tool here. One particularly debated issue is the literary relationship between the Marcionite Gospel and Luke. The traditional explanation holds that Marcion abbreviated 28 Justin, 1 Apol. 26; 58. Reference critical editions: Munier 2006 and Minns and Parvis 2009. Early testimony does not provide an independent copy of Marcion’s Gospel.

This work does not adopt a general solution before examining specific passages; its priority is to distinguish what ancient sources attest to from what modern historiography infers. In the current state of research, the most widely accepted explanation is that Marcion worked with a form of Luke and revised it according to his theological project. This position retains weight because it coincides with the general direction of patristic testimony and with numerous features of the textual relationship. However, it can no longer be presented as an indisputable fact. Among the serious alternatives are the priority of the Marcionite Gospel over the canonical form of Luke and the hypothesis that both depend, in different ways, on an earlier Gospel form. Luke 5:39: a case in which silence cannot become omission Modern tradition, from Harnack onwards, frequently attributed the omission of Luke 5:39 to Marcion because the preference for “old” wine seemed incompatible with a theology of rupture between the Creator God and the Father of Jesus Christ. However, Dieter T. Roth insists on a methodologically crucial point: indirect Marcionite sources attest neither to the presence nor to the absence of this verse. Harnack reconstructed its omission on grounds of dogmatic expediency, but this procedure creates negative evidence where the sources are silent. The absence of Luke 5:39 from Codex Bezae (D) and in part of the Western tradition demonstrates, moreover, that the omission of the verse is not in itself a distinctively Marcionite trait. Therefore, this locus should be used as an example of critical discipline: one can discuss why the verse would have been inconvenient for a Marcionite reading, but one cannot assert that Marcion eliminated it. Roth classifies the Marcionite text of this verse as unattested. Methodological consequence: the reconstruction of the Gospel attributed to Marcion cannot be completed through theological expectations. The apparatus must record “not attested” where Tertullian, Epiphanius, and the other sources do not provide data.

Luke 10:21: “Lord of heaven” and the absence of “the earth” In Luke’s critical text, Jesus addresses the Father as “Lord of heaven and earth.” Tertullian, Adv. Marc. IV.25, and Epiphanius transmit a form attributed to Marcion’s text in which the reference to earth is missing. Roth reconstructs with considerable confidence a reading containing κύριε τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, “Lord of heaven,” without καὶ τῆς γῆς. The divergence has evident theological potential within the Marcionite controversy because it permits the Father of Jesus to be distinguished from explicit sovereignty over the earth. However, the argument must be expressed carefully: the philological fact is the difference in reading; the explanation that the alteration was deliberately made to express a dualistic cosmology belongs to the level of historical interpretation. The causal sequence cannot be deduced solely from the variant. This locus is particularly valuable because it shows the interaction between patristic reconstruction and general textual criticism. The apparatus of NA28 records no Greek variant omitting “and of the earth” at this point; the short reading comes from the patristic tradition about Marcion, and its priority over the long text requires further argument. The question of priority requires further argument. 3.5. Locus 3. Luke 13:28: Patriarchs and prophets versus “all the righteous” The canonical text mentions Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and “all the prophets” in the kingdom of God. For the recension attributed to Marcion, Tertullian and Epiphanius allow the expression πάντας τοὺς δικαίους, “all the righteous,” to be reconstructed in its place. Roth considers this locus sufficiently attested to incorporate it into his critical reconstruction. The difference is historically significant. The Marcionite reading generalises the category of those admitted to the kingdom and eliminates the explicit enumeration of founding figures of Israel. It is reasonable to relate this textual form to the Marcionite dispute over the continuity between the Gospel and the Scriptures of Israel; however, the apparatus must distinguish between the given fact—the reading “all the righteous”—and the explanation of its origin. The substitution offers one of the clearest examples of what a comparative edition can and cannot establish: the variant is documented; the specific editorial intention remains a historical inference.

74 early christianity 3.6. Locus 4. Luke 20:35–36: punctuation, syntax and “the god of that age” This passage calls for an important correction to overly free reconstructions. Tertullian does not accuse Marcion here of simply omitting the “flesh” or the idea of resurrection. The controversy revolves around how the phrase is segmented. The Marcionite tradition could read the sequence so that “of that age” modified “God,” producing the meaning “the god of that age”; Tertullian insists on punctuating after “God,” so that “that age” pertains to what the worthy will attain. Roth reconstructs for Luke 20:35 a sequence that preserves both the reference to attaining that age and “the resurrection from the dead.” Consequently, it is incorrect to describe this locus as a simple Marcionite suppression of the bodily resurrection. The problem is syntactic, hermeneutical, and theological: the same sequence of words could be divided differently to produce a different Christology and cosmology. This example is especially useful for the monograph because it demonstrates that textual criticism is not limited to words present or absent. Punctuation, segmentation, and reliance on a patristic Latin translation can radically alter the reconstruction of a lost Greek text. 3.7. marcion, scripture and the formation of… 75 4. The Apostolikon: Paul as textual authority Marcion also compiled a collection of Pauline letters, traditionally called the Apostolikon. Ancient sources and modern reconstructions agree that Paul held exceptional authority within his scriptural project. This selection should not be explained simply as personal preference: it shows that, by the middle of the second century, the Pauline letters could already function as a transmissible corpus, susceptible to systematic ordering, editing, and interpretation. Tertullian, in Adversus Marcionem V, discusses the Pauline epistles in turn and preserves information about the order and certain titles of the Marcionite collection; for example, he reports that the writing known to him as Ephesians appeared under the name Laodiceans in Marcion’s corpus. This information should be evaluated within the broader discussion of the titles, circulation, and stabilisation of the epistles. The existence of the Apostolikon does not mean that Marcion “invented” Paul, nor that he was the first to collect letters. There are indications of earlier Pauline circulation, and the very reception of Paul in 2 Peter (2 Pet 3:15–16) presupposes a plurality of letters. However, Marcion provides exceptional evidence for the programmatic use of a delimited Pauline corpus. 4.1. P46 and the materiality of an early Pauline collection The history of the Apostolikon must be compared with the material evidence from non-Marcionite Pauline collections. The papyrus known as P46 (P.Mich. inv. 6238 and corresponding leaves in the Chester Beatty Library) is the oldest surviving manuscript of an extensive collection of Pauline letters. It is usually dated palaeographically to the late second or early third century; the University of Michigan describes it in general terms as written about the year 200. The codex preserves a significant order: Hebrews appears immediately after Romans, a sequence that differs from that of most modern Bibles. The sequence shows that early Pauline collections could be organised in different ways and that the order of the letters was not yet universally fixed. P46 demonstrates neither dependence on Marcion’s Apostolikon nor Marcionite influence on later codices. Its value is comparative: it physically shows that, around the same chronological horizon in which the controversies surrounding Marcion were still active, collections of Pauline letters existed in codex form, each with its own selection and order. The history of the canon must therefore be constructed from specific communities, codices, and collections, not solely from normative lists.

The Antitheses and the problem of the two gods The Antitheses are not directly preserved. Tertullian mentions them as a fundamental argumentative device of Marcion and attacks them chiefly in Books I–II and IV of Adversus Marcionem. The reconstruction must avoid two extremes: treating them as a book whose content could be restored word for word or reducing them to a caricature without historical substance. The general principle attributed to Marcion contrasts the God of creation and the Law with the God revealed by Jesus Christ. Irenaeus summarises this opposition by distinguishing the God proclaimed by the Law and the Prophets from the Father of Jesus (Haer. I.27). The rhetoric of his adversaries intensifies these differences through pairs such as justice/goodness, known/unknown, and creator/Father. The

A second example revolves around punitive fire. The God of the Scriptures of Israel can punish by fire; in Luke 9:54–56, however, Jesus rejects the disciples’ initiative to call down fire from heaven. The value of this locus for an antithetical argument is evident. At the same time, because we know this opposition only through an adversary, we must distinguish between Marcionite reasoning and the way in which Tertullian reorganises it to refute it. A third type of antithesis contrasts the promises and signs of the Creator with the appearance of a Christ considered separate from that God. Here, it is not only moral maxims that are opposed: the debate centres on which Scripture can claim Christ as its own fulfilment. This level shows that the Antitheses constituted a theory of interpretation and divine economy, not simply a collection of paradoxes. It is methodologically imprecise simply to classify Marcion as “Gnostic.” His thought shares problems with other movements of the second century, but his relationship with creation, Scripture, Christ, and Paul has a configuration of its own. Lieu’s work clearly demonstrates that Marcion must be situated within the Christian debate of the second century and not within a rigid, retrospectively constructed taxonomy. 6. A first New Testament? The formula “first New Testament” is useful only if carefully defined. Jason BeDuhn has used it to highlight that Marcion brought together a gospel and a set of Pauline letters into a coherent scriptural collection (BeDuhn 2013). However, this formulation does not imply that Christian collections did not circulate before Marcion, nor that later communities simply adopted his model. It is preferable to distinguish three phenomena: the circulation of individual writings; the formation of collections; and normative canonical delimitation. These processes overlap, but are not identical. Marcion clearly belongs to the second and contributes to the third, because his selection forced other authors to specify more precisely which texts they recognised and why. Even so, the formation of the canon of four Gospels and the New Testament corpus was gradual and cannot be attributed to a single reaction.32 32 Gallagher and Meade 2017; Barton 1997; Lieu 2015. Normative reading, physical collection and closed list are distinguished.

marcion, scripture and the formation of… 81 7. Irenaeus and the defence of the fourfold gospel At the end of the second century, Irenaeus provides decisive testimony to a new phase. In Adversus haereses III, he explicitly defends the authority of four Gospels and links them to the apostolic tradition. The historical force of this argument lies not only in the well-known symbolism of the number four, but also in the fact that it presupposes a body of Gospels already in circulation whose delimitation he needs to defend against real alternatives. The response to Marcion, to Valentinian groups, and to other adversaries did not consist simply in establishing a list of books. It involved articulating a relationship between Scripture, the rule of faith, apostolic succession, and ecclesial reading. The canon must therefore be studied as part of a technology of authority: texts, interpreters, institutions, and apostolic memories legitimised one another. In this context, “orthodoxy” does not designate an essence that existed complete from the beginning. It designates a historical configuration that acquired mechanisms of self-reproduction: lists, episcopate, genealogies of teaching, liturgy, and criteria of interpretation. Recognising this process does not mean denying the existence of early shared convictions; it means explaining how certain convictions managed to become translocal norms.33 8. Non-canonical gospels and ecologies of transmission The formation of the fourfold gospel cannot be understood solely from the four texts that eventually acquired canonical authority. The second century and the centuries immediately following transmit a much wider constellation of writings presented as gospels, revelations, collections of sayings, or narrative expansions of episodes absent from Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. The term “non-canonical” is used here descriptively: it indicates the later position of these writings in relation to the dominant church collections, not an intrinsic literary quality or a uniform date of exclusion. The modern category of “apocryphal” also requires precision. Current scholarship increasingly uses the expression “early Christian apocryphal literature” to avoid the impression that there is a closed corpus perfectly parallel to the New Testament. These texts circulated in different ways, were read by different audiences, and did not always function as Scripture for separate communities. Manuscript evidence and ancient references require each work to be studied individually. 33 Irenaeus, Haer. III.11.8. Reference: Rousseau and Doutreleau 1974, SC 210–211. The fourfold argument is not used as a document of an identical canon in all communities.

82 early christianity The aim of this section is not to reconstruct a supposed homogeneous “alternative canon,” but to show the diversity of forms in which Christians of the second to fourth centuries continued to write about Jesus, the apostles, Mary, revelation, and salvation. Comparison with the canonical gospels must be made on a case-by-case basis, taking into account genre, language, manuscript transmission, literary dependence, and context of use. 8.1. Gospel of Thomas: sayings, dependence and dating The Gospel of Thomas, preserved in its entirety in Coptic as NHC II,2 and also known from Greek fragments from Oxyrhynchus, contains 114 sayings attributed to Jesus. It lacks a continuous narrative of passion and resurrection and organises its material as a collection of logia. This literary form makes it a central source for the study of the memory of Jesus’s sayings, but it does not, on its own, demonstrate independence from the Synoptic Gospels. The dating and literary relationship of Thomas to Matthew and Luke remain a subject of debate. Some scholarship has argued for an early, independent core; other studies, including those by Simon Gathercole and Mark Goodacre, have argued in detail that the known version of Thomas presupposes knowledge of the Synoptic Gospels. This monograph does not use Thomas as automatic proof of a pre-Synoptic tradition: it distinguishes between the possible antiquity of individual sayings and the date/composition of the writing as a whole. From a material standpoint, the difference between the Nag Hammadi Coptic manuscript and the Greek fragments is methodologically decisive. The Coptic codex is considerably later than the text’s composition; the Greek fragments demonstrate earlier circulation and support the view that the Coptic version derives from a Greek tradition.34 8.2. Judeo-Christian gospels: fragments and modern categories The so-called Gospel of the Hebrews, Gospel of the Nazarenes, and Gospel of the Ebionites do not survive as complete books. They are reconstructed from fragments quoted or paraphrased by authors such as Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Epiphanius, and Jerome. The tripartite taxonomy is modern, and it is not always possible to determine whether each ancient reference refers to a different work. 34 Gospel of Thomas, NHC II,2; fragments P.Oxy. I 1, IV 654 and IV 655. Gathercole 2012 and Goodacre 2012 discuss the synoptic dependence; the date of individual sayings is distinguished from the composition of the writing.

84 early christianity for studying traditions that modern historiography has linked to so-called “Sethianism.” Its value, however, lies not in representing a universal Gnostic doctrine, but in documenting a specific form of Christian exegesis, myth, and revelation. The Gospel of Truth, NHC I,3 and XII,2, is not a narrative gospel either. It is a homiletic or meditative composition centred on the knowledge of the Father, error, and revelation. Its affinity with Valentinian traditions is widely recognised, but its direct attribution to Valentinus cannot be considered certain. It is preferable to speak of a Valentinian text, or one close to that milieu, rather than presenting it as the master’s own work. The Gospel of Judas, preserved in the Codex Tchacos, offers a particularly illustrative case of the distance between composition and manuscript. Towards the end of the second century Irenaeus knew of a text called the Gospel of Judas; the surviving version is a Coptic translation in a later codex, probably from the late third or fourth century, and presupposes a Greek original. The text reverses the conventional assessment of Judas and places him within a cosmological revelation; its exact relationship to the work mentioned by Irenaeus must be formulated with caution, although the identification is widely accepted. 8.4. Infancy gospels and narrative expansion The Protoevangelium of James expands upon the accounts of Jesus’ origins through a narrative centred on Joachim and Anne, the birth of Mary, her consecration, and her virginity. The text demonstrates how, as early as the second century, the silences of the canonical gospels could become spaces for narrative and devotional elaboration. Its historical importance lies less in providing biographical information about Mary than in documenting the formation of Marian memory and piety. The Infancy Gospel of Thomas recounts episodes from Jesus’ childhood through miracles, punishments, and demonstrations of power. The tone of some accounts may seem strange to modern sensibilities, but precisely for this reason, it is a relevant source for studying how different communities imagined the childhood of a figure about whose early years the canonical gospels say very little. These writings should not be classified simply as “late fiction” in a pejorative sense. They are reception documents: they reveal questions that the canonical texts left open and show how the memory of Jesus and his family continued to expand in Christian narrative practice.

marcion, scripture and the formation of… 85 8.5. Gospels of passion and apostolic authority: Peter and Mary The Gospel of Peter is a particularly important witness to the reception of the passion and resurrection traditions. Recent research has strongly argued for its direct or indirect dependence on Synoptic materials; its value lies in showing how the passion narratives continued to be rewritten in the second century, incorporating new theological and narrative features. The Gospel of Mary, preserved only in fragments in Coptic and Greek, shifts the focus of interest to Mary’s revelatory authority and the conflict among disciples. Its importance for this monograph lies not in identifying a specific community behind the text, but in documenting that apostolic authority and the legitimacy of revelation could be articulated through figures and hierarchies different from those that dominated later ecclesial memory. 8.6. Nag Hammadi: material status, language and transmission The discovery of the Nag Hammadi codices in 1945 transformed the study of early Christianity because it provided access to texts, some of which had until then been known only through their adversaries. However, the discovery does not eliminate the problem of transmission: the surviving codices are Coptic manuscripts from Late Antiquity, while many of the works they contain were composed centuries earlier and, in several cases, translated from Greek originals. This distance must be recorded in every analysis. A text composed in the second century and preserved in a fourth-century Coptic codex does not constitute direct material evidence from the second century. Its content may date back to that period, but the preserved copy belongs to a different historical, linguistic, and monastic or ascetic context whose interpretation remains a subject of debate. The variations among different Coptic versions also show that the translation and copying were not mechanical processes. For this reason, this monograph systematically distinguishes between the date of the manuscript, the probable date of composition, and the date of the first external references. The same distinction is applied to the canonical gospels and all early Christian literature.35 35 King 2003; Brakke 2010; Williams 1996. The Nag Hammadi discovery does not demonstrate a uniform community behind all the works in the collection.

86 early christianity 8.7. The myth of the “forbidden gospels” The popular expression “forbidden gospels” oversimplifies a long and uneven process. There was no single act in the second century by which a central authority eliminated all alternative texts at once. Some writings were condemned by specific authors; others ceased to be copied in certain networks; still others continued to circulate for centuries in different contexts. The survival of manuscripts depends on multiple factors: liturgical use, pedagogical value, attributed apostolic prestige, availability of copies, networks of copyists, language, writing material, doctrinal changes, and, in some periods, explicit censorship. Reducing this process to a conspiracy, or at the opposite extreme, to a purely spontaneous selection, distorts the material history of books. Therefore, the problem of the canon is formulated as a history of circulation, selection, copying, reading, and delimitation. The authority of a text was produced in concrete practices before crystallising into normative lists. 8.8. Scroll, codex and the materiality of the collection The early Christian preference for the codex is one of the most striking material features of Christian written culture. In a world where the scroll remained a common medium, Christian manuscripts of the second and third centuries show a disproportionately high presence of the codex. The phenomenon is well documented, although its causes remain debated. The codex offered practical advantages for gathering various writings within a single physical unit, locating passages, and transporting collections. This capacity proved especially significant for corpora such as the Pauline epistles or, later, collections of gospels. However, it should not be claimed that the codex “caused” the canon: the relationship between book technology and textual delimitation is facilitative, not deterministic. The history of the canon, therefore, must incorporate the material technology of writing. Selecting four gospels or compiling Pauline epistles was not merely an intellectual decision; it involved copying, arranging, binding quires, financing manuscripts, and ensuring their circulation.36 36 Nongbri 2018; Hurtado 2006. Book form, selection of writings and copying chronology are considered related but distinct problems.

The transmission gap and the text of the canonical gospels Textual criticism must apply the same rigour to the canonical gospels as it applies to Marcion and apocryphal literature. We possess no autographs of Matthew, Mark, Luke, or John. The first-century texts are reconstructed from later manuscripts, patristic quotations, and early versions, all of which belong to a history of copying with variants. P52 , a small fragment of John, has traditionally been dated to the first half of the second century, although the precision of this palaeographic dating has been questioned and it is now better expressed as a broad range. P75, which preserves extensive portions of Luke and John, is usually dated to the early third century— although Brent Nongbri (2016) has argued for a fourth-century date—and is among the oldest witnesses to both Gospels in a single codex. The existence of these manuscripts reduces the gap between composition and the surviving copies, but does not eliminate it. The methodological consequence is important: “canonical” does not mean “transmitted without variants.” The relative stability of large portions of the text can coexist with local differences, omissions, additions, and different orderings. 92 early christianity 8.11. From the catalogue to the history of circulation The historical value of this repertoire lies not in counting titles “outside the canon,” but in observing the persistence of gospel production after the composition of the four Gospels that ultimately became canonical. The second and third centuries simultaneously show narrative expansion, collections of sayings, post-resurrection revelations, rewritings of the Passion, and the elaboration of infancy traditions. The canonical closure was a process of selection and standardisation within a literary field that continued to produce texts. Material transmission confirms this plurality: Oxyrhynchus preserves Greek fragments of Thomas and other gospels; Nag Hammadi preserves Coptic translations of earlier Greek works; the Tchacos Codex transmits Judas in Coptic; the Judeo-Christian gospels survive mainly through adversarial quotations. The documentary map is therefore asymmetrical: late manuscript abundance does not equate to widespread early circulation, and a lost work known only through quotations may have had a circulation that the vagaries of preservation have obscured. 8.12. Heresy, classification, and the construction of boundaries The case of Marcion clarifies the vocabulary of “heresy.” The Greek αἵρεσις could initially mean choice, school, or party; in second-century Christian literature, the term acquired an increasingly normative function. Irenaeus not only describes doctrines: he orders them within a genealogy of deviations and, by contrast, constructs a legitimate apostolic continuity. Heresiology is therefore a dual source. It informs us about groups, teachers, texts, and practices that would otherwise be less well known, but at the same time it reconfigures these materials according to a strategy of refutation. Historical research must take advantage of its documentary density without automatically adopting its taxonomies. In the chapters dedicated to Valentinians and other movements, the same rule applies. “Valentinian” designates, when the evidence allows, networks and traditions related to Valentinus and his successors; “Sethian” is used as a modern category for certain texts and mythologies, not as if it were necessarily a uniform ancient self-designation.

94 early christianity 10. Spread and persistence of the Marcionite churches The historical importance of Marcion did not end with the Roman controversy of the mid-second century. Justin presents him as a teacher whose teachings had spread widely; Tertullian, several decades later, attacks still-active Marcionite communities; later sources preserve accounts of his presence in various eastern regions. Although these testimonies are adversarial, their convergence rules out reducing Marcionism to an ephemeral intellectual circle. The Greek inscription from Deir Ali (ancient Lebaba, south of Damascus), dated 318/319 CE and naming a ‘synagogue of the Marcionites’, provides material evidence independent of heresiology. The Marcionite churches must have possessed sufficient structures to sustain communities, ministers, liturgical readings, and textual transmission. This persistence is crucial to the history of the canon: a collection of Scriptures acquires historical efficacy when a community copies, reads, interprets, and transmits it. The heresiological condemnation and social disappearance were not simultaneous processes. Ecclesiastical memory was able to classify Marcion as an adversary early on, while communities that identified with his tradition continued to exist for generations. The discussion carefully distinguishes between contemporary testimonies, later accounts, and geographical claims whose accuracy cannot be verified. 11. Conclusion of the chapter Marcion brings into sharp relief a qualitative shift in second-century Christianity: texts are no longer merely vehicles for memory and teaching, but also explicit instruments for defining identity and authority. His Gospel and his Apostolikon demonstrate a coherent selection of Scripture; the responses of Irenaeus and Tertullian show that this selection was perceived as a dispute over the continuity between Jesus, the apostles, Israel, and the Church. The convergence of Marcion, Tatian— whose Diatessaron (c. 170) harmonised the four gospels into a single narrative—and Irenaeus makes it possible to describe three second-century editorial technologies without turning them into a linear sequence: the selection and delimitation of corpora, narrative harmonisation, and the stabilisation of a fourfold plurality. The contrast offers a macro-narrative of gospel formation: not an inevitable passage towards the canon, but concurrent responses to the same problem of textual authority. The formation of the canon cannot be reduced to “Marcion brought about the New Testament.” The evidence points to earlier processes of collection and circulation, and subsequent stabilisation was gradual. But Marcion was a catalyst of extraordinary importance because he forced the formulation of questions that could

The following chapter examines how these questions developed within the Christian plurality of the second century, with particular attention to Ignatius, 1 Clement, the Didache, the Shepherd of Hermas, Justin, and Irenaeus. The focus is not on a linear progression from “diversity” to “orthodoxy,” but rather on the historical formation of mechanisms of authority in specific communities. Summary This chapter examines Marcion, the authority of Scripture, and the formation of Christian textual collections. It studies the lost Marcionite Gospel and the Apostolikon through the testimonies of their adversaries, with explicit levels of reconstruction. P46 and P75 provide material evidence for the circulation and organisation of the texts. The non-canonical gospels and the Nag Hammadi writings are studied as distinct transmission histories. The chapter distinguishes between authoritative readings, codex collections, and closed canonical lists. Keywords: Marcion; canon; textual transmission; P46; P75; non-canonical gospels.

chapter iii Community Plurality and Mechanisms of Authority in the Second Century The transition from the first to the second century is not simply the maturation of an already defined institution. On the contrary, the sources from this period reveal a landscape of communities simultaneously experiencing geographical expansion, doctrinal diversification, ritual elaboration, and competition for legitimacy. The memory of Jesus and the apostles, the interpretation of the Scriptures of Israel, the circulation of Christian texts, and the organisation of community life become explicit sources of authority. What in previous decades might have remained implicit or locally negotiated now begins to be formulated with greater precision and, in many cases, with greater combativeness. This chapter examines that process without projecting onto it the retrospective image of an already consolidated “Great Church.” Categories such as orthodoxy, heresy, and Gnosticism are employed with methodological caution: they are recorded when ancient sources use them or when they prove analytically useful, but they do not become the pre-established framework for organising the narrative. The aim is not to draw a straight line from plurality to uniformity, but to analyse how, in specific contexts, mechanisms of legitimation—episcopate, succession, rule of faith, collections of texts, liturgical practice, and heresiological discourse—were constructed that would later allow for more stable forms of collective identity. Modern discussion of this problem largely starts from Walter Bauer, Rechtgläubigkeit und Ketzerei im ältesten Christentum (1934; Eng. trans. Orthodoxy and Heresy in Earliest Christianity, 1971), whose thesis on the local priority of forms later declared heretical has been corrected on many points but still sets the agenda of the debate. The sources from this period are diverse in genre and should not be harmonised. The letters of Ignatius of Antioch document a passionate defence of unity around the bishop and of the bodily reality of Christ’s Passion. 1 Clement intervenes in a 96

community plurality and mechanisms… 97 conflict within the Corinthian community by appealing to the order and memory of the apostles. The Didache preserves practical instructions on ethics, baptism, fasting, prayer, and the Eucharist, along with tensions between itinerant prophets and local authorities. The Shepherd of Hermas offers a visionary and moral testimony of the Roman community, concerned with repentance and the social composition of the Church. Justin Martyr, through apologetics and dialogue, develops an interpretation of the Scriptures and the “memoirs of the apostles” that seeks to define the movement in relation to both Judaism and other Christian currents. Irenaeus of Lyons, for his part, represents a decisive moment in the articulation of the rule of faith, the fourfold gospel, and a genealogy of truth that is constructed in opposition to what he presents as deviations. Each of these texts responds to particular situations. Ignatius writes in chains, in a context of crisis and on a journey towards martyrdom; 1 Clement intervenes from Rome in a conflict not its own; the Didache reflects the concerns of communities still negotiating the relationship between charism and office; Justin addresses both external and internal audiences; Irenaeus develops a far-reaching project in response to what he perceives as doctrinal threats. The diversity of genres, geographical horizons, and argumentative strategies is, in itself, a historical fact of major importance. The chapter thus proceeds by successively analysing these testimonies, paying attention to their contexts, their vocabulary, and the mechanisms of authority that each one employs. Only after this particular examination is a synthesis offered of the main mechanisms by which the communities of the second century attempted to define, delimit, and transmit what they considered legitimate teaching and practice. The result is not the image of a uniform institution, but rather that of a field of forces in which real plurality and the search for coherence coexisted and shaped each other. This approach connects the present chapter with the preceding ones. If the first century showed the emergence of the movement within Judaism and the conflicts arising from the incorporation of Gentiles, the second century reveals how these communities, now larger and more diverse, began to develop more explicit instruments of identity and regulation. The formation of boundaries was neither a single episode nor a homogeneous process; it was the cumulative result of local decisions, controversies, ritual practices, and memory strategies that, over time, acquired greater translocal reach.

98 early christianity 1. The sources of the period and the diversity of its genres The second-century sources do not form a homogeneous archive. A pastoral letter, a liturgical instruction, an apology addressed to imperial power, a prophetic vision and a treatise against doctrinal opponents construct their subject matter differently. The first methodological requirement is therefore to resist turning them into chapters of a single ecclesiastical history organised in advance. 1 Clement and the letters of Ignatius belong to epistolary networks, but they do not fulfil the same function. The former intervenes in a leadership crisis in Corinth and argues using biblical examples, cosmic order, apostolic memory, and community discipline. Ignatius, on the other hand, writes from a personal situation of captivity and makes unity around the bishop, the presbyters, and the deacons a repeated theme of exhortation. The Didache offers a different kind of access. Its interest lies less in grand doctrinal formulations than in the regulation of practices: moral catechesis, baptism, fasting, prayer, hospitality, the Eucharist, discernment of prophets, and the appointment of local authorities. It is precisely this everyday materiality that makes it an extraordinary source for observing how a community attempts to transform charism and mobility into sustainable norms. The Shepherd of Hermas combines vision, command, parable, and moral exhortation. Its historical value does not depend on reading its visions as a literal description of events, but on recognising the social and disciplinary problems that these visions presuppose: wealth, repentance, authority, exclusion, and reintegration. Justin’s Apologies and Dialogue with Trypho belong to still distinct registers. The author mounts a public defence of Christianity, claims rationality for Christian belief, and, at the same time, delimits his position in relation to Jews and other groups that also identify with Christ. With Irenaeus, finally, the classification of rival doctrines achieves a systematic structure: describing the adversary and defining one’s own truth become inseparable operations.39 2. 1 Clement: order, conflict and apostolic memory The so-called First Letter of Clement is a particularly important witness to the ways in which one community could intervene in the life of another without yet possessing the legal structures that would characterise later centuries. It was sent by the church 39 Holmes 2007, texts and translations of the Apostolic Fathers; Gregory and Tuckett 2005, transmission and reception studies. Scholarly commentaries are identified by author in the bibliography.

community plurality and mechanisms… 99 at Rome to Corinth in response to a crisis in which some leaders had been removed from their positions. The letter does not present itself as a decree from an individual Roman bishop; it speaks on behalf of the sending community and builds its authority through argumentation, memory, and exhortation. The conventional date of c. 95– 97 CE rests on the allusion in 1 Clem. 1:1 to misfortunes that had befallen the Roman community and on the tradition reported by Eusebius (HE III.16), although some studies allow a wider chronological range. The Corinthian conflict is interpreted through the vocabulary of order. The term τάξις—order, arrangement—appears within a broader vision according to which God has arranged creation, worship, and community in an orderly manner. The argument is not merely administrative: transforming a local conflict into a problem of τάξις allows it to be endowed with theological and scriptural depth. Philologically, τάξις belongs to a broad semantic field that can designate disposition, order, rank, or arrangement. The term circulated far beyond Christian vocabulary, in philosophical, civic, military, and cultic contexts. Its use in 1 Clement does not demonstrate a direct dependence on a particular school; it shows how a GrecoRoman lexicon of order could be put at the service of scriptural and communal argumentation. One of the decisive passages is found in 1 Clement 42–44. There, the apostles appear as sent by Christ and, in turn, as those who established leaders in the communities and ensured the continuity of that ministry. The text is fundamental to the history of succession, but it must be read with precision. It does not yet unequivocally describe the monarchical episcopal system that Ignatius would defend in some cities of Asia Minor. It speaks of ἐπίσκοποι and διάκονοι—and, in 44.4–5, of πρεσβύτεροι, without clearly distinguishing the two terms—and seeks to legitimise continuity of service in response to a deposition deemed unjustified. The use of Peter and Paul in 1 Clement 5 is equally revealing. Both serve as recent examples of perseverance and suffering. Rome does not base its intervention solely on geographical proximity or institutional precedence; it mobilises a shared apostolic memory to define models of conduct. Authority is thus built through example rather than through a fully developed legal theory. The important historiographical point is twofold. On the one hand, 1 Clement shows that certain communities could attempt to correct others and that Rome possessed the symbolic resources to do so. On the other, to treat it at once as proof of an already established papal jurisdiction would be anachronistic. The evidence supports the conclusion that translocal intervention occurred and that apostolic memory was

100 early christianity invoked; the exact institutional form of this authority must be reconstructed without projecting later structures.40 3. Ignatius of Antioch: unity, episcopate and the reality of the Passion The letters of Ignatius of Antioch offer a much more explicit picture of the bishop as a focus of unity. Written while their author was being taken under guard to Rome, the letters combine martyrological autobiography, communal exhortation, doctrinal polemic, and concern for the cohesion of the churches. The traditional dating under Trajan (c. 110 CE), based on Eusebius, has been questioned: some scholars propose the 130s or 140s (e.g. T. D. Barnes, “The Date of Ignatius,” 2008). The question does not diminish their value as evidence for an episcopal model under construction, but it does affect where they stand in the second-century sequence. In several passages, Ignatius articulates a triad formed by bishop, presbyters, and deacons. The rhetorical force of this structure is undeniable. In Smyrn. 8.1, for example, he urges his readers to follow the bishop as Jesus Christ followed the Father, and the presbytery as they would the apostles. The text reveals a clear ecclesiological project: visible communion must be organised around recognisable authorities. However, the programmatic nature of the exhortation is precisely a reason not to universalise it. Ignatius insists on obedience because unity is contested. His letters document the existence and defence of an episcopal model in certain communities, rather than demonstrating that all the churches of the Empire had already adopted the same structure. Significantly, his letter to the Romans mentions no bishop of Rome. The institutional problem is intertwined with the Christological one. Ignatius insists that Jesus truly suffered, was truly crucified, and rose again. The adverb ἀληθῶς—“truly”—acquires a polemical value in this context. The defence of the flesh of Christ is not an abstract speculation: it defines communion, the Eucharist, and authority against adversaries whom Ignatius considers incompatible with the community’s identity. The polemical value of ἀληθῶς stems precisely from its ordinary adverbial function: “truly,” “in truth.” Ignatius exploits this lexical simplicity to transform the reality of birth, suffering, and resurrection into a criterion of belonging. This is not a philosophical technicality imported without mediation, but a common word that, repeated within a Christological controversy, acquires confessional weight. 40 1 Clem. 5.1–7; 42.1–5; 44.1–6. Jaubert, SC 167; Holmes 2007. The loci and institutional scope are discussed in the documentary appendix.

The word should not be automatically interpreted as the name of a religion already defined according to modern categories. In Ignatius, it functions within a discourse of differentiation and belonging, in tension with Ἰουδαϊσμός. Precisely for this reason, it is an important testimony that certain boundaries could be formulated with increasing clarity in some circles at the beginning of the second century. Ignatius’ contribution to the chapter’s general problem is clear: episcopate, Eucharist, Christology, and discipline appear united as mechanisms of cohesion. Institutional authority does not arise separately from doctrinal content; both reinforce each other.41 4. The Didache: practice, ritual and negotiation between charisma and office The Didache reveals a different kind of authority. Its opening teaching on the “Two Ways” places moral formation before dogmatic definition. The text then goes on to regulate baptism, fasting, prayer, the Eucharist, hospitality, and discernment of teachers and prophets. Chapter 7 prescribes baptism “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” preferably in running water, but allows for adaptations when material conditions do not permit it. This detail is historically valuable: the norm does not ignore contingency, but rather incorporates alternatives. Early ritual practices already appear regulated, but not rigidly confined to a single material form. Chapters 8–10 distinguish days of fasting and transmit Eucharistic prayers whose form does not exactly coincide with the Pauline or Synoptic accounts of institution. This divergence rules out reducing second-century liturgy to a single uniform line. The Didache preserves a communal tradition with its own vocabulary and accents. Especially significant is the treatment of itinerant apostles and prophets in chapters 11–13. Charisma still possesses authority, but it needs criteria for discernment. The length of their stay, their relationship with money, and the consistency between teaching and conduct serve as practical indicators of authenticity. Chapter 15 urges the community to appoint ἐπισκόπους καὶ διακόνους, “bishops and deacons,” worthy of the Lord. The passage shows the coexistence of itinerant and local authority. Rather than a simple transition from charism to institution, the Didache documents an attempt to articulate both levels. 41 Ignatius, Smyrn. 8.1–2; Philad. 4; Eph. 20.2. Reference to the middle recension: Holmes 2007; commentary by Schoedel 1985. The vocabulary of unity also constitutes an exhortation.

102 early christianity This combination makes the Didache a central source for the monograph’s overall argument: authority is also produced through regulated practice. Baptising, fasting, receiving travellers, discerning prophets, and celebrating the Eucharist are acts that build identity as much as a doctrinal formulation.42 5. The Shepherd of Hermas: repentance, wealth, and a church in the making The Shepherd of Hermas offers one of the densest testimonies on the moral and social life of Roman Christian communities in the second century. Its visionary form does not diminish its historical value; on the contrary, the images of towers, stones, women, angels, and commandments transform conflicts about belonging, sin, and restoration into a narrative grammar capable of disciplining the community. The image of the tower built with stones of varying quality represents the Church as a reality that is simultaneously present and incomplete. Some stones are accepted, others are provisionally rejected, and still others can be readmitted after transformation. The metaphor presents a conception of belonging that is not reduced to instantaneous inclusion or exclusion: discipline is linked to the possibility of repentance. The problem of post-baptismal repentance is central. Hermas recognises the gravity of sins committed after baptism, but does not build a community incapable of reintegration. Granting an opportunity for μετάνοια serves as a pastoral response to the tension between the ideal of purity and social reality. The work also pays attention to wealth. The visions and parables presuppose believers with resources, businesses, houses, and social obligations. The Roman Christianity that emerges from Hermas is not a socially homogeneous community. Wealth, dependency, and patronage are part of the moral problem, making the work an indispensable source for a social history of the urban Church.43 6. Justin Martyr: apology, Scripture and boundary-making Justin represents a shift in register. His Apologies present Christianity to imperial and learned interlocutors; the Dialogue with Trypho constructs an extensive dispute on Scripture, promise, and identity. In both cases, Christian authority is articulated through public argumentation and exegesis. 42 43 Did. 7.1–4; 9–10; 11–15. Critical edition identified: Rordorf and Tuilier 1998, SC 248. Local norms are compared with Ignatius without assuming an exact institutional synchronicity. Hermas, Vis. II.4.2–3; Mand. IV.3.1–7. Holmes 2007; Osiek 1999.
