community plurality and mechanisms… 103 In 1 Apol. 67, Justin describes a Sunday gathering in which “the memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets” are read as long as time permits. The passage does not yet offer a definitive list of books, but it documents communal reading of apostolic writings alongside prophetic Scripture. In Dial. 103, the “memoirs” are linked to the Gospels. This terminology is crucial for reconstructing the transition between circulating texts and liturgically authorised repertoires. Justin also names and classifies adversaries. His treatment of Marcion shows that the external demarcation against the Empire coexisted with internal demarcations between groups that claimed the Christian name. Apology and heresiology are not separate processes: defining what Christianity is before imperial power also entails deciding who can legitimately represent it. The relationship with Judaism must be treated with equal precision. The Dialogue is neither a stenographic transcription of an actual discussion nor a neutral representation of second-century Judaism. It is a Christian composition that uses a Jewish interlocutor to expound an interpretation of Scripture and of the identity of God’s people. Its historical value lies both in the arguments it preserves and in the literary form in which it constructs the distinction.44 7. Irenaeus of Lyons: rule of truth, fourfold gospel and succession With Irenaeus, the construction of authority reaches a systematic scale. Adversus haereses is not merely a catalogue of doctrines considered erroneous; it is an architecture of legitimation. To refute his adversaries, Irenaeus must explain why a particular reading of Scripture, a particular tradition, and certain communities have a stronger claim to represent apostolic teaching. The so-called regula veritatis functions as a normative summary of the framework within which the Scriptures must be interpreted. Its importance lies not in its being a fixed creed identical everywhere, but in enabling Irenaeus to assert that Christian truth possesses coherence prior to the fragmentary exegeses he attributes to his adversaries. In Adv. haer. III, Irenaeus links this rule to the succession of bishops and to the public tradition of the churches. The Roman list in III.3 should not be read as mere administrative information: it serves a polemical function. The continuity of individuals and communities serves as an argument against teachers whose genealogy Irenaeus presents as recent or deviant. 44 Justin, 1 Apology 65–67; Dialogue 103.8. Editions of the Apologies: Munier 2006; Minns and Parvis 2009. Dialogue: Bobichon 2003. The distinction between works is maintained.

104 early christianity The defence of four gospels in Adv. haer. III.11.8 represents another mechanism of delimitation. Irenaeus does not merely acknowledge the existence of four texts; he argues that there must be four, no more and no less. The well-known analogy with the four winds and the four corners of the world has rhetorical value, but the most important historical fact is that at the end of the second century an author could defend a fourfold gospel as a normative collection against alternative selections. Heresiology thus functions as a technology of authority: it names, classifies, genealogises, and orders. This observation does not compel us to accept Irenaeus’s reconstructions of each adversary without question. On the contrary, it requires them to be read in two ways: as information—sometimes irreplaceable—about rival groups and as an active production of the boundaries it purports to describe.45 8. Valentinus, Valentinian traditions and the problem of “Gnosticism” The label “Gnosticism” is too broad if used as an explanation before analysing the documents. For the second century, it is preferable to begin with specific teachers, schools, and corpora. Valentinus and the traditions that scholarship calls Valentinian constitute one of the best-documented cases of speculative, exegetical, and ritual Christianity that competed to define the legitimate interpretation of revelation. Einar Thomassen’s research has shown that “Valentinianism” does not designate a single, homogeneous organisation either. Texts, teachers, and communities exhibit internal diversity. The study must distinguish between what we know of Valentinus, what is attributed to his disciples, and what is preserved in Nag Hammadi writings related to Valentinian traditions. The same caution applies to the texts that modern historiography groups as “Sethian.” The category can be useful for comparing myths, divine names, and cosmological structures, but it should not automatically become the name of a unified historical Church. David Brakke has insisted precisely that the diversity of groups and practices necessitates a revision of the major inherited taxonomies. The crucial point for this chapter is that these movements do not represent an irrelevant periphery. The need to respond to them helped to lead authors such as Irenaeus to formulate more sharply their criteria of tradition, Scripture, succession, and the rule of truth. The boundary was constructed in interaction.46 45 Irenaeus, Haer. I.10.1–3; III.3.1–4; III.11.8. The books are identified according to the relevant SC series; for III, SC 210–211. The origin of a rule and its subsequent reception are different problems. 46 Thomassen 2006; Williams 1996; Brakke 2010. community plurality and mechanisms… 105 8.1. Critical catalogue of speculative currents and rival schools The category “Gnosticism” does not reliably designate a unified religion, a common institution, or a continuous historical genealogy. Recent research has shown that ancient authors such as Irenaeus constructed polemical classifications grouping together very different teachers and groups, while modern historiography has added its own taxonomic categories. Therefore, the following catalogue does not offer a chain of “heresies,” but rather a comparative map of teachers, networks, and corpora whose relationships to one another must be demonstrated on a case-by-case basis. It is also necessary to separate textual provenance from social geography. The fact that a codex was found in Egypt does not prove that the group that originally produced each work lived in the place of discovery. Similarly, a heresiological account of Rome or Alexandria is not enough to reconstruct a stable organisation without independent evidence. 8.2. Simon and the construction of a heresiological origin Acts 8 presents Simon as a Samaritan figure associated with magical practices and opposed to apostolic authority. Justin, Irenaeus, and later authors develop a much more extensive tradition in which Simon appears accompanied by Helena and becomes the ancestor of successive heresies. This genealogy should be read as a later heresiological construction, not as a demonstrable history of the formation of Gnosticism. The phrase in Acts that refers to Simon as “the Great Power of God” is an early literary fact; the detailed doctrines later attributed to the Simonians come from later, polemical sources. Consequently, this book avoids presenting Simon as the “founder of Gnosticism” and instead studies how the memory of Simon was used to produce a genealogy of error. 8.3. Cerdo: a figure known almost exclusively through adversaries Cerdo appears in Irenaeus and later heresiological traditions as an active teacher in Rome before or around the arrival of Marcion. He is credited with distinguishing between the God proclaimed by the Law and the Prophets and a higher God revealed by Christ. However, none of his writings survive, and biographical information depends on authors interested in constructing doctrinal genealogies. For this reason, Cerdo should not be described as a “proven link” between a Syrian Gnosticism and Marcion. One can speak of affinities attributed by heresiological

106 early christianity tradition and of chronological proximity, but not of demonstrated doctrinal transmission. 8.4. Valentinus and Valentinian traditions Valentinus was a Christian teacher active in the second century and associated with Alexandria and Rome by ancient sources. Later tradition even claimed that he aspired to the Roman episcopate, but this should not be taken as fact. What is well documented, however, is the breadth and diversity of the traditions that later authors identified as Valentinian. Contemporary research, especially since the work of Einar Thomassen, insists that Valentinianism was not a monolithic organisation. Different schools, teachers, and texts shared certain schemata concerning the Pleroma, Sophia, ignorance, and restoration, but they developed them in different ways. The Gospel of Truth, the Tripartite Treatise, and other texts related to Valentinian circles demonstrate a sophisticated Christian exegesis in dialogue with Scripture, apostolic tradition, and philosophy. It is not necessary to imagine these groups as completely external to the mainstream churches; in various contexts, the boundary was precisely the subject of dispute. 8.5. The so-called “Sethians”: a historiographical category The term “Sethian” is a modern category applied to a group of texts that share names, myths, and cosmological structures, including the Apocryphon of John. Seth plays an important role in several of these writings, but the existence of a unified Sethian Church, with a clearly defined organisation and geography, cannot be taken for granted. Nor should an Egyptian origin be inferred simply because many texts were preserved in the Nag Hammadi codices. The find-spot of the codices, which were copied in the fourth century, is an archaeological datum; the social and geographical origin of each composition may be earlier and different. The systems included in this category usually distinguish the transcendent God from demiurgic figures like Yaldabaoth and rework Genesis within complex narratives of emanation and revelation. But not all share the same degree of dualism or the same Christology, and “docetism” should not be automatically applied to the entire corpus.

community plurality and mechanisms… 107 8.6. Basilides and the Basilidians Basilides taught in Alexandria during the first half of the second century and is known through Clement of Alexandria, Irenaeus, and other adversaries. Reconstructions of his system diverge markedly depending on the source. Hippolytus, for example, transmits a cosmogony different from that attributed to him by Irenaeus. Concepts such as the 365 heavens or the name Abraxas belong primarily to the heresiological tradition concerning the Basilidians and should not be taken as a definitive exposition of Basilides’ personal teaching. This case provides an excellent example of why it is necessary to distinguish between the master, the later school, and the polemical description. 8.7. Carpocrates and the Carpocratians Carpocrates and his circle appear in Irenaeus, Clement, and other authors as representatives of a radical current. The accusations of promiscuity, debauchery, and ritual transgression are part of a polemical repertoire frequently used against rival groups and cannot be accepted literally without corroboration. Sources attribute to the Carpocratians ideas about cosmic powers, transmigration, and the liberation of the soul. More important for a critical history is to observe how authors like Irenaeus used this group to define, by contrast, the moral and doctrinal limits of the legitimate community. 8.8. Marcion: polemical parallel, not “gnostic” by definition Marcion frequently appears alongside so-called Gnostic currents because he radically distinguishes the Creator God from the Father revealed by Christ. However, his theology lacks many of the cosmological, genealogical, and mythological features characteristic of Valentinian traditions or the texts known as Sethian. Therefore, this monograph does not classify Marcion as an unqualified “Gnostic.” It studies Marcion and his movement as a rival Christian current with its own canon, churches, and theology, in dialogue and conflict with other forms of Christianity in the second century. 8.9. Manichaeism: independent late religion, not automatic culmination of Gnosticism Manichaeism, founded by Mani in the third century within the Sasanian Empire, shares with certain earlier traditions a language of light, matter, knowledge, and dualism. However, it was an autonomous universalist religion, with its own scriptures,

108 early christianity missionary structure, and a self-understanding that integrated Christian, Iranian, and Buddhist traditions. Simply classifying it as the “culmination of Gnosticism” obscures more than it explains. For the chronological scope of this monograph, it is relevant because it demonstrates that the Mediterranean and the late Roman Near East continued to produce transregional religious movements capable of competing with imperial Christianity. Augustine’s later experience as a Manichaean hearer confirms the religion’s presence in Roman Africa during the fourth century, but that episode belongs to a historical context much later than that of Valentinus or Basilides. 8.10. 110 early christianity 8.11. Methodological consequence This catalogue confirms that “Gnosticism” is only useful if employed as a secondorder term and with an explicit definition. The procedure of this work consists of starting with the texts and the teachers, reconstructing their context, and only then deciding whether a typological comparison adds value. Ancient heresiology is treated as a dual source: it provides information about real adversaries, but at the same time fabricates genealogies, exaggerates similarities, and uses moral accusations to create boundaries. The historian must study both levels. 8.12. Other voices from the second century: Polycarp, Diognetus, Tatian and Athenagoras The reconstruction of the second century gains depth when texts that do not fit directly into the Marcion–Irenaeus axis are also incorporated. Polycarp’s Letter to the Philippians conveys moral exhortation, uses Pauline traditions, and commemorates Ignatius; the Martyrdom of Polycarp, discussed in the following chapter, shows how that authority was transformed into martyrial memory. The so-called Epistle to Diognetus, whose author and date are disputed (the second or early third century), offers a rhetorical portrayal of Christians as city dwellers who participate in social life without fully identifying with the surrounding religious order. It should be read as a literary apologetic, not as a sociological survey. Tatian, a disciple of Justin, composed the Diatessaron, a gospel harmony that exerted enormous influence on Syriac Christianity. Its existence demonstrates that the reception of four gospels did not always imply four volumes read separately: the collection could be harmonised into a single liturgical narrative. Athenagoras of Athens, in his Legatio pro Christianis, responds to accusations of atheism, incest, and cannibalism through a philosophical defence of Christian rationality. His work shows that apologetics in the second century was not a marginal genre, but rather a space in which Christians learned to translate their claims into categories understandable to the educated elites of the Empire.47 47 Polycarp, Phil. 1–14; To Diognetus 5–6; Athenagoras, Leg. 1–4. Clement of Alexandria: philosophical culture and intellectual Christianity Clement of Alexandria represents an intellectual Christianity that does not define Greek philosophical culture solely as an enemy. In Protrepticus, Paedagogus, and Stromata, philosophy can function as preparation, an educational tool, and a field for debate. He is particularly important as a safeguard against a simplistic opposition between “Christianity” and “Hellenism.” At the beginning of the third century, Christian authors could use Platonic, Stoic, and philological categories while still constructing an explicitly Christian identity. The term “Gnostic” even acquires a positive connotation in Clement when he describes the perfect believer, confirming that the vocabulary of gnosis did not belong exclusively to the groups classified by Irenaeus as heretics.48 8.14. From the first century to heresiological classification: the limits of retrospective chronology The search for “heterodox movements” in the first century requires special caution. The earliest sources do not offer a map of churches clearly demarcated by systematic doctrines comparable to those described by Irenaeus, Hippolytus, or Epiphanius. The Pauline epistles, Revelation, the Johannine epistles, and other writings reveal real conflicts—over shared meals, circumcision, apostolic authority, prophecy, Christology, food sacrificed to idols, or sexual discipline—but turning every anonymous adversary into a direct ancestor of a second-century heresy is often a backward projection. This monograph therefore distinguishes three levels: first-century controversies documented by contemporary sources; names or groups whose existence is attested in near-contemporary texts; and heresiological genealogies constructed retrospectively by later authors. 48 Clement of Alexandria, Paed. Nicolaitans, Balaam and Jezebel: adversaries of the Apocalypse Revelation 2 mentions the Nicolaitans in connection with Ephesus and Pergamum and links the “teachings of Balaam” and the symbolic figure of “Jezebel” within the same polemical context. The text suggests that some communities in Asia Minor debated participation in sacrificial meals, sexual practices, and adaptation to the civicreligious environment. However, it does not allow for the reconstruction of a complete Nicolaitan theological system. Irenaeus and later authors identified the Nicolaitans with Nicholas of Acts 6:5 and attributed libertine behaviour to them. This genealogy should be treated as a heresiological reception, not as an independent fact about the first century. The historical interest of the passage lies precisely in observing how a local controversy could become, two or three generations later, a heretical identity established by the literature of controversy. 8.16. Cerinthus and the difficulty of reconstructing a teacher from the turn of the century Cerinthus occupies a peculiar place between the end of the first century and the beginning of the second. Irenaeus presents him as an adversary of the Johannine tradition and attributes to him a Christology that distinguishes between Jesus and the Christ who descended upon him; the millenarian eschatology ascribed to him derives instead from Gaius of Rome and Dionysius of Alexandria, as quoted by Eusebius (HE III.28). Epiphanius and other heresiologists expand the dossier with data whose dependence and chronology are difficult to establish. The famous anecdote of Polycarp about John fleeing from a bathhouse upon recognising Cerinthus, transmitted by Irenaeus, has value for the polemical memory of Asia Minor, but cannot be used as a contemporary record. Cerinthus must be preserved as a probable historical figure, even though the exact content of his teaching remains partially reconstructed from the accounts of his adversaries. 8.17. Judeo-Christianities: Ebionites, Nazarenes and the problem of labels The terms “Ebionites” and “Nazarenes” appear in patristic sources to describe groups that combined adherence to Jesus with various forms of Jewish observance. Modern scholarship has shown that it is unsafe to treat these labels as designating two stable, homogeneous, and clearly distinguishable churches over several centuries. Irenaeus, Origen, Eusebius, Epiphanius, and Jerome transmit partial, sometimes incompatible,

community plurality and mechanisms… 113 information on Christology, observance of the Law, use of the Gospels, and evaluation of Paul. The name “Ebionite” may also have acquired a generalising heresiological meaning. Consequently, this study speaks of Jewish Christianities and reconstructs each testimony by author and date. The fundamental fact is not the existence of a single “Ebionite Church”, but the persistence, during the second–fourth centuries, of forms of Christian identity that maintained different positive relationships with the Torah, circumcision, the calendar and the memory of Jerusalem. 8.18. The Elkasaites: revelation, baptisms and Mesopotamian Jewish Christianity The Elkasaites are known primarily through Hippolytus, Origen—cited by Eusebius—and Epiphanius. Sources connect them with a revealed work attributed to Elchasai/Elxai, with repeated baptismal practices, observances of a Jewish character, astrology, and a Christology difficult to reconstruct. Their location in Syro-Mesopotamian environments and their chronology of the early second century are plausible, but the details depend heavily on hostile testimonies. The group is important because it unsettles the overly simple narrative according to which Judaising Christianity disappeared rapidly after 70 CE. It also forces us to differentiate between continuity of Jewish practices, new prophetic revelations, and the development of hybrid community identities. 8.19. Docetism: Christological category, rather than a single church “Docetism” derives from δοκεῖν, “to seem”, and is used to describe Christologies in which Christ’s suffering or corporeality is understood as an appearance or is reformulated in such a way that the Passion does not fully affect his divine being. As early as the beginning of the second century, Ignatius of Antioch was attacking adversaries who denied that Jesus Christ truly suffered “in the flesh.” However, Docetism does not designate a single institution or an identical doctrine in all authors. It can appear combined with different anthropologies and cosmologies. Historiography must therefore avoid labelling every high Christology, or every distinction between Jesus and Christ, as “Docetism” without textual analysis. Its usefulness lies in describing a recurring Christological problem: how to articulate divinity, humanity, suffering, and salvation.

114 early christianity 8.20. Encratism and ascetic networks: Tatian, continence and discipline The term “Encratites” comes from ἐγκράτεια, meaning continence, and was used by heresiologists to classify ascetic tendencies that rejected or restricted marriage, meat, and wine. Tatian was later associated with the Encratites, although the relationship between his personal history, the Diatessaron, and a supposed Encratite organisation requires caution. What is historically relevant is the existence, during the second and third centuries, of Christian networks in which sexual renunciation, fasting, and certain dietary practices acquired particular soteriological significance. These currents should be studied alongside proto-orthodox asceticism, not as a completely separate world: the boundary between rigorous discipline and “heresy” was constructed differently depending on the author, region, and context. 8.21. Montanism or “New Prophecy”: charism, gender and authority The so-called New Prophecy movement arose in Phrygia during the second half of the second century, associated with Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla. Its adversaries described it as an aberrant, ecstatic prophecy, while its supporters understood it as an intensification of the Spirit’s action. The sources are largely filtered through Eusebius and Epiphanius, but also through Tertullian’s later adherence to the New Prophecy. The movement cannot be reduced to a marginal extravagance: it raises central questions of Christian history—who may prophesy, how revelation is recognised, what authority women prophets possess, how charisma and episcopate relate to each other, and what discipline should be required of the baptised. Its spread beyond Phrygia also demonstrates the transregional reach of second-century Christian networks. 8.22. Adoptionisms and monarchianisms: categories of the second–third centuries The labels “adoptionism,” “dynamic monarchianism,” and “modalistic monarchianism” group together distinct controversies concerning the relationship between God, Christ, and the Holy Spirit. Theodotus of Byzantium, active in Rome in the late second century, was accused of holding that Jesus was a man upon whom divine power descended; Artemon appears in later sources within a similar genealogy. In another register, Noetus, Praxeas, and Sabellius were associated with forms of theology that so strongly defended divine oneness that their adversaries considered the distinction

community plurality and mechanisms… 115 between Father and Son insufficient. Later labels simplify debates whose vocabulary was still developing. Their study is essential for understanding why the Trinitarian and Christological languages of the fourth century did not emerge from nothing, but rather from more than a century of controversies concerning unity and distinction in God. 8.23. Novatian and the “pure”: penitential discipline and schism in the third century The Novatianist conflict developed in Rome after the persecution of Decius and was linked to the readmission of the lapsi, Christians who had yielded to sacrificial demands. Novatian, a Latin theologian of considerable stature, was consecrated by a group opposed to Cornelius in 251. The controversy cannot be adequately explained as a clash between “heresy” and “orthodoxy,” since the two sides held much doctrinal ground in common; the immediate core was ecclesiological and disciplinary: who had the authority to grant reconciliation for grave sins and under what conditions. The Novatianist communities survived for centuries and were known in some regions as katharoi, “the pure.” Their persistence demonstrates that disciplinary schisms could produce lasting institutions, their own hierarchies, and alternative memories of sanctity. Chronological control note. The properly late-antique cases—Donatism, the post-Nicene controversies called “Arian,” Priscillian and Manichaeism—are not analysed here as components of the second-century ecclesial landscape. Their substantive treatment belongs to Chapters XI–XII and the relevant regional sections. They are retained only in the diachronic comparative matrix that follows, as a long-term historiographical control with their chronology made explicit, in order to avoid both their artificial subordination to the second century and their disappearance from the comparative framework.

From polemical designation to historical category: how to use “pseudo-Christian”, “heresy” and “Gnosticism” In ancient and modern confessional literature, expressions equivalent to “false Christian,” “pseudo-apostle,” or “pseudo-Christian” appear. These are useful as demarcation markers, but not as neutral categories for the historian. To call a group “pseudoChristian” before analysing its own texts would turn the conclusion of an ancient controversy into a premise of the investigation. Where possible, this monograph uses the names by which groups identified themselves, or the most precise historical designations; when only a name transmitted by adversaries is available, that dependence is indicated. Similarly, “Gnosticism” is reserved for explicitly defined comparisons and does not function as a general receptacle for all dualistic, ascetic, or non-Nicene theology. 8.25. 118 early christianity 8.26. Consequence for the history of early Christianity The panorama of the first–fourth centuries should not be understood as a linear progression from initial diversity to inevitable orthodoxy. Nor should it be understood as an indefinite coexistence of equivalent Christianities without dominant institutions. The sources reveal a more concrete historical process: communities competing for texts, teachers, apostolic memories, rituals, and spaces; episcopal networks growing in density; councils producing formulas of communion; civil authorities increasingly intervening; and authors retrospectively classifying their adversaries. The result was the formation of powerful normative traditions, but this normativity must be explained historically. Studying the groups that were defeated, marginalised, or classified as heretical is not a digression: it is a privileged path to understanding how canon, creed, episcopate, discipline, and memory were constructed. 9. Rome: from apostolic memory to episcopal succession 9.1. The problem of the Roman episcopal lists: memory, succession and anachronism The history of the Roman episcopate requires distinguishing three levels that later traditions tended to conflate: the apostolic memory of Peter and Paul, the existence of diverse leaders and ministries within the Roman community, and, finally, the formation of a retrospective sequence of individual bishops. The list transmitted by Irenaeus of Lyons in Adversus haereses III.3.3, written towards the end of the second century, is the earliest surviving testimony that offers an ordered chain from the apostles to Eleutherius. Its historical value is considerable, but it does not warrant simply projecting onto the decades between 60 and 100 the institutional form of the monarchical episcopate that the sources document more clearly elsewhere during the second century. The letter known as 1 Clement, sent from Rome to Corinth towards the end of the first century, speaks of episkopoi and deacons and defends an orderly transmission of the ministry; however, it does not identify Clement as “bishop of Rome” in the later institutional sense. The Shepherd of Hermas, also linked to Rome and usually placed in the second century, suggests a community with prophets, presbyters, deacons, teachers, and other leaders; in Vis. II.4.3 it refers, in the plural, to “the presbyters who preside over the church”, without mentioning a single bishop. These texts

community plurality and mechanisms… 119 advise caution regarding an image of a monarchical succession perfectly established from the outset. Accordingly, the early names in the Roman list are preserved here as part of an ancient succession tradition, while a clear distinction is maintained between the probable existence of leading figures and the later reconstruction of a continuous episcopal line. Irenaeus deploys that sequence polemically, presenting the teaching he regards as apostolic as traceable through public and known churches in contrast to rival claims of secret tradition. The list is therefore both a historical datum and a heresiological argument. From the last third of the second century onward, the documentation becomes denser. The Easter controversies associated with Victor, the Christological and disciplinary disputes of the time of Zephyrinus and Callistus, the schism of Hippolytus according to modern reconstructions, the crisis of Cornelius and Novatian, and the baptismal conflicts of Stephen and Cyprian reveal a Roman see with a growing capacity for coordination, correspondence, and arbitration. This increasing centrality should not be described teleologically as if all its later forms were already present from Peter onward, but neither can it be reduced to a retrospective fiction: during the second and third centuries, a real process of institutionalisation is documented. 9.2. From Linus to Eleutherius: the ancient succession according to Irenaeus and its limits Irenaeus lists, after Peter and Paul, Linus, Anencletus/Anacletus, Clement, Evaristus, Alexander, Sixtus, Telesphorus, Hyginus, Pius, Anicetus, Soter, and Eleutherius. The tradition is not homogeneous in the form of the names or in the chronology. Later sources, especially Eusebius and the Late Antique Roman catalogues, provide episcopal durations and synchronisms that cannot always be independently verified. Critical practice, therefore, consists of distinguishing between an early attested nominal succession and a much more uncertain exact chronology. Clement occupies an exceptional position because 1 Clement constitutes a Roman witness from the end of the first century, although the text is presented as a letter from the church of Rome and not as a personal writing of an episcopal monarch. Telesphorus is remembered by Irenaeus as a martyr; Anicetus appears in the tradition concerning Polycarp’s visit to Rome and the discrepancy over the date of Easter; Eleutherius is a contemporary of Irenaeus and, therefore, represents the chronologically most secure end of the list. This gradation of certainty is not a flaw in the analysis: it is precisely the difference between a critical history of institutions and the mere reproduction of a traditional list.

120 early christianity 9.3. Victor I and the Easter controversy: authority, communion and limits of intervention With Victor I, towards the end of the second century, the documentation reveals a Roman intervention of supralocal scope. Eusebius, in his Ecclesiastical History V.23– 25, preserves accounts of the Quartodeciman controversy: communities in Asia Minor maintained the celebration of Easter linked to the fourteenth of Nisan, while other groups defended the Sunday celebration. Victor attempted to exclude from communion those churches in Asia that maintained the Quartodeciman practice; Irenaeus, although he shared the Sunday practice, urged him to show moderation in a letter partly quoted by Eusebius (HE V.24.11–17). This episode is important because it simultaneously reveals the capacity for initiative and resistance to that initiative. Rome could convene, communicate, and threaten to break off communion, but it did not yet possess an operational universal jurisdiction in the legal sense of later periods. The conflict illuminates the construction of authority through networks of letters, apostolic memory, ecclesial communion, and the capacity to forge regional consensus. 9.4. Zephyrinus, Callistus and Hippolytus: internal conflict and retrospective construction of legitimacy The transition from the second to the third century is marked by openly polemical sources. The Refutatio omnium haeresium, traditionally attributed to Hippolytus, presents an extremely hostile image of Zephyrinus and, above all, of Callistus. It accuses its targets of Christological errors, lax discipline, and personal irregularities. The source is indispensable, but its genre demands a reading symmetrical to that applied to Irenaeus or Epiphanius: the adversary cannot automatically become a neutral narrator. The disputes reveal central questions for Roman institutionalisation: who has the authority to readmit grave sinners, how marital discipline is structured, what Christological language is acceptable, and who can define it. The existence of rival groups presenting themselves as the legitimate church shows that the “succession” was not merely a chronological line, but a continually contested claim.

community plurality and mechanisms… 121 9.5. Cornelius and Novatian: penance, episcopal election and sociology of the church at Rome The crisis following the persecution of Decius offers exceptional documentation. Cornelius and Novatian were elected by rival factions in Rome in 251, and the problem of the lapsi—Christians who had sacrificed, obtained certificates, or yielded under pressure—became a major ecclesiological issue. Cyprian of Carthage and the documents preserved by Eusebius support a partial reconstruction of the controversy. Eusebius (HE VI.43) transmits a letter from Cornelius that describes a Roman community with forty-six presbyters, seven deacons, seven subdeacons, numerous acolytes, exorcists, lectors, and doorkeepers, in addition to a large body of people receiving support. Although the figures come from a partisan source and must be read in their polemical context, they provide unusually detailed evidence for the organisational and welfare scale of urban Christianity in the mid-third century. Novatian was not simply a doctrinal “heretic”: his break was primarily related to discipline, penance, and episcopal legitimacy, even though his movement later developed its own lasting ecclesial identity. This case demonstrates that the boundaries between schism, discipline, and heresy are not interchangeable, ahistorical categories. 9.6. Stephen I and Cyprian: baptism, communion and conflict between sees The controversy over baptism administered outside the Catholic communion pitted Stephen of Rome against Cyprian of Carthage and African synods in the 250s. The issue was not secondary: it affected the understanding of sacramental efficacy, the identity of the Church, and the authority of regional traditions. Cyprian defended the rebaptism of those who came from groups considered heretical; Rome maintained a different practice, accepting in certain cases the laying on of hands without repeating the baptism. The Cyprianic letters reveal a network of churches that recognised one another, engaged in intense disputes, and appealed to memory, custom, and apostolic tradition. Presenting the episode as a mere exercise in “papal primacy” or, conversely, as proof that Rome lacked any supralocal authority impoverishes the evidence. The conflict documents precisely a stage of institutional negotiation in which prestige, antiquity, communion, and episcopal autonomy were still being balanced in uneven ways.

From Valerian’s persecution to the Tetrarchy: cemeteries, memory and community government During the third century, the history of Roman church leaders became intertwined with the administration of cemeteries, charitable assistance, and the commemoration of martyrs. Sixtus II died during Valerian’s persecution; the tradition concerning Lawrence belongs to a reception history that must be analysed in layers. The development of funerary complexes and the use of catacombs do not in themselves prove an early centralised structure, but they do show that the management of burials, anniversaries, and the commemoration of martyrs acquired increasing institutional importance. The Liberian Catalogue and the Depositio episcoporum of the Chronograph of 354 (the so-called Philocalian calendar) provide, as early as the fourth century, an organised record of Roman bishops and martyrs. These are fundamental Late Antique documents for studying how Rome constructed a sacred chronology of its own leaders. Their testimony is especially valuable when combined with funerary epigraphy and contemporary sources, but it should not be uncritically projected back to the first and second centuries. 9.8. Miltiades and Sylvester: from persecution to imperial patronage The Constantinian shift radically altered the material conditions of the Roman episcopate. Miltiades appears linked to the resolution of the Donatist conflict through the Synod of Rome in 313, convened within a context of imperial intervention. The relationship between emperor and bishops introduced new possibilities regarding arbitration, property ownership, construction, and public representation. Sylvester I, bishop for much of Constantine’s reign, occupies a disproportionately large place in later legend and a relatively limited one in contemporary sources. He did not personally preside over Nicaea: the Roman see was represented by legates. Medieval narratives that portray Sylvester as Constantine’s baptiser and recipient of a territorial “Donation” belong to later phases and cannot be used as evidence for the fourth century. The contrast between the historical Sylvester and the legendary Sylvester offers an exemplary case of the medieval construction of institutional memory.

Liberius, Damasus and Siricius: doctrinal conflict, monumentalisation and decretals Liberius’s episcopate unfolded against the backdrop of the post-Nicene controversies and the imperial pressure of Constantius II. His exile and the problem of the Formulas of Sirmium demonstrate the extent to which the bishop of Rome could become entangled in imperial doctrinal politics. Sources are biased, and assessments of his conduct vary; the episode must be studied through letters, ecclesiastical historians, and modern reconstructions, not through later categories of institutional impeccability. Under Damasus I (366–384), the Roman see acquired a new monumental and epigraphic visibility. His election was accompanied by violence between rival factions; subsequently, he promoted the memory of martyrs through metrical inscriptions and reinforced the Christian topography of Rome. Jerome’s activity in his circle and the growing importance of biblical Latin belong to this same cultural horizon, although the relationship between Damasus and the Vulgate must be formulated precisely and without oversimplification. Siricius, elected in 384, already stands on the threshold of a new documentary practice. His letter to Himerius of Tarragona, from 385, is generally considered the first papal decretal preserved in a fully developed form. The importance of the document lies not in demonstrating that the later papacy existed fully from the first century, but in showing how, towards the end of the fourth century, the Roman see was developing normative genres, claims to disciplinary action, and a more defined institutional vocabulary. 9.10. Rome as an observatory of liturgy, discipline and ministries The evolution of Roman authority cannot be studied solely through lists of bishops. Ritual practices and the ordinary organisation of communities reveal how the institution developed from the ground up. Justin, in First Apology 65–67, describes baptism, Sunday gatherings, the reading of the memoirs of the apostles and the writings of the prophets, prayer, the kiss of peace, the Eucharist, distribution by deacons, and the collection for the needy. This description is not a “Roman missal” in the later sense, but it is one of the richest sources for urban Christian practice in the midsecond century. The Didache, although not Roman, offers an indispensable point of comparison: baptism in running water when possible, fasting, prayers, the Eucharist, itinerant prophets, and the election of bishops and deacons. Comparison among the Didache,

community plurality and mechanisms… 129 Justin, Ignatius, 1 Clement, and the Apostolic Tradition—whose attribution, date, and location are debated—supports a reconstruction of families of practice without assuming a uniform universal liturgy. Baptism functions simultaneously as a rite of incorporation, a communal boundary, and a problem of authority. Its specific form varies in the sources; its theology is not monolithic either. The controversy between Stephen and Cyprian demonstrates that, in the third century, the question of whether a baptism administered outside of communion should be repeated could divide regional churches without either side considering the matter trivial. The Eucharist provides another privileged vantage point. Paul offers the oldest surviving Christian testimony on the communal meal and its conflicts; the Didache preserves formulas different from the Pauline and Synoptic ones; Ignatius links the Eucharist, unity, and the episcopate; Justin describes a Sunday rite with reading, exhortation, prayer, offerings, and distribution. Historical development should not be presented as a linear sequence from a simple form to a fixed liturgy, but rather as a gradual convergence of local practices. Penance clearly illustrates the institutional transformation. The Shepherd of Hermas debates the possibility of repentance after baptism; the controversies surrounding the lapsed after Decius necessitated the definition of reconciliation procedures; Novatian and Cornelius represent divergent responses to post-persecution discipline. Episcopal authority became visible, among other things, in the capacity to administer exclusion, reconciliation, and communion. The ministries also reveal a process. Paul mentions apostles, prophets, teachers, episkopoi, and deacons in various contexts; 1 Clement rationalises ministerial continuity through a record of appointment and succession; Ignatius insists on a triad of bishop-presbytery-deacons; the Didache still preserves a tension between local ministers and itinerant charismatics. There is no single date on which the monarchical episcopate “was born” for all the churches. The evidence necessitates regional and chronologically staggered reconstructions. Assistance to the poor, widows, orphans, prisoners, travellers, and confessors is not a social appendix to institutional history: it is one of its infrastructures. Paul’s collections, the charity mentioned by Dionysius of Corinth regarding Rome, and the figures transmitted in Cornelius’s letter show that redistribution, hospitality, and care helped to produce networks of dependence, reputation, and authority.

Methodological note on episcopal titles and primacy Throughout this book, early references to the church of Rome are not translated automatically into later legal categories. “Primacy”, “apostolic see”, “pope”, and “jurisdiction” have distinct semantic histories. When such terms are used for the first through fourth centuries, the evidentiary level is specified: apostolic memory, honorific precedence, capacity for mediation, disciplinary intervention, reception of appeals, or normative formulation. The aim is neither to deny nor to presuppose historical continuities, but to describe them at the precise point at which the sources permit them to be observed. The history of the leaders of the Christian community in Rome requires a distinction between tradition of succession and institutional reconstruction. Linear lists of “bishops of Rome” are ancient, but not contemporary with the earliest names they contain. Irenaeus of Lyons, at the end of the second century, offers in Adversus haereses III.3.3 the first preserved sequence of Linus, Anacletus, Clement, and their successors up to Eleutherius; Eusebius reproduces and expands upon it in the fourth century. These lists are fundamental historical sources for the Roman church’s memory of continuity, but they do not, in themselves, demonstrate that Rome possessed from the 60s onward a form of monarchical episcopate identical to that of the third century. Clement’s First Letter itself is significant. The writing speaks on behalf of the church of Rome and does not present Clement as an individual author or as a monarchical bishop issuing a personal decision. The traditional attribution to Clement is ancient and plausible as the memory of a prominent Roman figure, but the document, as it survives, does not bear an episcopal signature. Therefore, the monograph distinguishes between “Clement” as a traditional figure in the Roman succession and 1 Clement as an anonymous community letter. Modern research has proposed various models to explain this documentary tension. One influential line of thought—represented above all by Peter Lampe, Die stadtrömischen Christen in den ersten beiden Jahrhunderten (1987; Eng. trans. From Paul to Valentinus, 2003)—maintains that Rome retained a relatively collegial structure for much of the second century, composed of several domestic communities and local leaders, before the consolidation of a more centralised monarchical episcopate. Other studies emphasise that the succession lists reflect an institutional memory already sufficiently strong in Irenaeus’s time. It is not necessary to resolve the entire institutional history with a single model; what is necessary, however, is to avoid retroactively projecting the third-century form onto the first century.

Thomas and India as a problem of memory and transmission The tradition linking the apostle Thomas to India belongs to a long history of reception. The Acts of Thomas preserve a narrative of mission, asceticism, and martyrdom, the composition of which is usually placed in the third century, in an environment related to Syriac Christianity. Its distance from the first century prevents it from being read as a contemporary diary of the apostle. Its value is, however, considerable for studying the eastern projection of apostolic memory.51 The appearance of the name Gondophares in this literature may be related to an Indo-Parthian context known from other sources. The identification of a real name makes a historical horizon of composition or of tradition plausible, but it does not confirm all the episodes of a narrative. Similarly, ancient trade networks with the Indian Ocean demonstrate possibilities for circulation, not the individual itinerary of a character without sufficient contemporary documentation. For this monograph, it is essential to separate four questions: when was the work composed, what prior memory could it have used, which communities transmitted its different versions, and when were the local traditions linked to Thomas consolidated? This distinction preserves the theme of eastern expansion without presenting it as a first-century fact established with the same degree of certainty as Paul’s activity attested in his letters. The reception of Thomas also shows that apostolic authority was not constructed solely in Rome or Asia Minor. Syriac traditions organised their own space of memory, translation, and belonging. Their study is part of a broader Mediterranean and Eastern history, but it requires a specific apparatus for each language and version. A reference to a modern translation does not replace the examination of ancient recensions. 51 Acts of Thomas, especially the initial mission narrative and the account of martyrdom. Open questions and limits of reconstruction The evidence examined supports a reconstruction of specific mechanisms of authority, but it does not eliminate several open questions. The intervention of 1 Clement from Rome demonstrates a translocal capacity for exhortation and correction, although it does not, in itself, authorise projecting later legal categories onto the end of the first or beginning of the second century. Similarly, Ignatius’s insistence on the bishop can be read as evidence of a strong institutional model and, simultaneously, as an indication that this model still required defence. The normative force of discourse should not be automatically confused with sociological uniformity. The Didache presents a different problem: its composition and possible stratification affect how its practices are reconstructed. The instructions on prophets, local authorities, baptism, and the Eucharist must be read with regard to the possibility of distinct layers and contexts of transmission. These issues do not weaken the reconstruction; they define its limits. The second century can be described with sufficient historical density without turning every documentary difference into a single evolutionary sequence. 13. Pagan criticism and apologetic response: an arc between the second and fourth centuries The delimitation of Christian identity did not occur solely through internal controversies. From the second century onward, learned pagan authors examined the historicity of the traditions about Jesus, the coherence of Scripture, the conduct of the apostles, and the Christian claim to religious exclusivity. These criticisms compelled Christian apologists and exegetes to respond on the same philological, philosophical, and historical ground as their adversaries. The documentation presents a specific problem: much of the anti-Christian literature is not preserved in independent manuscript transmission. Celsus is known primarily through Origen; Hierocles, through Eusebius; Julian, mainly through Cyril of Alexandria; and the anti-Christian corpus attributed to Porphyry must be reconstructed from scattered testimonies whose attribution to a single work remains a subject of debate. Therefore, each argument must indicate whether it comes from a direct quotation, a paraphrase, or a later attribution. Furthermore, it is not advisable to simply group Celsus and Porphyry under the same philosophical label. Celsus belongs to the horizon of Middle Platonism of the second century; Porphyry, on the other hand, writes within the Neoplatonism of the

Celsus: historical, social and philosophical criticism Celsus’s Logos Alēthēs, probably composed in the second half of the second century, has been lost and must be reconstructed from Origen’s Contra Celsum. The Christian apologist quotes extensive passages from his adversary, but the modern reconstruction should not present Celsus’s text as if we possessed a continuous manuscript. Celsus introduces, among other strategies, a Jewish interlocutor who questions the birth of Jesus and reproduces the polemical tradition according to which Mary conceived a child with a soldier named Panthera. This detail belongs to a polemical construction from the second century and does not constitute independent biographical evidence about Jesus. Its importance lies in showing that the legitimacy of Jesus’ birth and miracles had already entered the realm of public controversy. Celsus also ridicules the social composition of Christian communities, mentioning artisans, uneducated people, women, and children as recipients of the preaching. Origen responds that the ethical transformation produced by the message constitutes an indication of its power. The contrast shows how the same social phenomenon could be interpreted as a sign of vulgarity by the critic and as moral efficacy by the apologist. On a philosophical level, Celsus questions the incarnation, bodily resurrection, and the idea that the universal divine order could be concentrated in a particular history. His critique reveals a conflict between different conceptions of providence, matter, revelation, and religious citizenship.52 13.2. Porphyry: philology, Daniel and the critique of apostolic coherence Porphyry of Tyre, a disciple of Plotinus, was remembered by Christian authors as one of their most formidable intellectual adversaries. Tradition speaks of an antiChristian work in fifteen books, but the reconstruction of this corpus is problematic: fragments and testimonies have been gathered since Harnack, while recent research debates which materials actually belonged to a single work entitled Contra Christianos. 52 Origen, Cels. I.28; I.32; I.68; III.44; III.55; VIII.55. References: Koetschau 1899 and Chadwick 1953. The accusation about Panthera is identified as a polemic transmitted by Origen.

Modern scholarship independently dates the final form of Daniel to the context of the Maccabean crisis; this does not make Porphyry the founder of modern biblical criticism, but it does demonstrate the antiquity of a historical reading of the problem. Porphyry was also associated with objections based on scriptural discrepancies and directed against the consistency of apostolic authority. The case of Galatians 2:11–14 proved especially fertile: the confrontation between Paul and Cephas could be read as evidence of a real conflict among apostolic leaders. Jerome explains in Epistle 112 that earlier Christian commentators had proposed an interpretation of the scene as a prearranged strategy, precisely to respond to Porphyry’s accusation. Augustine rejected this solution because, in his view, it compromised the veracity of Scripture.53 13.3. Hierocles and Apollonius of Tyana: the comparative problem of miracles At the beginning of the fourth century, Hierocles composed the Philalēthēs, an antiChristian work preserved only indirectly. Eusebius of Caesarea responds in Against Hierocles and cites the most distinctive core of the argument: the comparison between Jesus and Apollonius of Tyana. Hierocles argues that Christians proclaimed Jesus divine based on miracles, while pagan observers could accept prodigies attributed to Apollonius without thereby making him a god. Eusebius responds by subjecting Philostratus’s Life of Apollonius to a critique of its credibility and coherence. This episode is methodologically important because it illustrates a dispute over criteria for evidence. The work, probably in three books, does not survive directly; most of the known fragments come from Cyril of Alexandria’s Contra Iulianum, written decades later. Modern scholarship insists that the reconstruction should not be printed as if it were a reliable, continuous text. Julian questions the Christian appropriation of the Scriptures of Israel, contrasts Hellenic civic and cultic traditions with Christian claims, and attacks the historical coherence of a religion that, in his view, had distanced itself as much from Jewish practices as from traditional Greco-Roman religion. His testimony is especially valuable because it comes from an emperor initially raised in a Christian environment and later committed to a policy of restoring traditional cults. Contra Galilaeos thus belongs to both the intellectual and the political history of the relationship between Christianity and the Empire.55 13.5. In turn, Christian responses preserved many of the criticisms they sought to refute. Epidemics, crises and persecution: avoiding automatic causality The great epidemics of the second and third centuries coincided with periods of political and religious tension, but this chronological overlap does not justify attributing persecutions to epidemics, nor plagues to religious conflicts. The Antonine Plague developed from the 160s onward, and the so-called Plague of Cyprian from the midthird century; the measures taken by Decius and Valerian addressed issues of loyalty, sacrifice, imperial discipline, and governance, which require their own documentary analysis. At the same time, the epidemics disrupted mobility, mortality, taxation, recruitment, markets, and assistance networks. In this context, Christian communities could interpret illness through eschatological or providential categories while simultaneously organising care, burials, and material aid. Chapter XIII specifically examines this intersection between illness, medicine, ritual, and charity. Conclusion The second century did not immediately produce a uniform Church; rather, it produced mechanisms capable of making increasing unification possible. Ministerial order, succession, rule of truth, liturgy, collections of texts, and classification of adversaries arose in different contexts and did not advance at the same pace.

144 early christianity Plurality was real, but so was the search for coherence. The communities differed and, in that context, apostolic memory and public continuity acquired value; multiple texts circulated and some collections began to function as preferred repertoires; rival teachers existed and the definition of a rule of truth became a polemical necessity. These correlations do not by themselves prove a causal relation: they describe conditions that coexisted and that the authors of the period themselves invoke to justify their proposals. The formation of borders was, therefore, a productive process. It not only excluded: it also created vocabulary, institutions, practices, and archives. Later centuries would inherit these instruments and deploy them on a new scale when the relationship with the Empire, persecution, martyrdom, and finally imperial patronage transformed the conditions of existence of the communities. Summary This chapter examines second-century Christian plurality through the mechanisms by which communities constructed and authorised their collective identity. It analyses 1 Clement, Ignatius, the Didache, the Shepherd of Hermas, Justin, Irenaeus, the Roman succession traditions, the Valentinian and other second-century movements, and the pagan intellectual response from Celsus to Julian. It distinguishes teachers, schools, corpora, and heresiological constructs in the study of “Gnosticism.” It argues that episcopal structures, apostolic memory, rules of truth, textual collections, ritual practices, polemical classifications, and external philosophical criticism developed unevenly but together created mechanisms that made later forms of Christian unity possible. Keywords: second-century Christianity; authority; apostolic succession; episcopate; heresiology.

chapter iv Persecution, Martyrdom and Imperial Administration (Second–Fourth Centuries) Relations between Christian communities and Roman power cannot be described as a uniform and uninterrupted persecution from Nero to Constantine. The sources show an irregular sequence of local episodes, casuistic administrative procedures, and imperial measures of varying scope. Only in the third century did genuinely empire-wide policies emerge that systematically affected Christian communities. This distinction is essential for a critical history. Later Christian memory tended to organise episodes of violence within a continuous narrative of witness and martyrdom. That memory has enormous historical value, but it is not the same thing as a single state policy sustained over three centuries. 145

146 early christianity Prelude. From the burning of Rome to Pliny’s correspondence: coercion and memory in the first century The first century offers no evidence of a continuous imperial policy against all Christian groups. The best-documented episode is the Neronian repression following the fire of Rome in 64, known chiefly from Tacitus (Ann. XV.44), who wrote several decades after the event. The passage presents the Christians as an already identifiable group in Rome and describes exemplary punishments, but it does not support the reconstruction of a general edict applicable throughout the Empire. Its historical value lies in showing an action of imperial power confined to the city of Rome and the availability of a religious minority as an object of public stigmatisation. Later Christian memory transformed this episode into a pivotal point in the tradition concerning Peter and Paul, whereas the surviving evidence allows us to speak with confidence only of a specific situation in Rome. Suetonius’s account of Claudius and the riots instigated by Chrestus (Claud. 25.4) pertains to a different problem: it does not describe a Christian persecution in the technical sense, and its interpretation depends on whether Chrestus refers to Christ—and thus to intra-Jewish conflicts over the messianic proclamation—or to an agitator of that name. The expulsion, or restriction, of certain Jews from Rome around 49 CE must therefore be methodologically separated from the Neronian repression. This distinction allows the chapter to cover the period from the first century to the Great Persecution without fabricating an uninterrupted line of coercion.

persecution, martyrdom and imperial… 147 1. Pliny and Trajan: procedure before programme The correspondence between Pliny the Younger and Trajan, Epistulae X, 96–97, constitutes the clearest administrative evidence from the beginning of the second century (c. 110–113). As governor of Bithynia-Pontus, Pliny consulted the emperor because he did not know exactly how to proceed against people accused of being Christians. His uncertainty shows that he was not acting on the basis of a specific and uniform penal statute dedicated exclusively to Christianity. Trajan replies that Christians should not be actively sought out, that anonymous accusations should not be admitted, and that those who deny being Christian and demonstrate adherence to public worship by sacrificing should be released. The procedure is fundamentally administrative and political: persistence in refusing a legitimate order from a magistrate, and refusal to participate in public worship, could become grounds for condemnation. Pliny also provides valuable information about Christian practices: meetings before dawn, singing to Christ quasi deo (“as to a god”), and moral commitments. This information nevertheless comes from interrogations and the perspective of a Roman governor.56 2. Martyrdom of Polycarp: memory, exemplary conduct and discipline The Martyrdom of Polycarp, composed in Asia Minor after the death of the bishop of Smyrna, is one of the earliest Christian accounts of martyrdom developed as an exemplary narrative. It is not a literal court record: it combines local memory, epistolary features, biblical exegesis, and a typology of the imitation of Christ. Its historical value lies precisely in this elaboration. The text defines what constitutes legitimate martyrdom, discourages the reckless pursuit of arrest, and constructs the memory of the body and relics within a community that celebrates the martyr’s anniversary. The judicial event thus becomes a ritualised memory.57 56 57 Pliny, Ep. X.96–97. Reference edition: Mynors 1963. de Ste. Croix 2006 and Rebillard 2012 help to distinguish administrative action from local identities. Mart. Pol. 9–10; 15–18. References: Holmes 2007; Musurillo 1972. The narrative scenario is distinguished from the procedural data that can be verified.

The text combines first-person narration, martyr narrative and communal shaping. Perpetua, a young woman of relatively high social standing, and Felicity, an enslaved and pregnant woman, show how gender and legal status permeate Christian memory. The narrative does not erase the social hierarchies of the Empire, but rather reorders them around confession and martyrdom.58 4. The obligation to sacrifice nevertheless bore particularly heavily on those who considered the act incompatible with their religious identity. The standard study of the general character of the measure is J. B. Rives, “The Decree of Decius and the Religion of Empire,” Journal of Roman Studies 89 (1999). The crisis created categories of those who had sacrificed, obtained certificates, or resisted, and opened a lasting conflict over the readmission of the lapsed. The measures included the destruction of meeting places and Scriptures, the loss of legal privileges, and, in later phases, demands for sacrifice. Its application varied considerably between regions. Eusebius and Lactantius are primary sources, but both write from highly interpretive Christian perspectives. Their accounts must be considered alongside legislation, papyri, epigraphy, and regional chronologies. The intensity of persecution in the East was not identical to that observed in the territories ruled by Constantius Chlorus. 60 Cyprian, Ep. 80.1, on the measures of Valerian; Eusebius, HE VII.10–13. Galerius and the Edict of Toleration of 311 In 311 Galerius issued an edict of toleration that acknowledged the failure of the repressive policies and once again permitted Christian gatherings, on the condition that public order was respected and prayers were offered for the welfare of the state. Lactantius preserved the Latin text, and Eusebius a Greek version. According to Lactantius, the edict, issued when Galerius was already mortally ill, was posted at Nicomedia on 30 April 311 (Mort. pers. 35.1: pridie Kalendas Maias). The document rules out any account of toleration as an initiative of Constantine alone in 313. The legal transformation started within the Tetrarchy itself and must be understood as a broader political process.62 8. Martyrdom acts: document, memory and literature The category of Acta martyrum does not in itself guarantee a literal transcription of the judicial process. Some works preserve plausible formulas and frameworks of interrogation; others are later literary compositions that develop hagiographic themes. For each piece, the date of the event, the date of composition, the manuscript tradition, and the degree of reworking must be distinguished. The historical question is not only whether an episode occurred, but also how it was remembered, what elements were added, and what function it fulfilled in the community that transmitted the story.63 Conclusion Between the second and early fourth centuries, the Christian experience of state coercion was real, but uneven. The memory of martyrdom transformed local episodes into translocal models of identity. Persecution, therefore, must be studied simultaneously as administrative history and as a history of memory. 62 63 Lactantius, Mort. pers. 34; Eusebius, HE VIII.17. The edict of 311 is earlier than the agreement of 313 and has its own formulation. Musurillo 1972; Moss 2012. Acts and passions require analysis of transmission, genre and purpose, in addition to the possible procedural core.

152 early christianity Summary This chapter examines Roman measures against Christians from Pliny and Trajan to the Great Persecution and Galerius’s Edict of Toleration in 311. It rejects the model of uninterrupted persecution throughout the Empire and distinguishes between administrative procedure, imperial policy, judicial practice, and the memory of martyrdom. It pays particular attention to the Martyrdom of Polycarp, the Passion of Perpetua and Felicity, the libelli from the time of Decius, the measures of Valerian, and the documentary asymmetry between Christian accounts and administrative evidence. Keywords: persecution; martyrdom; Decius; Valerian; Diocletian; Galerius.

chapter v Space, Manuscripts and Early Christian Iconography Material culture is not merely a secondary illustration of what we already know from texts. Objects, inscriptions, manuscripts, funerary spaces, and buildings possess their own chronologies and contexts. In this chapter, they are treated as autonomous sources capable of confirming, qualifying, or contradicting reconstructions based exclusively on literature. The central methodological problem lies in avoiding two extremes: considering every ancient symbol as unequivocally Christian or, conversely, denying specificity to images and objects when their archaeological context allows for a reasonable attribution. Christian visual identity emerged through the selection, reuse, and reinterpretation of repertoires shared with the Greco-Roman world. 1. The codex and the materiality of the collection The surviving Christian manuscripts show an early preference for the codex. This preference was not absolute, but it was marked enough to set Christian practice apart from large sectors of Greco-Roman literary culture, in which the roll remained of great importance. The codex facilitated the gathering of various writings into a single physical unit, the location of passages, and the transport of collections. P46 is a prime example for the Pauline epistles; P75 , for Luke and John. Material technology did not create the canon, but it conditioned the concrete possibilities of collection and reading. Each manuscript must be analysed separately: writing material, format, number of columns, nomina sacra, order of books, hands, and corrections. Textual criticism is also the archaeology of the book.64 64 Hurtado 2006; Nongbri 2018. The Christian use of the codex does not prove that every ancient codex is Christian nor that every collection constitutes a complete canon. 153

154 early christianity 2. Staurogram and nomina sacra Among the most striking palaeographic features of certain early Christian manuscripts is the staurogram, a ligature of tau and rho used in some abbreviations related to σταυρός and σταυρόω. In certain manuscripts, the sign has been interpreted as an early form of visualising the cross within the writing itself. The interpretation must remain tied to the specific manuscripts and their dating. The sign should not be turned into a universal emblem of early Christianity. Its relevance lies in showing how writing and image could be superimposed on the page. Figure 12. Detail of the staurogram in Luke 14:27, P75 (Bodmer XIV–XV, now Pap. Staurogram and chrismon as distinct signs The tau-rho ligature and the chi-rho monogram must be distinguished graphically and functionally. The staurogram incorporates letters associated with the abbreviation of words from the σταυρός family. The chi-rho monogram combines the first letters of Χριστός and acquired particularly important public visibility during the fourth century. Sharing a rho neither makes them necessary stages of a single evolution nor demonstrates a common origin for all their uses.

156 early christianity 2.2. Tau, Ezekiel 9 and the formation of a visual grammar of the cross The relationship between the letter tau, Ezekiel 9, and the earliest Christian symbols of the cross must be approached through a strictly philological and palaeographic reformulation. The starting point is not a universal symbolic genealogy, but rather a problem of texts, spellings, and receptions. In Ezekiel 9:4–6, the sign placed on the foreheads of the righteous depends on the textual tradition and the history of the letter’s graphic forms. The ancient Hebrew taw and later Greek forms should not be confused, nor should it be assumed that every ancient cruciform sign inherently possessed a Christian meaning. The Septuagint offers a particularly important field of study here because Greekspeaking Christian communities received Ezekiel through a Greek text whose terminology could be typologically reactivated. Later Christian reception interpreted Ezekiel’s protective sign in light of the cross, but this reading must be distinguished from the historical sense of the prophetic passage. The typological procedure is a fact of reception; it does not constitute proof that the author of Ezekiel anticipated a Christian form. It should also be noted that the Septuagint renders the Hebrew ‫ָּתו‬ as σημεῖον; the explicit reference to the letter tau derives from the versions of Aquila and Theodotion, as reported by Origen (Selecta in Ezechielem 9). Early manuscript documentation necessitates a second distinction. The staurogram—the tau-rho ligature that appears in some Christian manuscripts—is not equivalent to the chi-rho monogram, nor should it be confused with a cross drawn independently. Its importance lies in showing how a scribal convention could acquire a visual dimension within the text. Papyri such as P66 , P75 , and P45 have been central to the discussion, although each example must be dated and described with palaeographic caution. The interpretation of the staurogram as one of the earliest visual representations of Jesus crucified is suggestive because the rho can evoke a head above the tau crossbar. However, the analysis should be presented as a historiographical interpretation and not as self-sufficient evidence. The abbreviative function, the tradition of sacred names, and the graphic context of the codex are equally relevant. The strength of the argument arises from the convergence of form, use, and Christian context, not from an isolated geometric resemblance. The history of the Christian cross does not gain rigour by connecting it to every previous cruciform figure; on the contrary, such accumulations obscure the routes

space, manuscripts and early christian… 157 of transmission that can actually be demonstrated. A legitimate comparison must specify object, date, origin, medium, function, and historical chain of reception. The subsequent development of the cross as a public symbol also requires distinct chronologies. Before the fourth century, the cross could appear allusively, textually, or graphically, without yet occupying the monumental position it would acquire in imperial Christian culture. The Constantinian transformation did not create the symbolism of the cross from scratch, but it changed the possibilities for its display. Therefore, manuscripts, gems, graffiti, sarcophagi, inscriptions, and literary narratives must be studied in separate series before being integrated into a comprehensive history. A comparison of tau, the staurogram, the chi-rho monogram and the simple cross requires attention to date, medium, context, certainty of identification and bibliography. This approach preserves the historical value of the evidence without turning a sequence of similarities into an imaginary genealogy. The Alexamenos graffito: mockery, the cross and external perceptions The so-called Alexamenos graffito was found in the Paedagogium on the Palatine Hill and depicts a human figure to the left, with a raised arm, facing a crucified figure with a donkey’s head on the right. The Greek inscription is usually interpreted as a mockery: “Alexamenos worships his god.” Its dating is generally placed between the late second and third centuries, with different proposals depending on the archaeological context. The scene is often interpreted as an anti-Christian caricature. Its importance lies in documenting how crucifixion could function as an object of ridicule precisely because the shameful execution was central to Christian identity. The donkey’s head also connects with ancient accusations of onolatry levelled against both Jews and Christians. The graffito is not a Christian image produced for devotion; it is a hostile image. It is therefore a particularly valuable testimony to external social perception.66 66 The graffito of Alexamenos, Paedagogium of the Palatine; Tertullian, Apol. 16 and Nat.
