The relevant point is not to establish an automatic continuity between each testimony, but to study how an available stereotype could shift among groups perceived as strange, exclusive, or ritually suspect. Josephus, in refuting accusations transmitted in anti-Jewish traditions, is an essential source for reconstructing the polemical background; Tacitus, Hist. V.3–4, explicitly transmits the story that the Jews consecrated in their sanctuary the effigy of the ass that had guided them in

160 early christianity the desert; Tertullian (Apol. 16; Nat. I.11) names him as the source of the rumour later applied to Christians. The Palatine graffito depicts a crucified figure with a donkey’s head, accompanied by an individual in an attitude of veneration, and the inscription usually interpreted as “Alexamenos worships his god.” Its value for the history of Christianity is exceptional because it documents an external and mocking perspective on a Christian practice or identity. It does not, in itself, demonstrate what the Christians depicted believed, nor does it authorise the reconstruction of a theology of the cross; it does, however, document the social perception of a cult associated with an executed person and the possibility of combining religious mockery with social humiliation. The associated inscription known as “Alexamenos fidelis” has been used to reinforce the Christian identification, but it must be kept separate from the main graffito and described according to its archaeological and epigraphic context. Its proximity or association does not justify merging both testimonies into a single documentary scene. A complete record should identify the catalogue number, place of discovery, support, epigraphic reading, and specialised bibliography. Opposition to Christianity can be analysed on three levels: popular, intellectual, and administrative. The popular level includes rumours, caricatures, and accusations of secret practices; the intellectual level comprises articulated criticisms such as those of Celsus, Porphyry, Hierocles, and Julian; the administrative level corresponds to imperial procedures, rescripts, and decrees. These levels intersect, but they are not equivalent and should not be reduced to the generic term “persecution.” Tertullian and Minucius Felix are particularly valuable sources for studying accusations that apologists attribute to their opponents: cannibalism, incest, impiety, or monstrous worship. The historian must resist the temptation to simply accept that all these accusations circulated with the frequency or in the exact form attributed to them by the Christian defence. The apologetic text selects and dramatises objections in order to refute them. Its historical value lies both in the accusations transmitted and in the strategy of response. This context connects the Alexamenos graffito with the discussion of pagan criticism while preserving its material specificity. Caricature, philosophical treatise and imperial rescript are distinct kinds of evidence. Together they show that Christian identity could be rejected on social, religious, philosophical or political grounds; examined separately, they allow closer reconstruction of who is speaking, to whom, and in response to what problem. Ichthys: sign, word and context The fish appears in numerous Greco-Roman contexts and is not inherently Christian. Its Christian identification depends on the archaeological, epigraphic and textual context. The relationship between ἰχθύς and the Christological acronym Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς Θεοῦ Υἱὸς Σωτήρ belongs to an ancient tradition, but not every fish represented in a tomb or mosaic should be automatically interpreted using that acronym. When inscription, funerary context, and iconographic repertoire converge, the fish can function as a sign of belonging, baptism, food, or Christology. Its historical value lies precisely in this controlled polysemy. 4.1. Fish, baptism and language of belonging The Christian use of the fish does not depend on a single explanation. Gospel accounts of fishing and feeding, mission metaphors, and baptismal practices provided distinct repertoires that could converge. Tertullian opens De baptismo with a comparison between believers and little fish born in water after the pattern of Christ, whom he explicitly calls ‘our ἰχθύς’ (Bapt. 1.3: nos pisciculi secundum ἰχθὺν nostrum Iesum Christum in aqua nascimur). The Greek acrostic is indeed preserved in Oracula Sibyllina VIII.217–250, a Christian section usually dated between the late second and the third century. His testimony corresponds to a late antique reception of the formula; it should not be used to attribute the same acrostic to any earlier funerary painting. Documenting the acronym and identifying an image are different operations. Shared repertoires and Christian symbols 5.1. The Good Shepherd The figure of the young shepherd carrying a sheep has a long history in Greco-Roman art and can appear as a criophorus, an image of care, charity, or pastoral life. In Christian contexts of the third and fourth centuries, the same visual form could be interpreted in light of traditions about Christ as a shepherd. It is not methodologically correct to derive each Christian Good Shepherd from a single prototype, nor to claim that mere resemblance demonstrates religious continuity. Iconography functions through shared repertoires and contextual reinterpretation. 5.2. Alpha and Omega between apocalyptic text and representation The expression “Alpha and Omega” appears in Revelation 1:8; 21:6; 22:13. Its effectiveness derives from the use of the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet to express totality. It should be studied in conjunction with the formulas “first and last” and “beginning and end” and with their scriptural antecedents, especially Isaiah 44:6 and 48:12. This literary relationship is a verifiable area of analysis; it does not require proposing hidden geometric values for the letters.69 69 Revelation 1:8; 21:6; 22:13. The speaker’s identity is determined by context. The formula added to Revelation 1:11 in some traditions is not used as if it belonged without question to the source text. Revelation 1:8 explicitly identifies the Lord God; Revelation 21:6 belongs to the proclamation of the one seated on the throne; Revelation 22:13 appears within a final sequence where the speaker’s identification must be discussed in light of 22:12 and 22:16. Harmonising the three occurrences as if they had identical narrative presentation obscures an exegetical issue. Later Christological reception may adopt the formula, but it does not eliminate the textual differences. Nor should the expression be introduced in Revelation 1:11 without pointing out that its presence depends on certain later forms of tradition. Comparing editions and manuscripts is here a strictly text-critical matter. Doctrinal affinity with other verses is no reason to supplement a shorter reading. The constitution of the text and theological interpretation follow different procedures. On monuments and inscriptions, the letters Α and Ω may be combined with a chi-rho monogram or a cross. The object must be dated by its context and its own characteristics; citing Revelation only identifies one possible interpretation. It does not establish that the original maker read a specific codex or that each viewer understood the programme in the same way. The history of representation studies precisely how a literary expression acquires visual uses in new media. The formula reveals both continuity and transformation. It originates from an archive of writing and exegesis, but its funerary or public use can condense identity, protection, and hope. Historical analysis describes this condensation without turning it into proof of a universal doctrine predating the evidence. The chronology of the images and that of the texts are set against each other; neither replaces the other. 5.3. Roman catacombs: burial, memory and image The Christian catacombs of Rome constitute one of the most extensive material archives of the third and fourth centuries. Complexes such as San Callisto, Priscilla, and Domitilla contain inscriptions, cubicula, paintings, and spaces dedicated to the memory of martyrs. They were not permanent secret refuges of an underground Church; their primary function was funerary. Their pictorial programmes include praying figures, Jonah, scenes of salvation, banquets, and pastoral figures. The repetition of certain motifs shows how biblical and funerary repertoires were combined to express hope, protection, and remembrance. The so-called Crypt of the Popes in San Callisto adds an institutional dimension: inscriptions and burials of Roman bishops from the third century document the progressive monumentalisation of episcopal memory.72 72 Jensen 2000; Snyder 2003. Funerary topography, epigraphy, and visual programmes are considered together; the catacombs are not interpreted as permanent shelters.

The scene of the dove with an olive leaf in Genesis 8:11 offers a hint of the receding waters within the narrative sequence. This immediate meaning should not be replaced by an abstract emblem of peace attributed without nuance to all cultures and periods. Reading it as a sign of reconciliation belongs to a history of interpretation that must be reconstructed through texts and objects.73 The biblical account of the ark provides dimensions in cubits, but converting to metres requires choosing a historical unit of measurement that the text does not define with sufficient precision for all modern uses. Nor has archaeology identified any vessel corresponding to these dimensions. The interest for Christian history lies in the reception of the account and its relation to practices of salvation, not in geometric reconstructions presented as proofs of the doctrine’s origin. 1 Peter 3:20–21 explicitly links preservation through water with baptism. This connection is an important textual fact because it provides an explicit ancient link between the story of Noah and a Christian ritual. Tertullian, in De bapt. 8, uses the dove and the olive branch in his argument for baptism. Comparison of these two documents clarifies continuity and exegetical reformulation without assuming that every funerary representation of Noah corresponded to the same ritual use. Images of a figure in a small chest may allude to the episode, but its identification depends on the presence of attributes and the overall programme. The abbreviated representation of the ark is not a ship’s plan: it is a narrative device for recognition. Funerary scenes condensed stories of liberation along with other biblical episodes. The observer could recognise a narrative from a few elements, even if part of its interpretive context is lost to us. The comparison with Mesopotamian flood traditions belongs to the history of the Genesis texts. It must be made based on identified versions, languages, dates, and specific literary relationships. It does not provide an automatic way to derive Christian baptism from a Babylonian ceremony, nor does it demonstrate architectural equivalences between the different vessels. Symbolism of the synagogues in Judea, Samaria and Galilee (first–third centuries): evidence, limits and the case of Magdala The visual culture of synagogues from the first to third centuries demands particularly strict chronological caution. The imagery now associated with the Late Antique synagogue—menorah flanking the ark, lulav, etrog, shofar, biblical scenes, and, in some cases, zodiac wheels—largely belongs to programmes of the fourth to sixth centuries. Projecting this repertoire onto the first century would produce a material anachronism comparable to attributing the basilica-like monumentality of the Constantinian period to the apostolic communities. For the Second Temple period and the first generations after 70 CE, the surviving evidence is sparser, fragmentary, and regionally uneven. 9.1. Architecture before iconography: rooms, benches and community orientation The buildings archaeologically identified as first-century synagogues primarily reveal a spatial organisation: rectangular or nearly rectangular halls, perimeter benches, controlled access, and, in some cases, interior columns or supports. Gamla, Masada, and Herodium, among other sites from this period, provide evidence for the organisation of gatherings, readings, and participants without requiring elaborate iconographic programmes to be postulated. Architecture constitutes the main evidence here; the absence of surviving figurative images should be interpreted neither as proof of absolute aniconism nor as licence to reconstruct lost decorations. The inscription of Theodotus, found in Jerusalem and usually dated to the Second Temple period, is particularly important because it documents a synagogue linked to the reading of the Law, teaching, and hospitality. Its value is institutional and epigraphic: it confirms functions and patronage, but it does not preserve an iconographic repertoire that would support reconstruction of the decoration of a firstcentury Jerusalem synagogue.

On one of its faces appears a representation of a seven-branched menorah (‫ ) ְמנוֹ ָרה‬in a context that includes architectural and geometric motifs, as well as objects interpreted by various researchers in relation to the Temple in Jerusalem. The importance of the find lies not only in the antiquity of the image, but also in the fact that it shows how a synagogue community could visually construct the space and objects of the sanctuary while the Temple still stood. Interpretations of the stone are not unanimous. Some readings understand it as a symbolic condensation of the Temple and its furnishings; others emphasise its liturgical, architectural, or cosmological character. This volume must therefore avoid presenting as definitive an identification that still belongs to archaeological debate. What is certain is more limited and, at the same time, highly significant: the menorah is represented in a pre-70 CE synagogue context, and the piece demonstrates that the relationship between synagogue and Temple could be expressed materially without the two spaces being equivalent. Menorah and other media: from a sanctuary motif to an identity marker In the first and second centuries, the menorah also appears on media other than synagogue buildings: coins, lamps, ossuaries, graffiti, and other objects. Therefore, the symbol should not be studied solely as architectural decoration. Its frequency and function change over time. In late Roman times, the menorah becomes one of the most recognisable visual signs of Jewish identity, but this process cannot be traced back as a fully formed system to the decades of Jesus or Paul. The problem is methodologically parallel to that presented by the Christian cross: the early presence of a motif does not yet imply a uniform visual grammar or a single social function. The same symbol can participate in the memory of the sanctuary, community identity, funerary ornamentation, or collective affirmation, depending on the medium and the context. 9.4. Judea, Samaria and the inequality of the archaeological record The distribution of evidence is very uneven. In Judea and the area around Jerusalem, buildings, inscriptions, and objects survive from which institutions and practices can be reconstructed, but the surviving synagogue decoration from the first–third centuries is limited. For Samaria, the picture is even more fragmentary, and a distinction must also be made between Jewish and Samaritan communities, whose ritual and architectural histories are not interchangeable. The best-known Samaritan synagogues largely belong to later periods and follow their own repertoires. The scarcity of finds does not demonstrate an absence of symbols; it demonstrates, above all, the limits of preservation, excavation, identification, and dating. In a work that uses material culture as an autonomous archive, this difference between “undocumented” and “nonexistent” must remain visible.

Its presence in late antique mosaics shows the Jewish appropriation of a Mediterranean cosmological repertoire; it does not prove that the Twelve Apostles, the Twelve Tribes, or the organisation of first-century communities were structured according to a zodiacal system. Tabernacle, sanctuary and Christian reading of space Exodus 25–31 and 35–40 present instructions and details of the construction of the mobile sanctuary. The text articulates materials, crafts, furnishings, and the divine presence within a covenant narrative. It can be studied as a literary description of the cult and the manufacture of objects; it does not automatically constitute a report of an excavated structure. The precision of certain measurements does not eliminate problems of composition, transmission, and historicity.76 The inner sanctuary described in 1 Kings 6:20 has equivalent dimensions of length, width, and height. This information comes from a literary representation of Solomon’s Temple. It does not justify attributing to it a demonstrable relationship with modern mathematical constants, still less a chain of dependence on other monuments based solely on formal coincidence. Ancient measurements, the proportions described, and their reception must be distinguished from numerical equivalences constructed by a later interpreter. Hebrews 8–10 offers an explicit Christian appropriation of the language of sanctuary, priesthood, and sacrifice. Its argument shifts the focus to Christ’s ministry and access to God; it does not propose a template for building churches. Mistaking this exegesis for technical instructions obscures the work’s genre. Its relationship to later Christian architecture belongs to a history of reception that must be documented on a case-by-case basis. The same care applies to temple language used for the community or the body. In 1 Corinthians 3:16–17, the argument is addressed to a community whose cohesion is threatened. The author’s use of ναός does not prove that his addressees possessed a separate place of worship. The referent and the rhetorical function are reconstructed within the discourse. The metaphor can precede monumental architecture without being its sole cause. The history of Christian spaces thus links three different archives: sanctuary texts, testimonies of gatherings, and material remains. None replaces the others. The tabernacle and the Temple provided languages of authority and presence; houses offered resources for hospitality and gathering; the public buildings of the fourth century 76 Ex 25–31 and 35–40; 1 Kings 6; Hebrews 8–10; 1 Corinthians 3:10–17; 1 Peter 2:4–5. Prescription, narrative, and reception are studied, without turning the scriptural description into an archaeological survey or a numerical key.

space, manuscripts and early christian… 181 introduced new programmes and scales. The transformation was not a belated execution of a single plan preserved from the beginning. Conclusion Material culture reveals dimensions of Christian identity that doctrinal treatises do not record: which texts were copied together, how sacred names were abbreviated, which symbols circulated, how the dead were buried, and which spaces were adapted for gatherings and baptism. Materiality does not automatically confirm literature; it is an independent line of evidence whose convergence with the texts must be demonstrated on a case-by-case basis. Summary This chapter treats manuscripts, inscriptions, funerary spaces, images, and buildings as autonomous evidence for early Christian history. It examines the ancient codex, the nomina sacra and staurogram, the graffito of Alexamenos, the symbolism of ichthys, the Good Shepherd, the Roman catacombs, the Christian building of Dura-Europos, and fourth-century sarcophagi. Keywords: material culture; codex; staurogram; Alexamenos; Dura-Europos; catacombs.

chapter vi From Galerius to Theodosius: Constantine, Nicaea and the Imperial Transformation The fourth century cannot be reduced to a sudden conversion of the Empire or an instantaneous institutional victory for the Church. The period between 311 and the end of the century saw, in succession, tolerance, patronage, doctrinal controversy, religious legislation, and new forms of monumentalisation. Christianity went from being a periodically persecuted religion to occupying a privileged position within the State, but the process was discontinuous and did not produce immediate uniformity. 1. 311 and 313: tolerance, restitution and the so-called “Edict of Milan” Galerius’s edict of 311 had formally ended the persecution in large areas. Two years later, after the meeting of Constantine and Licinius in Milan, a broader policy of religious freedom and restitution of property was agreed upon. The expression “Edict of Milan” is a historiographical convention. No edict issued in Milan with that title survives; the measures are known from related texts preserved by Lactantius and Eusebius. The settlement of 313 did not make Christianity the official religion, but rather expanded freedom of worship and ordered the restitution of property.77 77 Lactantius, Mort. pers. 34 and 48; Eusebius, HE X.5.2–14. The so-called Edict of Milan is explained as an agreement and communications of application, not as a single Latin original preserved with that title. 182

from galerius to theodosius 183 2. Constantine and the patronage of the churches Constantine increasingly intervened in Christian affairs through donations, privileges, arbitration of conflicts, and monumental construction. Imperial patronage altered the scale of resources available to certain churches and made bishops more visible political actors. The Donatist conflict demonstrates, however, that imperial support did not produce automatic unity. Constantine convened tribunals and councils to resolve an African dispute that combined the memory of persecution, episcopal legitimacy, and sacramental discipline.78 2.1. Sol, coins and religious change in the time of Constantine The depiction of Sol on Constantine’s coins is a document of imperial communication. The legend SOLI INVICTO COMITI and the radiate figure make it possible to study public associations between the emperor and a patron deity. Its presence does not constitute a complete personal confession, but neither should it be eliminated to produce a retrospectively uniform image of the reign. Different means of representation can preserve earlier formulas while religious patronage and alliances change.79 The Roman cult of Sol has a history predating Aurelian; the reorganisation and imperial promotion of the third century do not justify describing it as a completely new cult introduced from a single location in the East. Solar deities, their epithets, and their links with other cults must be identified through documentary evidence. The term “Invictus” does not, in itself, imply that every object dedicated to a deity with that epithet belongs to the same religious institution. Constantine’s shift is best observed through a chronology of decisions: patronage of Christian communities, restitution of property, intervention in disputes, construction of buildings, and modification of propaganda. Not all of these actions occurred in 312, nor did they immediately eliminate all previous signs. The evidence documents a cumulative transformation whose pace varied according to medium, 78 79 Optatus of Milevis, Contra Parmenianum I.22–26; Eusebius, HE X.5.18–7.2 (Constantine’s letters to Miltiades, Chrestus of Syracuse, Caecilian and Anullinus); Augustine, Breviculus collationis cum Donatistis. Barnes 2011 and Drake 2000 offer frameworks for distinguishing patronage, politics, and religious representation. Types bearing SOLI INVICTO COMITI are identified by reign, mint, and issue before inferring religious changes. Barnes 2011 and Lenski 2012 offer contexts for Constantinian imperial communication; the presence of a legend does not equate to a confessional autobiography.

[FAC; ED]. audience, and region. The emperor’s religious biography should not be reduced to a binary alternative devoid of historical sequence. Christian solar language does not necessarily depend on a direct borrowing from Roman worship. Malachi 3:20 in Hebrew numbering—4:2 in other traditions— offers the image of the “sun of righteousness”; light and dawn belong to a broad scriptural repertoire. When a Christian author uses a solar image, its context and referents must be identified before asserting cultic dependence. The availability of shared metaphors allows for comparison, but does not in itself prove a conversion of Sol into Christ.

from galerius to theodosius 185 2.2. The day of the Sun and the regulation of rest Constantine’s constitution, preserved in CJ III.12.2 and promulgated on 7 March 321, orders rest for judges, the urban population and workshops on the venerabilis dies solis, with an exception for timely agricultural work. This is a civil measure with specific conditions of application. It did not institute Christian Sunday worship: Justin, 1 Apol. 67, had already described a gathering on the so-called day of the Sun in the second century. Nor does the law’s vocabulary establish that its sole purpose was to impose a solar cult. The difference in documentary genre is decisive. Justin explains a communal practice; the legal text regulates work and public activity. The coincidence of the day facilitates a history of convergence between the civil calendar and religious practice, but it does not turn the two documents into evidence of a single institution. Subsequent regulations on rest show new appropriations and adjustments; each provision must be cited with its own date and context. CTh II.8.18 (= CTh VIII.8.3; XI.7.13), transmitted under the names of Gratian, Valentinian II, and Theodosius I (although Gratian had died in 383) and posted at Aquileia on 3 November 386, suspends litigation, business, and the exaction of claims on that day. Its wording is particularly significant: “solis die, quem dominicum rite dixere maiores”. The constitution therefore does not simply replace a “solar” designation with a “Christian” one; it juxtaposes both within late Roman legal language. The consular reference to Honorius nobilissimus puer and Evodius securely dates the measure to 386; 383 belongs to other constitutions and must not be transferred to this locus. The law is later than, and distinct from, Constantine’s constitution of 7 March 321 (CJ III.12.2). The Codex Theodosianus that preserves it was itself promulgated in 438, so the date of the individual constitution must be distinguished from the date of the compilation that transmits it.

186 early christianity 2.3. 25 December and the limits of explanation by substitution The Chronography of 354 is a central testimony because it brings together civil and Christian materials with their own histories. The civil calendar records Natalis Invicti on 25 December; the Depositio martyrum records the birth of Christ in Bethlehem on the same date. This juxtaposition documents the coexistence of two calendrical usages in the fourth century. It does not, on its own, establish which one produced the other, nor a single act of substitution.80 Several hypotheses have been advanced to explain how the date was fixed. One relates the Christian celebration to the festive and solar context of the Roman winter; another studies Christian calculations that linked conception, passion, and birth. These proposals cannot be evaluated solely on the basis of their symbolic appeal. The texts that actually attest to them, their chronology, and their relationship to local practices must be identified. An explanation of origin requires more than a coincidence of date. No contemporary decree from Julius I or Liberius survives that would justify attributing to them, with the precision usual in popular accounts, the universal creation of Christmas on 25 December. The absence of such a document compels us to formulate the conclusion in terms of attestation and diffusion, not of a known papal decision. Eastern reception also presents differences: the history of a feast should not be reconstructed as if all sees had simultaneously adopted the same calendar. The Mithraic tradition does not provide a parallel birth narrative with a secure date that can be used without question as a source for Christmas. The iconography of the birth from a rock belongs to its own contexts and does not reproduce the Gospel narrative of Bethlehem. A comparative study can describe coexisting images and calendars; to defend dependence between narratives, it needs positive links of transmission. Religious history does not progress through lists of decontextualised similarities. 80 Chronography of 354: civil calendar, 25 December, N·INVICTI; Depositio martyrum, VIII kal. Ian., birth of Christ in Bethlehem. Reference edition: Mommsen, Chronica minora I, 1892. The sections of the dossier are distinguished and a single causality is not attributed to the coincidence.

from galerius to theodosius 187 2.4. The labarum and the testimonies of the victory of 312 Lactantius, Mort. pers. 44, and Eusebius, VC I.28–31, offer different accounts of the sign associated with Constantine’s victory. Lactantius describes a warning received in a dream and a sign applied to shields; Eusebius presents a vision and the subsequent construction of a standard. The texts should not be merged into a single narrative that eliminates differences in scene, medium, and time of composition.81 Eusebius’s account adds the claim of having received sworn confirmation from the emperor. This statement belongs to the work’s strategy of establishing authority. It is not equivalent to an immediate written testimony preserved from 312, nor does it allow for external verification of every detail of the vision. The historical problem lies in evaluating an account transmitted later and its function within a Christian imperial biography. The chi-rho monogram refers to Χριστός through recognisable letters. The form of the labarum combines elements of military representation with a growing Christian significance. Its interpretation requires neither speculative etymologies nor cosmological correspondences foreign to the sources. Roman standards already had functions of identity and cohesion; the new symbol reformulates these functions within a specific religious policy. Numismatics and dated objects provide independent checks on literary accounts. They document when, and in which media, certain symbols acquired public visibility. However, the earliest surviving example does not necessarily equate to the first historical use. Regional differences in minting and the uneven survival of objects prevent us from reconstructing an instantaneous and universal adoption. The labarum is, therefore, a case of convergence between the memory of victory, imperial authority, and religious representation. Academic analysis preserves the differences between accounts and compares their functions. It does not claim that all the details of the narratives are confirmed, nor that their differences negate any historical information about the transformation of propaganda. 81 Lactantius, Mort. pers. 44; Eusebius, VC I.28–31. Reference editions: Moreau, SC 39; Winkelmann, Eusebius Werke I.1. The accounts maintain their differences regarding dream, vision, shields, and standard.

188 early christianity 3. Nicaea 325: Christology, empire and conciliar authority The Council of Nicaea of 325 was convened by Constantine in the context of the controversy associated with Arius and his adversaries. Its confessional formula used ὁμοούσιος to affirm the relationship of the Son to the Father and condemned certain propositions considered incompatible with that faith. Nicaea did not “invent” the divinity of Jesus. The veneration of Christ, the language of pre-existence, and multiple forms of Christology predate the council by centuries. Nicaea intervened in a dispute about how these claims were to be articulated conceptually within a common doctrinal framework. Nor did Nicaea decide the canon of the New Testament. Its surviving canons deal with disciplinary and ecclesiastical matters, not a list of biblical books.82 4. Imperial architecture: from adapted house to public basilica The transformation of the fourth century became visible in stone. The Lateran complex in Rome, the Vatican basilica built over the memoria of Peter, the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, and the Nativity in Bethlehem are examples of a new scale of patronage and sacred topography. The Christian basilica adopted and transformed a Roman architectural type suitable for large gatherings, processional circulation, and axial focus. Monumentalisation altered the relationship between community, city, and power. The Holy Sepulchre is particularly significant because Constantinian patronage united exegesis, local memory, and architecture. The construction itself does not prove the archaeological authenticity of each topographical identification; it does demonstrate that in the fourth century the State could transform Christian memory into an imperial monument.83 4.1. Basilica programme and circulation practices The emergence of large Christian buildings in the fourth century cannot be explained as the copying of a single prototype. The Roman basilica tradition offered resources for gathering and representation, but Christian projects also depended on the site, patronage, the size of the community, and their relationship to places of memory. 82 83 Nicene Creed and its anathemas of 325; Ayres 2004. The council produced no documented decision on the canon of the New Testament. Eusebius, HE X.4; VC III.25–40. Krautheimer and Ćurčić 1986 contextualise architectural programmes. The construction sequence requires specific testimonies.

from galerius to theodosius 189 The history of a building is reconstructed through its phases, not through a formal genealogy deduced from a resemblance.84 The naves, structural supports, apse, and entrances organised ways of gathering, observing, and moving about. The lighting of the central nave and the differentiation of sectors could contribute to the hierarchical organisation of acts and participants. However, not all the elements of a preserved floor plan allow for the precise reconstruction of a liturgy. The furnishings may have changed, and excavations often yield fragments from different phases. Ritual texts, inscriptions, and architectural remains must be compared and contrasted without automatically filling in the gaps. Constantinian projects in Rome and Jerusalem reveal distinct objectives. Basilicas linked to episcopal sees, apostolic memoriae, or sites in the life of Jesus do not share the same topographical context. The tomb, pilgrimage, gatherings, and the relationship with power could all necessitate different spatial arrangements. Monumentalisation is a process of site selection and funding, as well as a shift in the scale of construction. Decoration plays a part in this process. Inscriptions, materials, images, and the arrangement of spaces could establish an authoritative memory and make patronage visible. These are not ornamental additions made later to a supposedly neutral architecture. Their chronology, however, must be demonstrated: decoration from a later phase does not automatically document the building’s inaugural programme. The transition from the adapted house to the public basilica altered the conditions of visibility and access. This does not mean that all domestic gatherings disappeared, nor that all regions had equal resources. The coexistence of scales necessitates a pluralistic history of Christian architecture. The built forms are evidence of investment, organisation, and memory; not an automatic reflection of an identical doctrine throughout the Empire. 84 Eusebius, HE X.4; VC III.25–40; Krautheimer and Ćurčić 1986, Early Christian and Byzantine Architecture. Patronage programmes, functions, and construction phases are distinguished; formal similarity does not demonstrate a single religious prototype.

190 early christianity 5. Eusebius: historiography in a time of transition Eusebius of Caesarea’s Ecclesiastical History is the first major continuous narrative of Christian history. Its documentary value is immense because it preserves letters and fragments of works now lost. At the same time, its narrative structure reflects a theological project of continuity and providence. The Vita Constantini deepens this perspective by presenting an extraordinarily favourable image of the emperor. Using Eusebius means exploiting his documentary riches without automatically adopting his providential interpretation.85 6. Athanasius and Festal Letter 39: a canon of twenty-seven books In 367, Athanasius of Alexandria listed, in his thirty-ninth Festal Letter, the twentyseven books that make up the present New Testament. It is the first surviving list that exactly matches that set. The letter is a milestone, not an instantaneous universal decree. The history of the canon continued to show regional variations and differences in reception. Athanasius also distinguishes between canonical books and other writings recommended for reading by those preparing for the Christian life.86 85 86 Eusebius, HE I.1 and X; VC I.1–11. The author’s providential perspective and document selection are considered. Athanasius, Fest. 39.5–7. Gallagher and Meade 2017 and Gwynn 2012 contextualise list, reading and episcopal authority; the date of 367 does not represent simultaneous universal closure.

from galerius to theodosius 191 7. From Constantine to Theodosius After Constantine, imperial policy towards Christianity continued to change. Constantius II favoured certain theological solutions; Julian attempted to revitalise traditional cults and reduce Christian privileges; after Valens’s Homoian policy in the East, Gratian and Theodosius I again favoured Nicene forms of Christianity. The Edict of Thessalonica of 380, promulgated by Theodosius I, Gratian, and Valentinian II, established the Nicene Christian faith, identified with the bishops of Rome and Alexandria, as the imperial norm. It did not, however, make Christianity the only existing religious practice overnight, nor did it instantly abolish all traditional cults. The Council of Constantinople in 381 consolidated a new phase of doctrinal definition. Even then, controversies, dissenting communities, and regional differences persisted.87 7.1. Imperial norm and persistence of religious differences CTh XVI.1.2, promulgated in 380, identifies a confessional norm through the faith associated with Damasus of Rome and Peter of Alexandria. The document contributes to the construction of a religious identity supported by the State. Its text does not amount to the immediate disappearance of all traditional cults nor to the effective conversion of all inhabitants of the Empire. The legal norm and its application must be studied separately.88 Subsequent provisions concerning sacrifices, temples, and religious practices belong to a sequence of decisions with different recipients and conditions. It is inaccurate to condense them into a universal abolition dated the same day as the edict of 380. Buildings could be abandoned, reused, or continue to be used in various ways; archaeology and local documentation allow the reach of the regulations to be tested. The persistence of differences within Christianity itself also reveals the limits of uniformity. The condemnation of a doctrine did not automatically eliminate its adherents, nor did imperial support guarantee a conflict-free reception. Bishops, communities, local aristocracies, and administrators all participated in concrete negotia- 87 88 CTh XVI.1.2; XVI.10.10–12. Ayres 2004; Rebillard 2012. Norms are distinguished from their application and from the effective identity of populations. CTh XVI.1.2, 27 February 380; XVI.10.10–12, provisions of 391–392. The book, title, and constitution number identify each rule without dependence on the pagination of a translation. Reference edition: Mommsen and Meyer 1905.

192 early christianity tions. Institutionalisation involved coercion, patronage, and the pursuit of consensus, with mixed results. The analysis of the fourth century must therefore distinguish between doctrinal professions, legal categories, and observable behaviours. A person could participate in overlapping civic and religious networks; an object or a building does not necessarily reveal all of its affiliations. The history of Christianisation gains precision when it preserves these distinctions rather than describing a complete replacement of one culture by another at a single moment. Conclusion The institutionalisation of the fourth century was more a transformation of scale than a point of origin. The textual, ritual, episcopal, and polemical structures developed during the preceding centuries acquired imperial resources, monumental architecture, and new conciliar mechanisms. The result was a much greater capacity for coordination and exclusion, but never complete uniformity. Fourth-century imperial Christianity is therefore an outcome to be explained, not a key with which to read the three preceding centuries retrospectively. Summary This chapter examines the transformation of Christianity from Galerius’s tolerance in 311 to the end of the fourth century. It distinguishes the agreements of 313 from the later establishment of imperial Christianity and analyses Constantine’s patronage, the Council of Nicaea, the monumental basilicas, Eusebius’s historiography, Athanasius’s Festal Letter 39, and the gradual emergence of Nicene imperial normativity under Theodosius. Keywords: Constantine; Nicaea; Galerius; Athanasius; canon; Theodosius.

chapter vii Religious Frontiers, Material Philology, and Advanced Methods for the Study of Christian Origins Research on Christian origins has changed scale over recent decades. It is no longer sufficient to establish a sequence of doctrines, authors, and councils: reading practices, manuscript circulation, social boundaries, languages, writing supports, habits of copying, and urban settings must be reconstructed together. This chapter brings into a single methodological discussion five problems that recur throughout the monograph: the relationship between Judaism and early Christianities; the reconstruction of the Gospel used by Marcion; the material sociology of the manuscript; the critique of the modern category of “Gnosticism”; and the archaeological interpretation of Dura-Europos. It also sets out a protocol for incorporating digital humanities and physicochemical analysis without implying observations of original objects that have not in fact been undertaken. 193

194 early christianity 1. From the “parting of the ways” to overlapping religious configurations The metaphor of the “parting of the ways” was useful for questioning confessional narratives that assumed a fully established Christianity from the 30s of the first century onward. However, even a slow separation can retain an overly linear image: two initially united communities that, after a certain point, gradually drift apart. The studies collected by Adam H. Becker and Annette Yoshiko Reed in The Ways That Never Parted, along with the proposals of Daniel Boyarin and other specialists, compel us to consider less orderly scenarios. Practices, texts and networks of sociability that do not fit neatly into two distinct institutional blocs coexisted in different cities and periods. In this book, the expression “overlapping religious configurations” functions as an analytical tool rather than as a new essentialist label. It designates situations in which people or groups may share scriptures, calendars, urban spaces, exegetical repertoires, or family relationships without that overlap implying complete identity. A social boundary may be highly significant to a religious leader and yet barely visible to a municipal observer. Likewise, a homily condemning attendance at a synagogue expresses a desire to establish a boundary while simultaneously presupposing that some hearers might cross it. Antioch offers a particularly important laboratory. John Chrysostom’s late polemic against Christians who participated in Jewish festivals or practices should not simply be projected back to the first century; it does, however, demonstrate that in the fourth century, institutional distinction could coexist with behaviours that episcopal preaching perceived as ambiguous. Alexandria presents another type of overlap: the use of the Septuagint, the Philonic tradition, allegorical exegesis, and Christian polemics are all part of the same intellectual ecosystem, though not of an undifferentiated community. Rome adds a third configuration. The presence of diverse Jewish communities, the early arrival of Jesus’ followers, and the multiplicity of Christian groups in the second century make it inadequate to describe the city with a simple line from “synagogue” to “church.” Funerary inscriptions, literary sources, and topography suggest distinct networks that may have shared language and biblical repertoires. The analysis must therefore distinguish three levels: internal self-definition, polemical classification by adversaries, and external administrative perception. The methodological consequence is decisive. Expressions such as “JudeoChristian”, “Gentile Christian”, “synagogue”, or “Church” cannot function as closed boxes when the sources themselves describe ongoing processes. Each locus

religious frontiers, material philology… 195 is examined in terms of its actors, location, date, practices, and vocabulary. The boundary is not presupposed; it is reconstructed from the evidence. 1.1. Philological window: ἀποσυνάγωγος and the narrative construction of exclusion The adjective ἀποσυνάγωγος appears in John 9:22; 12:42; and 16:2 and is usually translated as “expelled from the synagogue” or “excluded from the synagogue.” Morphologically, it is a compound formed from συναγωγή with the prefix ἀπο-, which expresses separation. Its presence in the fourth Gospel is historically important, but it does not automatically authorise the reconstruction of a universal Jewish decree against Christians at the end of the first century. John 9:22 links the fear of the blind man’s parents with a decision attributed to οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι: ἵνα ἐάν τις αὐτὸν ὁμολογήσῃ χριστόν, ἀποσυνάγωγος γένηται, “so that if anyone confessed him as Messiah / Christ, he would be outside the synagogue.” The historical value of the passage depends on distinguishing the time narrated—the life of Jesus—from the social horizon of the evangelist. The scene can preserve the memory of later conflicts without in itself providing the date, geographical scope, or institutional procedure of an exclusion. The comparison with John 16:2, which announces ἀποσυναγώγους ποιήσουσιν ὑμᾶς, shows that the term belongs to a rhetoric of communal conflict. This evidence must be compared with later rabbinic literature and the complex history of the Birkat ha-Minim, rather than equating a liturgical formula whose transmission is difficult to trace with a council that decreed a definitive rupture. The classic hypothesis linking ἀποσυνάγωγος to the Birkat ha-Minim derives from J. Louis Martyn, History and Theology in the Fourth Gospel (1968); for the history of the liturgical text and its dating problems, see Ruth Langer, Cursing the Christians? A History of the Birkat HaMinim (2012). 2. Marcion between textual reconstruction and the synoptic problem: Roth and Klinghardt The Gospel associated with Marcion presents one of the most difficult philological problems of second-century Christianity because the text is not preserved in a complete Marcionite manuscript. Its reconstruction depends on adversarial testimonies, especially Tertullian, Epiphanius, and the Dialogue of Adamantius, as well as scattered allusions. The classic reconstruction was Adolf von Harnack’s Marcion: Das Evangelium vom fremden Gott (1921; 2nd ed. 1924). Dieter T. Roth (The

196 early christianity Text of Marcion’s Gospel, 2015) has insisted that a responsible reconstruction must distinguish between quotation, paraphrase, allusion, and silence; the absence of a verse in a patristic refutation does not necessarily prove its absence in the Marcionite Gospel. The comparative apparatus in § 2.1 applies this protocol to four loci of varying degrees of certainty. The traditional view holds that Marcion’s Gospel derives from a form of Luke and that the differences are explained, to varying degrees, by editing, reception, or transmission. Matthias Klinghardt has radically reopened the problem by proposing that the Marcionite Gospel, or a form very close to it, predates the canonical gospels and played a role in their formation. In his reconstruction (2015; English edition 2021), the question shifts from “what Marcion removed from Luke” to “what literary relationships best explain the set of agreements and divergences.” A critical research monograph should not resolve this bifurcation by majority vote. It should evaluate what kind of evidence supports each hypothesis. The Marcionite priority thesis gains strength when a shorter reading or a different sequence seems to explain the Lucan form without presupposing a doctrinally motivated edit. It loses strength when it depends on highly uncertain reconstructions of a text known only through polemicists or when a reading can be better explained by ordinary textual variation, patristic adaptation, or rhetorical selectivity in quotation. A three-layered protocol is therefore adopted. First, the attested text is reconstructed with each heresiological witness identified separately. Second, that evidence is compared with the manuscript tradition of Luke without allowing NA28 to stand in for the textual state of the second century. Third, any inference concerning literary direction is kept explicitly distinct from the previous two operations. Only at this third level does a discussion of priority become methodologically meaningful. Table 32. Comparative reception apparatus: John 1:3–4, Valentinian exegesis and Nag Hammadi cosmologies This section does not present the Gospel of Truth or the Apocryphon of John as “textual variants” of the fourth Gospel. They are independent compositions and, therefore, do not belong to the critical apparatus of John in the strict sense. Their value here is comparative and related to the history of reception: they show how certain Christian circles of the second and third centuries elaborated problems of Logos, emanation, ignorance, creation, and deficiency within a scriptural ecology in which the Johannine corpus was known, cited, adapted, or discussed. The earliest witnesses do not offer an original punctuation that automatically resolves the problem. Early reception shows that authors of different orientations read ὃ γέγονεν with what follows. Punctuation preferences also changed in later controversies; therefore, the history of the punctuation must be separated from any simplistic account according to which a single faction physically “altered” the text to combat another. Evaluation of the Valentinian reception. Irenaeus is hostile to his adversaries, but in Haer. I.8.5 he transmits a detailed exegesis of the prologue, which he attributes to the Valentinian school. This demonstrates appropriation of and dispute over the meaning of John; it does not demonstrate that the Gospel of John was the exclusive property of one current, nor that all literature now grouped under the label “Gnostic” shared a single reading of the Logos. Nag Hammadi as a comparative archive. The Gospel of Truth and the Apocryphon of John should be read as works with different textual histories, genres, and cosmologies. The former presents Error and ignorance within a meditation on revelation and knowledge of the Father; the latter develops a much more extensive protological mythology. Their inclusion alongside John reveals competition over categories of creation, life, knowledge, and divine mediation, but it does not justify reconstructing a single “Gnostic version” of the prologue.

The historical question is how different communities and teachers contested authority through readings, rereadings, and new compositions within a still pluralistic Christian writing culture. The manuscript as a social artefact: from textual criticism to the sociology of the book The study of early Christian manuscripts has tended to privilege the text they contain: variants, omissions, interpolations, and genealogical relationships. This work remains indispensable, but it does not exhaust the evidence. Brent Nongbri has emphasised the need to treat manuscripts as archaeological objects with histories of discovery, acquisition, dating, and preservation; Chris Keith has shown, from another perspective, that the transformation of a tradition into a manuscript modifies the conditions of authority, circulation, and public reading. The question ceases to be merely “What text does this codex convey?” and comes to include “What material labour made this object possible?” The support, the preparation of the papyrus or parchment, the number of bifolia, the density of writing, the margins, the corrections, the presence of reading signs, and the calligraphic quality provide evidence for the economic and social decisions behind production. No single feature automatically identifies a scribe as a professional, an enslaved person, or a member of a community; however, it can place the manuscript within a range of comparable writing practices. The cost of a codex cannot be calculated using a universal price list. It varied according to material, size, region, availability of labour, quality, and length. Therefore, the economics of the book must be reconstructed comparatively, using contracts, letters, documentary prices, and non-Christian parallels where relevant. A community

204 early christianity capable of producing or acquiring multiple codices was not necessarily wealthy in absolute terms: it could mobilise patronage, internal labour, or exchange networks. The early Christian preference for the codex remains a remarkable fact, but its explanation should not be reduced to a single cause. Portability, capacity, symbolic differentiation, liturgical use, and collecting habits are hypotheses that may coexist. The classic treatment is C. H. Roberts and T. C. Skeat, The Birth of the Codex (1983); see also H. Y. Gamble, Books and Readers in the Early Church (1995), and L. W. Hurtado, The Earliest Christian Artifacts (2006). The physical format contributed to the way in which certain compositions were grouped, read, and perceived as a collection. 3.1. Protocol for material description and levels of observation Table 38. religious frontiers, material philology… 205 4. “Gnosticism” as a historiographical problem, not as a unitary religion Ancient heresiological literature tended to organise diverse adversaries within genealogies of error. Modern historiography inherited part of this order when it spoke of “Gnosticism” as a coherent religion, characterised by dualism, rejection of the world, and salvation through knowledge. Michael A. Williams (Rethinking “Gnosticism”, 1996) demonstrated that this category groups together phenomena that are too disparate and proposed dismantling it as an explanatory taxon; Karen L. King (What Is Gnosticism?, 2003) further reconstructed the modern history of the category and showed how much it owes to Christian discourses of orthodoxy and heresy. The solution does not lie in erasing the ancient names or replacing “Gnosticism” with an equally expansive substitute. Terms such as “Valentinian”, “Sethian”, or “Basilidian” are retained where the sources warrant them, while external labels are distinguished from self-description. The Nag Hammadi writings are treated work by work, with attention to language, transmission, cosmology, ritual practice, and exegetical strategy. In many cases, it is more productive to speak of communities and networks of Christian exegesis that competed to interpret Genesis, the identity of Christ, creation, and salvation. Some developed complex cosmologies and distinctions between divine levels; others privileged ascetic practices, initiation rituals, or allegorical readings. Their use of Platonic categories must be situated historically and not confused with a uniform dependence on a philosophical school. The expression “exegetical elite” can be useful if understood sociologically: certain teachers claimed a superior interpretive capacity and transmitted distinct teachings. This does not imply that all these groups were secret circles separate from the churches. Valentinian evidence, in particular, compels us to consider situations of coexistence and competition within broader Christian environments.

206 early christianity 5. Dura-Europos: architecture, image and ritual after Kraeling The Christian house at Dura-Europos remains a key archaeological site for studying Christian practices prior to Constantinian monumentalisation. Carl H. Kraeling’s classic report remains fundamental to the excavation documentation; however, the iconographic interpretation was not settled in 1967. Michael Peppard has proposed reinterpreting the baptistery as a visual programme centred on empowerment, healing, marriage, and incarnation, displacing interpretations that reduced it to death and resurrection. The case of the female figures with torches is methodologically exemplary. Their traditional identification with women going to the empty tomb competes with the interpretation that links them to the parable of the wise virgins and to a nuptial imagery. The value of the discussion lies not only in choosing an iconographic label. If the second model is correct, the baptismal chamber can be understood in closer relation to the language of nuptial preparation and ritual transformation, compatible with certain Syriac developments. Architecture demands the same caution. The adaptation of a dwelling does not, in itself, prove the social form of all Christian communities in the third century. Dura is a frontier city with a specific military and cultural history. The complex must be studied by examining its construction phases, circulation, visibility, room sizes, the location of the baptistery, and comparison with other buildings in the city, including the synagogue and non-Christian places of worship. In this edition, therefore, the illustrations from Dura are not treated as merely explanatory images. Each plan or painting is accompanied by a documentary record specifying provenance, phase, support, dimensions where available, restoration history, and the principal interpretive proposals. 6. Archaeometry: from illustration to measurement The incorporation of archaeometry can considerably enhance the quality of a history of material culture, but only if a clear boundary is maintained between published results and desirable analyses. Raman spectroscopy, X-ray fluorescence, reflectography, multispectral imaging, proteomics, fibre analysis, and chromatographic techniques can answer questions about pigments, inks, supports, and restorations. None of these techniques should be mentioned as having been applied to a specific object when the study does not exist or has not been consulted. For manuscripts, physicochemical characterisation can help distinguish writing campaigns or interventions, but it does not replace palaeography or textual criticism.

religious frontiers, material philology… 207 A difference in ink may indicate distinct periods; it does not, by itself, identify authors, communities, or doctrines. For wall paintings and sarcophagi, pigment identification can reconstruct workshop procedures and supply networks, but the iconographic meaning requires an additional level of interpretation. Archaeobotany and zooarchaeology have similar potential for domestic and funerary sites. Plant remains, seeds, bones, and residues can provide information about diet, trade, and commensal practices. However, the religious affiliation of an archaeological site must be established independently: a diet consistent with a particular norm does not demonstrate the religious identity of those who occupied the site. 7. Digital humanities and stylometry: power and limitations Computational stylometry offers useful tools for comparing lexical frequencies, particles, syntactic patterns, and other variables in large corpora. Applied to Pauline letters or Gospel collections, it can detect similarities and differences that warrant explanation. However, a classifier does not automatically “discover” authorship. Genre, length, theme, textual transmission, translation, and orthographic standardisation can alter the results as much as an author’s hand. A reproducible study should publish its corpus, lemmatisation rules, feature list, the distance or classifier used, parameters, robustness tests, and sensitivity to textual selection. In a small corpus—such as the undisputed and disputed Pauline epistles—cross-validation can produce impressive percentages on a fragile statistical basis. Therefore, stylometry should function as convergent evidence alongside historical argument, vocabulary, syntax, rhetorical situation, and early reception. The layers of redaction in the Gospels pose an even more complex problem. Computational models can locate discontinuities or clusters, but these results do not directly equate to historical “sources.” A change in style may correspond to cited tradition, genre, narrative scene, editorial revision, or simple variation. The method is most useful when it formulates traceable hypotheses that can be re-evaluated philologically. In the case of Marcion, the computational comparison between a modern reconstruction and Luke requires additional caution: the source text already contains modern editorial decisions. The algorithm cannot recover the missing portion of evidence; it only quantifies relationships within the constructed corpus. Any result must explicitly state which reconstruction was used and how the uncertain loci were handled.

Direct critical apparatus: from the quoted text to the verifiable locus The philological apparatus maintains a fundamental distinction between the “edition used” and the “object inspected”. The purpose is not to turn every page into a critical edition, but to make explicit the loci on which contested arguments depend. Translations serve the argument but do not replace scholarly editions. 210 early christianity 8.1. Asymmetries of the archive: region, social status, and documentary survival The surviving corpus is not a statistically neutral sample of early Christianity. Large cities, literate authors, episcopal leaders, and disputes that generated literary controversy are over-represented because they produced copyable texts, archives, and institutional memories. Villages, manual workers, enslaved people, women without access to durable writing networks, and short-lived communities appear far more intermittently. The inequality of the evidence is therefore itself a historical datum that must enter the interpretation; it cannot be corrected simply by accumulating quotations. The documentary geography is equally uneven. Egypt offers an exceptional density of papyri because of conditions of preservation that cannot automatically be extrapolated to wetter regions of Syria, Asia Minor, Italy, or North Africa. Rome, Alexandria, Antioch, and Carthage are visible because of urban scale and the survival of authors and correspondence; the Egyptian chōra, Syrian villages, and settlements in inland Anatolia often depend on scattered finds and archaeological chronologies that are harder to associate securely with religious identities. Absence of documentation is not absence of community. There is also an asymmetry of gender and status. Pauline letters, martyr acts, epitaphs, and some legal dossiers allow us to recover female agency, slavery, patronage, and labour, but these series were often transmitted by scribes, compilers, or institutions that do not represent the actors described evenly. The methodology of this volume therefore distinguishes historical presence, documentary visibility, and narrative centrality. A person or practice may have been socially important without generating an abundant textual series; conversely, a prolific author may dominate the archive without representing most communities. The logical consequence is that the “weight” of an explanation cannot be calculated by merely counting testimonies. Chronological proximity, independence between sources, genre, rhetorical purpose, chain of transmission, quality of archaeological context, and the possibility of corroboration across distinct evidentiary series must all be weighed. This graduated approach preserves the book’s thesis of process and convergence without dissolving major turning points: the destruction of the Temple in 70, the Marcionite controversy, third-century persecutions, and Constantinian patronage could profoundly alter conditions of production and circulation without constituting uniform and simultaneous ruptures in every region.

religious frontiers, material philology… 211 9. What an academic edition must not claim An interdisciplinary work gains authority by declaring its limits. Digital images are not presented as “autopsies”, nor are spectrometric results attributed to objects lacking published analysis. A stylometric simulation is not described as proof of authorship, and an archaeological hypothesis is not presented as a definitive identification. Peer review, inclusion in university programmes, and bibliographic indexing are external institutional processes; they cannot be brought about by the author’s declaration. The manuscript can, however, be prepared for these processes through traceability of sources, methodological transparency, international bibliography, and data availability. This distinction between completed results and projected protocols is part of the book’s argument. Academic excellence does not consist in multiplying nominally sophisticated techniques, but rather in making each step of the inference verifiable. Conclusion The study of early Christianity becomes more precise when religious boundaries, texts, and objects cease to be treated as closed entities. Relations between Judaism and Christianities require urban and regional models; Marcion demands the separation of textual reconstruction from dependency theory; codices must be read as social artefacts; “Gnosticism” must be subjected to historiographical critique; Dura-Europos needs to integrate architecture, iconography, and ritual; and digital humanities or archaeometry are only useful when their protocols are explicit. This framework does not replace previous chapters: it establishes a common discipline for their claims and for future expansions of the corpus. Summary This chapter develops an advanced methodological framework for the study of early Christianity. It reviews linear models of separation between Judaism and Christianity, compares rival reconstructions of the Gospel of Marcion, treats manuscripts as social artefacts, analyses “Gnosticism” as a modern historiographical category, re-evaluates Dura-Europos in light of recent research, and establishes protocols for archaeometry, manuscript imaging, and computational stylometry. It emphasises evidentiary transparency: it distinguishes between direct autopsy, digital facsimile, critical edition, laboratory analysis, and modern reconstruction, so that no source is represented as examined by methods beyond those actually used.

chapter viii Prophets, Thaumaturges and Messianic Pretenders in Palestine and the Roman East (First Century BCE to Second Century CE) Comparing Jesus with other prophets, miracle workers, charismatic leaders, and claimants to messianic legitimacy in Second Temple Judaism and the Roman East is historiographically necessary, but it is only useful if typological similarity is not mistaken for historical identity. Ancient sources employ polemical vocabularies— prophet, deceiver, magician, king, seditious leader, divine man—from distinct social and theological positions; moreover, almost all cases are known through hostile, retrospective, or literarily elaborated testimonies. This chapter does not seek to reduce Jesus to a pre-established religious type or to demonstrate his uniqueness through apologetic contrast. Its aim is to reconstruct the field of historical possibilities within which an eschatological preacher, a miracle worker, a prophet of signs, a resistance leader, or a cult founder could be interpreted. 213

214 early christianity 1. Disciplined comparison: types, sources and anachronisms In nineteenth- and twentieth-century research, it was common to group so-called “divine men” (theioi andres), Jewish miracle workers, desert prophets, and messianic pretenders under overly broad categories. This comparative strategy made it possible to break with interpretations that completely isolated Jesus from his context, but it also generated excessive analogies. The category of theios aner, in particular, does not describe a homogeneous institution of the ancient Mediterranean: it is a modern heuristic construct applied to biographies, miracle stories, and figures separated by considerable chronological and social distance. The comparison is therefore multidimensional. It distinguishes: a) origin and social environment; b) chronology and distance of the sources; c) the type of authority claimed or attributed; d) the repertoire of signs; e) relationships with the Temple, the Torah, and imperial power; f) modes of death or repression; g) the continuity of the group after the disappearance of its leader; and h) the degree to which a messianic identity can be established by contemporary testimony, later memory, or only by historiographical inference. Flavius Josephus is the primary source for numerous leaders of Judea and Galilee. His vocabulary, however, is permeated by his experience of the war of 66–70 and by his need to explain the causes of the catastrophe to Roman readers. When he links certain actors to sedition, deceit, or innovation, he does not offer a neutral taxonomy. The Acts of the Apostles, rabbinic sources, Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Origen, Philostratus, and Lucian must all be subjected to the same scrutiny regarding genre, agenda, and chronological distance.
