Honi and Hanina ben Dosa: effective piety and thaumaturgic memory Honi, known in rabbinic tradition as the “Circle Drawer,” belongs to a generation before Jesus. Josephus presents him as a righteous man whose prayer was associated with rain and whose death occurred during the struggle between Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II. The Mishnah, on the other hand, preserves the famous scene in which Honi draws a circle and declares that he will not leave it until God sends rain (m. Ta’anit 3.8). The comparative value lies not in postulating dependence between accounts, but in observing that Late Hellenistic and Roman Judaism could attribute extraordinary efficacy to the prayers of individuals considered especially pious. Hanina ben Dosa dates from the first century, but his profile is primarily known through later rabbinic memory. The Mishnah preserves a tradition concerning his

prophets, thaumaturges and messianic… 217 prayer for the sick (m. Berakhot 5.5), while the Talmuds considerably expand his repertoire of miracles. The dossier reminds us that his thaumaturgical reputation could be integrated within frameworks of Jewish piety without necessarily creating a separate sect or a Christology. Precisely for this reason, comparisons with the Gospels must distinguish between functional similarities—healing, effective prayer, charismatic recognition—and differences in the eschatological and post-mortem interpretation of the person of Jesus. 4. Judas the Galilean and the “fourth philosophy”: divine sovereignty, tribute and resistance The census associated with Publius Sulpicius Quirinius in 6 CE provided the context for the protest of Judas, called the Galilean or Gaulanite, along with a certain Zadok. Josephus makes him the founder of a “fourth philosophy,” characterised by exclusive adherence to the rule of God and the refusal to call any man lord (Ant. XVIII.1–10; XVIII.23–25; BJ II.117–118). Josephus’s construction is retrospectively biased: the historian links this current of thought to the chain of events that, in his view, culminated in the war of 66 CE. It is therefore preferable not to write that Judas “founded the Zealot movement” as if a stable and continuous organisation existed from 6 to 66 CE. It can be stated, however, that Josephus attributes to Judas an ideology of divine sovereignty and tax resistance that found later echoes. In relation to Jesus, the episode illuminates the political potential of the question of tribute and the language of divine kingship, but it does not automatically transform every proclamation of the “kingdom of God” into an insurrectionary programme.

218 early christianity 5. The Samaritan prophet of Gerizim: sacred sign and repression under Pilate Josephus recounts that a Samaritan leader promised to display on Mount Gerizim the sacred vessels that, he claimed, Moses had placed there. A crowd gathered for the expedition, and Pilate responded forcefully; the subsequent Samaritan protest contributed to his removal (Ant. XVIII.85–89). The episode is important because it combines scriptural memory, sacred geography, the expectation of revelation, and collective mobilisation without Josephus presenting the figure as a “messiah.” The comparison with Jesus requires attention to the internal diversity of Israelite traditions. Gerizim, not Jerusalem, structures the sacred horizon here. The existence of this type of prophet demonstrates that the desire for restoration could be articulated through signs linked to Moses and hidden objects, without necessarily adopting a Davidic ideology. 6. Theudas and the “Egyptian”: sign prophets, exodus and eschatological geography Theudas appeared under the procurator Cuspius Fadus, probably around 44–46 CE. According to Josephus, he persuaded a crowd to take their possessions to the Jordan and promised to part the river at his command; the Roman cavalry dispersed the group, and Theudas was beheaded (Ant. XX.97–99). The account reuses a biblical grammar of water-crossing associated with Moses and Joshua. Acts 5:36 also mentions a Theudas, but places him, within Gamaliel’s speech, before Judas the Galilean. The chronological discrepancy has generated a long discussion and should not be resolved by automatic harmonisation. The figure known simply as “the Egyptian” gathered followers and led them to the Mount of Olives, from where—according to Josephus—he promised a spectacular transformation of Jerusalem’s defences. Felix suppressed the movement, although the leader escaped (BJ II.261–263; Ant. XX.169–172). Acts 21:38 shows that the memory of this episode could function as an identifying reference point. Both Theudas and the Egyptian illustrate a form of sign prophecy: the leader calls for territorial action that awaits God’s decisive intervention. The figures for followers reported by Josephus and Acts do not coincide and should not be taken as precise statistics. More important is the narrative structure: desert, river, mountain, Jerusalem, and liberation form a symbolic landscape in which Scripture becomes a script for collective action.

prophets, thaumaturges and messianic… 219 7. Jesus ben Ananias: prophecy of doom and the fate of the Temple Among the figures described by Josephus, Jesus son of Ananias offers one of the most evocative prophetic comparisons. From approximately 62 CE, according to BJ VI.300–309, he wandered through Jerusalem, incessantly proclaiming woes against the city, the Temple, and the people. He was beaten by Jewish leaders and brought before the procurator Albinus; under interrogation and flogging, he continued to repeat his message. He died during the siege, struck by a Roman projectile, after years of announcing calamity. The similarities with gospel traditions—prophecy against Jerusalem, conflict with authorities, appearance before Roman power, physical suffering—do not justify postulating literary dependence. The Josephian narrative possesses its own tragic architecture. Its value lies in showing that the prophecy of judgement concerning the Temple could be an intelligible public practice within first-century Judaism and could simultaneously provoke local violence and evaluation by the Roman administration. In contrast to the Jesus movement, no lasting community is known to have formed around the death or vindication of Jesus ben Ananias. 8. Menahem and Simon bar Giora: insurgent kingship and the language of liberation During the revolt of 66, Menahem, linked by Josephus to the family of Judas the Galilean, held a prominent position in Jerusalem and adopted a royal appearance before being assassinated by rivals (BJ II.433–448). The episode supports an analysis of the theatricalisation of authority and competition between factions, but it does not compel us to attribute to him a fully reconstructible messianic programme. Simon bar Giora attained even greater military authority during the final phase of the war. His entry into Jerusalem, his retinue, and, finally, his display at the Flavian triumph have favoured interpretations of a royal or messianic character. However, Josephus writes from the perspective of defeat and portrays the leaders of the revolt as responsible for the national ruin. Prudence demands that we distinguish between royal gestures, popular military leadership, and a messianic self-proclamation that our sources do not unequivocally preserve.

220 early christianity 9. Bar Kokhba: the best-documented case of political messianisation after Jesus The revolt of 132–135 CE offers an incomparably more direct body of documentation thanks to letters and documents from the Judean Desert linked to Simon ben Kosiba. These texts document administration, orders, supplies, and territorial control without relying exclusively on later literary narratives. The epithet Bar Kokhba, “son of the star,” refers in tradition to Numbers 24:17 and is associated with the messianic interpretation of the leader. The celebrated tradition that Rabbi Aqiva identified ben Kosiba as messiah derives from later rabbinic sources and should be presented as traditional memory, not as a contemporary record. Cassius Dio retrospectively describes the scale of the war and its devastation (Roman History LXIX.12–14). Unlike Jesus, ben Kosiba exercised effective territorial and military command. This contrast shows that “messiah” could take on very different political configurations and that the leader’s defeat did not, in this case, produce a transimperial expansion comparable to Christianity. 10. Simon of Samaria and Dositheus: charisma, magic and heresiological genealogies Acts 8 describes Simon in Samaria as a practitioner of magic to whom the population attributed “the Great Power of God.” The narrative subordinates him to the apostolic mission through the episode of the purchase of the power to confer the Spirit. In the second century, Justin, a native of Flavia Neapolis in Samaria, and Irenaeus transformed Simon into a figure of much greater significance: founder of error, object of veneration, and the starting point of heresiological genealogies (Justin, 1 Apology 26; Irenaeus, Haer. I.23). This growth of the tradition should be studied as a history of reception, not projected entirely onto the Simon of the first century. Justin’s assertion that Rome had erected a statue to Simon with the inscription Simoni Deo Sancto is particularly instructive. The discovery of an inscription dedicated to the Sabine deity Semo Sancus on Tiber Island made it plausible that Justin had misinterpreted a monument. The case shows why even a relatively early and geographically informed author can err in the material identification of a religious object. Dositheus is even more difficult to reconstruct. Origen and later traditions place him within the Samaritan milieu and link him to prophetic or messianic claims, but the scarcity and lateness of the sources prevent a precise definition of his chronology and doctrine. He should be included on the map of Samaritan possibilities, not on a list of certain “messiahs.”

prophets, thaumaturges and messianic… 221 10.1. The historical problem of Dositheus: Mosaic prophet, messiah and sectarian memory Reconstructing Dositheus’s story demands a particularly rigorous approach to sources. Origen refers to him as a Samaritan figure and claims that he presented himself as the prophet foretold in Deuteronomy 18:15, or even as the expected Christ; elsewhere, he mentions books attributed to Dositheus and the claim by his followers that their master had not died. The documentation, however, is late, polemical, and partly contradictory. Hegesippus (preserved by Eusebius), the Pseudo-Clementines, Hippolytus and Epiphanius transmit differing genealogies of the relationship between Dositheus and Simon. Therefore, a linear succession of “John the Baptist → Dositheus → Simon → Gnostics” should not be reconstructed as if it were a proven historical chain. The Samaritan expectation of a prophet like Moses provides a more solid context than the later category of “Gnosticism.” Samaritan tradition is articulated around the Pentateuch and Mount Gerizim; within that horizon, the eschatological figure of the restorer—often associated in scholarship with the Taheb—offers a plausible framework for understanding why a prophetic claim based on Deuteronomy 18 could gain traction. Even so, the specific identification of Dositheus with the Taheb, the exact chronology of his activity, and the content of a supposed Dosithean doctrine must remain open questions, not established facts. Stanley J. Isser’s classic monograph and A. D. Crown’s studies show precisely the extent to which Dositheanism constitutes a problem of Samaritan history rather than merely a preliminary chapter of Christian heresiology.

222 early christianity 10.2. Simonians and Menander: polemical continuity and limits of heresiological genealogy The movement attributed to Simon of Samaria is the closest parallel in Christian sources. Acts 8 presents him as a magician to whom the Samaritans attributed “the Great Power of God”; Justin, Irenaeus, and later authors expand the narrative to make him the paradigmatic founder of subsequent deviations. This construction should be read as a heresiological genealogy: the fact that a second-century source traces several schools back to Simon does not demonstrate a real institutional continuity among them. The account of Menander, also a Samaritan according to Irenaeus, belongs to the same polemical archive and shows the tendency of heresiologists to organise religious diversity into master-disciple chains. The comparison with Dositheus is useful if it remains at a typological level: a claim to special revelation, individual charismatic authority, reinterpretation of Israelite traditions, and subsequent recollection of extraordinary powers. It is not methodologically legitimate to infer from these similarities that Dositheans, Simonians, and Menandrians formed a single “Samaritan Gnostic religion.” The category must be broken down into specific groups, texts, chronologies, and witnesses. 10.3. Baptists, Hemerobaptists and Masbotheans: repeated purification and late taxonomies Ancient sources mention various groups characterised by practices of repeated immersion. The so-called Hemerobaptists—literally, “daily baptists”—appear in heresiological lists and rabbinic or patristic testimonies that are difficult to date; the Masbotheans are even more obscure, and their exact location varies according to modern reconstructions. These names should not be taken as designations of well-known communities. Their value lies in showing that immersion, bodily purity, and ritual discipline could structure diverse sectarian identities in Palestine, Syria, and neighbouring regions. The disciples of John the Baptist documented in Acts 18–19 present a different case: there, the persistence of a memory and baptismal practices associated with John outside Judea is evident. However, the evidence does not justify automatically identifying these groups with Dositheans or with the movements described by Epiphanius. It is more appropriate to speak of a “Baptist field” as a comparative tool, not as a unified historical organisation.

prophets, thaumaturges and messianic… 223 10.4. The Elkasaites and other Judeo-Christian communities: affinities without direct descent The Elkasaites, known primarily through Hippolytus, Origen—via Eusebius—and Epiphanius, appear in the second century associated with a revealed book, Jewish observances, and repeated purification practices. These characteristics allow for comparison with Dosithean and Baptist circles, but do not prove a historical lineage. Their circulation between Syria, regions east of the Jordan, and Mesopotamia, the combination of observance of the Law with new revelations, and the repeated use of water reveal a broader religious landscape in which the boundaries between “Jewish,” “Christian,” and “sectarian” were constructed differently depending on the source. For the same reason, Mandaeism should be used only as a comparison of the longue durée. Its surviving texts are late, and its historical formation is complex. Hypotheses that directly connect it to John the Baptist, Dositheus, or first-century Samaritan circles remain debated and cannot be presented as proven genealogy. 10.5. Qumran, purity and eschatology: structural comparison, not genealogy The Qumran literature provides another point of comparison, though not a “similar cult” in the strict sense. The Community Rule, ritual baths, membership discipline, interpretive authority, and eschatological expectations show that the production of intensive identities through purity, exegesis, and separation was possible within Second Temple Judaism. But there is no evidence to derive Dositheus, Simon, or the Baptist groups directly from Qumran. The comparison is structural: it helps define available repertoires within the religious landscape, not lines of descent.

It only orders similarities of practice, authority, and documentary memory. In particular, “Baptist,” “Samaritan,” “Judeo-Christian,” and “Gnostic” are not interchangeable categories: each depends on a different textual tradition and historical context. Overall, Dositheus should remain in the book as a borderline case: a figure remembered from Samaritan, Christian, and heresiological archives whose importance lies precisely in showing that the first century was not composed of already consolidated religious blocs. Comparison with Simonians, Baptist groups, Elkasaites, and Qumran helps reconstruct shared repertoires—purification, exegesis, prophecy, charismatic authority—without turning them into a single underground tradition.

226 early christianity 11. Apollonius of Tyana: the problem of the pagan parallel Apollonius of Tyana, a Neopythagorean philosopher from Cappadocia active in the first century, became one of the most frequently cited pagan parallels to Jesus. The fundamental difficulty lies in the documentation: the main surviving biography, Philostratus’s Life of Apollonius, was composed in the third century under the patronage of Julia Domna, at a considerable remove from the life of its subject. Philostratus presents Apollonius as an ascetic, itinerant sage, exorcist, prophet, and performer of extraordinary deeds, including a scene of a young woman’s apparent return to life. During the Great Persecution, Hierocles used Apollonius in anti-Christian polemics to challenge the inference drawn from Jesus’ miracles to his divinity; Eusebius responded in Against Hierocles. Therefore, the Apollonius-Jesus parallel is not a modern invention: it was already part of the Late Antique controversy. However, using Philostratus’ Life as an independent basis for reconstructing the milieu of Galilee in the 20s–30s would conflate two chronological levels. Its greatest value lies in the history of the cultural competition to define what distinguishes a sage, a miracle worker, and a being favoured by the gods. 12. Alexander of Abonoteichos and Glycon: cult founder, oracle and material evidence Alexander of Abonoteichos, active in Paphlagonia during the second century, founded or institutionalised the oracular cult of Glycon, a serpent-like manifestation linked to Asclepius. Our main account comes from Lucian of Samosata, whose Alexander, or the False Prophet, is deliberately satirical and hostile. Lucian portrays Alexander as an impostor skilled at manipulating religious expectations, producing oracles, and exploiting his clients. Unlike many figures known only through polemicists, the Glycon cult possesses independent material corroboration: coins, inscriptions, and artistic representations attest to its spread and civic recognition. This evidence does not verify every accusation made by Lucian, but it demonstrates that the phenomenon cannot be reduced to satirical fiction. The case provides a comparative benchmark for studying how personal charisma, ritual, the economy of the oracle, elite patronage, and material reproduction could transform a local religious innovation into a transregional network.

prophets, thaumaturges and messianic… 227 13. In what sense can Jesus be compared to these figures? The comparison reveals partial affinities distributed among different figures. Honi and Hanina illuminate the charismatic efficacy of prayer; Theudas, the Egyptian, and the Samaritan of Gerizim, sign prophecy and territorial mobilisation; Jesus ben Ananias, the prophecy of judgement upon Jerusalem; Judas, Menahem, Simon bar Giora, and ben Kosiba, the relationship between divine sovereignty, resistance, and royal forms; Simon of Samaria, the polemical boundary between miracle and magic; Apollonius and Alexander, the Greco-Roman construction of the sage, thaumaturge, or cult founder. None of these parallels, taken separately, reproduces the combination documented in the earliest sources on Jesus: eschatological proclamation of the reign of God, teaching within Jewish frameworks, healings and exorcisms attributed to him by his followers, conflict culminating in Roman crucifixion, and, decisively for the later history of the movement, the very early assertion that God had raised and exalted him. This last conviction already appears in the Pauline epistles—including the traditional formula of 1 Cor 15:3–8—decades before the writing of Philostratus or most of the rabbinic dossier on miracle workers. Nor should the difference be expressed through the circular argument that “none of them succeeded, but Jesus did.” Some movements were militarily relevant, others survived for generations, and some cults expanded geographically. The historical problem lies in explaining why the execution of Jesus did not produce the expected dissolution of his group, but rather a reworking of his death through Scripture, visionary experience, ritual practices, and translocal mission. This explanation belongs to the social history of memory and networks, not to an abstract table of miracles. 14. Sources, hostile memory, and degrees of certainty This dossier requires an explicit grading of evidence. The letters of ben Kosiba possess a documentary value distinct from the rabbinic memory of Aqiva; Josephus is closer to Theudas or the Egyptian than Philostratus is to Apollonius, but he still writes with his own political objectives; Lucian is a rough contemporary of Alexander, although his genre is invective; the Church Fathers transform Simon of Samaria into an ancestor of heretical systems that cannot be projected backwards without qualification. Therefore, in the apparatus of this monograph, each comparative statement can be classified as: [DOC], if it comes from contemporary or near-contemporary documentation; [LIT], if it depends on an ancient literary narrative; [MEM], if it belongs to later traditional memory; [POL], if it is preserved mainly in polemics; and [HYP],

228 early christianity if the messianic identification or precise function is a modern inference. This gradation prevents a comparative table from producing a false appearance of documentary equivalence. Conclusion The religious and political landscape of Palestine and the Roman East between the first century BCE and the second century CE was populated by sign prophets, pious men renowned for their efficacy, resistance leaders, royal figures, ritual specialists, ascetic philosophers, and cult founders. Jesus can be historically situated within this field without being exhausted by any of its categories. The most productive comparison does not ask which figure was “most similar,” but rather what repertoires of authority were available and how each community transformed the memory of its leader. Christianity emerged from a Jewish matrix in which prophecy, Scripture, healing, eschatology, and divine sovereignty were living languages; its subsequent trajectory, however, depended on a specific combination of memory of the crucifixion, affirmation of resurrection, scriptural rereading, and missionary networks that turned an infamous death into a principle of expansion. Summary This chapter compares Jesus with documented prophetic, charismatic, thaumaturgical, and insurgent figures in Palestine and the Roman East from the mid-first century BCE to the second century CE. It distinguishes the genres of the sources, chronology, authority, political context, repression, and post-death memory. The dossier includes Honi, Hanina ben Dosa, Judas the Galilean, Theudas, the Egyptian, Jesus son of Ananias, Bar Kokhba, Simon of Samaria, Apollonius of Tyana, and Alexander of Abonoteichos. The comparison situates Jesus within a historically intelligible repertoire without reducing him to a single ancient type.

chapter ix Women in Paul’s Letters: Agency, Authority, and Memory in the Early Communities The study of women in the Pauline epistles is one of the most sensitive historiographical laboratories for reconstructing the early Christian communities. The difficulty lies not only in identifying female names, but also in distinguishing documentary strata, literary genres, urban contexts, and functional vocabularies. A historically disciplined reading must separate the seven letters generally considered authentic— Romans, 1–2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, and Philemon— from the letters of disputed or later authorship, especially Ephesians, Colossians, and the Pastoral Epistles. Otherwise, ecclesial restrictions from the beginning of the second century may be retrospectively projected onto communities in the 50s. This chapter adopts four rules. First, prosopography precedes theology: each woman is studied by name, place, relationship, verb or title, and documentary context. Second, Greek terms are analysed within their contemporary semantic field and not through later ecclesiastical equivalents. Third, internal tensions within the corpus—for example, between women who pray and prophesy in 1 Corinthians 11 and the command to silence in 1 Corinthians 14:34–35—are left open as textual and historical problems. Fourth, domestic space is treated as social infrastructure: household, patronage, work, mobility, hospitality, and epistolary circulation condition concrete forms of authority. 229

230 early christianity 1. Corpus, authorship and chronology: why it is important to separate the Pauline strata The undisputed letters are occasional documents. They do not offer a systematic treatise on gender or an ecclesiastical constitution, but rather responses to specific conflicts and relationships. Their occasional character explains why vocabulary concerning women appears scattered: greetings, recommendations, internal conflicts, ritual instructions, marital problems, and references to female collaborators. Historical reconstruction must resist the temptation to transform situational phrases into a homogeneous normative system. The attribution of Ephesians, Colossians, 2 Thessalonians, and, much more markedly, 1–2 Timothy and Titus remains a subject of debate, but critical scholarship generally distinguishes the Pastoral Epistles from the undisputed letters. This distinction is crucial for the history of women: 1 Tim 2:11–15 and 5:3–16 belong to an institutional setting different from that of Rom 16:1–16 or Phil 4:2–3. The comparison is legitimate if it is framed as a history of Pauline reception and discipline, not as if all the texts stemmed from a single situation and a single decade. 2. Female prosopography of the undisputed Pauline corpus Romans 16 contains the densest concentration of female names in the corpus. Its value transcends mere anecdote: it reveals a translocal network of mobility, hospitality, work, and authority. The names should not be read as decoration in a list of greetings, but as evidence of real social relationships that sustained the circulation of people, letters, and resources. Table 43. 232 early christianity 3. Phoebe: διάκονος and προστάτις in Romans 16:1–2 Romans 16:1–2 is among the most important passages for early institutional history. Paul presents Phoebe as “our sister”, διάκονος of the ekklēsia at Cenchreae, and προστάτις of many, including himself. These terms must be interpreted within their ancient semantic fields. Διάκονος can mean servant, agent or minister, and Paul also applies it to men and to his own ministry. Precisely because of this breadth, reducing it here to a female domestic helper with no communal significance introduces an asymmetry that the Greek does not require. Προστάτις is even more significant. It can imply protection, assistance, or patronage. In the language of associations and dependent relationships in the urban Mediterranean, the capacity to receive, represent, or finance was not neutral. Paul’s request that the Roman community “receive her in the Lord in a worthy manner” and assist her in whatever she needs suggests that Phoebe travels with sufficient relational authority to be recommended to networks that may not have known her personally. The hypothesis that she was the bearer of the letter to the Romans is plausible and widely discussed, although the text does not explicitly state this. 4. Prisca: mobility, household and apostolic collaboration Prisca appears in several geographical settings and offers an exceptional case for studying the mobility of an artisan couple within Christian networks. In Romans 16:3–5, Paul calls her, along with Aquila, συνεργός (“co-worker”) and recalls that they risked their necks for his life; moreover, a community (ekklēsia) meets in their home. 1 Corinthians 16:19 places the couple at another time in Ephesus. Acts adds narrative episodes, but for a minimal reconstruction, the Pauline letters suffice: the couple travels, hosts, and acts as a link between communities. The fact that Prisca is frequently mentioned before Aquila has generated various interpretations. It should not automatically be taken as proof of hierarchical superiority, but it does prevent us from assuming that the order in which women are mentioned is irrelevant in all contexts. The combination of mobility, home, and collaboration makes Prisca a prime example of how authority and domesticity were not separate spheres.

women in paul’s letters 233 5. Junia and the problem of ἐπίσημοι ἐν τοῖς ἀποστόλοις Romans 16:7 greets Andronicus and Junia, Paul’s “relatives,” fellow prisoners, and people who were in Christ before him. The name Ἰουνίαν is now generally understood to be feminine; the earlier suggestion of a masculine “Junias” lacks comparable onomastic documentation. The main question thus shifts to the syntax of ἐπίσημοι ἐν τοῖς ἀποστόλοις: it can be understood as “notable among the apostles” or, according to another reading, “well known to the apostles.” The standard case for the feminine name is Eldon Jay Epp, Junia: The First Woman Apostle (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2005); the exclusive reading (“well known to”) was argued by M. H. Burer and D. B. Wallace (New Testament Studies 47, 2001) and contested by L. L. Belleville (New Testament Studies 51, 2005). The exegetical decision should not obscure two firm facts: Junia joined the movement before Paul (“they were in Christ before me,” Rom 16:7) and shares with Andronicus a memory of imprisonment and missionary prestige. The passage warns against anachronistically restricting ἀπόστολος to the circle of the Twelve. In Paul, the term can designate envoys and missionaries more broadly. The discussion about Junia is, therefore, simultaneously philological, prosopographical, and historiographical. 6. Euodia and Syntyche: conflict between collaborators, not marginalisation Philippians 4:2–3 is often read as a minor episode of personal discord. However, the vocabulary Paul uses carries significant missionary weight: both women “fought together” with him for the gospel, along with Clement and other συνεργοί. Public mediation suggests, without proving it, that their dispute affected the community; it does not allow their rank to be measured. The scene also shows that leadership and conflict are not opposing categories. Later church historiography tended to remember male controversies as doctrinal debates and female disputes as personal problems. Philippians helps correct this documentary bias: Paul places Euodia and Syntyche in the shared memory of evangelistic work. 7. Chloe and economies of information 1 Corinthians 1:11 attributes the news of the Corinthian divisions to “Chloe’s people.” This expression could refer to members of her household, dependents, freedmen, or people connected to her patronage. The text does not establish Chloe’s

234 early christianity legal position with certainty, but it reveals a structure of information that spanned households and cities. Communication with Paul depended on messengers capable of travelling, being aware of conflicts, and being considered credible sources. From a network perspective, Chloe functions as an information node even though she does not physically appear in Corinth within the narrative. This case illustrates a methodological rule applicable to the entire chapter: ancient authority does not always take the form of a title. Controlling hospitality, resources, the flow of messages, or reputation could generate a capacity for intervention comparable to functions formalised only later. 8. 1 Corinthians 11: prayer, prophecy, and body 1 Corinthians 11:2–16 presupposes that women pray and prophesy in the assembly. The controversy does not centre on whether they can do so, but on how they should present themselves physically and how that presentation communicates honour, sexual difference, and authority. The complexity of the passage is increased by the vocabulary of κεφαλή (kephalē), by the references to creation and angels, and by the ambivalence between hierarchy and reciprocity in 11:11–12. Any historical reconstruction must keep three levels separate: the documented practice—women praying and prophesying; Paul’s regulation of that practice; and the subsequent interpretations that transformed the text into the foundation of much more developed ecclesial systems. Prophecy, in 1 Corinthians 12–14, is a gift of high communal relevance; therefore, the female presence within that practice cannot be reduced to silent participation. 9. 1 Corinthians 14:34–35: silence, manuscripts and literary coherence The command that “women should remain silent in the assemblies” is one of the most debated loci in the Pauline corpus. The tension with 1 Corinthians 11:5 is evident: a few pages earlier, Paul regulates women’s prayer and prophecy. Furthermore, in some Western witnesses, verses 34–35 appear displaced after 14:40 (D 06, F 010, G 012 and part of the Old Latin tradition), a fact that has fuelled the hypothesis of a marginal interpolation later incorporated into the text, argued in particular by Gordon D. Fee, The First Epistle to the Corinthians (NICNT; Grand Rapids: Eerdmans, 1987). The manuscript evidence does not warrant dogmatic excision of the passage: it is widely attested, although its position varies. The principal interpretations fall into three broad families: a) later interpolation; b) a contextual prohibition of a particular

women in paul’s letters 235 kind of disruptive or interrogative speech; and c) a more general regulation that must be read alongside 11:5. The question is not resolved here by confessional preference; instead, the variant position, the internal tension, and the literary arguments for each hypothesis are set out explicitly. 10. Galatians 3:28: baptismal formula, equality and social limits “There is neither Jew nor Greek, neither slave nor free, nor is there male and female” is probably a traditional formula incorporated by Paul. Its rhetorical power lies in redefining belonging “in Christ” and not in describing the empirical disappearance of social hierarchies. Precisely for this reason, the text must be considered in dialogue with practices where status differences continue to operate: slavery, marriage, citizenship, honour, and economic resources. The expression οὐκ ἔνι ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ evokes the language of Genesis 1:27 and has been interpreted both eschatologically and in a baptismal context. Historically, its importance lies in the fact that it offers a grammar of belonging that can be mobilised in different directions by later communities. It is not a modern constitution of legal equality, but neither is it an empty formula without social consequences. 11. Marriage, celibacy, and agency in 1 Corinthians 7 1 Corinthians 7 offers exceptional documentation on sexual negotiation, marriage, continence, and eschatological expectation. Paul formulates reciprocal obligations between husband and wife in a way that was remarkable for his time: each spouse has authority over the other’s body. This rhetorical symmetry does not eliminate the patriarchal structures of the Roman world, but it introduces an argumentative pattern that must be studied in its own terms. The chapter also presupposes unmarried women, widows, and mixed marriages. Paul’s personal preference for continence is framed within his “present distress” and an expectation that the time was short. The subsequent history of Christian virginity should not be projected directly onto this passage. Here, abstinence is an eschatological and missionary choice rather than a monastic institution.

236 early christianity 12. Philemon and female invisibility: Apphia and the household The brief letter to Philemon also greets Apphia and Archippus, in addition to the ekklēsia gathered in the house. Apphia frequently disappears from reconstructions focused exclusively on Philemon and Onesimus. However, her inclusion among the initial recipients suggests that the conflict concerned a broader domestic and communal unit. The house is not a backdrop: it is the space where property, slavery, kinship, and religious gathering intersect. This supports a prosopographical caution: not every female name can be assigned a position that does not exist in the source, but omitting it reproduces a reverse bias. The method of this monograph records presence, syntactic position, and context before attributing functions. 13. From Paul to the Pauline tradition: Ephesians, Colossians, and Pastoral Epistles Diachronic comparison reveals a shift towards domestic and institutional stabilisation. The so-called domestic codes of Colossians and Ephesians regulate relationships between wives and husbands, children and parents, and slaves and masters. The Pastoral Epistles, likely written after Paul, address widows, teaching, and female authority with greater intensity. This movement should not be described simply as a “fall” from an original equality, but rather as evidence that the Pauline legacy was reappropriated within communities facing challenges related to reputation, discipline, and generational transmission. 1 Timothy 2:11–15, in particular, should be cited as evidence of Pauline reception and not as a key to automatically reconstructing the Corinthian assemblies several decades earlier. Similarly, Romans 16 should not be idealised as documenting an egalitarian system without hierarchies. The historical reality lies between these two extremes: real female agency within deeply stratified ancient structures. 14. Thecla and the imagination of a Pauline female authority The Acts of Paul and Thecla, probably from the second century, is not a contemporary source for the historical Paul. However, it is essential to the history of his reception. The figure of Thecla transforms Paul’s preaching on continence into a narrative of female autonomy, family conflict, mobility, and teaching. Tertullian (De baptismo 17) testifies that the text could be used in debates about women’s authority precisely because some readers treated it as a significant apostolic account.

women in paul’s letters 237 Thecla must therefore appear in this chapter as a second body of evidence: she does not prove what happened in the communities of the 50s, but she demonstrates what possibilities of agency Christian communities of the second century could imagine when rereading Paul. 15. Women, slavery and domestic vulnerability The ancient household contained deep-rooted legal hierarchies. Enslaved women could participate in the same assembly as free owners and, at the same time, remain subject to sexual coercion, forced labour, and a lack of legal autonomy. Christian fraternal language did not automatically eliminate these conditions. A social history of women must avoid confusing ritual equality with legal emancipation. The importance of studying gender and status simultaneously is later observed in figures like Felicity, an enslaved and pregnant woman in the Passio Perpetuae et Felicitatis, or in epitaphs where freedwomen and patron-client relationships continue to structure Christian identity. Although these sources are later than Paul, they help us perceive which dimensions are silenced in letters written from male positions of literacy and authority. 16. Prosopography, networks and centrality: a transparent quantitative model The women in the undisputed corpus can be incorporated into a social network analysis if a distinction is made between explicit and inferred links. A minimal graph would have people and communities as nodes, and textually attested relationships as edges: collaboration, cohabitation, recommendation, kinship, hospitality, shared imprisonment, or circulation of information. No arbitrary weights would be assigned to theological terms; metrics should be derived from published, reproducible rules. In an initial model, Prisca and Aquila appear as translocal nodes due to their presence in more than one city; Phoebe as a bridge between Cenchreae and Rome; Euodia and Syntyche as internal collaborators in Philippi; Chloe as an informational node; and Junia and Andronicus as a link to believers whose adherence preceded Paul’s. Mathematical centrality does not equate to ecclesiastical hierarchy, but it reveals a density of relationships that a linear reading of the letters would obscure.

238 early christianity 17. Historiography: from invisibility to critical reconstruction Modern historiography on early Christian women has gone through several phases. An initial tradition tended to interpret women’s titles through later ministerial categories or to minimise them as informal language. Feminist and social research in the last third of the twentieth century recovered the agency of women as patrons, prophetesses, widows, enslaved women, and domestic leaders. Works by Elisabeth Schüssler Fiorenza, Ross Shepard Kraemer, Margaret Y. MacDonald, Carolyn Osiek, and others shifted the focus from “what office they could hold” to the concrete social conditions of authority, domestic space, kinship, and memory. The most recent reassessment also demands avoiding a compensatory narrative in which every mention of women is transformed into formal leadership. The standard must be symmetrical: neither minimising nor maximising. Name, verb, title, position in the letter, epigraphic comparison, and urban context constitute the basis for grading certainty. 18. Epigraphy, martyrdom, and female authority in the third and fourth centuries Evidence later than Paul allows the question to move from literary memory into material culture. Epitaphs, funerary inscriptions, and Christian dedications identify women through kinship, legal status, and, occasionally, titles or functions. Such evidence should be read without automatically converting every designation into an “office” equivalent to ministries standardised in later centuries. Its value lies precisely in revealing local vocabularies of prestige, service, widowhood, patronage, and belonging. The martyr acts provide a different register. Perpetua and Felicity show, in early third-century Africa, how gender, slavery, maternity, vision, and narrative authority could converge within a single dossier. In the fourth century, the expansion of female asceticism and aristocratic Christian networks made new forms of patronage, foundation, hospitality, and spiritual authority more visible. These forms do not simply continue the Pauline pattern unchanged, but they allow the transformation of women’s possibilities for action to be followed across different social and institutional settings.

Conclusion The undisputed Pauline epistles document a female participation that cannot be reduced to a single model. Women pray and prophesy, collaborate in mission, offer homes, protect, carry information, intervene in conflicts, and are remembered for work and imprisonment. The same corpus preserves regulations concerning the body, marriage, and assembly order, showing that this agency operated within patriarchal and slave-owning societies. The historical convergence that characterises this monograph appears here with particular clarity: charismatic authority, domestic patronage, urban mobility, and subsequent institutionalisation do not follow one another as pure stages, but rather overlap and are negotiated.

Summary This chapter reconstructs the agency of women in the undisputed Pauline letters through prosopography, philology, and social history. It distinguishes these letters from later Pauline traditions, analyses Phoebe, Prisca, Junia, Euodia, Syntyche, Chloe, and the women who prophesy at Corinth, and examines disputed passages such as 1 Corinthians 14:34–35. chapter x Textual Ecologies of the Second Century: Literature, Science, Administration and Christianities in the Roman Empire The second century should not be reconstructed from a retrospective canon of “great authors.” Textual circulation depended on language, region, literacy, school networks, private libraries, administration, associations, and copying markets. The aim of this chapter is to situate Christian literature within a broader documentary ecology: Latin historiography, the Greek Second Sophistic, philosophy, medicine, astronomy, legal and administrative texts, Jewish traditions, and diverse Christian production. Comparison helps measure both cultural continuity and innovation. 1. What does it mean to say that a text “circulated”? For the ancient world, circulation did not mean mass production. It could mean public reading, school copying, private lending, transmission through patronage networks, preservation in libraries, or indirect reception through citation. Therefore, rankings such as “most read texts” should be avoided unless specific evidence exists. The history of the book in the second century deals with uneven survival: Egypt preserves papyri that other regions have lost, and authors transmitted through late antique education survive better than popular or administrative literature. 2. Science, medicine and cosmography: Galen and Ptolemy Galen and Claudius Ptolemy remind us that the intellectual history of the second century is not limited to philosophy and religion. Galen produced a vast body of medical and philosophical work; his reflections on demonstration, schools, and textual authority provide important context for understanding how the ancients evaluated rival traditions. Ptolemy systematised astronomy, geography, and mathematical astrology. Christian vocabulary concerning cosmos, body, and nature circulated within a world where technical disciplines possessed their own criteria for proof and transmission. Comparisons must be functional. No direct dependence of a Christian author on Galen or Ptolemy will be asserted here without textual evidence. Their usefulness lies in reconstructing the horizon of specialised literacy and the coexistence of different forms of knowledge.

textual ecologies of the second century 245 5. Second-century Judaism: from the catastrophe of 70 to rabbinic reorganisation The second century in Jewish history was marked by the memory of the destruction of the Temple, the Diaspora rebellions, and the Bar Kokhba revolt. The traditions that would culminate in the Mishnah should not be imagined as a fixed book throughout the century. Rather, they were the product of a process of teaching, discussion, and compilation associated with rabbinic circles whose authority grew unevenly. The redaction of the Mishnah is conventionally placed towards the end of the second or the beginning of the third century under Judah ha-Nasi. The Septuagint continued to circulate among Greek-speaking communities, while Jewish translations such as those associated with Aquila reflected new needs for precision and exegetical debate. The relationship between Judaism and Christianity remained regionally variable; therefore, textual history must avoid the illusion of two completely separate libraries. 6. Apostolic Fathers: a corpus created retrospectively The label “Apostolic Fathers” is modern and brings together heterogeneous texts that their authors did not conceive of as a unified collection. Ignatius writes en route to martyrdom; 1 Clement intervenes in a Corinthian conflict; the Didache combines ethical instruction, ritual discipline, and organisation; the Shepherd of Hermas articulates visions, commandments, and parables; Polycarp writes from Smyrna; Papias survives only fragmentarily through later transmission. Apologists and negotiation with imperial culture In the mid-second century, an apologetic literature emerged, adopting forms of petition, philosophical discourse, and religious polemic. Justin Martyr is central because he combines defence before the authorities, exegesis, ritual description, and debate with Judaism. Athenagoras, Tatian, Theophilus of Antioch, and Melito of Sardis show that “apologetics” does not designate a homogeneous school either. Strategies range from appropriation of Greek philosophy and radical critique of pagan culture to petitions for legal recognition. Justin is particularly important for the history of the book because his “memoirs of the apostles” cannot simply be identified with a closed canon identical to the later one. His testimony belongs to a phase in which certain Gospel narratives possess liturgical authority while the limits of collection remain open.

textual ecologies of the second century 247 8. Marcion and the material reorganisation of textual authority Marcion must be situated within the textual ecology of the second century and not as an external anomaly. His Gospel, Apostolikon, and Antitheses articulate a collection and a reading of apostolic authority. The question of whether he edited Luke or whether his Gospel preserves an earlier form cannot be resolved by the label “heretical”; it requires philological reconstruction based on Tertullian, Epiphanius, and other witnesses, as well as comparison with the Lucan text. The historical importance of Marcion also lies in the materiality of selecting, ordering, and transmitting a corpus. The second century shows that the canon did not appear all at once: collections, lists, liturgical preferences, and polemics interacted for generations. 9. Irenaeus and the production of a memory of plurality Adversus haereses is an indispensable and dangerous source. Irenaeus preserves names, fragments, practices, and doctrinal outlines of groups that often do not survive in their own archives, but he does so within a polemical project that constructs genealogies of error and a rule of truth. His defence of the fourfold gospel is a concrete historical intervention, not the neutral description of an original consensus. Comparison with Nag Hammadi texts has shown that some systems described by heresiologists possessed vocabularies, myths, and practices that were indeed attested, while other categories appear to have been artificially aggregated. Therefore, Irenaeus must be used in two ways: as both witness and constructor. 10. Clement of Alexandria and the end of the second century Clement of Alexandria stands at the threshold between the second and third centuries. His Protrepticus, Paedagogus, and Stromata reveal a Christian intellectual community engaged in dialogue with philosophy, paideia, exegesis, and asceticism. His work demonstrates that Alexandrian Christianity cannot simply be described as a transition from “Gnosticism” to “orthodoxy”: internal boundaries are more porous, and the vocabularies of knowledge, perfection, and allegorical reading are both shared and contested.

248 early christianity 11. Non-canonical gospels and revelations: plural literary imagination The second century produced or transmitted a variety of gospels, acts, apocalypses, and dialogues. The category “apocryphal” is retrospective when used as if the authors knew beforehand that they were writing outside a closed New Testament. The Gospel of Thomas, the Gospel of Peter, the Protoevangelium of James, infancy traditions, the Acts of Paul and Thecla, and Valentinian literature must be studied within a plural literary imagination. The production of new revelations did not cease when certain collections began to stabilise. Canonisation and creativity are not mutually exclusive processes: they can advance together. This perspective makes it possible to overcome the “illusion of the canon,” that is, the modern tendency to order every second-century text according to its final destination within or outside fourth-century lists. 12. Valentinian literature and the limits of “Gnosticism” Valentinus and authors associated with Valentinian currents share the same world of Christian exegesis as their adversaries. Texts such as the Gospel of Truth, the Tripartite Treatise, or the Gospel of Philip—with distinct problems of authorship and dating—should not be introduced as documents of an already established external religion. In many cases, they reflect intensive reading of Scripture, baptismal language, Christology, and debates on creation and salvation within urban Christian networks. The critique by Michael A. Williams, Karen King, David Brakke, and Einar Thomassen compels us to abandon overly rigid taxonomies. The category “Gnosticism” can be retained as a historiographical term if it is defined and limited; it should not replace the description of each corpus. 13. Lucian, Peregrinus and Alexander: satire as an external source Lucian of Samosata is an invaluable external source precisely because he writes with satirical intent. In The Death of Peregrinus, he depicts Christians providing material support to a prisoner and mobilising solidarity; Alexander, or the False Prophet portrays the workings of oracles, credulity, religious competition and the formation of cults. Neither text can be read at face value, but both illuminate how a pagan intellectual could represent new communities and charismatic leaders.

textual ecologies of the second century 249 14. Papyri, the codex and the market for copies The literary history of the second century must come down to the material supports of writing. The growth of the codex among Christians is one of the most debated material features. The earliest surviving Christian papyri are fragmentary and often of broad palaeographical date ranges; they do not allow for precise annual chronologies. P52, P66, P75 and other witness es must be presented by date ranges and comparison of scribal hands, not as precisely dated fossils. The production of a codex required materials, time, planning of quires, and scribal work. The graphic quality varied enormously, from relatively competent hands to less formal copies. Rather than inferring the readers’ social class directly from this, it is more appropriate to consider material investments and different production contexts. The sociology of the manuscript must distinguish between price, availability, patronage, and scribal skill. The codices themselves are also autonomous evidence: format, nomina sacra and reading aids reveal communal practices that literary texts do not describe (Hurtado 2006). 14.1. textual ecologies of the second century 251 Conclusion The second century thus emerges as a densely connected textual ecology. Christian literature did not develop in an isolated chamber, but alongside imperial historiography, rhetoric, medicine, philosophy, Jewish translation, satire, and administration. The consolidation of Christian collections coincided with an extraordinary surge of creativity in gospels, revelations, and commentaries. Recognising this simultaneity dispels two linear narratives: that the canon quickly stifled alternative production, and that Christian identity was constituted outside the cultural practices of the Empire. annotated chronology of christian history 257 Fourth century. Imperial patronage and conciliar normativity The fourth century should not be read as a linear transition from persecution to a fully formed imperial Church, but as a sequence of legal, material, and doctrinal changes whose intensity varied considerably by region. The Great Persecution begun in 303 left an archive of confiscations, destruction of meeting places, surrender of books, and disputes concerning the lapsi and traditores. Galerius’s edict of toleration in 311 and the measures of 313 conventionally associated with “Milan” established a new framework of legality and restitution; they did not amount to the immediate Christianisation of the Empire. Constantinian patronage nevertheless altered the public scale of particular Christian communities. Restitution of property, clerical privileges, donations, and basilican building programmes created an unprecedented relationship between episcopal institutions and imperial power. Nicaea (325) set an enduring precedent for conciliar deliberation under imperial patronage, although its Christological formula did not end controversy and remained subject to negotiation for decades. Athanasius’s Festal Letter 39 (367) is the earliest extant witness to list exactly the twenty-seven books of the present New Testament; its documentary importance does not demonstrate immediate or uniform reception in every church. Under Theodosius I, Nicene definitions acquired increasing legal support, and several constitutions restricted sacrifice and particular forms of traditional cult. Enforcement, however, was uneven, and non-Christian cults persisted well beyond the fourth century. Laws preserved in the Codex Theodosianus must be cited by the original date of each constitution: the compilation itself dates to 438 and is not a unitary contemporary document of fourth-century events. Key dynamics include imperial patronage, conciliar authority, monumental architecture, the delimitation of scriptural corpora, and the progressive legal regulation of religious identities.

chapter xi Textual and Intellectual Ecologies of the Third Century: Imperial Crisis, Philology, Controversy, and New Christian Cultures The third century was not only a time of political and military instability. It was also a period of extraordinary intellectual density in which Christian communities, philosophical schools, Roman jurisprudence, rabbinic tradition, and religious movements of the Eastern Empire developed new forms of knowledge production, classification, and transmission. For the history of Christianity, this century is decisive because it saw the convergence of processes that in the second century were still dispersed: the professionalisation of exegesis, the expansion of libraries, the consolidation of episcopal networks, transregional disciplinary conflicts, and the emergence of authors capable of simultaneously engaging in philology, philosophy, pastoral care, and public debate. The documentation, however, must be read with particular caution. The so-called “crisis of the third century” did not produce a uniform experience throughout the Empire; the chronologies of civil war, fiscal pressure, epidemics, inflation, and military mobility affected each province differently. Similarly, there is no single Christian culture of the third century. Alexandria, Caesarea, Carthage, Rome, Antioch, and the Syriac communities all exhibit distinct institutional and linguistic profiles. The periodisation that follows uses these differences as an organising principle and avoids turning the century into a teleological prelude to Nicaea. 258

textual and intellectual ecologies of… 259 1. Tertullian and the formation of a Latin Christian vocabulary Tertullian offers a particularly revealing linguistic laboratory for Latin Christianity. His work, composed between the end of the second century and the first decades of the third, shows how theological, legal, and ritual categories of Greek origin were translated, reformulated and, at times, displaced by the Latin lexicon. Apologeticum, Adversus Marcionem, De praescriptione haereticorum, De baptismo, De oratione, and the disciplinary treatises should not be read as pieces of a homogeneous system. Their chronologies, intended audiences, and shifts in position necessitate the reconstruction of an intellectual and ecclesial trajectory. His historiographical value lies both in what he affirms and in the adversaries he presupposes. The polemic against Marcion shows that Marcionite communities remained real interlocutors; the discussions on discipline, prophecy, the female veil, marriage, and penance reveal internal disagreements that a retrospective history of “orthodoxy” tends to flatten. Tertullian also offers a privileged case for studying the relationship between forensic rhetoric, categories of private law, and ecclesiastical language, without implying that the Church had already acquired a uniform legal personality. 2. Cyprian of Carthage: episcopate, crisis and correspondence as a social archive The Cyprianic documentation provides unusually detailed evidence for reconstructing an episcopal network in the Latin West during the mid-third century. His letters, De lapsis, and De unitate ecclesiae are situated at the crossroads of persecution, penitential discipline, financial assistance, and the negotiation of authority. The persecution of Decius and the issue of the lapsed generated specific procedures: certificates, intercessions of confessors, synods, letters of recommendation, and disputes over the pace of readmission. It is not merely a matter of penitential theology; it is an archive of community logistics and the administration of people. Cyprian’s correspondence allows for a network analysis of the transmitted dossier. Carthage links African communities, Rome, and other Mediterranean centres, but the frequency of letters does not, in itself, establish institutional primacy. The prosopographical appendix offers a pilot network with sources and reproducible metrics; the direction of exchange and the preservation of each letter are recorded separately from the simplified graph representation.

260 early christianity 2.1. Documentary infrastructure and social network analysis (SNA): the Cyprianic epistolary archive as a system of flows The correspondence attributed to Cyprian of Carthage forms one of the densest epistolary archives of third-century Latin Christianity. Its value lies not only in penitential or ecclesiological theology: letters, delegations, messengers, and synods support reconstruction of a system of information circulation between Africa, Rome, Hispania, and the East. The following model does not transform the preserved correspondence into a complete picture of the historical network; it represents only explicit or strongly documented relationships within the transmitted corpus. SNA protocol. Node = identifiable person, community, or episcopal see; edge = epistolary link or documented delegation; direction = sending/receiving when it can be established; weight = number of loci selected in the verification dossier, not total volume of historical communication. The metrics express the structure of the modelled corpus and not an actual ecclesiastical hierarchy. Figure 24 (SNA-2). Selected flows from the Cyprianic archive. Restrained analytical visualisation of documented exchanges; the dashed line to Arles indicates the intervention requested from Stephen of Rome (Ep. 68), not a preserved letter sent to Arles. The term “Cyprianic archive” here designates the transmitted collection of correspondence associated with Cyprian, not a fully preserved ancient administrative archive. The usual numbering comprises 81 letters dating from approximately 249– 258. It contains writings by Cyprian, synodal letters, and letters from other correspondents; the conventional attribution distinguishes 59 letters by him, 6 synodal letters, and 16 by other authors (Letters 1–81, Fathers of the Church 51). Its order and delimitation depend on manuscript transmission and editorial work.

Novatian and the dispute over the purity of the Church Novatian illustrates the fragility of the later categories of “schism” and “heresy.” His De Trinitate shares broad doctrinal assumptions with other Latin authors, while the conflict between him and Cornelius centred on episcopal authority and the discipline of reconciliation. The controversy demonstrates that the creation of ecclesial boundaries did not depend solely on Christological differences. It could also arise from rival elections, local legitimacies, and incompatible models of penance. Sources on Novatian largely come from adversaries or later ecclesiastical narratives. Therefore, any reconstruction must distinguish between the self-understanding of his communities and the labels imposed by rival networks. The persistence of Novatianist communities for centuries confirms that this was not an ephemeral deviation, but an alternative ecclesial structure with its own episcopate, places of worship, and a memory of its own.

textual and intellectual ecologies of… 263 4. Origen: library, Hexapla and professionalisation of Christian philology The work of Origen represents the most important qualitative leap in preConstantinian Christian philology. His activity in Alexandria and Caesarea combined biblical commentary, teaching, polemics, comparative editing, and library work. The project known as the Hexapla should not be imagined as a modern “critical Bible,” but rather as an extraordinary device for textual comparison: Hebrew, Greek transliteration, and various Greek versions were aligned to expose divergences and translation problems. Against Celsus, On First Principles, the commentaries, and the homilies reveal an intellectual culture that engages with philosophy, grammar, and literary criticism. The importance of Origen for this book lies not in making him a doctrinal arbiter, but in observing how a Christian community could develop complex philological procedures before imperial patronage. Biblical variants appear as problems of interpretation, not as marginal incidents. At the same time, the subsequent transmission of Origen—including Latin translations, condemnations, and selective extracts— necessitates distinguishing between the original work, its reception, and modern reconstruction. 5. Clement of Alexandria, Gregory Thaumaturgus and intellectual pedagogy Clement of Alexandria, whose activity extended into the early third century, linked biblical exegesis, ethics, Greek paideia, and social critique. His Protrepticus, Paedagogus, and Stromata do not simply form a systematic “trilogy”; they reveal distinct registers of pedagogical intervention. Read together, they illuminate the social composition of educated urban audiences, debates over wealth, marriage, food and clothing, and the selective use of philosophy as a conceptual repertoire. Gregory Thaumaturgus, for his part, offers a disciple’s memory of Origen’s school. His speech of gratitude to Origen combines praise, intellectual autobiography, and the construction of authority. The comparison between the two authors helps to avoid an abstract representation of the “school of Alexandria” and to reconstruct personal trajectories, movements, and teaching networks. 6. Hippolytus and the problem of attributions The name of Hippolytus of Rome encapsulates one of the classic problems of attribution in early Christian literature. The Refutatio omnium haeresium, exegetical works, and the so-called Traditio Apostolica were long treated as the coherent output

264 early christianity of a single Roman author. Modern scholarship has shown that this simplification is untenable. For historical purposes, each work must be evaluated separately and not used as a transparent window onto a single, third-century “Church of Rome.” The Apostolic Tradition is especially important because its liturgical prescriptions have frequently been used to reconstruct baptism, ordination, and the Eucharist. Its textual and compositional history, however, is complex. It is therefore treated here as a layered ecclesiastical tradition, not as a normative enactment straightforwardly datable to the Roman activity of a historical Hippolytus. 7. Dionysius of Alexandria and episcopal communication Dionysius of Alexandria is known largely through fragments and letters preserved by Eusebius. This mediation conditions the evidence, but does not diminish its value. His interventions in debates on rebaptism, persecution, discipline, and doctrinal controversies reveal an Eastern network of episcopal correspondence that extends beyond a single city. Eusebius’s selection should be treated as an edited archive: it preserves documents while simultaneously rearranging them within a narrative of the Church’s past. 8. Methodius of Olympus, virginity and exegetical competition Methodius’s Banquet of the Ten Virgins shows that Christian asceticism could appropriate prestigious classical literary forms. The imitation of Plato’s Symposium does not constitute an automatic doctrinal continuity with Platonism; it is a literary and rhetorical choice. The text is particularly useful for studying represented female authority, virginity, the body, and exegesis in an environment where ascetic discourse was acquiring increasing centrality. 9. Martyrdom, records and documentation of coercion The third century produced a martyrdom archive whose reading requires distinguishing between acts with a possible documentary basis, literary compositions, and hagiographic reworkings. The Passio Perpetuae et Felicitatis, dating from the beginning of the century, combines first-person sections, narrative editing, and a theological construction of martyrdom. Its exceptional nature should not be overlooked: precisely for this reason, it is a primary source for studying gender, visionary authority, family, imprisonment, and community memory.

textual and intellectual ecologies of… 265 During the persecutions of Decius and Valerian, papyrus and epistolary documentation permits a contrast between martyrial rhetoric and administrative procedure. The sacrificial libelli show formulae, names, witnesses, and local bureaucracy. They do not, in themselves, record “Christian persecution” in every case, but they permit reconstruction of how ritual compliance was verified and how specific civic commissions functioned. 10. Plotinus and Neoplatonism as a documented historical context Plotinus belongs to the intellectual horizon of the third century and should be treated as such, without turning Neoplatonism into a secret key to explaining Christianity. The Enneads, edited by Porphyry after the master’s death, reveal debates about the soul, intellect, unity, and philosophical ascent that circulated in learned circles of the Empire. Certain Christian authors may have shared vocabulary or problems with these schools, but each convergence requires specific textual evidence. This book maintains a firm methodological separation: the historical presence of Middle and Late Platonisms is indispensable for understanding the intellectual landscape, but it does not justify esoteric genealogies or doctrinal equivalences. Comparison is restricted to concepts, teaching networks, and situations of explicit controversy. 11. Porphyry and the scholarly critique of Christianity Porphyry is one of the most sophisticated critics of early Christianity. His Against the Christians survives only in fragments, and its reconstruction depends on Christian responses and later testimonies. This state of transmission prevents us from quoting it as if we possessed a continuous text. However, the information we have about his arguments—including the Maccabean dating of Daniel—reveals a critique based on philology, chronology, and literary coherence, not solely on religious mockery. The case of Daniel is especially significant because it shows that issues associated with modern biblical criticism—dating, prophecy ex eventu, textual layers—could already be formulated in antiquity. The comparison between the Masoretic Text, the Greek versions, and the Qumran fragments should be presented as a history of transmission and interpretation, avoiding attributing anachronistic methodological categories to Porphyry.

266 early christianity 12. Philostratus and the literary construction of Apollonius of Tyana The Life of Apollonius of Tyana, written by Philostratus at the beginning of the third century, is a central source for studying the literary construction of the “divine man.” Its relationship to Jesus should not be framed as either dependence or equivalence. The comparative interest lies in the narrative techniques: travels, teaching, asceticism, miracles, conflicts with authorities, and posthumous memory. The work was later used in anti-Christian polemics, but its original purpose cannot be reduced to a response to the Gospels. 13. Cassius Dio and the political memory of the Empire Cassius Dio’s Roman History provides a valuable senatorial account of imperial politics, although its social location and chronological perspective differ markedly from those of Christian sources. Here it is used chiefly in political and military contexts, especially where it supplements or corrects chronologies transmitted by ecclesiastical authors. Its evidentiary value depends on comparison with inscriptions, papyri, and other historians, not on any presumption of neutrality. 14. Mani and the formation of a trans-imperial religion Mani’s preaching from the mid-third century onward generated a religious tradition that crossed linguistic and political boundaries. His communities used Syriac, Middle Persian, and other languages, and developed an extraordinarily mobile manuscript culture. Manichaeism interacted with Christian, Iranian, and Mesopotamian vocabulary, but it must be distinguished from the second-century Christian movements that ancient heresiology and modern historiography indiscriminately grouped under labels such as “Gnostics” and “Gnosticism.” The inclusion of Manichaeism in this history is justified by religious competition and by the way fourth-century Christian authors perceived it, not because it constitutes a branch of Christianity. Augustine’s biography also reminds us that the boundaries between communities could be crossed by individuals in the course of a lifetime.

textual and intellectual ecologies of… 267 15. Mishnah, Tosefta and rabbinic recomposition The compilation of the Mishnah around the beginning of the third century and the formation of Tannaitic corpora offer an indispensable counterpoint. The history of rabbinic Judaism should not be narrated as a mere inverted mirror of Christian episcopal development. Rabbinic collections respond to their own processes of memory, legal classification, and authority. Their comparison with Christian texts is only valid when chronology, genre, and context of transmission are taken into account. 16. Jurisprudence, rescripts and the language of administration The third century was also the era of great late classical jurisprudence. Papinian, Ulpian, Paulus, and other jurists formulated categories that encompassed administration, property, associations, and personal status. Christian communities existed within this legal order, even though they did not possess a single, unified legal status. To understand confiscations, restitution of property, or the liability of associations, it is preferable to work with specific legal documents rather than with the anachronistic label of religio licita/illicita as if it were a general statute.
