Zoroastrianism, Second Temple Judaism and historical mediation The most solid historiographical approach to these contacts is not a direct line “Zarathustra → Jesus”, but rather the long interaction between Jewish populations and Iranian worlds from the Achaemenid period, followed by the Parthian and Sasanian contexts. Eschatological concepts could circulate, be transformed and combine with Judaism’s own biblical traditions. Qumran, apocalyptic literature, and other texts from the period show that Second Temple Judaism was not a passive recipient, but a creative laboratory capable of reworking any external influence within its own Scriptures and categories.

zoroastrianism and early christianity 321 12. Conclusion: similarity, contact, and dependence The interaction between Jewish and Iranian worlds has a secure historical basis. Judea was a province (Yehud) of the Achaemenid Empire from 539 to 332 BCE; Isaiah calls Cyrus “anointed” (Isa 45:1) and Ezra presents the return under Persian sponsorship; biblical Hebrew and Aramaic preserve Iranian loanwords of administrative, legal and religious vocabulary (pardēs, “park, paradise”; rāz, “secret”, in Dan 2 and in the Qumran manuscripts). The Magi, as ritual specialists, appear in Greek sources from Herodotus on and are studied by A. de Jong. This basis allows us to speak of contact; it does not decide which concepts were transmitted or in which direction. Against that background the symmetries among Zoroastrianism, Second Temple Judaism and first-century Christianity should be graded. (a) Dualism. The “Instruction on the Two Spirits” in the Community Rule (1QS III:13–IV:26), with its Prince of Lights and Angel of Darkness, is the closest parallel to the language of light and darkness, truth and falsehood that reappears in John 3:19–21; but the Qumran text subordinates both spirits to a single creator God, whereas the opposition of Ohrmazd and Ahriman is formulated in terms of two principles, with nuances that scholarship (Shaked) distinguishes between the Gāthās and Pahlavi literature. (b) Resurrection and judgement. Dan 12:2 is the clearest biblical affirmation of bodily resurrection for judgement; the Zoroastrian expectation of a resurrection (tan ī pasēn) is documented in detail only in Pahlavi texts, and the most cited ancient testimony, that of Theopompus transmitted by Diogenes Laertius (1.9), according to which the Magi taught that men would be resurrected, is brief and disputed. (c) Final renewal. The frašō.kərəti, with its definitive defeat of evil, admits typological comparison with the “new heavens and new earth” of Isa 65:17 and Rev 21:1; the comparison does not imply borrowing, because the idea of cosmic renewal has prophetic antecedents of its own. (d) Ordeal by fire. The molten-metal ordeal of the Pahlavi texts recalls the rivers of fire in Dan 7:9–10 and the fire of judgement in 2 Pet 3:7, but the dating of the Iranian texts prevents a direction being fixed. (e) Saving figure. The Saošyant, who renews the world, and the Jewish Messiah or Son of Man fulfil related functions in the structure of the end, but differ in origin and mission; late traditions about a virgin birth of the Saošyant should not be projected onto Matt 1–2. A synthesis, strictly speaking, can be formulated in four grades. Secure historical contact: Persian rule over Judea, lexical loans, the presence of the Magi in Greek sources. Real conceptual parallels: moral dualism, judgement, resurrection and final renewal. Possible mediation: Enochic and Danielic apocalyptic and the Qumran texts, where material could be reworked within Jewish Scripture. Hypotheses with-

322 early christianity out proof: that Jesus, Paul or the evangelists knew Zoroastrian doctrines directly, that the Magi of Matt 2 are identifiable Zoroastrian priests, or that the Saošyant is a model for Christology. First-century Christianity stands at the end of that chain: it receives the eschatological repertoire already Judaised, not by way of the Avesta. The symmetry is therefore one of form—a history with beginning, conflict, judgement and renewal—and not of social process: what Christianity adds, and what comparative Zoroastrianism does not offer, is the anchoring of that scheme in an executed historical person, a community of shared table and, in the long run, a collection of writings. This result is consistent with the book’s thesis. To show that the vocabulary of the end—kingdom, judgement, resurrection, renewal—was available in a space of exchange stretching from Persia to Judea and Rome reinforces the reading of Christian formation as a convergence of fields of influence, and the Pauline reading of that convergence, because it was Paul who translated that repertoire for a community of Gentiles. Nothing obliges us to explain Christianity by Iranian dependence, and nothing authorises us to exclude contact as one more component of the environment. Zoroastrianism and Christianity share a keen interest in the moral outcome of history, the defeat of evil, and ultimate justice. The similarities are too significant to ignore, but too general—and the sources too disparate—to automatically translate into direct dependence. The contribution of a critical comparison lies precisely in grading the evidence: certain historical contact, genuine conceptual parallels, possible Jewish mediations, and, finally, a core of claims for which there is no proof of borrowing. This criterion preserves comparative value without restoring esoteric or syncretic genealogies that this edition has excluded from the historical framework. Summary This chapter offers a controlled comparison between Zoroastrian eschatology and early Christianity. It examines cosmic opposition between good and evil, resurrection, final judgement, the Saošyant, the final renewal (frašō.kərəti), the kingdom of God, Satan, the forty-day temptation narrative, and the Magi in Matthew. It distinguishes historical contact from typological similarity and foregrounds the chronological difficulty posed by the late Pahlavi sources. Iranian influence on Jewish and Christian eschatologies remains a significant and contested hypothesis; claims of direct derivation require specific evidence.

chapter xix Sages, Rabbis and Judaisms (First–Fourth Centuries): Comparison with the Jesus Movement and External Testimonies This chapter brings together three problems that often appear scattered: the history of Jewish teachers and rabbis between the end of the Second Temple period and Late Antiquity; a disciplined comparison between first-century Judaism and the Jesus movement; and the dossier of Jewish and non-Jewish references to Jesus and the early Christians. The aim is not to construct two fully formed “religions” from the year 30 CE onward, but rather to trace processes of differentiation that shared scriptures, languages, institutions, practices, and conflicts. The use of the term “rabbi” requires caution: for Hillel, Shammai, or Gamaliel I, it is preferable to speak of sages or teachers; the institutionalisation of the rabbinic title belongs primarily to the period after 70 CE. 323

Method and vocabulary: from the sages of the Second Temple to Tannaitic and Amoraic rabbis The surviving rabbinic literature—Mishnah, Tosefta, Midrashim, and Talmuds— reached written form long after the lifetimes of many of the figures it recalls. Therefore, any doctrinal attribution to Hillel, Shammai, Yohanan ben Zakkai, or Aqiva must distinguish between the possible historical memory of a teaching and its formulation within a collection written or transmitted generations later. The chapter uses the Tannaitic and Amoraic designations as historiographical categories of period, not as evidence of a uniform rabbinic institution from the first century onward. Three levels are distinguished: [A] person and activity securely located in history by convergence of sources; [B] probable historical figure whose specific teaching depends on later traditions; [C] attribution or biographical detail of uncertain historicity. After 70: Yavne, rabbinisation and Christianisation as asymmetrical processes The destruction of the Temple in 70 CE forced numerous Jewish groups to reconfigure authority, worship, and memory. Later rabbinic tradition located a series of decisive figures and controversies in Yavne, but current historiography avoids imagining a central academy capable of instantly legislating for all synagogues. Similarly, the communities of Jesus’ followers did not immediately transform into a uniform “Church.” Both processes were regional, competitive, and uneven. The second century simultaneously reveals continuity, conflict, local separation, appropriation of Scripture, and a redefinition of categories of belonging.

Evaluation protocol: testimony, reception and controversy Jewish references to Jesus, his family, and figures associated with his followers do not form a homogeneous archive. The corpus combines Josephus, a first-century Jewish author writing in Greek for an imperial audience, with rabbinic traditions committed to writing several centuries later, and with medieval polemical compositions. This section does not accumulate “proof” of historicity; rather, it classifies testimonies according to date, proximity, independence, transmission, and rhetorical function. The question is not only what each text says, but when it says it, in what genre, for what purpose, and what distance exists between the narrated referent and the preserved literary form. The scale used is: [A] chronologically proximate and philologically controllable testimony; [B] early testimony whose transmitted form presents significant textual intervention or debate; [C] late tradition which may preserve earlier materials but whose specific historicity cannot be safely isolated; [D] polemical construction or late reception, useful for the history of representations but not as a direct source for the first century. The gradation applies to the passage, not to the person in the abstract. Rabbinic literature requires additional caution. The Mishnah was compiled around the beginning of the third century; the Tosefta and the Tannaitic midrashim

XVIII.63–64 (18.3.3), the so-called Testimonium Flavianum, is preserved in Greek manuscripts with unequivocally Christian formulations. Modern scholarship ranges from complete interpolation, through a retouched Josephan core, to substantial authenticity with glosses. This monograph adopts a position of minimal certainty: the received text cannot be cited as if all its content came without modification from Josephus; however, it is methodologically legitimate to discuss the possibility of a non-Christian core prior to the reworking. Ant. XX.200 (20.9.1) is quite different: here Josephus mentions the execution of “James, brother of Jesus called Christ.” The passage is integrated into the narrative of the high priest Ananus and lacks the confessional density of the Testimonium. Although all ancient manuscript traditions must be subjected to criticism, this locus possesses a considerably greater degree of historical acceptability. The expression “called Christ” functions as an identifier and does not imply Josephus’s adherence to the Christian confession. The difference is methodologically decisive: there is no single category of “Josephus’s testimony about Jesus.” Each locus has its own textual history, narrative function, and probative value. Celsus, Panthera and the counter-narratives about the birth of Jesus The oldest surviving testimony associating the birth of Jesus with a figure named Panthera (Πανθήρα) comes from Celsus, a pagan author of the second half of the second century. His Ἀληθὴς λόγος does not survive independently: it must be reconstructed through Origen’s refutation. In Contra Celsum I.28, Celsus’s Jewish interlocutor rejects the virgin birth, and in I.32 he identifies the supposed father as a soldier named Panthera. The status of the passage is polemical and mediated [B/C]. Celsus wrote more than a century and a half after the events, and his formulation is known only through selection, quotation, and paraphrase by a Christian adversary. The text demonstrates the circulation, in the second century, of an anti-Christian counter-narrative concerning the parentage of Jesus; it does not constitute contemporary or independent evidence of his birth. The nominal similarities with ben Pandera/Pantera in later rabbinic materials warrant comparison, but do not demonstrate a continuous documentary chain from the first century. 340 early christianity 7. Conclusion: from plural Judaism to rabbinic and Christian trajectories Between the first and fourth centuries, there was no simple replacement of “Judaism” by “Christianity,” nor were there two blocs that separated all at once. There were diverse forms of Judaism, movements of followers of Jesus, expanding Gentile communities, and, after 70 and 135 CE, parallel processes of textual, ritual, and institutional reorganisation. Rabbinic tradition attained its own normative forms through the Mishnah, the Tosefta, the Midrashim, and the Talmuds; the churches developed canons, episcopates, liturgies, and theological languages. Scholarly comparison is most fruitful when it describes these trajectories as asymmetrical historical processes of selection, memory, and authority, not as predetermined destinies. Summary This chapter presents prominent Jewish sages and rabbis from the first–fourth centuries, compares first-century Jewish configurations with the Jesus movement, and brings together Jewish and non-Jewish references to Jesus and the early Christians. It distinguishes the Second Temple sages from later rabbinic institutionalisation, treats Yavne as a complex process after 70 CE, and evaluates Josephus, rabbinic traditions, Tacitus, Pliny, Suetonius, Mara bar Serapion, Lucian, and Celsus according to their chronology, independence, transmission, and polemical context.

chapter xx Architecture, Surveying and Infrastructure in the Roman Empire (First–Fourth Centuries): Technical Texts and the Transformation of Christian Space This chapter examines the written sources for reconstructing the architectural and technical culture of the Empire between the first and fourth centuries CE. It does not automatically identify “Christian architecture” with its own treatise tradition: for most of the period, Christian groups inhabited, adapted, and reinterpreted spatial forms produced by Roman, Hellenistic, and provincial architecture. Therefore, three levels of evidence are distinguished: technical and administrative treatises; literary descriptions of buildings; and independent archaeological evidence. Vitruvius is included as a Republican and Augustan antecedent whose work continued to be reused, not as an author of the first century CE. 1. Vitruvius as a technical antecedent received in the imperial era Marcus Vitruvius Pollio composed De architectura in the first century BCE. Its presence in this chapter reflects the enduring relevance of its technical vocabulary: ordinatio, dispositio, distributio, firmitas, utilitas, and venustas; materials; water supply; public and private buildings; temples; machines; and gnomonics. For the history of Christianity, its significance lies not in postulating a doctrinal transmission between architecture and religion, but in describing part of the technical framework within which cities, houses, basilicas, baths, porticoes, and hydraulic systems were built and later used by Christian communities. The sequence of the ten books of De architectura is used here solely as the material organisation of a technical treatise and as long-term testimony on the city, building resources, public and private buildings, hydraulics, machines and measurement. It is not credited with a hidden numerological structure or a symbolic architecture that 341

342 early christianity the text does not document. For the present study, its value lies in offering a technical and typological vocabulary open to historical comparison with later building practices, without turning that terminological continuity into religious dependence. 2. Frontinus and water administration: De aquaeductu urbis Romae Sextus Julius Frontinus, appointed curator aquarum in 97 CE, wrote De aquaeductu urbis Romae as a technical and administrative record of Rome’s water supply system. The text combines the history of aqueducts, flow measurement, pipe sizes, fraud, maintenance, easements, and personnel organisation. For this monograph, its importance is twofold: it documents the infrastructure that made urban concentration possible and shows that the material conditions for gathering, hygiene, water sources, baths, and population density depended on complex public systems. It should not be used to infer that Christian communities controlled these infrastructures; it provides the urban framework within which they operated. 3. Pliny the Elder and Pliny the Younger: materials, monuments and the administration of building Books XXXIV–XXXVI of Pliny the Elder’s Natural History gather information on metals, pigments, stones, marbles, sculpture, and buildings. His encyclopaedic perspective does not amount to a design manual, but it preserves material vocabulary, information on provenances, and monumental records indispensable for understanding the building culture of the High Empire. Pliny the Younger adds another archive: his correspondence with Trajan reveals funding problems, unfinished works, baths, aqueducts, theatres, and provincial oversight. These letters document architecture and public works as an administrative practice rather than merely an aesthetic form. 4. Surveying and territory: the Corpus agrimensorum Romanorum The literature of the surveyors—Frontinus in his gromatic role, Hyginus Gromaticus, Siculus Flaccus, and other texts transmitted in the Corpus agrimensorum Romanorum—documents boundaries, centuriation, land categories, disputes, and measurement procedures. Roman territory thus appears as a legally constructed space. This corpus is of interest to early Christianity because cities, cemeteries, foundations, rural properties, and roads did not exist on neutral ground: they were subject to regimes of possession, taxation, and delimitation. The date and authorship of each

architecture, surveying and infrastructure… 343 treatise must be addressed separately; the “corpus” is a later manuscript compilation of diverse materials. 5. Pseudo-Hyginus, De munitionibus castrorum: military architecture and spatial order De munitionibus castrorum, formerly attributed to Hyginus and now conventionally referred to as Pseudo-Hyginus, describes the layout of a military camp. Its dating within the High Empire remains debated, with proposals ranging from the Trajanic period to later in the second century. The work shows how military space could be organised through measurements, hierarchies, circulation, and functional allocation. It is particularly useful for frontier cities like Dura-Europos, but its principles should not be mechanically applied to the Christian building excavated there: camp, city, and adapted house belong to different scales of evidence. 6. Faventinus and the practical transmission of Vitruvius Marcus Cetius Faventinus, probably between the third and fourth centuries, composed a compendium of architectural technique known as Artis architectonicae privatis usibus adbreviatus liber, also transmitted under titles similar to De diversis fabricis architectonicae. The work abbreviates and reorganises Vitruvian material for domestic and private use. Its existence is crucial for the history of Vitruvius’s reception: it demonstrates that Vitruvius was not merely an ancient literary monument, but a wellspring that could be summarised and adapted to later needs. Precisely for this reason, its transmission must be studied through specific texts and not through supposed symbolic continuities. 7. Eusebius and the Christian description of the monumental building With the Constantinian peace, the scale of documentation changed. Eusebius of Caesarea, in his Ecclesiastical History X.4, preserves the panegyric dedicated to the reconstruction of the church of Tyre, and in his Vita Constantini, descriptions of imperial programmes linked to Jerusalem and other centres. These texts are not treatises on architecture: they are theological-political discourses that transform building, patronage, and liturgy into signs of restoration. Therefore, they must be compared with archaeology, topography, and construction phases. Their value lies precisely in showing how monumental architecture began to be narrated as an argument for Christian legitimacy.

344 early christianity 8. Mishnah Middot and other Jewish spatial texts The Mishnah, compiled around the beginning of the third century CE, though preserving earlier traditions, contains in Middot a normative description of the Temple in Jerusalem. It is neither a Roman architectural treatise nor a precise modern archaeological plan. It is, however, a major source for studying the remembered spatial order of the sanctuary, its measurements, access points, courtyards, and hierarchies. Comparison with Josephus and with archaeology reveals how different corpora construct sacred space textually after the destruction of 70 CE. 9. From the domus and the insula to the basilica: typological continuity and change of scale Documentation from the first to third centuries forces us to resist an overly simplistic genealogy according to which the “house-church” evolved linearly into the basilica. Communities gathered in homes, workshops, and adaptable spaces; DuraEuropos offers an exceptional archaeological case, not a universal model: a private house adapted for worship and sealed by the city’s destruction after the Sasanian siege of 256/257, whose chronology derives from stratigraphy rather than from literary tradition. In the fourth century, the basilica provided scale, axiality, visibility, and processional capacity, but its adoption depended on patronage, urban land, and political circumstances. The change is both institutional and material: not the sudden invention of a specifically Christian architectural type. 10. Architecture and Christianity: what can be demonstrated The historical result is not a continuous “Christian architecture” from Jesus to Constantine, but a sequence of spatial appropriations within pre-existing imperial infrastructures. Technical texts document materials, measurements, hydraulics, ownership, and typologies; fourth-century Christian sources reveal the new capacity for monumentalisation; archaeology serves as a control on both archives. This method avoids two reductionisms: reading architecture as a mere illustration of theology and, conversely, deducing doctrine directly from a building form. Conclusion Between the first and fourth centuries, the Empire’s building culture was sustained by technical knowledge circulated in treatises, compendia, regulations, administrative correspondence, and construction practices. Christianity emerged within this material world. The Constantinian transformation did not introduce architecture into Christian history; rather, it changed the economic, legal, and monumental scale of a relationship with space that already depended on houses, streets, ports, necropolises, water, roads, and urban networks. Comparison of Vitruvius, Frontinus, the surveyors, Faventinus, and Eusebius makes it possible to narrate this transition without equating technical continuity with ideological continuity.

chapter xxi The Canonical Gospels in Comparison: Chronology, Literary Dependence, Divergences, and Christologies This chapter compares Mark, Matthew, Luke, and John as four related but not interchangeable ancient literary compositions. Its aim is neither to produce a continuous gospel harmony nor to transform every divergence into an insoluble contradiction. The historical-critical comparison begins with a more demanding principle: each Gospel must first be read according to its own narrative architecture, language, sources, community context, and theological programme; only then can the parallel accounts be compared. In a monograph on the first to fourth centuries, this comparison is crucial because the four Gospels were transformed, during the second century, into a normative collection without thereby losing their differences. The Gospels cannot be dated with absolute years. The proposed dates depend on internal evidence, their relationship to the Jewish-Roman War and the destruction of the Temple, the literary dependence between texts, the history of their reception, and the earliest manuscript evidence. Working ranges and degrees of probability are therefore used. The dates of the surviving manuscripts are also not dates of composition: a papyrus from the second century proves the text was in circulation by that time, but not the exact year the Gospel was written. 347

348 early christianity 1. Probable dates and composition context Mark is usually placed roughly between 65 and 75 CE, with a concentration of proposals around 70. The prophecy concerning the destruction of the Temple in Mark 13 can be read as an earlier prophetic tradition, as redacted in light of the war, or as a combination of both. The date cannot be mechanically deduced from a single verse. Matthew and Luke-Acts are placed, in most contemporary scholarship, after Mark and usually between 80 and 95, although earlier and later proposals exist. Dependence on Mark, when accepted, establishes a relative terminus: Matthew and Luke must be later than the Markan text they used. John presents a different problem. The fourth Gospel shares characters, events, and traditions with the Synoptic Gospels, but it organises the ministry differently and presents its own Christological language. A dating to around 90–100 CE remains a common working hypothesis, although the composition history may have been layered and some materials may be earlier. John’s presence in second-century papyri rules out excessively late chronologies, but it does not justify converting the palaeography of P52 into an exact date of composition. Table 76. Do not automatically identify “expulsion from the synagogue” with a universally datable measure. 2. Mark: narrative priority, messianic secret, and passion Mark is the shortest of the canonical Gospels and, according to the most widely accepted view today, the primary narrative text used by Matthew and Luke. Its opening lacks an infancy narrative: Jesus appears as an adult in relation to John the Baptist. The narrative moves rapidly from Galilee to Jerusalem. Jesus’ identity is revealed gradually and paradoxically. The demons know who he is; the disciples understand incompletely; Peter makes a messianic confession that must immediately be redefined by the announcement of the Passion. The so-called “messianic secret” should not be reduced to a single key, but it aptly describes the tension between manifestation and concealment that structures numerous episodes. The Passion occupies an extraordinary proportion of the narrative. The centurion at the foot of the cross marks a point of narrative recognition, while the older ending of Mark 16:1–8 concludes with the women’s fear and silence. The expansion in 16:9–20 belongs to the later history of transmission and reception. This fact is philologically important: the comparison of the Easter appearances must distinguish the oldest reconstructible Markan text from the secondary endings that harmonise or expand the narrative.

350 early christianity 3. Matthew: fulfilment, Torah and community Matthew reworks much of Mark’s Gospel, but reorganises the material through large discursive blocks and a dense network of fulfilment quotations. His Gospel introduces a genealogy tracing back to Abraham and an infancy narrative centred on Joseph, the Magi, Herod, the flight to Egypt, and the return. This sequence situates Jesus within the history of Israel through Mosaic, Davidic, and prophetic motifs. The phrase “so that it might be fulfilled” should not be treated as mere evidence of isolated predictions; it forms part of a scriptural hermeneutic in which events and texts from Israel are reread as shaping the identity of Jesus. The relationship with the Law is more complex than an opposition between “Judaism” and “Christianity.” Matthew 5:17–20 affirms that Jesus did not come to abolish the Law and the Prophets; the antitheses of the Sermon on the Mount intensify or reorient commandments rather than offering an undifferentiated abolition. At the same time, Matthew contains very severe polemics against scribes and Pharisees. Historically, this language may reflect conflicts of proximity between groups that disputed authority over Scripture, practice, and the memory of Israel. One should not project onto the 80s CE a universal institutional separation as though it had already taken place. 4. Luke: salvation history, Spirit and openness to the nations Luke begins with a historiographical prologue that acknowledges the existence of “many” earlier accounts and declares a plan for ordering them. His Gospel should be read together with Acts as a two-volume work, although the exact conditions of its publication and circulation remain a subject of debate. The infancy narrative focuses alternately on John the Baptist and Jesus, introduces hymns, and situates the events against the backdrop of imperial and priestly history. The genealogy traces back to Adam, not just Abraham, and fosters a universalising perspective. Luke develops with particular intensity the action of the Spirit, prayer, the reversal of status, wealth and poverty, the inclusion of marginalised figures, and the journey of the word from Galilee to Jerusalem and, in Acts, from Jerusalem to Rome. Lucan theology does not eliminate judgement or eschatology; it integrates them into a narrative that must explain the continuity of the movement over a longer historical period. The question of the “delay of the Parousia” must be formulated carefully: Luke does not abandon future expectation, but rather reconfigures the temporality of the mission.

the canonical gospels in comparison 351 5. John: pre-existence, signs and a different chronology John opens with a prologue about the Logos, not with genealogy or baptism. The pre-existence of Christ is formulated in language that connects creation, life, light, and revelation. Throughout the Gospel, miracles are “signs” that point to the identity of Jesus; the “I am” discourses develop a Christology in which the relationship between Father and Son is central. This elevated formulation does not justify describing John as merely a product of external Greek philosophy: his vocabulary is also constructed through Jewish Scripture, festivals, the Temple, Wisdom, Exodus, and messianic traditions. The Johannine chronology differs from that of the Synoptic Gospels on several substantive points. John mentions multiple Passovers and presents a ministry that may extend over more than two years; the cleansing of the Temple appears at the beginning, not in the final week. Jesus’ death is linked to the preparation for Passover in a way that differs from the Synoptic sequence of the Last Supper. These differences cannot be erased by automatic harmonisation. They constitute narrative and chronological choices that require independent evaluation. 6. The synoptic problem: dependence, sources, and limits of reconstruction Mark, Matthew, and Luke share sequences, vocabulary, and episodes with a degree of overlap that necessitates some kind of literary relationship. The Two-Source Hypothesis explains this relationship through the priority of Mark and a hypothetical source, Q, for material shared by Matthew and Luke but absent from Mark. Q is a critical reconstruction, not a surviving manuscript. Its usefulness depends on whether it better explains the double tradition than the alternatives. The Farrer hypothesis (Austin Farrer, “On Dispensing with Q”, 1955) dispenses with Q and proposes that Luke used Matthew in addition to Mark; other theories posit different patterns of dependence. Q is treated here as a critical hypothesis rather than as a materially attested source, and Luke’s use of Matthew is not regarded as established. The comparative apparatus adopts Markan priority as a robust working hypothesis while marking explicitly those loci at which the direction of dependence remains disputed. Source criticism is paired with redaction criticism: where Matthew or Luke systematically recasts a Markan formulation, the alteration may illuminate an evangelist’s theological or narrative priorities, although its precise motivation cannot always be recovered.

352 early christianity 7. Infancy narratives: genealogies, conception and geographies requiring mediation to be reconciled Only Matthew and Luke contain birth narratives. Both affirm the virginal conception and birth in Bethlehem, but they differ in characters, sequence, motifs, and geographical movements. Matthew begins with a family apparently linked to Bethlehem, which receives the Magi, flees to Egypt and finally settles in Nazareth for fear of Archelaus. Luke’s narrative begins in Nazareth, brings Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem for a census, introduces shepherds and, after the rites in Jerusalem, returns to Nazareth. Attempting to merge both sequences into a single, comprehensive chronology requires introducing events that neither evangelist narrates. The genealogies also diverge from David to Joseph and attribute different names to Joseph’s father. Matthew organises three symbolic groups and traces the Davidic line through Solomon; Luke traces back from Jesus to Adam and follows another line from Nathan. Ancient explanations using legal and natural genealogies belong to reception history but are not explicitly stated in the Gospels. For historical criticism, this divergence shows that genealogies fulfil theological and scriptural functions in addition to any biographical claims. 8. Ministry, geography and chronology The Synoptic Gospels present a ministry dominated by Galilee, culminating in a final ascent to Jerusalem. John distributes the movement between Galilee and Judea from an early stage and mentions several festival visits to Jerusalem. The chronology of the cleansing of the Temple is the most visible example: at the beginning in John 2, at the end in the Synoptic Gospels. It is possible that John displaced the episode for theological reasons, that the Synoptic Gospels concentrated it within the Passion narrative, or that there were two separate episodes; the last possibility should not be adopted simply to eliminate the divergence, as we lack independent corroboration of two distinct events. Nor can the duration of the ministry be deduced by a simple addition. The Synoptic Gospels do not explicitly state that it lasted only one year, but their narrative mentions a final Passover; John offers a broader festal framework. Historically, the fourth Gospel can preserve independent chronological data and, at the same time, rearrange them theologically. The appropriate method is locus by locus, not a global preference for one Gospel as if it were a neutral chronicle.

the canonical gospels in comparison 353 9. Kingdom of God, eschatology and temporality In Mark and Matthew, the Kingdom is an explicit focus of preaching. Luke retains this language and integrates it with a perspective on the “time of the Church” and of the Spirit. John uses the expression “Kingdom of God” less frequently and emphasises eternal life, judgement, resurrection, and relationship with the Son. This lexical difference does not imply an absence of eschatology in John. In John 5, for example, future resurrection and judgement coexist with the present realisation of life for those who hear and believe. Different temporal perspectives are crucial for reconstructing the Christian diversity of the late first century. Some formulations maintain an intense expectation of imminent intervention; others explain the historical permanence of the community. It is incorrect to draw a simple line from “early apocalypticism” to “late deeschatologisation.” The same writings can combine present and future, imminence and delay, everyday ethics and final judgement. 10. Comparative Christologies The four Gospels identify Jesus through overlapping titles and narratives: Messiah / Christ, Son of God, Son of Man, Lord, teacher, and prophet. However, the distribution and weight of each title vary. Mark articulates identity and suffering; Matthew intensifies themes of fulfilment, Emmanuel, and teaching authority; Luke links identity with Spirit, salvation history, and lordship; John formulates pre-existence and functional unity with the Father in a particularly explicit way. The comparison should not be constructed as a simplistic scale from a “low” to a “high” Christology. Paul’s letters, which predate the Gospels, already contain elevated formulations about Christ; Mark can narrate divine authority without employing Johannine vocabulary; John, in turn, preserves humanity, death, and conflict. It is more accurate to describe Christological profiles: different ways of articulating divine agency, sonship, messiahship, pre-existence, death, and vindication. 11. Passion: Last Supper, date and words from the cross The Passion narrative offers a broad common ground: entry into Jerusalem, conflict, arrest, trial, crucifixion under Pontius Pilate, death, and burial. However, the details present significant divergences. The Synoptic Gospels describe the Last Supper within a Passover context; John situates Jesus’ death in relation to the preparation for Passover and constructs his own Passover symbolism. The exact chronology remains

354 early christianity debated. It is not methodologically legitimate to claim that the two sequences say the same thing when the texts organise the feast differently. The words of Jesus from the cross also vary. Mark and Matthew preserve the cry of abandonment; Luke presents words of forgiveness and trust; John includes the relationship between Jesus, his mother, and the beloved disciple, and culminates with “τετέλεσται”. The traditional “seven last words” are a later devotional harmonisation formed by combining the Gospels. As objects of reception, they are historically important; as a reconstruction of a single spoken sequence, they should not be confused with the independent testimony of each source. 12. Resurrection: similarities and differences All four canonical Gospels place women among the first witnesses of the empty tomb, but they differ in the number of women, messengers, reactions, and appearances. Mark, in its earliest ending, concludes at 16:8 without an appearance of Jesus. Matthew locates a decisive appearance in Galilee; Luke concentrates the first day and the appearances around Jerusalem and culminates in the ascension; John combines Jerusalem and Galilee and offers his own scenes with Mary Magdalene, Thomas, and the miraculous catch of fish in John 21. These differences are historically productive. They show that the Easter confession was narrated through multiple traditions before its canonical stabilisation. Paul’s letters, especially 1 Corinthians 15, predate the Gospels and offer another list of appearances. Critical history must compare the traditions without assuming that one list exhausts all others or that every divergence invalidates the common core: death, burial, conviction of appearance/vindication, and the rapid centrality of the resurrection in the Christian proclamation. Law, Israel and Gentiles The Gospels emerged from a movement born within Judaism and must be interpreted without turning their internal controversies into a later racial or religious map. Matthew can be intensely polemical against Jewish leaders and, at the same time, profoundly scriptural and legal. Luke-Acts establishes continuity with Israel while narrating an expansion to Gentiles. John uses polemical expressions about “the Jews” whose referent shifts from scene to scene and which, read out of context, contributed to later anti-Jewish receptions. A scholarly edition must distinguish ancient narrative conflict from generalisations against Judaism as a whole. The mission to the Gentiles also does not appear in an identical form. Matthew combines an initial restriction of the mission with a final universal commission; Luke anticipates a light for the nations from infancy and develops the expansion in Acts; John formulates universality through language of world, life, and attraction. The differences correspond both to traditions and to the situations of communities that were negotiating their heritage from Israel, ethnic identity, and Mediterranean expansion.

356 early christianity 14. Textual transmission: literary divergence and manuscript variant are not the same The comparison of the Gospels must distinguish between two phenomena. A divergence between Mark and Matthew pertains to the relationship between different works; a variant among manuscripts of Mark pertains to the transmission of the same work. Modern textual criticism reconstructs the text from papyri, uncials, minuscules, versions, and patristic quotations. Some loci acquired special importance precisely because later scribes harmonised parallel texts, added endings, or made titles explicit. Mark 16:9–20 and John 7:53–8:11 are classic examples of textual units whose manuscript history requires a critical apparatus. The pericope of the adulteress circulated in different positions and is absent from several early witnesses; its extraordinary importance in Christian reception does not automatically make its Johannine placement part of the earliest reconstructible textual state. A scholarly edition must preserve both textual history and reception history. 15. Why do the Gospels differ? The divergences do not require a single explanation. Some stem from literary dependence: one evangelist abbreviates, expands, or rearranges a source. Others may derive from different oral or written traditions. Some reflect narrative theology: Matthew organises the material around fulfilment and teaching; Luke integrates episodes into a geography of salvation; John reconfigures feasts and signs. Other differences may reflect distinct historical information, local memory, or the development of community controversies. Finally, manuscript transmission introduced additional variations. Therefore, the critical question is not “Which gospel tells the truth?” in the singular, but rather what kind of claim each makes, what evidence supports it, and what can be reconstructed through independent comparison. In ancient history, complete agreement is not a condition of documentary value. Partially dependent, biased, and divergent sources are the normal material for historical reconstruction. The historian’s discipline lies in neither granting a source a neutrality it lacks nor dismissing its testimony simply because it is theologically constructed.

358 early christianity 16.1. Redaction criticism and intertextuality with the Scriptures of Israel Redaction criticism remains useful provided that it is not made to recover inaccessible authorial psychology with unwarranted confidence. The final form of each Gospel displays observable literary decisions: Matthew reorganises and expands Markan material around scriptural fulfilment, teaching, and communal discipline; Luke relocates episodes within a narrative geography that moves from Galilee to Jerusalem and, in Acts, from Jerusalem into the Mediterranean world; John constructs a sequence of signs and discourses that cannot be reduced to a simple enlargement of the Synoptic scheme. These are textual observations; identifying a specific community behind each decision requires a further degree of inference. Intertextuality requires the same discipline. Isaiah, the Psalms, Daniel, Zechariah, and other scriptural repertoires provide vocabulary, scenes, and narrative patterns for all four Gospels, but the relationship ranges from explicit quotation to probable allusion and broad thematic resemblance. Mark opens with a composite scriptural citation; Matthew multiplies fulfilment formulae; Luke shapes canticles and prophetic scenes; John rereads signs, festivals, and biblical figures through a Christology of preexistence. Analysis is most precise when it identifies the locus, the relevant Greek or Hebrew textual form, and its literary function rather than accumulating undifferentiated parallels. 17. Kloppenborg, works on Q; and critical studies on the Farrer and Two-Source Hypotheses. For Mark, Joel Marcus and Adela Yarbro Collins; for Matthew, Ulrich Luz and W.D. Davies/Dale Allison; for Luke-Acts, Joseph Fitzmyer, François Bovon, and C. Kavin Rowe; for John, Raymond E. Brown, C.K. Barrett, J. Louis Martyn, and later works that revise the model of an overly unified “Johannine community.” For the historical Jesus, the comparison is made independently of any single criterion of authenticity, taking into account memory, tradition, and context. Greek text editions should be checked against Nestle-Aland 28 and UBS5, with consultation of specialised critical apparatuses when a locus requires it. A Gospel synopsis should not replace the continuous reading of each Gospel. Papyri such as P52, P66, P75, and P45 are used for transmission history, not as absolute calendars of composition. Patristic quotations from Papias, Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, and

the canonical gospels in comparison 359 Origen belong to reception history and should be dated according to the surviving testimony. Conclusion The four Gospels preserved four portraits that Christian communities of the second to fourth centuries did not reduce to a single, harmonised biography. This gradually achieved canonical configuration is a historical fact of major importance: subsequent norms were built upon an internal plurality. Mark, Matthew, Luke, and John share a fundamental plot—Jesus, ministry, conflict, crucifixion, and Easter proclamation— but differ in chronology, selection, language, and Christology. The scholarly task consists of keeping these differences visible and explaining, when the evidence allows, their literary and historical causes. Where a decision cannot be reached, uncertainty must be preserved as part of knowledge. Read alongside Marcion and Tatian, the fourfold Gospel emerges as a third editorial response to the problem of plurality: in contrast to the selection of a single corpus and to harmonisation into one continuous narrative, the solution defended by Irenaeus preserves four distinct compositions within a common normative framework. This synthesis links Chapters II and XXI and avoids treating canon, harmonisation, and synoptic criticism as separate histories. Summary This chapter compares the four canonical Gospels as related but distinct ancient compositions. It examines probable dating, the Synoptic Problem, infancy narratives, chronology, geography, Torah and Gentile mission, Christology, passion and resurrection traditions, and textual transmission. Each divergence is assessed in relation to literary dependence, redaction, independent tradition, historical memory, theological construction, and manuscript transmission. The fourfold Gospel canon is therefore treated as preserving, from the second century onward, an internal plurality of narratives rather than erasing it.

chapter xxii Christian Apocalypses and Eschatological Horizons of the First and Second Centuries: Christ, Empire, Nero Redivivus and Interreligious Comparison The Book of Revelation is one of the richest witnesses for studying how a Christian current of the late first century imagined Christ, the empire, judgement, and the consummation of history. Its language cannot be reduced to a code of modern predictions. It belongs to the apocalyptic genre, combining prophetic vision, circular letter, liturgy, scriptural exegesis, and symbolic critique of power. This chapter places it alongside Jewish and Christian apocalypses of the first and second centuries and, with greater caution, alongside Iranian eschatological traditions and the politico-religious themes of the Roman world. Interreligious comparison demands a strict rule. A structural similarity—final judgement, resurrection, saviour, cosmic battle, destruction of evil—does not, in itself, demonstrate textual dependence. Three cases must be distinguished: (a) typological parallels, which can arise in different cultures; (b) historically possible contact, when compatible networks, chronology, and geography exist; and (c) probable or demonstrable dependence, when the transmission of specific forms, vocabulary, or sequences can be identified. This hierarchy, refined into four levels in section 14, avoids both the confessional isolation of the Book of Revelation and indiscriminate comparativism. 360

christian apocalypses and eschatological… 361 1. Date, genre and situation of the seven churches Revelation is frequently dated towards the end of Domitian’s reign, approximately 90–96 CE, partly due to the early reception associated with Irenaeus (Adv. haer. V.30.3, quoted by Eusebius, HE III.18.3). There are proposals for a Neronian or immediately post-Neronian date, especially when the motifs of 666 and Nero redivivus are emphasised. Internal evidence does not establish an unequivocal year. It is more prudent to speak of the end of the first century and to acknowledge that some images may preserve earlier material. The seven churches of Asia—Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea—form a specific historical geography. The letters in Revelation 2–3 depict conflicts over wealth, suffering, participation in civic-religious practices, prophecy, and authority. They do not necessarily describe a uniform imperial persecution. The pressure may include local hostility, social exclusion, the memory of martyrdom, and tension over the imperial cult. A historically accurate reading must avoid turning every metaphor of violence into evidence of a centralised state policy. Figure 26. The seven churches of Revelation 1:11 and Revelation 2–3 in Asia Minor. The points are approximate city centres; neither a route for John nor confessional boundaries are shown. 362 early christianity 2. The vision of Christ in Revelation 1 Revelation 1:12–18 presents a figure “like a son of man” among seven lampstands. The description combines motifs from Daniel 7 and 10 with priestly imagery, light, fire, a powerful voice, and authority over death and Hades. The result is not a physical portrait of Jesus, but a Christological theophany. Traits that in Daniel belong to the Ancient of Days and heavenly beings are reconfigured around the exalted Christ. This appropriation shows the extent to which apocalyptic Christology engages with the language of divine identity and agency without erasing the narrative distinction between God and the Lamb. The formula “the first and the last” connects the visionary Christ with language that in Isaiah belongs to the God of Israel. Similarly, the doxologies and worship scenes of Revelation 4–5 place the Lamb within heavenly worship. However, one must avoid translating this observation directly into fourth-century conciliar categories. The text offers material that later contributed to Trinitarian and Christological elaboration, but its own grammar is apocalyptic, liturgical, and scriptural. 3. The Lamb: victim, victor, and sovereign Revelation 5 constructs one of the central images of early Christianity: the seer hears the announcement of the Lion of Judah and sees, instead, a Lamb standing “as though it had been slain.” The paradox redefines victory through death and vindication. The Lamb receives the scroll, shares in the scene of worship, and appears as the agent of judgement and salvation. The image draws on Paschal, sacrificial, Isaian, and Messianic repertoires, but it is not limited to a single source. Compared to John 1:29, 36, where ἀμνός appears, Revelation predominantly uses ἀρνίον. The lexical difference does not prove two incompatible Christologies; rather, it cautions against automatically identifying all language of the “Lamb” as a fixed formula. In Revelation, the Lamb is simultaneously sacrificed, living, enthroned, and a warrior. This combination explains part of the power of its subsequent artistic and liturgical reception. 4. Son of Man, Messiah and divine titles The figure of the Son of Man links Revelation with Daniel, the Gospels, and other Jewish traditions. Revelation 14 presents “one like a son of man” with a crown and sickle, associated with the eschatological harvest. The text does not offer a systematic treatise on the natures of Christ; it operates through superimposed images. Davidic

christian apocalypses and eschatological… 363 Messiah, Lamb, faithful witness, rider, Word of God, and Son of Man converge in a single narrative figure without eliminating their different symbolic genealogies. Comparative study must also consider imperial titles. Emperors and benefactors could receive language of salvation, lordship, victory, epiphany, and divine filiation in inscriptions, coins, and ceremonial practices. The existence of this vocabulary creates an environment of political resonance, but it does not mean that every Christian title derives from the imperial cult. “Son of God” has biblical, Davidic, and Jewish roots; the imperial field functions as a competitive context where words of power could acquire an additional polemical edge. 5. Rome as Babylon and the problem of the empire Revelation 17–18 symbolically identifies a great city with Babylon, a woman drunk with blood, commercial power, and luxury. The association with Rome is historically strong due to the reference to seven hills, dominion over kings, and the memory of violence. “Babylon” allows for a reinterpretation of Rome through the biblical history of oppressive empires. The critique is neither exclusively economic nor exclusively religious: commerce, violence, idolatry, prestige, and domination form a single representation. The book cannot be reduced to a simple anti-Roman pamphlet. It uses the Empire’s own communication infrastructure to circulate among cities in Asia and employs a cosmological language in which Rome is a historical manifestation of a broader struggle. This universalisation makes its subsequent reception possible in very different contexts, but it also compels us to distinguish the initial historical referent from modern applications.

364 early christianity 6. 666/616, the beast and Nero redivivus Revelation 13:18 invites us to calculate the number of the beast. The reading 666 is strongly attested; 616 also has ancient manuscript support (P115 and Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus, C) and is crucial to the history of interpretation. The Hebrew transliteration ‫נרון קסר‬, “Nero Caesar,” totals 666; the form ‫נרו קסר‬, corresponding to the Latin name Nero without the final nun, totals 616. The calculation is performed using Hebrew letters, not the Latin letters of Nero Caesar. This correspondence is the main argument for the Neronian interpretation, which remains a hypothesis: 616 admits other explanations (for example, Γάιος Καῖσαρ also totals 616 in Greek), and Irenaeus (Haer. V.30) does not name Nero; problems of spelling, reception, and transmission also remain. The motif of Nero redivivus must be carefully distinguished from the Christological figure. After Nero’s death in 68, rumours circulated that he was still alive or would return from the East; impostors appeared, and the Sibylline traditions developed a returning Neronian figure of increasing eschatological significance. In Revelation 13 and 17, the wounded and restored beast and the king who “was, is not, and is to come” may resonate with this complex of expectations. The connection is plausible and, for many interpreters, strong; however, it does not warrant the assertion that the Roman world uniformly believed in a “Nero, the resurrected son of God, who returns as judge.” Imperial titulature could style an emperor divi filius, “son of the deified one,” and the imperial cult can bestow upon him superhuman honours. This is distinct from a doctrine of resurrection comparable to the Christian proclamation of Jesus. Nero redivivus functions best as a political and eschatological counter-figure: a returning king, enemy, persecutor, or instrument of catastrophe. It is precisely this difference that allows for a more rigorous comparison between the dead and living Lamb and the imperial parody of a beast that seems to survive its mortal wound. 7. Daniel, 1 Enoch and the Jewish archive of apocalypticism The immediate horizon of Revelation is the Jewish Scriptures. Daniel provides imperial beasts, thrones, judgement, a time of tribulation, and the figure “like a son of man.” Ezekiel contributes visions, scrolls, measurements of the Temple, and Gog/ Magog; Isaiah contributes to the new creation and the defeat of powers; Exodus structures plagues and deliverance. Revelation rarely quotes by explicit formula: it rewrites and combines images, so that intertextuality must be analysed by density and function, not just by exact verbal coincidence.

Both reflect on divine justice, Israel’s suffering, the fate of the world, and consummation. 4 Esdras presents intense dialogues on the problem of evil and the small number of those who will inherit the world to come; 2 Baruch combines lamentation, instruction, and messianic expectations. The parallel with Revelation lies less in direct dependence than in the way roughly contemporary texts transform historical catastrophe into an eschatological question. The differences are equally important. Revelation organises the conflict around the testimony of Jesus and the identity of the Lamb; 4 Esdras and 2 Baruch respond from Jewish frameworks that do not share that Christology. Comparison reveals the same historical problem—empire, destruction, justice—and distinct theological responses. This avoids defining apocalyptic literature solely by its spectacular imagery and frames it as a discourse on the legitimacy of God when history appears to be dominated by unjust powers.

Christian apocalypses of the first and second centuries The Ascension of Isaiah, in its complex compositional history, combines martyrdom, celestial journey, and a Christology of descent/ascent. Its stratified structure makes a single date difficult, but Christian elements belong to the early centuries. The Apocalypse of Peter, probably from the second century, develops scenes of post-mortem reward and punishment with a concreteness that would influence later imagery. The Shepherd of Hermas, while not an apocalypse in the same sense as John’s, uses visions, angels, symbols, and penitential exhortation to address the moral situation of a Roman community. These texts show that the Christian apocalyptic genre did not follow a single direction. John articulates empire, martyrdom, and new creation; the Apocalypse of Peter emphasises the destinies of the afterlife; Hermas transforms vision into communal discipline; the Ascension of Isaiah imagines movements through heavens and powers. The comparison shows how revelation could legitimise authority and conduct rather than merely predict the end. 10. Zoroastrianism: Saoshyant, resurrection and renewal The Iranian tradition offers one of the most illuminating—and methodologically hazardous—comparative dossiers when chronology is neglected. The late Avesta attests the Saoshyant, the final victory over evil, the resurrection of the dead, and the renewal of existence (frašō.kərəti). Yt 19 describes a future world without old age, decay, or death. These motifs predate the medieval Pahlavi treatises, although the more systematic narratives of the final stages, the molten metal, and the sequence of saviours are preserved in later sources and should not be projected wholesale back onto the first century. The comparison with the Book of Revelation can be organised around five axes: cosmic conflict between good and evil; eschatological agent; resurrection; judgement; and renewal of the world. In both systems, history does not end in mere destruction but in transformation. However, the differences are profound: the Lamb is defined by the death and vindication of Jesus within a Jewish biblical framework; the Saoshyant belongs to an Iranian tradition and remains, in its classical formulation, an eschatological human agent linked to Zarathustra. The similarity of function does not make one a copy of the other. Long-term contact among the Iranian, Mesopotamian, Jewish, and Hellenistic worlds made the circulation of motifs historically possible. Demonstrating a specific influence on the Apocalypse of John, however, requires a more concrete chain of

Zoroastrian traditions therefore serve here as a major comparative horizon and as a possible remote component in the eschatological environment of Second Temple Judaism; they are not presented as evidence of direct dependence by John. 11. Judgement, resurrection and new creation Revelation 20–22 culminates in the defeat of hostile powers, judgement before the great white throne, resurrection, the lake of fire, and the new Jerusalem. The sequence combines the Jewish tradition of resurrection with an eschatological city in which the Temple disappears because God and the Lamb constitute its sanctuary. The final image is not a simple return to Eden: it is a garden city where the river, the tree of life, nations, and glory reconfigure Genesis, the prophets, and expectations of restoration. In 4 Esdras and 2 Baruch, final justice responds to the trauma of history; in Iranian traditions, renewal ultimately eliminates corruption and death; in the Apocalypse of Peter, the emphasis is on rewards and punishments. This comparison identifies a shared grammar of deferred justice: the present order does not offer a sufficient correspondence between virtue and destiny, so revelation imagines a judgement that restores justice. The differences lie in who judges, how the cosmos is transformed, and what role the Messiah or Christ plays. 12. The “Son of God” in a world of sovereigns, heroes, and saviours The title “son of God” must be contextualised within various registers. In Israel, it can be applied to the Davidic king, the people, or celestial beings; in the GrecoRoman world, there are divine genealogies of heroes and rulers, and the imperial prince could be defined as the son of a deified emperor. Christianity reused an available vocabulary but integrated it into a Jewish narrative of creation, messianism, the cross, and resurrection. The comparison must analyse specific functions and not assume that the mere coincidence of an expression establishes historical filiation. Nero illustrates the problem. His membership in the imperial house and the language of deification in the Principate form part of the political backdrop, but the traditions of his return do not amount to the proclamation of a benevolent resurrected saviour. In Sibylline and Christian sources, he can become a destructive figure. If Revelation plays with a monstrous imitation of death and return, the

380 early christianity 13.4. Daniel, Isaiah, and Zechariah as scriptural matrices of Revelation The scriptural density of Revelation depends less on formal quotations than on a network of allusions. Daniel supplies beasts, horns, thrones, judgement, and the language of sovereignty; Isaiah contributes imagery of new creation, nations, and restoration; Zechariah offers horses, lampstands, and visionary scenes that John reconfigures. Ezekiel, Exodus, and the Psalms complete a repertoire in which Roman imperial language is interpreted through biblical images already charged with political and theological memory. Intertextuality should therefore not be reduced to a search for linear “sources”. John combines, displaces, and superimposes formulations within a new visionary architecture. Philological analysis must distinguish lexical coincidence, shared motif, and structural reuse; historical analysis must also allow for the textual plurality of the Greek Scriptures and that an allusion may depend on liturgical or mnemonic repertoires without implying direct copying from a single scroll. 14. The comparative method adopted here does not confuse similarity with filiation. Two traditions may share images of judgement, resurrection, cosmic combat, or renewal without either having borrowed the motif from the other. A claim of historical dependence requires more than resemblance: it must also be supported by chronological proximity, a plausible route of transmission, sufficiently specific correspondences, and an account of the significant differences. Four levels of evaluation are used. [P] Parallel: typological similarity without any claim of contact. [C] Possible contact: geographical or cultural coexistence that makes circulation of the motif conceivable, but without a demonstrable chain. [T] Probable transmission: specific convergence accompanied by identifiable historical mediations. [D] Demonstrable dependence: a textual or documentary relationship sufficiently strong to support a line of transmission. Most ancient interreligious comparisons do not rise above the first two levels. This scale is especially necessary when comparing with Zoroastrianism. Persian rule over Jewish populations, Mesopotamian networks, and the continuity of Jewish communities in Iranian territories constitute real historical conditions of contact. However, an eschatological system reconstructed from medieval Pahlavi texts cannot be directly transposed to the first century. The analysis therefore separates the motif, source, and date of the witness. The same principle applies to the Sibylline Oracles and Nero redivivus. Here, the chronological proximity and the imperial context are greater, but the relationship with Revelation remains one of historical reconstruction: John nowhere identifies the beast with Nero by name. The 666/616 dossier, the healed wound, the sequence of kings, and the return traditions constitute a convergent whole, not an explicit inscription of the emperor’s name in the text. Numerological, geometric, or Neoplatonic constructions that cannot be supported by an ancient documentary chain are excluded from the explanatory apparatus. The number of the beast is studied through manuscript tradition, ancient procedures of nominal calculation, the imperial context, and early reception; not through modern correspondences or retrospective symbolic systems.

Christian reception: from expectation to canon The status of the Book of Revelation was debated in different regions. It was strongly received by authors such as Justin Martyr (Dial. 81.4) and Irenaeus, especially in relation to millenarian expectations, while other contexts showed reservations. Dionysius of Alexandria, as transmitted by Eusebius (HE VII.25), used stylistic arguments to question the attribution of Revelation to the John who wrote the Gospel. This fact is crucial: Christians of the second and third centuries could accept the text as scripture and, at the same time, discuss its authorship, interpretation, and relationship to other Johannine writings. Canonisation did not eliminate exegetical diversity. Millenarian, allegorical, historicist, liturgical, and political readings coexisted. For a history of Christianity across the first four centuries, it is less important to decide which later reading is “correct” than to observe how the book offered a vocabulary for thinking about persecution, empire, heresy, martyrdom, Christ’s triumph, and consummation. Its plasticity explains both its centrality and its hermeneutical danger when it is disconnected from its ancient context.

christian apocalypses and eschatological… 383 16. Critical apparatus and verification sources Greek text: Nestle-Aland 28/UBS5, with special attention to Revelation 13:18 (666/ 616), Revelation 1:8, 11, and other loci where tradition presents significant variants. For historical-literary commentary, the works consulted include David E. Aune, Revelation; Adela Yarbro Collins, Crisis and Catharsis; Craig R. Koester, Revelation; Richard Bauckham, The Climax of Prophecy; and the works of John J. Collins on Jewish apocalyptic literature. The relationship with the imperial cult should be tested against epigraphy, numismatics, and the provincial history of Asia and not inferred solely from the Christian text. For 4 Esdras and 2 Baruch, critical editions and studies of post-70 CE apocalyptic literature are used. For the Ascension of Isaiah, Shepherd of Hermas, and Apocalypse of Peter, dates are expressed as ranges, and composition is distinguished from the date of surviving manuscripts. For Nero redivivus, Suetonius, Tacitus, Cassius Dio, the Neronian impostors, and the Sibylline Oracles are considered, distinguishing the date of each stratum. For Iranian eschatology, the Avesta, especially Yt 19, and studies by Mary Boyce, William Malandra, and the Encyclopaedia Iranica are consulted; late Pahlavi texts are cited as sources of reception and systematisation, not as first-century documents. 17. Conclusion: the vision of Christ at the end of the first century The Book of Revelation testifies to a Christology of the late first century in which Jesus does not appear simply as a remembered teacher. He is the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, the slain and enthroned Lamb, the victorious rider, the Word of God, and a figure like a son of man. He shares the roles of judgement and worship within a reconfigured monotheistic vision. This profile should be compared with contemporary gospels and letters to understand the plurality of Christological languages before the councils, not to project Nicene definitions back onto it. The eschatological horizon of the text is likewise multifaceted. Its primary source is the Jewish Scriptures; its historical enemy is formulated through the language of empire and Babylon; the Neronian motif offers a powerful political key; and comparisons with other Jewish, Christian, and Iranian apocalyptic texts show that the expectation of judgement and renewal was part of a much broader religious context. John’s historical originality lies not in having invented each motif, but in the particular arrangement that brings them together around the Lamb and concrete communities in Asia Minor.

384 early christianity Summary This chapter situates the Apocalypse of John within the apocalyptic cultures of the late first and second centuries. It examines the visionary Christ, the Lamb, the images of the Son of Man, Rome as Babylon, 666/616, and the Nero redivivus complex; it compares the work with Daniel, 1 Enoch, 4 Esdras, 2 Baruch, early Christian apocalypses, and Zoroastrian eschatology. It distinguishes structural parallels, historically plausible contacts, and demonstrable dependencies. Zoroastrian resurrection and renewal provide a relevant comparative horizon, but later Pahlavi systematisations must respect their own chronology. Nero is treated as a returning imperial adversary, without being equated with the resurrected Christ.

chapter xxiii Asceticism, Continence, and the Formation of Monasticism (First–Fourth Centuries) Christian asceticism long predates the institutional consolidation of monasticism. Fasting, sexual continence, renunciation of property, consecrated widowhood, and disciplines of the body are already attested in first- and second-century sources, yet they do not amount to a homogeneous monastic institution. The task, therefore, is to distinguish these earlier ascetic practices from the eremitic and cenobitic forms that took more recognisable shape in the course of the third and fourth centuries. 1. Paul, marriage and continence 1 Corinthians 7 provides the earliest substantial documentary point of departure. Paul values continence within an eschatological horizon, while at the same time recognising marriage and articulating reciprocal obligations between spouses. His personal preference for celibacy should not be retrojected as a monastic rule into communities for which no such institution yet existed. The Pastoral Epistles, whatever their precise dating, reflect a different social configuration, marked by households, widows, and increasingly explicit criteria for ecclesial office. The contrast underscores a central methodological point: asceticism must be studied as a historically situated option rather than treated as an intrinsic essence of earliest Christianity. 385

386 early christianity 2. Widows, virgins, and ascetic continence in the second and third centuries The Didache, the Shepherd of Hermas, Ignatius, Tertullian, Clement of Alexandria, and Cyprian attest to disciplines of fasting, sexual continence, and widowhood. Yet these categories are not socially or institutionally equivalent across regions: a widow maintained by a community, an ascetic virgin, and an Encratite teacher occupy distinct positions and cannot be collapsed into a single type. Traditions associated with Tatian and with so-called Encratism show that the renunciation of marriage could acquire explicit doctrinal force. The label “Encratite”, however, is largely inherited from classificatory and heresiological authors and should not be assumed to denote a single, coherent organisation. 3. Thecla and the ascetic imagination The Acts of Paul and Thecla, generally dated to the second century, display with particular clarity the narrative force of female asceticism: Thecla rejects marriage, teaches, confronts martyrdom, and is associated with baptism. The work is therefore an important witness to ideals of continence and female authority, but not an independent biography of a historical collaborator of Paul. 4. Egypt: Antony, Pachomius, and the institutionalisation of monastic life Athanasius’s Life of Antony, composed in the fourth century, was decisive in the wider diffusion of the eremitic ideal. Yet the Antony presented there is also a literary and episcopal construction. Letters, parallel traditions, documentary evidence, and monastic archaeology make it possible to place that influential portrait within a more complex historical field. Pachomius and the Egyptian cenobitic communities represent a different configuration: rules, labour, common meals, internal hierarchies, and forms of collective ownership organised a durable communal life. Eremitism and cenobitism should not, however, be arranged as successive stages in a single linear evolution.

asceticism, continence, and the formation… 387 5. Syria, Cappadocia and monastic diversity Syrian and Mesopotamian ascetic traditions developed distinctive vocabularies and institutional forms; in Cappadocia, Basil and the networks associated with Macrina bring ascetic discipline into relation with communal life, hospitality, and organised care. Late-antique monasticism is thus best understood as a polycentric history rather than as the simple diffusion of a single Egyptian model. 5.1. Egyptian trajectories before cenobitic codification The emergence of Egyptian monasticism cannot be reconstructed solely from the biographies of celebrated founders. Papyri, letters, property documents, and archaeological remains reveal a far more varied landscape of withdrawal, labour, and ascetic association. The “desert” itself was crossed by villages, routes, estates, quarries, and links with urban centres; physical distance from the city could therefore operate as an ascetic discipline without entailing complete social isolation. This evidence requires a careful distinction among anchorites, small ascetic groups, and formally regulated communities. Antony cannot stand for the whole of eremitic life, any more than Pachomius can be treated as the inventor of every form of collective asceticism. Fourth-century sources construct normative genealogies within a more heterogeneous reality, in which bodily discipline, manual labour, reading, patronage, and charismatic authority could be combined in markedly different ways. 5.2. Syria and Mesopotamia: continence, covenant, and non-Egyptian ascetic forms In Syria and Mesopotamia, ascetic vocabulary followed trajectories of its own. The valuation of continence, the “sons and daughters of the covenant”, and other forms of dedicated life show that rigorous asceticism could remain embedded within urban and ecclesial communities without assuming the form of Egyptian desert withdrawal. Fourth-century Syriac sources disclose combinations of celibacy, ecclesial service, hymnody, and communal discipline, and thus caution against writing the history of monasticism as a one-way diffusion from Egypt to passive peripheries.
