chapter xxiv Magic, Amulets, Exorcism, and Protective Material Culture in Early Christianity The category of “magic” is historically unstable. In the Roman world, practices of protection, healing, divination, and ritual coercion could be classified as superstition, magic, medicine, philosophy, or religion depending on the observer, genre, and polemical setting. Analysis should therefore begin with objects, formulae, agents, and contexts of use rather than with a modern boundary between legitimate religion and illegitimate magic. 1. Acts and the polemic against ritual specialists Acts 8, 13, and 19 construct figures such as Simon, Elymas, and the Ephesian practitioners who burn their books. These episodes disclose competition over ritual authority and thaumaturgical power, but they cannot be read as a neutral catalogue of magical professions or practices. 2. Exorcism and healing The Gospels place exorcism at the centre of Jesus’ public activity, and Christian sources of the second and third centuries continue to present it as a manifestation of divine power. Justin Martyr, Tertullian, and Origen also deploy exorcism apologetically. Historical analysis must therefore distinguish the practice itself from literary representations that may magnify its scope or effectiveness. 389

390 early christianity 3. Papyri, gems and amulets Egyptian papyri and amulets preserve psalms, divine names, signs, abbreviations, Gospel incipits, and protective formulae. Some objects can be identified as Christian with considerable confidence; others combine Jewish, Greek, Egyptian, and Christian repertoires. Such mixtures of vocabulary do not in themselves demonstrate a stable syncretic identity and may instead reflect the pragmatic logic of the object and its intended efficacy. The so-called Greek magical papyri are a modern editorial corpus that brings together materials from widely differing dates and contexts. They should not be treated as though they represented a single, unitary “magical religion” existing in parallel with Christianity. 4. Medicine, relics and ritual boundaries A protective formula, the laying on of hands, oil, a relic, or a medical prescription may all serve therapeutic or apotropaic functions without belonging to the same regime of authority. Comparison becomes historically informative when medium, agent, formula, recipient, and context are specified; it becomes misleading when functional resemblance is allowed to stand as evidence of dependence. 4.1. The amulet as object: medium, inscription, and bodily use The analysis of an amulet cannot end with the transcription of its formula. Material, dimensions, folding, perforation, container, traces of use, and archaeological context all require documentation, since these features bear directly on the ways in which the inscribed text was intended to operate upon the body and within domestic space. A Gospel fragment worn at the neck, an inscribed lamella deposited in a grave, and an engraved gem may share an apotropaic purpose without belonging to the same chain of production or ritual repertoire. The presence of nomina sacra, crosses, voces magicae, angelic names, or biblical incipits is likewise insufficient, on its own, to classify an artefact as “orthodox”, “magical”, or “syncretic”. Attribution must rest on the convergence of formula, palaeography, iconography, provenance, and comparanda. This discipline is particularly important for unprovenanced material, since the modern antiquities market may have severed an object from precisely the contextual information required for responsible interpretation.

magic, amulets, exorcism, and protective… 391 4.2. Defixiones, cursing, and the limits of attribution Greco-Roman defixiones provide an indispensable comparandum because they document technologies of ritual writing—names, binding formulae, invocations, and deposition in particular places—that could coexist with other protective uses of text. Yet identifying a curse tablet as Christian requires more than the appearance of a biblical name or a cross. Religious repertoires across the Empire shared signs and names, while formulae could circulate without stable confessional ownership. Attribution should therefore remain graded, explicit, and open to revision. Table 89. chapter xxv Childhood, Family, Marriage and Household in Christian Communities (First–Fourth Centuries) Early Christianity developed within households, kinship networks, workshops, and relations of dependency. The “Christian family” was never a homogeneous social unit: married couples, widows, enslaved people, freedpeople, patrons, children, ascetics, and religiously mixed households coexisted within the same social world. This chapter reconstructs that domestic sphere without projecting the assumptions of the modern nuclear family onto the Roman Mediterranean. 1. Oikos, domus, and household communities The Pauline letters attest assemblies meeting in houses and networks of hosts who made such gatherings possible. The household was not merely a private space: it could also be an economic unit, a workshop, a locus of patronage, and a setting for communal meetings. “House church” should therefore be understood primarily as a mode of gathering, not as evidence for a specialised Christian architecture in the first century. 2. Marriage, sexuality and mixed households 1 Corinthians 7 attests marriages between believers and non-believers, separation, continence, and reciprocal obligations. The Deutero-Pauline and Pastoral Epistles reflect other forms of domestic discipline. The so-called Haustafeln should be compared with wider Greco-Roman moral discourse, but not reduced to the direct reproduction of any single philosophical school. 392

childhood, family, marriage and household… 393 3. Children, birth and baptism Children appear unevenly across the sources. The infancy narratives of Matthew and Luke are theological compositions concerning Jesus, whereas letters and ecclesial texts permit a different set of social-historical questions. Evidence for infant baptism becomes clearer in the second and third centuries: Tertullian’s advice in De baptismo 18 that baptism be delayed in certain cases presupposes that the practice was already known. Later patristic testimony should not be projected automatically onto Pauline communities. References to the baptism of an entire “household” in Acts and the Pauline corpus do not, by themselves, establish the age of each person baptised. 4. Exposure, adoption and child vulnerability The exposure of newborns and various forms of fosterage belong to the legal and social world of the Roman Empire, but their incidence is difficult to quantify securely. Christian authors condemn practices they present as homicidal or immoral; such rhetoric must be tested against papyrological evidence, law, and demographic reconstruction before collective behaviour is inferred. 5. Education, memory and transmission Religious formation in childhood took place through listening, repetition, reading, psalmody, narrative, and domestic discipline. From the fourth century onwards, expanding ecclesiastical infrastructure made formal catechesis and specifically Christian forms of education more visible, although the household remained a decisive setting of transmission. 5.1. Funerary epigraphy, childhood, and family memory Funerary epigraphy considerably enlarges a literary archive in which children appear only intermittently. Age at death, kinship terms, affective formulae, and, in some cases, explicitly Christian markers allow grief, filiation, and family memory to be studied with greater precision. Epitaphs are not, however, a neutral demographic sample: their survival depends upon economic resources, local commemorative conventions, and material preservation. The frequency of a formula cannot be converted directly into a rate of mortality, literacy, or religious adherence. Read alongside sarcophagi, catacomb evidence, and legal documentation, these testimonies suggest a gradual Christianisation of domestic memory. Biblical images

394 early christianity and formulae of hope could coexist with wider Roman funerary conventions; Christian distinctiveness must therefore be located in particular combinations of signs and practices rather than in an assumed wholesale rupture with existing repertoires. 5.2. Household economy, slavery, and authority within the household A household that hosts an assembly is also an economic unit. Enslaved people, freedpeople, clients, artisans, and relatives could inhabit the same space without sharing legal status or equal control over resources and mobility. Networks of “house churches” should therefore be reconstructed through property, patronage, and labour as well as through kinship and religious affiliation. The hospitality that makes an assembly possible may indicate economic capacity, but it does not by itself identify the property-holder as the community’s sole leader. Table 90. chapter xxvi The Imperial Cult, Sacrifice, and Political Loyalty: From Augustus to the Tetrarchy The imperial cult was not a uniform institution imposed from Rome. Cities, provinces, associations, and local elites articulated their own forms of honouring living and deified emperors through temples, priesthoods, festivals, sacrifices, images, and oaths. Christian conflicts can be understood only by reconstructing this diversity rather than reducing every gesture of civic loyalty to a single “religion of the emperor”. 1. Asia Minor and the civic competition for imperial honours The cities of Asia Minor developed temples, priesthoods, and titles linked to the imperial cult, and competed for prestige as neokoroi. This environment is especially relevant to Revelation because the seven churches are situated within cities where civic religion, benefaction, and imperial power formed a visible network. 2. Images, sacrifice, and tests of loyalty Pliny’s correspondence with Trajan documents a provincial procedure in which invocation of the gods, sacrifice, and reverence before the imperial image could serve to test whether Christian identity had been renounced. The exchange does not constitute a universal code of persecution; it does, however, show the political and juridical weight that ritual gestures could acquire in a particular administrative setting. 395

396 early christianity 3. Revelation: beast, image, and economy Revelation 13 brings political authority, cult, image, and economic constraint together within a symbolic vision. Comparison with the imperial cult helps reconstruct the text’s horizon of intelligibility, but it does not justify treating every apocalyptic detail as a coded transcription of a specific municipal ceremony. The representation of Rome as Babylon in Revelation 17–18 places commerce, luxury, and violence within a broader theopolitical critique. The text draws simultaneously upon scriptural codes and the experience of imperial power. 4. Decius, libelli, and the empire-wide scale of sacrifice Decius’s policy of 249–251 marks a significant change of scale. The surviving Egyptian libelli document the certification of sacrifice, personal identity, and administrative procedure. The measure should not be described simply as a “persecution of Christians”: it required widespread ritual compliance, with particularly serious consequences for those who refused on account of Christian conviction. 5. The Tetrarchy and the transformation of conflict The Great Persecution initiated under Diocletian and his colleagues combined edicts, the destruction of buildings, the surrender or confiscation of books, and sacrificial demands, all with substantial regional variation. The imperial cult formed part of the language of loyalty, but the conflict must also be understood through administration, military discipline, legal authority, and the wider reorganisation of imperial power.

the imperial cult, sacrifice, and political… 397 6. Cults of the Empire and the limits of comparison with early Christianities The imperial cult belonged to a wider religious landscape in which traditional civic cults, Dionysiac associations, devotion to Isis and Serapis, the cults of Magna Mater, and Mithraic communities coexisted with many other local configurations. Older scholarship sometimes treated “mystery religions” as a homogeneous family from which Christian baptism, ritual meals, salvation, or initiation might be explained by analogy. That model is inadequate: each cult possessed its own chronology, agents, spaces, ritual structures, and degrees of secrecy, and formal resemblance acquires historical significance only where a concrete context of contact can be established. Mithras offers a particularly instructive comparison. The archaeology of mithraea documents relatively small meeting spaces, communal meals, and specialised iconography, while participation was organised predominantly through male networks and, in some regions, military milieus. The cults of Isis and Serapis, by contrast, could be highly visible in public space, with processions and Mediterranean networks operating on a different scale; Cybele/Magna Mater and Attis possessed still other ritual calendars and institutional settings. Comparison with Christian communities helps reconstruct the competitive religious plurality of the Empire; it does not establish automatic borrowing or a common genealogy. Chronology is equally decisive. A late literary description of a mystery rite cannot simply be used to explain a first-century Christian practice. Nor does shared vocabulary—salvation, initiation, banquet, purity—establish dependence by itself, since such language could belong to the broader religious lexicon of the Mediterranean. The method adopted here therefore compares institutions and practices within their documented settings and reserves claims of influence for cases in which chronological proximity, plausible contact, and specific correspondences converge. chapter xxvii From House to Basilica: Topography of Worship, Funerary Memory and the Sacralisation of Christian Space (First–Fourth Centuries) The preceding chapters dealt separately with the house of assembly (V and XXV), liturgy (XVI), martyrdom (IV) and imperial architecture (XX). This chapter brings them together in a question of topography: how and when Christians moved from meeting in houses to having places of their own, from honouring their dead in cemeteries to organising space around sacred memories, and which part of that transformation can rest on the inherited Scriptures and which required new elaborations. The answer is neither rupture nor unaltered continuity. Between the first and fourth centuries there was a progressive territorialisation, materialisation and institutionalisation of Christian memory and of its ritual practices. The chapter offers a timeline of places and spaces of worship (Table 92), an archaeological catalogue by region and century (Table 93) and a separate matrix of exegetical tensions (Table 94), so that it can be established when each practice appears, what evidence there is for it, and how far it is legitimate to relate it to the oldest Christian scriptures. 399

400 early christianity 1. Houses and assemblies in the Pauline letters and in Acts The Pauline letters offer the oldest evidence. Paul greets the assembly that meets in the house of Prisca and Aquila (Rom 16:5; 1 Cor 16:19), that of Nympha (Col 4:15) and that of Philemon (Phlm 2); in Corinth the Lord’s Supper takes place in a gathering that presupposes a domestic space with hierarchies of the table (1 Cor 11:17–34). Acts adds meetings in the house of Mary, mother of John Mark (Acts 12:12), in the upper room at Troas (Acts 20:7–8), in the house of Titius Justus next to the synagogue at Corinth (Acts 18:7) and in the hall of Tyrannus at Ephesus (Acts 19:9), while the Jerusalem community continues to frequent the Temple (Acts 2:46; 3:1) and Paul preaches in the synagogues (Acts 17:1–2; 18:4). Ἐκκλησία designates in these texts an assembly, not a building, and no specific Christian building of the first century is known. Medium-sized houses allowed a few dozen people to gather in a dining room and an atrium, not a crowd; the composition of the Pauline assemblies, made up of several articulated households, is compatible with that. This phase raises no exegetical tension: the domestic meeting is what the oldest texts describe. Tension appears when the community acquires places of its own. 2. Adapted houses, assembly halls and buildings in the second and third centuries Between the second century and the middle of the third, the literary sources and archaeology agree on one point: there are recognisable places of worship, but no basilicas. Dura-Europos preserves a house adapted c. 240–256 (Chapter V): two rooms joined together form an assembly hall of about five by thirteen metres, and another room is turned into a baptistery with paintings of the Good Shepherd, Adam and Eve, the healing of the paralytic and the women at the tomb. The name “house church” describes a function, does not prove a stable typological form, and recent revisions of the building’s phases counsel against fixing its internal chronology with more precision than the data allow. Kefar ʿOthnay (Megiddo), with its mosaic and the inscription of Akeptous, adds an assembly hall with features of its own around the third century. With an initial date of about 230, it is usually presented as the oldest identified Christian prayer hall in the region, earlier than the house at Dura-Europos; its inscription, which speaks of offering “the table to God Jesus Christ as a memorial”, is also one of the earliest mentions of Jesus Christ as “God” in a building. It should be made clear that it is a hall of simple plan, neither a converted house nor a basilica,

from house to basilica 401 part of a complex excavated in the Megiddo prison compound, and that proposals for a later date prevent the chronological priority from being treated as settled. The literary sources show the same from another angle. The Chronicle of Edessa records the destruction by flood, in 201, of “the temple of the church of the Christians” (Chronicle of Edessa 8); Eusebius states that before the persecution Christians built spacious churches “from the foundations” (Eusebius, HE VIII.1.5); Lactantius describes at Nicomedia the church that overlooked the palace and was razed in 303 (Lactantius, Mort. pers. 12); the edict of Gallienus restores “places of worship” and cemeteries (Eusebius, HE VII.13). The size and form of those buildings can only be inferred. At Rome, the houses beneath the titular churches (San Clemente, Santa Prisca) show that aristocratic residences existed beneath later churches, but their Christian use before the fourth century has not been demonstrated archaeologically: it is a hypothesis that starts from late traditions. 3. Cemeteries, funerary memory and the cult of the martyrs Funerary memory precedes monumental cultic buildings. The Martyrdom of Polycarp describes, around the middle of the second century, how the community gathered the martyr’s bones, “more precious than costly stones”, laid them in a suitable place and resolved to celebrate there the day of his birth, that is, of his martyrdom (Martyrdom of Polycarp 18.2–3). The same text distinguishes between Christ, whom we worship, and the martyrs, whom we love as disciples and imitators of the Lord (Martyrdom of Polycarp 17.3). Tertullian alludes to Christian burial “areas” (Tertullian, Ad Scap. 3), and according to Hippolytus the future bishop Callistus was put in charge of the Roman community’s cemetery by Zephyrinus (Hippolytus, Ref. IX.12.14), so that around 200 the Church of Rome owned and administered a cemetery. At Rome, the sites on the Vatican and on the Via Ostiensis, attested by Gaius around 200 (Eusebius, HE II.25.7), and the Memoria Apostolorum at San Sebastiano (Chapter V) show that the memory of Peter and Paul was materialised in monuments and funerary banquets before any basilica. Eusebius documents, in addition, individual journeys to the Holy Land for prayer or inquiry: Melito of Sardis travels to the East to learn about the place where the message was proclaimed and fulfilled (Eusebius, HE IV.26.14), and Alexander of Cappadocia visits Jerusalem “for prayer and to see the places” (Eusebius, HE VI.11.2). Two features emerge: the tomb receives ritual treatment (anniversary, banquet, invocation), and memory becomes attached to specific places.

402 early christianity 4. Places of gospel memory: Golgotha, Zion, Capernaum and the Constantinian Holy Land The traditions about Jerusalem show well the distance between text and place. Acts locates the first community in the Temple and in houses, among them the upper room (Acts 1:13) and the house of Mary, mother of John Mark, to which Peter goes when freed (Acts 12:12). A later tradition, preserved by Epiphanius, claims that when the disciples returned to Jerusalem after 70 they found on Zion a “small church of God” (Epiphanius, Mens. 14), and from the late fourth century the liturgy of Zion is associated with the upper room. Neither Peter’s “house” in Jerusalem nor the Cenacle can be verified archaeologically for the first century; they are identifications of local tradition whose antiquity cannot be fixed. From Constantine on, the system changes scale. According to Eusebius, the emperor ordered a basilica built at Jerusalem over the place identified with Christ’s tomb and a complex at Golgotha (Eusebius, VC III.25–40); foundations followed at Bethlehem and on the Mount of Olives (Eusebius, VC III.41–43) and at Mamre (Eusebius, VC III.51–53). The text is an imperial and apologetic narrative, and the identification of the tomb, close to the forum of Hadrianic Aelia Capitolina, is plausible but not verifiable beyond local tradition. Egeria’s Itinerarium, of the late fourth century, already shows a stational liturgy organised around those places and recalls at Capernaum the house of the prince of the apostles, turned into a church (Egeria, Itin. 20.5). Joan E. Taylor, in Christians and the Holy Places (1993), criticised the hypothesis of an uninterrupted Christian veneration of the places from the first century and stressed the role of Constantinian reworking; her reading is a methodological warning against using topographical traditions as independent witnesses. Capernaum illustrates the problem: beneath the fifth-century octagonal church lies a first-century dwelling remodelled in later phases; whether it was Peter’s house is an identification of local tradition whose early cultic continuity is disputed. 5. From hall to basilica: monumentalisation and sacralisation of space With Constantine and his successors the basilical form, taken from civic architecture, becomes the model of the public church: the Lateran, an imperial foundation at Rome c. 313–320; the Vatican basilica over the necropolis that guarded the memory of Peter; that of Tyre, dedicated c. 315 and described by Eusebius in a panegyric (Eusebius, HE X.4). Three features separate these buildings from earlier forms: scale (naves able to hold an urban congregation), the fixing of the altar and the clergy in an apse, and the economic endowment of imperial patronage.

from house to basilica 403 Monumentalisation raises tensions that the oldest texts do not resolve by themselves. Acts presents Stephen and Paul as asserting that God “does not dwell in temples made by hands” (Acts 7:48; 17:24), John places worship “in spirit and truth” (John 4:21–24), and the Pauline letters apply temple language to the community (1 Cor 3:16–17; Eph 2:19–22). Around 200 the apologists deny having altars and temples (Minucius Felix, Oct. 10.2; 32.1), and Origen, against Celsus, defends the absence of altars, images and temples (Origen, Cels. VIII.17–20). The patristic solution was to distinguish the temple-community from the house of assembly and, later, to attribute to the building a consecration of its own, so that one language covered two realities. Images offer a parallel case: the baptistery of Dura and the Roman catacombs present biblical scenes, while canon 36 of the Council of Elvira (c. 300–306) forbids paintings in churches; practice coexisted with the objection. 6. Historical-critical conclusion The findings do not allow us to maintain without qualification that the monumental churches of the fourth century were a betrayal of the teaching of Jesus, nor that they represented an architectural continuation, unaltered, of the apostolic communities. They allow a more precise thesis: between the first and fourth centuries there was a progressive territorialisation, materialisation and institutionalisation of Christian memory and of its ritual practices. That transformation created new forms of relation to places, the dead, images and ecclesiastical authority. Some could be justified by the inherited texts; others generated tensions that required new theological elaborations. The documentation on Golgotha, Dura-Europos, Megiddo, Capernaum and the Roman apostolic cemeteries offers an exceptional basis for studying that process without reducing it to a simplistic opposition between an “original” and a “later” Christianity. The chapter is, moreover, a case of the book’s general thesis: the convergence of memory, text, ritual practice, authority and material representation in a configuration that starts from the domestic assembly fixed in Paul’s letters and extends, over four centuries, to a system of places, cemeteries and basilicas. General conclusions The history of early Christianity between the first and fourth centuries cannot be reduced to the linear expansion of a fully formed institution from its origins. Literary, papyrological, epigraphic, archaeological, and iconographic sources show instead a sequence of partial stabilisations: communities negotiating belonging, texts acquiring unequal authority, practices becoming normalised, leaders transforming memory into succession, and symbols making an identity recognisable in ever wider social spaces. The first result of this investigation is therefore both negative and positive. It is negative because it forces us to abandon teleological explanations that project the institutional forms of the fourth century onto Jerusalem, Paul, or the communities of the second century. It is positive because the absence of a uniform Church at the beginning does not imply an absence of structures: from very early on there were mechanisms of memory, discipline, ritual, and authority whose combination produced verifiable historical effects. The incorporation of Gentiles offers an early test case for these mechanisms. The Pauline letters show that belonging to the messianic movement of Israel could extend to non-Jews without requiring a complete ethnic conversion. The tension between mission, table fellowship, circumcision, and Law generated different solutions and left a contested memory that Acts later reworked. During the second century, this diversity did not disappear. Marcion, Justin, Ignatius, the Didache, Hermas, and Irenaeus reveal different ways of constructing legitimacy. Authority could be based on an apostolic calling, a public succession, a rule of truth, a ritual practice, a bishop, a prophet, a collection of texts, or a genealogy of teachers. So-called orthodoxy was not an essence that simply manifested itself, but a historical position that learned to reproduce itself through institutions, archives, and forms of exclusion. The analysis of the non-canonical gospels reinforces this conclusion. Thomas, the fragmentary Judeo-Christian gospels, the Nag Hammadi texts, the Gospel of Peter, and the infancy narratives do not form a homogeneous “lost canon”. They consti414

general conclusions 415 tute different literary trajectories whose uneven transmission illuminates the process by which some works were copied, read liturgically, and gathered into collections of increasing scope, while others circulated in a more limited way or ceased to be reproduced. Material culture adds a dimension that doctrinal history alone cannot recover. The codex, the nomina sacra, the staurogram, the graffito of Alexamenos, the catacombs, and Dura-Europos show that Christian identity was written, drawn, buried, and constructed. None of these objects should be interpreted through free symbolism; their value depends on context, dating, medium, and comparison with nonChristian repertoires. In at least one case—the third-century halls of Dura-Europos and Kefar ʿOthnay—the material evidence corrects a generalisation of the literary sources, namely that Christians had no temples or altars; in the others, it complements, qualifies or limits the texts, and must therefore be treated as an autonomous source. Nor was persecution a continuous backdrop. Between Pliny and the Tetrarchy, there were different policies, varying scales of violence, and multiple local responses. Martyrdom literature transformed this administrative discontinuity into a coherent memory of witness, creating models capable of circulating among communities and generations. The fourth century finally altered the scale of the process. Galerius, Constantine, Nicaea, architectural patronage, and subsequent legislation did not create a new religion ex nihilo; they provided imperial resources to structures that had been developing for centuries. The result was an unprecedented capacity to convene councils, finance buildings, preserve archives, discipline communities, and transform certain doctrinal definitions into norms backed by imperial power. The general thesis of this monograph can therefore be formulated in terms of convergence. Early Christianity acquired increasingly stable forms as memory, text, ritual practice, institutional authority, and material representation began to reinforce one another. None of these processes was sufficient on its own, and none progressed at the same pace in all regions. The starting point of the whole process is the continuity of the movement after the execution of Jesus, which is explained by the reinterpretation of his death and by the expectation of his return within a generation; the delay of that return compelled the production of the memory, texts, authority and spaces that this book studies. This convergence did not occur in a neutral space. It took place at the crossing of diverse fields of influence—the literature and practices of Second Temple Judaism, Greco-Roman rhetorical and associative culture, imperial law and administration

416 early christianity and, on the eastern margins, Syriac and Iranian traditions—and its articulation was, in a precise sense, Pauline. Paul set the problem (Gentile belonging without full ethnic conversion), the medium (letters read in assemblies and copied into collections), the network (urban communities of the shared table) and the vocabulary (ἐκκλησία, Christ, faith, body) that later centuries debated, extended or combated: Marcion built his Apostolikon on Paul; Irenaeus and the formation of the canon reintegrated him against Marcion; P46 and the Pauline codices are the material evidence of that circulation. “Pauline” does not mean that Paul designed the outcome, but that most lines of convergence pass through the question and the texts that he inaugurated. The chapters on prophecy and women, magic, asceticism, the family, apocalyptic, epidemics and architecture are read within this frame as fields of influence or friction in which that convergence was tested, not as thematic appendices. The integration of the thematic chapters with this thesis can be made explicit. In the chapter on prophecy and women, charismatic authority (the prophetesses of Corinth, Phoebe, Prisca, Junia) appears as a mechanism earlier than episcopal succession, whose later reduction—the disputed transmission of 1 Cor 14:34–35, the Pastoral Epistles, the anti-Montanist polemic—shows that institutional stabilisation had documentable costs. In magic and medicine, the practice of healing, exorcising and blessing was negotiated against external categories of superstition and magic, and Christianity drew boundaries by accusing others of magic and defending itself against the same charge. In asceticism, from Pauline celibacy (1 Cor 7) to the apocryphal Acts and fourth-century monasticism, renunciation worked as a form of distinction and of alternative authority that the institution incorporated only in part. In family and slavery, the household codes (Col 3:18–4:1; Eph 5:21–6:9; 1 Pet 2:18–3:7) and the household as community unit show convergence with Greco-Roman culture rather than radical social novelty. In epidemics, the plagues of the second and mid-third centuries offer a field in which assistance and the interpretation of suffering tested internal cohesion, without a single causality being attributable to them. In apocalyptic and Zoroastrianism, Chapter XVIII compares the cosmic opposition of good and evil, judgement, resurrection, the Saošyant and final renewal (frašō.kərəti), and concludes that the symmetries are real but too general, and the sources too uneven, to prove dependence; if early Christianity received them, it did so through Second Temple Judaism, where Iranian influence is plausible but disputed. Within the frame of this book, Zoroastrianism is a distant and mediated field of influence, not a cause: its value is one of contrast, for it shows how much of the vocabulary of the end— kingdom, judgement, resurrection—was available before the Jesus community used it, and it reinforces the Pauline reading of convergence rather than replacing it.

general conclusions 417 The question the book raises in comparing the Jesus movement with other movements of its time—why the execution of Jesus did not dissolve the group—can now be given an articulated answer. The first reason is one of content: the followers of Jesus interpreted his death in the light of Scripture and of experiences they took to be appearances of the risen one (1 Cor 15:3–8; Gal 1:15–16), so that the execution ceased to be the refutation of the proclamation of the kingdom and became its decisive moment. The second is one of horizon: the earliest community lived in expectation of the imminent return of Jesus as Messiah or Son of Man. This is shown by the Aramaic preserved in 1 Cor 16:22 (μαραναθά), the consolation of the Thessalonians about “we who are alive” (1 Thess 4:13–18), Paul’s counsel about the time that has grown short (1 Cor 7:29–31) and the synoptic sayings about the generation that will not pass away (Mark 9:1; 13:30), whose authenticity is disputed but whose early circulation is not. In that horizon the movement did not need to foresee its own duration in order to persevere: mission was an eschatological duty before the end (Rom 11:25–26; Mark 13:10), and the nearness of the outcome justified rupture with the surrounding world, internal solidarity and the risk of martyrdom. Third, the delay of the parousia, far from dissolving the group, compelled it to produce what this book studies: written memory (the Gospels also respond to the delay; cf. Luke 19:11; John 21:22–23; 2 Pet 3:3–9), succession, discipline, liturgy and a theology of the interim. The Christian movement continued after Jesus because it expected his return, and that expectation, as it lengthened, crystallised the movement into an apocalyptic religion that became institutional by reinterpreting the end rather than abandoning it. Two cautions are in order. The expectation of the parousia explains the group’s continuity, not its relative success against other messianic or apocalyptic movements that did dissolve; for that, the inclusion of Gentiles, the Pauline network and the ritual practices treated in the earlier chapters count. And faith in the resurrection and hope for the return are facts that history can record as documented beliefs, not as truths that it is for history to adjudicate. The expectation of an imminent return of Jesus has explicit and graded support in the sources. In 1 Thess 4:15–17 (c. 50), the oldest surviving Christian document, Paul consoles a community whose members have begun to die and includes himself, with “we who are alive, who remain until the coming of the Lord”, among those who will see the event; 1 Cor 15:51 repeats that “we shall not all sleep”, and 1 Cor 7:29–31 modifies marital and social practices because “the time has grown short”. The Aramaic acclamation μαράνα θά (or μαραναθά) of 1 Cor 16:22, “Our Lord, come!”, preserved untranslated in a Greek letter to a Greek community, attests that the invocation came from the oldest Aramaic-speaking communities. The Synoptics set the limit at one

418 early christianity generation: “this generation will not pass away until all these things take place” (Mark 13:30; Matt 24:34; Luke 21:32) and “some standing here will not taste death before they see the kingdom of God come with power” (Mark 9:1); the authenticity of these sayings is disputed, but their circulation and their inclusion in Mark around 70 are not. James 5:8–9, of disputed date, affirms that “the coming of the Lord is near”. In the second century the motif persists, but now with awareness of the delay. Didache 16.1 orders watchfulness because “you do not know the hour”; 1 Clem. 23.5 answers those who doubt with the promise that the Lord “will come quickly and suddenly”; Barnabas 21.3 declares that “the day is near” and, according to Barnabas 15, places the present on the threshold of the last millennium of a cosmic week; and 2 Pet 3:3–9, of disputed date (c. 110–140), answers the “scoffers” who ask “where is the promise of his coming?” by reconfiguring the measure of divine time: “with the Lord one day is like a thousand years”. The passage from imminent to prolonged expectation is thus one of the processes this book can document. For the thesis this has a precise consequence. The Jesus movement did not dissolve with his execution because his followers believed that Jesus would return within a generation, and acted accordingly: they pursued the mission as a task before the end, maintained communal solidarity, accepted the risk of martyrdom and reinterpreted the cross, which ceased to be a public failure and became the prelude to judgement. It is plausible that the sharing of goods described in Acts 2:44–45 and 4:32–35 was also understood within that horizon, although Acts does not say so and both the historicity and the meaning of those summaries are disputed. When the generation passed and the return did not occur, the movement did not die out: it integrated the delay into its theology (2 Pet 3; Luke 19:11; John 21:22–23) and was compelled to produce written memory, succession, discipline, liturgy and spaces of assembly and memory, that is, the mechanisms studied in the earlier chapters. Apocalyptic expectation is therefore a principal factor in the initial continuity and the origin of the pressure that turned a waiting into an institution; by itself it does not explain, as noted, the later success against other movements. The thesis is falsifiable. It would be weakened if the evidence showed, for the first and second centuries, a uniform and already complete form in every region— a closed list of books, a general monarchical episcopate, a common liturgy—as the linear-development model under criticism supposed; if the stabilisation of a single field (the canon or the episcopate, say) had preceded and by itself explained the others, so that one factor sufficed; if the rhythm were uniform across regions instead of uneven; or if material culture—codices, nomina sacra, inscriptions, buildings— proved independent of the texts and of the authority attributed to it. It would also

general conclusions 419 be weakened in the opposite direction if early plurality turned out to be an artefact of late sources. These conditions are not rhetorical: the dating of the Pauline papyri, the regional distribution of the nomina sacra, the dates of Dura-Europos and Kefar ʿOthnay, or the earliest testimony to an episcopal triad can move the picture, and the book treats them as data open to revision. “Convergence” here designates a hypothesis of co-occurrence and mutual reinforcement among series that can be measured separately, not an explanatory wild card. Where the book explains a mechanism by its function, it must be read with a distinction. The causal explanations are local and rest on data from the period: Irenaeus organises his rule of truth and his succession list against Marcion and the Valentinians; the list of Roman bishops is drawn up in a controversy and not as a programme of unity; the cult of the martyrs answers persecution. Those decisions had a unifying effect their authors did not seek, and fourth-century unity is an unintended result of accumulated choices—some retained, others abandoned—not their final cause. The model is one of variation and retention, not of purpose. Where the book links reasons with “because”, it signals co-occurrence, and only where the source itself declares it, as in Irenaeus against Marcion, does it assert causality. The development of places of worship confirms this pattern. In the first century Christians met in private houses and rented spaces (Rom 16:5; 1 Cor 16:19; Phlm 2; Acts 19:9), and no specific building is known. In the second and third centuries there appear, alongside adapted houses (Dura-Europos), assembly halls with features of their own, such as that of Kefar ʿOthnay, and places of funerary memory—the Vatican necropolis, the Via Ostiensis, San Sebastiano on the Via Appia—that are not churches. Only from the fourth century, with imperial patronage, do basilicas become general. None of these forms derives from the synagogue by conversion: they coexist with it and imitate or reject it as the case may be. The book consults almost all this evidence through publications, editions and facsimiles, not by autopsy; the “autonomy” of the material series is therefore methodological, a matter of criterion and not of access, and its results remain open to correction by those who have studied the objects directly. This perspective makes it possible to explain both early plurality and the subsequent capacity for unification without turning one into an anomaly and the other into an inevitable destiny. Early Christian history thus emerges as a history of selection, transmission, conflict, and materialisation: a succession of documentable human decisions that, accumulated over four centuries, transformed a Jewish movement of the eastern Mediterranean into a religious institution of imperial scope, al-

420 early christianity though that institution never wholly absorbed the regional, linguistic, and doctrinal diversity that had preceded it and continued to accompany it. Summary This monograph reconstructs the formation of early Christianity as a historically plural process of stabilisation encompassing memory, texts, ritual practices, institutional authority, and material representation. From the Jesus movement of the first century to the imperial Church of the fourth century, the evidence does not support a linear development from a fully constituted original institution. Successive communities created mechanisms of legitimacy, transmission, discipline, and boundary demarcation whose convergence gradually produced more stable forms of collective identity. The study combines literary criticism, textual criticism, papyrology, epigraphy, archaeology, and iconography, and applies the same evidentiary criteria to canonical, non-canonical, Christian, Jewish, Roman, and anti-Christian sources. Keywords: early Christianity; historiography; canon; material culture; authority; Roman Empire.

prosopographical appendix and social network… 429 5. Social Network Analysis (SNA): protocol and pilot networks The SNA is applied as a descriptive tool for preserved relationships. E1 = explicit contemporary or near-contemporary relationship; E2 = declared contextual inference; E3 = subsequent tradition or retrospective association. The metrics for these pilot networks are calculated on simple, undirected, and unweighted graphs, using only E1. CSVs retain the direction of the documented exchanges; E2 is drawn in a distinct style, and E3 is excluded. The number of edges does not measure historical significance, population, or jurisdiction. A second run (E1+E2) is not presented as a calculated result. Figure 28 (SNA-1). Minimal Pauline prosopographical network. Analytical visualisation of 18 people and 20 explicit relationships in the corpus; all nodes have equal graphic hierarchy and Paul is not enlarged as a dominant centre. [ED; SNA]. Inclusion threshold and reproducibility An E1 edge enters the network only if it can be traced back to an identifiable primary locus; E2 requires an explicit and justifiable inference that the reader can accept or reject; purely plausible relationships are not drawn. Each graph must maintain a table of edges with source, direction, and classification. Number of nodes, number of edges, density, degree centrality, betweenness, and components are reported; no metric is interpreted on its own as legal primacy, doctrinal authority, or demographic size. SNA reproducibility. The edition is accompanied by edge CSVs with origin, destination, direction, locus, class, and relationship type, and a calculation script. Degree centrality is k/(n − 1); normalised betweenness follows Brandes’s algorithm for simple undirected and unweighted graphs. SNA-1: 18 nodes, 20 edges, density

430 early christianity 0.131, and one component. SNA-2: 5 nodes in E1, 4 edges, density 0.400, and one component. Arles belongs to E2 and is excluded from the exchange metrics. The uneven preservation of the texts limits the historical interpretation of the results. 5.1. Controlled extension to second-century networks The same protocol can be extended into the second century, but not by simply adding names to a single undifferentiated graph. The Ignatian corpus can model senders, recipients, messengers, and communities linked by explicit relationships; Polycarp introduces connections among Smyrna, Philippi, and traditions of martyr memory; Justin requires a different model because the surviving evidence concerns trajectories of teaching, polemical encounters, and Roman location rather than a comparable epistolary network. A combined graph would be legitimate only if edge type, evidentiary status, and chronology remained explicit. For that reason, the present analysis retains the published metrics for the two pilot networks and frames wider expansion as a reproducible protocol rather than as a fictitious numerical result. Any future corpus should publish its node list, edge table, locus, direction, E1/E2/E3 classification, and aggregation rules before density, centrality, or betweenness is calculated. The methodological priority is reproducibility: a reader should be able to reconstruct the graph directly from the cited evidence. Table 103. Bilingual appendix of fundamental loci The following passages provide brief selections in the original language alongside the author’s own English translations as a control. They do not replace the critical editions cited in the bibliography. Only textual units necessary for the argument are reproduced, and transmission problems are noted where relevant. B1. Romans 16:1–2—Phoebe Original text: Συνίστημι δὲ ὑμῖν Φοίβην τὴν ἀδελφὴν ἡμῶν, οὖσαν [καὶ] διάκονον τῆς ἐκκλησίας τῆς ἐν Κεγχρεαῖς... καὶ γὰρ αὐτὴ προστάτις πολλῶν ἐγενήθη καὶ ἐμοῦ αὐτοῦ. Translation: I commend to you Phoebe, our sister, who is also a deacon/servant of the church in Cenchreae... for she herself was a protector or patron of many, and also of me. Critical note: διάκονος and προστάτις must be analysed historically before being translated by later ecclesiastical offices. B2. Romans 16:7—Junia Original text: ἀσπάσασθε Ἀνδρόνικον καὶ Ἰουνίαν... οἵτινές εἰσιν ἐπίσημοι ἐν τοῖς ἀποστόλοις. Translation: Greet Andronicus and Junia... who are distinguished among/in relation to the apostles. Critical note: The editorial accentuation Ἰουνίαν corresponds to the widely accepted feminine reading of the name Junia. Ancient manuscripts without accents do not resolve this issue on their own. The syntactic interpretation of ἐπίσημοι ἐν τοῖς ἀποστόλοις and its scope with respect to the term “apostles” require separate discussion. 433

bilingual appendix of fundamental loci 435 B7. Pliny, Epistulae X.96.7—Christian practice Original text: carmenque Christo quasi deo dicere secum invicem... seque sacramento non in scelus aliquod obstringere. Morphosyntactic note: dicere, like convenire, is a complementary infinitive of essent soliti, within the quod-clause that spells out what affirmabant reports; secum invicem expresses the reciprocity of the action described. Translation: And sing among themselves, alternately, a hymn to Christ as to a god... and bind themselves by oath, not to commit any crime. Critical note: External administrative source; sacramentum here belongs to the Latin language of oath/commitment. B8. Tertullian, Apologeticum 39.5—common fund Original text: Modicam unusquisque stipem menstrua die, vel cum velit, et si modo velit, et si modo possit, apponit; nam nemo compellitur, sed sponte confert. Translation: Each person contributes a small amount on a day of the month, or whenever they want, and only if they want to and can; no one is compelled; each contributes voluntarily. Critical note: Apologetic testimony about a community fund; it is not evidence of an audited budget. B9. Cyprian, De mortalitate 14—epidemic crisis Original text: quod in faucium uulnera conceptus medullitus ignis exaestuat, quod adsiduo uomitu intestina quatiuntur, quod oculi ui sanguinis inardescunt. Translation: that a fire kindled deep within burns in the sores of the throat, that the intestines are shaken by continuous vomiting, that the eyes are inflamed by the force of the blood. Critical note: Three clauses from De mortalitate 14 are reproduced according to the text of Hartel, CSEL 3.1 (1868); the spelling of that edition is retained. The passage describes an epidemic experience through pastoral and rhetorical discourse. It does not allow for the reliable identification of an aetiological agent. The text was consulted in a digital edition [ED], without fresh autopsy of the manuscript or a comprehensive collation of the critical apparatus.

Translation: It is our will that all the peoples ruled by the moderation of our clemency should practise that religion... Critical note: Legal document from 380; its scope must be read within the process of late Roman coercion and administration.

438 early christianity Tacitus, Annals XV.44 The lemma per procuratorem Pontium Pilatum corresponds to the terminology of the historian, who is writing after Pilate’s tenure. The epigraphic evidence from Caesarea uses praefectus. The difference can be explained historically without correcting Tacitus’s Latin with conjecture. The account of Nero documents the Roman representation of Christians and their punishment, but its rhetoric does not constitute a statistical account of victims. Reference edition: Fisher, Cornelii Taciti Annalium ab excessu divi Augusti libri. Pliny, Letters X.96.7–9 and X.97.1–2 Pliny’s report mentions meetings, singing to Christ, and moral obligations; the sacramentum described in X.96.7 should not be translated in a way that presupposes the later sacramental meaning. Trajan’s reply contains conquirendi non sunt: “they should not be sought.” This rule refers to the procedure outlined by the governor and is consistent with the punishment of those who persist after being denounced. It expresses neither complete tolerance nor universal persecution. Reference edition: Mynors, C. Plini Caecili Secundi Epistularum libri decem. Conflict, memory and community organisation Galatians 2:1–10 and 2:11–14 The meeting and conflict at Antioch belong to a first-person epistolary argument. The opposition between Peter and Paul does not justify constructing two static parties throughout the first century. The reference to the poor in Galatians 2:10 and the accusation of inconsistent conduct in 2:13 belong to the argument about membership and table fellowship. The equivalence with Acts 15 is treated as a hypothesis of synchronisation, not as documentary identity. Reference edition for the text: NA28; specific readings require consultation of its apparatus. 440 early christianity Writing, reading and delimitation of texts Justin, First Apology 26 and 58 The passages identify Marcion as a known Christian adversary in the second century. They are testimonies predating Tertullian and Epiphanius, but do not provide an edition of the Marcionite Gospel or the Antitheses. The charge of wide dissemination belongs to the apologetic argument and should be distinguished from an inventory of communities. Critical editions identified: Munier, SC 507; Minns and Parvis, Justin, Philosopher and Martyr: Apologies. The book’s commentary verifies the loci and chronology, without attributing a new manuscript reading. Justin, First Apology 65–67 The reading of the “memoirs of the apostles” and the prophets appears within the description of the gathering. The testimony documents a literary and ritual practice in the author’s environment; it does not demonstrate that all communities used an identical collection or that the term implies a single codex. In chapter 67, the so-called day of the Sun is mentioned, a relevant detail for distinguishing Sunday worship from the legislation of 321. Reference editions: Munier; Minns and Parvis. The ANF translation is used only as a secondary content check. Irenaeus, Against Heresies III.3.1–4 Roman succession is used as an argument against teachings considered secret or divergent. In III.3.2, the Latin expression potentiorem principalitatem raises a problem of interpretation and transmission from the Greek original: translating it automatically as a universal legal competence can introduce later categories. The enumeration in III.3.3 includes Eleutherius and serves to study the construction of a public memory. It does not, in itself, establish the exact dates of all the leaders. Critical edition of reference: Rousseau and Doutreleau, SC 210–211. The ANF translation is used only as a secondary content check; a complete lexical discussion requires consultation of the text and apparatus of SC. Irenaeus, Against Heresies III.11.8 The defence of the fourfold gospel uses a symbolic argument about four regions and four winds. The monograph studies this symbolism as documented ancient reasoning; it does not adopt it as historical or mathematical proof. The passage

documentary and philological appendix 441 demonstrates that Irenaeus defended the delimitation of four gospels, but not that all second-century communities already possessed the same complete New Testament canon. Reference edition: SC 210–211. This locus relates to Chapter II and to the distinction between collection, normative reading, and closed canon. Tertullian, Against Marcion IV.7 and IV.19 The reports concerning the beginning of the Gospel and Lucan episodes are testimonies from an adversary. When Tertullian discusses a reading, it is necessary to separate the text he quotes, the explanation he attributes to Marcion, and his own rebuttal. The matrix in Chapter II does not replace this operation: it classifies loci and degrees of certainty. A complete Greek form is not attributed to the lost Gospel where the testimony is only indirect. Athanasius, Festal Letter 39.5–7 The letter of 367 lists the twenty-seven writings that comprise the later New Testament and distinguishes this set from other books useful for reading. It is a localised document of episcopal authority, not an act of a universal council that produced the canon in that year. Lists, pastoral use, and regional reception should be distinguished. For the presentation of lists and their texts, see Gallagher and Meade, The Biblical Canon Lists from Early Christianity. A supposedly collated pagination from a different edition is not printed. Objects and signs Gallio: FD III.4, no. 286; SIG³ 801 D The photograph records the epigraphic form ΓΑΛΛΙΩΝ; the rest of the chronological argument depends on the edited document and Claudius’s title. The coincidence with Acts 18:12–17 connects an administrative figure with the narrative, without turning the imperial letter into a testimony that names Paul. The entry for Chapter I preserves the photographed fragment, the editorial restitutions, and the contextual translation separately. Verification: Plassart’s epigraphic edition and Hanson’s presentation.

442 early christianity Theodotus: CIJ II 1404 The inscription links the synagogue to the reading of the Law and the teaching of the commandments. The selective transcription includes editorial brackets and normalised spelling; it is not presented as a line-by-line reproduction of the stone. The document provides a check on reconstructions of the variety of Jewish spaces prior to 70 CE, subject to discussion of its dating. Verification: Frey’s corpus and Hanson’s presentation. P46 and P75 The abbreviations designate different codices. The first brings together Pauline epistles and Hebrews; the second preserves Luke and John. The physical arrangement of a collection does not, in itself, demonstrate authorship, a closed canon, or the identity of all Christian libraries. Palaeographic dates are expressed as intervals or approximations. The documentary window on P46 reproduces the institutional transcription of a segment from the old page 158 and explains its numbering and abbreviations. The documentary window on P75 remains codicological: a catalogue identification is not converted into a collation of signs. Verification: editions of Kenyon and Sanders for P46 and of Martin and Kasser, Papyrus Bodmer XIV–XV (1961), for P75; Michigan guide and Vatican and CSNTM catalogues. Abercius and Dura-Europos The Epitaph of Abercius and the Christian building at Dura require different approaches. The former combines fragmentary epigraphy and literary transmission; the latter preserves spatial relationships and paintings from an excavated context. The words of the epitaph cannot be reconstructed from a partial photograph without prior warning. Architectural drawings are not equivalent to old photographs or newly made surveys. The presentation distinguishes between provenance, medium, interpretation, and reconstruction. documentary and philological appendix 443 Lactantius, Death of the Persecutors 34, 44 and 48 The three loci correspond to different matters: Galerius’s edict, the sign of the Constantinian campaign, and the text on restitution and religious freedom of 313. They should not be combined as a single edict. The author constructs an interpretation of the persecutors’ deaths that conditions his narrative, even where he preserves documents. Reference edition: Moreau, SC 39, De la mort des persécuteurs, 2 vols., 1954. The ANF translation is used only as a secondary content check. Comparison with Eus., VC I.28–31 preserves the narrative differences regarding the sign. CJ III.12.2 and CTh II.8.18 (= CTh VIII.8.3; XI.7.13) The first provision, CJ III.12.2 (7 March 321), uses venerabilis dies solis and contains an agrarian exception; the second regulates litigation and employs dominical vocabulary. The subscription of CTh II.8.18 (= CTh VIII.8.3; XI.7.13) corresponds to 3 November 386. These are two distinct norms and should not be confused chronologically. Legal designations are studied in conjunction with the regulated object, the addressee, and the date, without converting an administrative provision into the origin of a prior religious practice. Reference editions: Krueger for the Justinian Code; Mommsen and Meyer for the Theodosian Code. Verification of the second locus: Latin reproduction of the Grenoble Roman Law Project. CTh XVI.1.2; XVI.10.10–12 The edict of 380 defines a confessional norm. The provisions of 391–392 belong to a different period and regulate specific cultic practices more broadly. Distinguishing these documents prevents attributing all subsequent consequences to the former. The historical problem includes promulgation, jurisdiction, local application, and reception; a list of laws is not equivalent to a measure of the number of conversions. Reference edition: Mommsen and Meyer, Theodosiani libri XVI. The loci are cited by book, title, and constitution. Glossary Apocalyptic A modern category for writings and traditions that reveal a hidden order of history, the cosmos, or judgement through supernatural mediation. The literary form “apocalypse” and eschatological expectation are not equivalent. A text may share apocalyptic motifs without belonging to that genre. Critical apparatus An organised record of the witnesses, variants and editorial decisions of a textual edition. It is not to be confused with a bibliography or with historical notes. The appendix to this monograph is documentary and philological: it does not publish a new recensio of the cited authors. Apocryphal A reception label for writings that were not included in a particular canon. Its use does not establish a late date, a uniform doctrine, or a lack of historical value. Each work and its transmission must be identified. Apostolicity A claim to a link with the apostles through authorship, memory, teaching, succession or community origin. Its forms vary. The ancient attribution of a work to an apostle is a datum of reception before it can serve as proof of authorship. 446

glossary 447 Baptism Practice of incorporation and purification designated by βάπτισμα (baptisma) and related terms. Sources document differences in preparation, water, and procedure. A building with a baptismal installation provides evidence of a local practice; it does not establish an identical universal rite. Canon From the Greek κανών (kanōn), rule or measure. In textual history, a set of writings recognised as normative by a community. The authority of a book, its liturgical reading, its inclusion in a collection, and the closing of a list are related processes that must be distinguished. Charisma In the Pauline epistles, χάρισμα (charisma) refers to a gift. The modern sociological classification of “charismatic authority” constitutes another conceptual operation. Applying it requires explaining its usefulness without attributing the modern theory to an ancient author. Catacomb Common designation for underground burial complexes. Roman examples should be studied in terms of topography, phasing, epigraphy and visual repertoires. Their funerary function does not demonstrate that they were permanent refuges during continuous persecution. Codex A book made up of bound sheets, in contrast to a scroll. It may contain one or more works. The codicological form facilitates certain selection and consultation practices, but does not automatically determine the canon or the religion of its readers. Christology A modern category for the study of claims about the identity and role of Christ. It does not presuppose that all early texts responded to the questions or vocabulary of the fourth-century councils.

448 early christianity Chrismon Monogram formed by chi and rho, initial letters of Χριστός (Christos). It should be distinguished from the tau–rho staurogram. Its appearance in imperial or funerary contexts requires identification of the support and date of each case. Diaspora Distribution of Jewish populations outside of Judea and their relationships with places, practices, and memories of origin. It designates neither a homogeneous culture nor an absolute separation from Jerusalem. Diplomatic and semi-diplomatic A diplomatic transcription seeks to reproduce the relevant graphic features of the witness and its layout according to explicit conventions. A semi-diplomatic transcription introduces certain declared standardisations. Copying a continuous editorial text is not equivalent to either unless the procedure is explained. Domus ecclesiae A Latin expression used in modern times for domestic buildings adapted for Christian community functions. Its archaeological value depends on material evidence. A community that meets in a house, attested by a letter, does not, by that fact alone, constitute an excavated building of that type. Ekklēsia ἐκκλησία (ekklēsia) designates an assembly and, in Christian texts, a gathered community or a group of communities. Translating it invariably as “Church”, with a capital letter, can introduce a later institutional unity that the context does not require. Episcopate Function and organisation associated with ἐπίσκοπος (episkopos), supervisor or bishop. The relationship with presbyters and deacons changes between sources and regions. The presence of the word does not demonstrate a fully developed monarchical structure.

glossary 449 Eschatology The modern study of expectations regarding consummation, judgement, resurrection, and ultimate destiny. Ancient texts articulate these themes in different ways. An expectation of an imminent end does not by itself allow a text to be dated. Staurogram The tau–rho ligature used in certain abbreviations of words related to the cross and crucifixion. Its iconographic reading is a historical problem that requires identifying the manuscript and locus. It should not be attributed to P46 merely by generic association with early papyri. Eucharist εὐχαριστία (eucharistia) means thanksgiving. In Christian sources, it is related to meals, prayers, and liturgical practices whose organisation is not uniform. The descriptions in the Didache and Justin are studied as individual documents. Gospel εὐαγγέλιον (euangelion) can designate a proclamation and, later, a written work. The use of the term by an author does not guarantee that it names a volume or a collection similar to the current New Testament. Gentile In this work, a non-Jewish person. The term describes a historical relationship with Israel and with practices of belonging, without implying a single religious identity shared by all non-Jews in the Empire. Gnosticism A debated historiographical category that brings together heterogeneous systems and texts. It is used with an explicit definition, and the names of authors, traditions, and corpora are preferred when the documentation allows for greater precision. A single religion is not postulated as underlying all the Nag Hammadi writings.

450 early christianity Heresiology Production of classifications and refutations of doctrines considered erroneous. Its lists and genealogies are sources for opposing groups and for the strategies of those who describe them. Reproducing the ancient classification does not make it neutral. Heresy αἵρεσις (hairesis) was used in the senses of “choice”, “current of thought” and “school” before, and alongside, its sense of doctrinal deviation. The book identifies who applies the judgement and from what norm. The category does not replace the historical description of a group. Homoousios ὁμοούσιος (homoousios), “of the same substance” or “consubstantial.” The Nicene usage is studied in the fourth-century conflict. Its incorporation into the creed does not eliminate later disputes about meaning, reception, and alternative formulations. Iconography Identification and interpretation of themes and visual repertoires. It requires attention to support, context, date and comparanda. The similarity of two figures does not in itself prove a religious dependence or a chain of transmission. Jewish Christianity A modern category for Christian practices, groups, or writings specifically related to Jewish traditions. It should be specified whether it describes affiliation, observance, language, or content. It does not constitute a uniform ancient identity easily separable from others. Lapsi Latin designation for those who, according to community criteria, had yielded during a persecution. The forms of compliance and the conditions of readmission gave rise to controversy. A libellus documents administrative certification and does not, by itself, allow one to reconstruct the bearer’s inner convictions.

glossary 451 Libellus A brief document; in the Decian context, a certificate related to the performance of required sacrifices. Each must be recorded with its papyrological identification, date and formula. The document and the martyrdom narratives offer different perspectives on the same horizon. Locus An identifiable passage in a work or a precise textual location. The Latin plural is loci. The Index locorum records explicit references in the book and its notes; it does not attempt to list every possible literary allusion. Martyr μάρτυς (martys), witness. The association of the word with death for one’s religious confession has its own history. Martyrdom narratives can preserve procedural data and, simultaneously, construct examples, scenes, and community memory. Nomina sacra Convention of abbreviating certain names and titles by means of selected letters and a supralinear stroke. The set of abbreviated words and their form vary. Their presence is studied materially and not as a uniform numerical code. Orthodoxy A position recognised as correct teaching by specific actors and communities. The historian studies the processes of validation, transmission, and exclusion. The term does not justify projecting all subsequent definitions back to the first century. Palaeography The study of scripts and graphic practices. Comparative dating provides margins and probabilities, not absolute years. It must be supplemented with provenance, support, context, and independent data when available.

452 early christianity Patronage Relationships of support, resources, prestige, and dependence between people or institutions. Households and benefactors could facilitate Christian gatherings, but the analogy with Roman models does not automatically demonstrate the legal status of each participant. Pseudepigraphy Attribution of a work to a name other than that of its historical author. It is distinct from anonymity, later editing and traditional attribution. The judgement requires textual and transmission arguments, not merely doctrinal disagreement. Recension A textual form resulting from an identifiable process of revision or transmission. In Ignatius, the middle, long and short recensions present distinct problems. In textual criticism, recensio also designates the examination and classification of witnesses. Rule of faith or truth A formulation of teaching and a criterion of interpretation in certain authors. It can articulate creation, incarnation, and salvation without yet being a universal creed in identical verbal form. Its function must be established in each controversy. Synagogue συναγωγή (synagōgē) can designate a meeting, community, or building. The Theodotus inscription documents a programme of reading, teaching, and hospitality in Jerusalem. It does not imply architectural or institutional uniformity in all cases. Tradition Process and content of transmission. The appeal to an apostolic tradition is a historical claim of authority that must be examined through sources. Its declared antiquity and its effective continuity are not automatically equivalent. Textual variant Difference between witnesses to a text. The existence of a variant must be separated from its antiquity, distribution, and value for reconstruction. The monograph does not invent manuscript sigla or readings in order to complete an apparatus artificially.

Hebrew and Aramaic glossary of terms and names This glossary includes only Semitic terms that have a historical, philological, or onomastic function in the monograph. It does not repeat the conceptual entries of the general glossary. Spellings are offered as attested forms or plausible historical equivalents; when a New Testament form is preserved only in Greek transliteration, no attempt is made to reconstruct a supposed “original” phrase with greater certainty than the evidence allows. ‫ אַ ָּבא‬/ ‫—ܐܒܐ‬ʾabbā Aramaic: “father”. Preserved as ἀββᾶ in Mark 14:36; Rom 8:15; Gal 4:6. Transliteration within Greek shows Semitic linguistic memory, but does not by itself allow the reconstruction of the exact oral context. ‫— ָאמֵ ן‬ʾāmēn Hebrew, “certainly / so be it”, from the root ʾ-m-n associated with firmness and reliability. It passes into Greek as ἀμήν without a direct lexical translation in numerous Jewish and Christian texts. ‫— ַּבר אֱ נ ָׁש‬bar ʾĕnāš Aramaic, “son of man / human being”, especially Dan 7:13. It is a linguistic check for the debate on ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου; it is not assumed that all its gospel uses translate a single fixed Aramaic formula. ‫ ּ ֵכיפָ א‬/ ‫—ܟܐܦܐ‬Kēfā / Kēpā Aramaic, “rock, stone”. It underlies Κηφᾶς, the name of Peter in Paul and John. Πέτρος functions as a Greek onomastic equivalent, not as evidence of an original Hebrew spelling. 453

454 early christianity ‫ֵיה ּנֹם‬ ִ ‫ ּג‬/ ‫ֵיא־ה ּנֹם‬ ִ ‫— ּג‬gê-hinnōm “Valley of Hinnom”, base of γέεννα. The semantic history from toponym to eschatological image must be reconstructed through Second Temple and rabbinic Jewish literature, not from isolated etymology. ‫— ּגָלִ יל‬Gālîl Galilee. The Hebrew toponym is related to “district / region”. The Greek forms Γαλιλαία and Γαλιλαῖος belong to the linguistically mediated geography of the period. ‫ ּגֻלְ ֹּגלֶת‬/ Aram. gulgultā—gulgōlet / gulgultā “Skull”. Related to Γολγοθᾶ in the Gospels. The exact form of the first-century Aramaic place name is treated with caution; the Gospel explains its meaning for Greek readers. ‫—הַ לְ לוּ־י ָּה‬halləlû-yāh “Praise Yah.” Hebrew formula transmitted in the biblical tradition and as ἀλληλουϊά in Greek texts. Its preservation shows liturgical continuity of a Semitic expression. ‫—הוֹ ׁ ִשיעָ ה ּנָא‬hôšîʿâ-nnā “Save, please”, from Ps 118:25; base of ὡσαννά. In liturgical reception it shifted from petition to acclamation. ‫—יְהו ִּדי‬yəhûdî “Jew / Judean”, behind the semantic field of Ἰουδαῖος. The translation depends on the geographical, ethnic, political or religious context; the book avoids resolving all uses with a single English equivalent. ַ‫—י ֵׁשוּע‬Yēšûaʿ Late Jewish form of the name Joshua, related to the root y-š-ʿ, “to save”. Greek Ἰησοῦς. The etymology explains the form of the name, but does not in itself constitute historical proof of a messianic function.

hebrew and aramaic glossary of terms and names 455 ‫—יהוה‬YHWH Tetragrammaton of the divine name. The ancient pronunciation is not restored with absolute certainty. The Septuagint and Jewish manuscripts show different representation strategies; the Christian forms of nomina sacra belong to another graphic history. ַ‫— ָמ ׁ ִשיח‬māšîaḥ “Anointed,” verbal adjective (qāṭîl form) of the root m-š-ḥ, “to anoint.” The LXX usually translates it with χριστός. The history of the title encompasses kings, priests, and diverse eschatological expectations; “Messiah” does not designate a single, fixed profile. ‫ מַ לְ כוּת‬/ Aram. ‫—מַ לְ כו ָּתא‬malkût / malkûtā “Reign, sovereignty, kingdom.” Useful to contextualise βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ. The Greek gospel formula should not be automatically back-translated into a single Aramaic expression without contextual verification. ‫— ִמ ׁ ְשנָה‬mišnâ “Repetition / teaching”, name of the rabbinic Mishnah. Its redaction, c. 200 CE, does not justify projecting all its formulations onto first-century Judaism. ‫— ּ ֶפסַ ח‬pesaḥ Passover; Greek πάσχα. It designates a festival and, depending on the context, a sacrifice/meal. Its calendar was central to the chronology of the Passion and to later Christian controversies. ‫— ּ ְפרו ׁ ִּשים‬pərûšîm Hebrew form traditionally related to “separated”; Greek Φαρισαῖοι. The etymology does not replace the social history of Pharisaism nor prove a uniform self-designation in all periods. ‫— ַר ִּבי‬rabbî “My teacher / master”. Title transmitted as ῥαββί. Its use in first-century sources should not be equated without qualification with the fully developed rabbinic institution of later centuries.

456 early christianity ַ‫—רוּח‬rûaḥ “Wind, breath, spirit.” The Greek πνεῦμα offers a partially comparable field. Biblical equivalences do not eliminate semantic differences between Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek. ‫ש ָּבת‬ ַ ׁ —šabbāt Sabbath, “cessation / rest”. Greek σάββατον. The Christian discussion of the Sabbath must be situated within plural Jewish practices, not as an abstract opposition between “law” and “religion.” ‫ש ָטן‬ ָׂ —śāṭān “Adversary/accuser”; Greek Σατανᾶς and διάβολος depending on the context of translation and reception. In biblical Hebrew, ‫( ָׂש ָטן‬śāṭān) functions in various passages as a common noun, “adversary/accuser”; in Job 1–2 and Zechariah 3 it appears with the article, ‫( הַ ּ ָשׂ ָטן‬ha-śāṭān), as the functional designation of the accuser in the heavenly court. Its progressive development into a proper name and personification as a distinct figure belongs to the demonological development of Second Temple Judaism and later apocalyptic traditions. This personal sense should not be projected retrospectively as the sole meaning of all biblical strata. ‫— ׁ ְשמַ ע‬šəmaʿ “Listen.” Conventional name of Deuteronomy 6:4ff. The formula was and is central to the Jewish confession of divine oneness; it constitutes a relevant background for Jewish and Christian Christological debates. ‫— ּתוֹ ָרה‬tôrâ “Instruction / teaching”, usually “Torah” or “Law”. Greek νόμος in numerous contexts. In Paul, νόμος does not have an identical referent in every passage; Pentateuch, commandment, regime, and scriptural argument must be distinguished. ‫ ּתוֹ ָמא‬/ ‫—ܬܐܘܡܐ‬Tōmā Aramaic, “twin”; transliterated Θωμᾶς and glossed Δίδυμος in John. Clear example of a Semitic name accompanied by a Greek equivalent.

Colophon This book was typeset for its first bilingual edition (2026) by Sophia Lux Academic Editions, Franklin 2054, 1st Floor, Apt. B, Autonomous City of Buenos Aires. Editorial production, philological revision, textual verification and general direction of the work were the responsibility of Diego Kurilo. Typesetting. The text is set in EB Garamond—Georg Duffner and Octavio Pardo’s revival of Claude Garamont’s types after the Egenolff-Berner specimen of 1592—at 11/14.5 pt in the main text and in a smaller size in notes, tables and indexes, with polytonic Greek from the same family. Text block, hyphenation, running heads and pagination follow the conventions of the leading university presses; the pagination of the PDF is canonical for all cross-references and indexes. Greek, papyrological and epigraphic conventions. Diplomatic and semidiplomatic transcriptions preserve, where required by the witness, the lunate sigma (ϲ) and other graphic features; critical reconstructions employ standardised Greek. The distinction between facsimile, transcription, reconstruction and translation is made explicit in the apparatus. Semitic script. Hebrew and Aramaic strings are set in Noto Serif Hebrew and Syriac in Noto Sans Syriac, with bidirectional right-to-left direction, to avoid character inversion or loss of diacritics. Cartography and network analysis. Maps, SNA graphs, and synchronism tables use highly legible Unicode fonts and preserve their declared scales, legends, and metrics. In the minimal Pauline network, the normalised degree centrality of nodes with degree 1 is reported as 0.059 by symmetric rounding of 1/17 = 0.058823… References to manuscripts, inscriptions, coins, buildings and archaeological objects retain their explicit documentary status; the provenance and licence of each image are given in its caption.
